lean.note: The pictures are the same in both lessons. They read as a plausible half-done painting, but three pale trunks are already on the canvas at step 1 with no words to paint them. Step 16 turns the trunks into a blotchy camouflage pattern, and step 20 shows almost no visible change. A's step 1 stage summary admits the faint trunks, but its step 16 words call for gray heaviest on the shady side, and the picture shows no side shading at all.

base.note: The pictures and their faults are the same as A's. B's step 1 says outright 'There are no trees yet' while the picture shows three trunks, which is the clearest mismatch in either lesson. Elsewhere B tracks the pictures a little better: step 15 names the six birches and the small trunks behind the boulder, and step 16 describes the speckled pale patches the picture actually shows.

ab.note: The step pictures are identical, so only the words differ, and each lesson has one notable place where its words and pictures disagree (B at step 1, A at step 16). B is slightly more specific in the birch steps, but that is a small edge in the words, not a real difference for the painter. This is a toss-up.

base.note: The pictures are the same in both lessons. They read as a believable build until step 1, which already shows three far trunks before any trunk step. A's step 1 even says 'There are no trees yet', which the picture contradicts. Step 17 turns the gray trunks bright white using only a dark paint, and step 20's near-white barely changes anything. The other step words are concrete about where paint goes and match the pictures well (step 11's short back stretch of path, step 16's broken gray).

lean-low.note: The pictures and their faults are the same as A's: trunks already on the canvas at step 1, white bark appearing at step 17 from a dark-only step, and almost nothing visible from step 20. B's words are shorter and give fewer placements (step 15, step 19), so a beginner gets less to aim at. B also avoids A's outright 'no trees yet' contradiction at step 1.

ab.note: The step pictures are identical, so the same picture faults sink both lessons equally. The only difference is the words. A gives more exact placements but contradicts its step 1 picture. B is vaguer but contradicts less. Neither difference amounts to a real preference: a toss-up.

lean.note: The step pictures look like a believable painting in progress until the cow. Step 12 jumps from a flat silhouette to a furry, reshaped head and fringe from one umber shading pass. Step 19 reshapes the whole muzzle, chin and fringe under 'nostrils and a mouth', though A's words do mention darkening the hair around the muzzle, which covers part of that change. 'Nose pink' is an olive-grey mix (#77764b) used to shade the horns, which will confuse a beginner, and the cream glow in step 3 already lays down wavy bands that read as hills before step 4.

base.note: Same pictures and the same problems: the big texture and reshape jump in step 12, and step 19 remaking the face while the words only cover nostrils, a mouth and an outline around the nose. B's measurements are a little more specific (the nose's position, the size of each horn, how high the grass tips reach), but they don't fix the jumps. The olive 'Nose pink' mismatch is the same.

ab.note: Both lessons use the same paints, brushes and pictures, and their words differ only in small wording and order choices. A's step 19 covers a bit more of the face change, and B gives a few more measurements. Neither difference changes what the beginner would paint, so this is a toss-up.

base.note: The step pictures are shared, so the same faults count against both. Three trunks already stand in step 1 before any trunk step, the step 12 boulder is a hard flat cut-out dome, and step 20 shows almost no change for a step that claims to light every trunk. A's step 1 words say 'there are no trees yet', which the picture plainly contradicts. Elsewhere A places things well: the six birches and two small trunks in step 15, and the gray covering most of each trunk with pale patches and pale feet in step 16, both match the pictures.

lean.note: B has the same picture faults: early trunks in step 1, the flat boulder dome, and a step 20 that barely changes. B's stage line at least admits the faint trunks, but no step tells the painter to make them. B's step 15 is the weak point: it gives only the first trunk's position and says 'fill each one flat', so a beginner can't place the six birches or the two behind the boulder. B's step 16 asks for gray 'heaviest on the shady side', but the picture shows even gray all over.

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so this comes down to the words. A tells the painter where the birches go in step 15 and describes the bark shading the way the picture shows it; B leaves the trunk layout to guesswork. A's 'no trees yet' in step 1 is a real contradiction, so the edge is slight, close to a toss-up.

lean-sonnet.note: The pictures are shared and mostly read as a real painting in progress, but step 1 already shows three trunks while the words say 'don't paint any trees yet', and step 6 has odd blotches in the lower mist. Several steps tell the painter something the picture contradicts. Step 5 puts teal on the pines' sunny sides, but the picture shows teal haze around and below them. Step 13 says to keep the top and left of the boulder olive, but the picture shows it almost all dark. Step 16 says to shade only the right side, but the trunks go gray all over.

base.note: The pictures are the same, so they carry the same flaws: trunks in step 1 against 'no trees yet', stray blotches in step 6, and a big flat-trunk jump in step 15. Where the words differ from A, they follow the pictures more closely: the teal mist around the pines (step 5), the gold ground patches (step 9), the mostly dark boulder (step 13), the gray over most of each trunk (step 16), the gold trail on the right (step 19), and the two small trunks behind the boulder (step 15).

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words match them. B's words describe what each picture actually shows at steps 5, 9, 13, 15, 16 and 19, where A would send a beginner to paint something different from the reference. Both share the step 1 trunk problem, so the edge is moderate: slightly better than slight, not overwhelming.

base.note: The landscape builds cleanly from sky to meadow and the cow arrives as a flat shape, then gets shaded, horned and locked. That order is believable and paintable. The face is the weak point. Step 18's picture shows only a thin pink sliver, not the 1 in nose the words ask for. Step 19 then reshapes the whole muzzle and chin, which a liner and a few umber lines can't do. Step 12's picture also arrives already furry and sunlit on the fringe, more than one umber pass makes, and 'Nose pink' is mixed as an olive-grey.

lean.note: These are the same pictures, so the same problems: the nose barely appears at 18, then the whole muzzle forms at 19, and step 12 goes from flat to furry. B's step 19 words do name a shadow ring around the muzzle, which covers a little more of that jump, but not the new chin and face shape. Otherwise the words are as clear as A's, slightly less exact on placement in places and with a few more 'common mistake' tips.

ab.note: The pictures are identical and the words differ only in small ways. A gives a few more measurements, and B's step 19 explains the muzzle change a bit better. Neither fixes the real problems at steps 12, 18 and 19, so this is a toss-up.

lean-sonnet.note: The pictures are shared and have the same faults on both sides. Step 4, a wall step, suddenly shows full leaf clumps, a ghost post box and a stray dark triangle. In steps 20-21 eyes, nose and whiskers appear before their steps. A's words often describe what should happen rather than what the picture shows: steps 2-3 promise leaf clumps where the pictures show almost nothing, step 12 asks for a few fold lines but the picture shows the whole knit, and step 16 asks for shadow shading but the picture shows stripe bands. Step 23 asks for a nose that is already there.

base.note: B has the same picture faults: leaves appearing on the wall step, and the face showing up during the fur and light steps. B's words track the pictures more closely: the white cloud and tiny specks in steps 1-3, braided rows in step 12, stripe-base bands in step 16, and the left sun patch in step 9. Step 23 is titled 'Press in the pink nose' but its words warm the blanket gaps, and its picture shows no visible change, which would confuse a beginner.

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words match them. B describes what actually lands on the canvas more often (steps 1-3, 12, 16), while A repeatedly promises marks the pictures don't show. It is a slight preference, because both inherit the same step-4 and step-20/21 magic and B has its own muddled step 23.

lean.note: The pictures are shared, and the same faults run through both lessons. Step 4's wall step grows a full leafy tree and leaves ghost boxes for the post and sill. Step 12 jumps from a flat gold shape to a finished knit blanket. Steps 20 and 21 show eye lines, a pink nose and whiskers that their words never name, and step 23 is titled 'pink nose' but its words paint the blanket. A's words are clear and give sizes, and step 4 even accounts for the post band, but they can't cover what the pictures do.

base.note: The pictures are the same as A's, so B has the same magic and jumps: tree leaves appearing in step 4, the blanket finished in one go in step 12, and the face showing up in steps 20 and 21 unasked. Step 23 has the same title-versus-words mismatch. B's words place things a little more concretely (start points, distances from edges), but it skips the post band that A mentions in step 4, so overall the two even out.

ab.note: Both lessons share every picture, and their words differ only in small ways that don't fix the shared faults: the early leaves and ghosts, the one-step blanket, and the face appearing before its steps. Neither would get a beginner past steps 4, 12 or 20 better than the other. This is a toss-up, so no preference.

lean-low.note: Step 4 is called a wall blend, but full green tree clumps appear in the window. It also leaves ghost marks no brush makes: a dark box low left, a dark triangle at the right edge, and a brownish smudge where the sill and frame will go. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to a finished knit blanket. Steps 20 and 21 show the eyes, pink nose and whiskers arriving under words for gray fur and cream light, and step 23 is titled for the nose but its words go back to the blanket while the picture barely changes.

base.note: B has the same pictures, so the same problems: trees and ghost marks in step 4, the flat-to-knit jump in step 12, and the face showing up early in steps 20 and 21 with no words for it. Step 23 has the same nose-titled step that paints the blanket. B's words place things a little better, such as the tapering sun patch in step 9 and where the eyes and whiskers go, but they don't explain any of the magic either.

ab.note: Both lessons share every picture, and the pictures carry the problems that sink a lesson: ghosts and a big jump at step 4, a big jump at step 12, and the face appearing before its steps. B's words are a bit more specific, but that is polish, not a fix for what the pictures show. A toss-up, so none.

base.note: The landscape builds believably, and the words track the pictures closely. They explain the cream wavy bands over the lower sky in step 3, the gold glints between ridges in step 4, and the darker band widening to the right in step 5. The cow is the trouble, and it is the same in both lessons. Step 12 turns a flat rust blob into a furry, modelled cow with a head, which is more than 'shade the dark side' covers. Step 18's picture shows a thin pink line, not a 1 in pad. Step 19 makes a whole muzzle, chin and face appear from a liner and a few lines.

lean-sonnet.note: The pictures are the same, so the same jumps at steps 12 and 19 and the thin nose at step 18 apply. On top of that, B's words drift from the pictures in a few places. Step 3 says cream goes only on the cloud tops and to 'not touch the blue', but the picture reworks the whole lower sky into wavy cream-edged bands. Step 4 never mentions the gold glints between the ridges. Step 18 puts the nose 'in the middle of the face' when it sits at the right front.

ab.note: Both lessons share the same weak cow steps (12's magic rendering, 19's face appearing from a few liner lines), and those decide most of the scores. A's words match what each picture shows more often, especially at step 3, where B's words would actively mislead. The edge is slight but concrete.

lean-sonnet.note: The pictures build the scene in believable layers, but the face goes wrong: step 18 shows only a tiny pink sliver, not a 1 in nose, and step 19 makes a whole muzzle and chin appear from a few liner lines. The 'Nose pink' recipe (#77764b) mixes an olive grey, so paint and picture disagree twice. A's words also miss several pictures: step 3 says cream only on the upper cloud edges, but the picture puts most of it in wavy lines low in the sky. Step 4 says flat with no texture, but the picture has gold glints between the ridges. Step 12 asks for smooth round shading, but the picture shows hairy hanging streaks.

base.note: Same pictures, so the same nose-and-muzzle magic at steps 18 and 19 and the same olive 'Nose pink' mismatch. B's words track the pictures more closely where A's don't: the cream mostly in the low wavy lines at step 3, gold glints between the ridges at step 4, the darker ridge widest on the right at step 5, hairy streaks at step 12, locks mostly on the left at step 15, and only small glints at step 17. Step 16 still undersells how much straw gold covers the left of the body.

ab.note: The step pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words describe them. B matches what the beginner will see on about five steps where A's words point elsewhere. Both share the face problem at steps 18 and 19. Slight preference for B, not a toss-up.

base.note: The step pictures carry the same faults as B. In step 4 a full leafy tree appears in the window during a wall step. Step 4 also has ghosts before their steps: a faint post, a hard grey box low left, a dark triangle at the right edge and a brown blotch where the sill goes. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to finished knit in one step, and the nose and eye marks appear in steps 20–21 before the steps that name them. Step 23 is titled 'nose' but its words are about the blanket. A's words give real positions and amounts and match some picture details (paw outlines in step 16, the bar shadow on the sill), so it is somewhat easier to paint from.

lean-low.note: B has the same pictures and the same ghosts in step 4, the same jump in step 12, and the same nose and eyes appearing early in steps 20–21. B's step 4 words even tell the painter to 'keep the green trees showing' that were never painted. Most steps are vaguer than A's ('start on the head', 'scatter between stitches', a sill 'about 4 1/2 in tall' with no top line given), so a beginner has less to place marks by. The nose/blanket mismatch in step 23 is also present here.

ab.note: Both lessons share identical pictures with the same serious faults, so neither paints well. A's words locate each mark more concretely and agree a little better with what the pictures show. It is a slight preference, close to a toss-up, since the shared picture faults dominate both lessons.

base.note: Step 23 is named 'Press in the pink nose' but its words only warm the blanket gaps, so the nose, the centre of the face, is never painted; it appears untold in step 21. Step 4 has the same faults as B: the specks become full two-toned leaf clumps, and ghosts of the frame, the sill and a dark box show on the wall early. Steps 20-21 bring in eye lines, whiskers and the nose before their steps. Steps 2-3 (few specks) and 16 (bands as the base for the stripes) match their pictures better than B's.

lean-sonnet.note: Same pictures, so the same ghosts at step 4 and the same early face in 20-21. Steps 2-3 ask for two-toned leaf clumps the pictures don't show, though that at least sets up the clumps that appear at step 4. Every step's words match its title, including the nose at 23 (already in the picture by then), so a beginner always knows what to paint.

ab.note: Slight preference for B. Both share the same weak pictures (ghosts at step 4, the face appearing in 20-21). A has one broken step, though: its nose step paints the blanket, and that hits the focal point. A's words fit the early leaf and shading pictures better, so the margin is small.

lean-low.note: The pictures are shared and mostly read as a real painting in progress. The worst picture problem is three far trunks already standing on step 1, which is meant to be only the sky glow. In A the words often don't cover what the pictures show: the twig sprays high in step 6, the whole floor turning gold in step 9, and the two small trunks behind the boulder in step 15 are all missing from the words. Step 20 also claims a glow the picture barely shows.

base.note: These are the same pictures with the same problems: ghost trunks on step 1, a near-invisible change in step 20, and six flat trunks plus branches in one go at step 15. B's words do match the pictures better in several places: twig sprays in step 6, broad golden ground patches in step 9, the path's front left as leaves in step 11, and the trunks behind the boulder in step 15. Against that, step 1 says outright 'There are no trees yet' while trees are visible, which is a loud contradiction.

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so the choice rests only on how well the words describe them. B covers more of what each picture actually shows across steps 3 to 15. B's flat 'no trees yet' on step 1 and the empty step 20 keep the edge small. Slight preference, not clear.

lean-low.note: The landscape half builds believably, one coat at a time. The cow has two shared problems. Step 12 jumps from a flat blob to a nearly finished shaggy coat with one dark paint. Step 18's picture shows only a tiny pink fleck, and then step 19's liner step makes a full, larger muzzle appear, with lighter chin hair and a reshaped fringe that its words don't cover. Step 14 shades the horns with a 'Nose pink' that is really an olive grey. A's words are a little vaguer about placement, and step 5 mentions the lake corner before the lake exists.

base.note: These are the same pictures, so the same faults apply: the step 12 jump, the step 18 nose that doesn't match, the step 19 muzzle appearing by magic, and the step 14 'Nose pink' that is grey-olive. B gives more positions and sizes, and they mostly match the pictures: the cow about 7 1/2 in wide, the dark ridge widest on the right, the cream lying in the lower sky. It also says what isn't there yet. That helps a little, but it fixes none of the steps where the picture outruns the words.

ab.note: Both lessons share every picture, and the faults that would stop a beginner are in those pictures: steps 12, 18 and 19. B's words place things a bit more exactly, but that is a small edge in wording, not a real difference in what you could paint. I'm calling it a toss-up, leaning very slightly to B.

base.note: The pictures are shared and have real faults: three trunks already stand on the 'no trees yet' sky in step 1, the step 16 gray leaves odd white blotches and pale 'socks' on the trunks, and step 17 quietly whitens and textures the bark beyond the dark marks it names. A's words follow the pictures closely. Teal goes around the pines (step 5), broad gold glow lies on the ground (step 9), the boulder is mostly dark with a sliver of light (step 13), it places all six birches plus the two small trunks behind the boulder (step 15), and gray covers most of each trunk (step 16). A few garbled phrases ('bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy') cost a little.

lean-sonnet.note: B has the same pictures and the same flaws, but its words describe a tidier painting than the pictures show. The pictures don't match its teal light on each fir's sun side (step 5), its top and left of the boulder staying flat olive (step 13), or its gray shading only the right side of the trunks (step 16). Step 15 places only the first trunk ('Each is wide at its base') and never mentions the small trunks that appear behind the boulder, so a beginner has to guess.

ab.note: With identical pictures, the difference is how well the words match them, and A matches at the steps where B describes something the picture doesn't show (5, 13, 15, 16). A beginner comparing canvas to picture would be misled less often by A. I'm fairly sure of a slight but real preference, not a toss-up.

base.note: Both lessons share the same step pictures, and those pictures have serious faults. Step 4 is the worst: the wall picture already shows a ghost of the window post, a dark box, a pinkish blotch and a stray dark triangle on the right. The few leaf specks also become full sunlit tree clumps there. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to finished chunky knit in one go. The nose, eye marks and whiskers start showing at steps 20 and 21. Step 23 is titled for the nose, but its words only warm the blanket gaps. A's words are clear and well placed, but they don't explain any of this.

lean.note: Same pictures, with the same ghosts and the same leaf jump at step 4, the same flat-to-knit jump at step 12, and the face showing early at steps 20 and 21. B's step 4 does ask for a soft Deep wall blue band where the post will stand, which explains one of the ghosts. That doesn't cover the box, the blotch or the leaves. Step 23 has the same nose title with blanket words.

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so only the words differ, and they differ very little. A gives slightly more exact placements; B's step 4 accounts for the post ghost. Neither fixes the real problems: ghosts and magic leaves at step 4, the step 12 jump, the nose appearing early, and step 23's mismatch. It's a toss-up.

base.note: The step pictures mostly read as a real painting built up in layers, but step 12 jumps from a flat blob to a furry, modelled cow with lighter orange highlights that Dark umber can't make. Step 18 shows only a pink sliver where the words promise a 1 in nose, and the full muzzle with lit chin hair then appears in step 19 from liner lines alone. The words are specific about placement and size (horn tip at 2 1/2 in, nose 4 in from the right edge), but the step 16 picture puts straw-gold locks all over the left body where the words say only a few, and 'Nose pink' (#77764b) is an olive grey.

lean-low.note: Same pictures, so the same problems: the jump to a furry cow at step 12, the sliver nose at 18 and the muzzle appearing at 19, straw locks at 16 far beyond 'a few', and the olive-grey 'Nose pink'. Step 19 does mention dark touches around the muzzle and in the coat, which covers slightly more of that change. The words are terser and vaguer about where things go ('far side' horn, 'start at the top of the sky', 'dry brush flicked quickly upward').

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so the two differ only in the words. A gives clearer measurements and left/right placement, which slightly helps a beginner, but both share the same picture problems that would stop the painter at steps 12, 16, 18 and 19. That edge is small, so I call it none, leaning slightly to A.

base.note: The landscape steps (1-10) read as a real painting in progress, but the cow goes wrong. Step 12 jumps from a flat silhouette to a furry, shaded cow whose head has changed shape. Step 18 shows no nose, then step 19 shows the whole face appearing from two thin liner lines. Several recipes mix the wrong colour (olive 'Sunlit green' and 'Nose pink', a dark 'Golden ginger'), and the Known problems list fixes only some of them; for Sunlit cream and Sunlit green it gives no fix and talks about 'chains' and 'cards'.

f-lean.note: The pictures and words are the same as A's, so it has the same cow problems: the jump at step 12, the missing nose at 18 and the face appearing at 19. The difference is the Known problems list. It gives a plain fix for every wrong recipe (add yellow to Sunlit green, add white and gold to Sunlit cream, add red and white for the nose, lighten the ginger), which matters across steps 8, 9, 14, 15, 18 and 21. It also says plainly to follow the words where steps 17 and 18 show little change.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical and the diagrams are about equal: A's step 11 adds a useful 'rough up the edges' panel, while B's are a little cleaner. B wins because its Known problems list tells a beginner how to fix each wrong paint in plain words, and A's leaves the two most-used paints (Sunlit green and Sunlit cream) unfixed and talks in pipeline jargon. It is a slight preference, not a clear one.

base.note: The landscape steps (1-10) build plausibly, but the cow has magic in it. Step 12 is a shading step, yet its picture reshapes the head and legs. Step 18's picture shows only a streak where its words promise a broad pink nose, and step 19 then brings the whole face and fringe into focus on a step that only lines nostrils. The extra diagrams help: there is one for the shadow, the horn shading and the nose under the fringe, which partly covers step 18's gap. The Known problems list gives usable fixes for the dull ginger mix and the olive 'pink'.

f-split.note: B has the same step pictures, words and magic, with the same face appearing at step 19 and the same near-empty nose step. It has only three diagrams: block-in, horns and locks. Its Known problems entry for step 18 says 'the step's diagram shows the nose's shape and place', but B has no nose diagram, so the page contradicts itself just where the painter needs help. It does give a concrete dusty-pink mix for the nose, but no fix for the ginger locks being too dark.

ab.note: The steps are identical, so the choice rests on the extras. A's diagrams cover the hard cow steps (shadow, horn shading, the nose under the fringe), and its notes give fixes the painter can act on. B points to a nose diagram it doesn't have. Slight edge to A: neither one repairs the face jump at step 19.

f-split.note: Step 1 says 'there are no trees yet', but its picture already shows three pale trunks, so step 3 barely changes anything. Step 10's floor already shows the path gap. Later steps (the pines, boulder, birches, bark and leaf carpet) build well and believably. A's Known problems flags the early trunks only at step 2, missing step 1. Its small back-of-path diagram matches the words.

base.note: The same pictures and words, so the same ghost trunks in step 1 and the early path in step 10. B's Known problems is more honest: it names both. The bark-marks diagram for step 17 helps. But its path diagram shows a long strip from the front edge to the dot, which contradicts the words' 'only the back stretch'.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical; only the extras differ, and they cancel out. B's Known problems is more accurate and it adds a useful bark diagram, but its path diagram would mislead a beginner where A's matches the words. It's a toss-up.

f-split.note: The step pictures read as a real painting in progress, and the sky, hills and meadow build well. The face is the problem: step 18's picture shows only a streak, and step 19 brings in the whole face, with eyes under the fringe, a muzzle and a turned head, on a step that names only fine umber lines. Several recipes don't make the colors their names or the pictures show (Sunlit green, Golden ginger, Nose pink). The Known problems say a nose diagram covers step 18, but A's three diagrams cover only steps 11, 13 and 15, so that claim misleads the painter.

base.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same face jump at step 19 and the same off recipes. Its seven diagrams cover the steps where a beginner gets lost: where the shadow goes on the cow, how to shade the horns, and the nose tucked under the fringe. That last one really does fill the step 18 gap its Known problems point to. The Known problems are also accurate: they flag that step 17 barely changes, and they say how to adjust the ginger and nose mixes.

ab.note: The paintings are identical, so the choice rests on what each page adds. B's diagrams cover the shading and the nose, and its notes match what's on the page. A's notes point to a nose diagram that isn't there. The edge is slight to clear: the shared step 19 jump and the wrong recipes still hurt both.

f-lean-sonnet.note: The pictures are shared, so A carries the same flaws as B. Step 4 has leaf clumps that steps 2 and 3 never painted, ghosts of the frame and sill, and a stray dark arrow and box. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to finished knit. Step 23 is titled for the nose, but its words are about blanket commas and the nose was already there in step 21. A's diagrams for the two blanket steps (11 and 12) are broken and draw nothing, which leaves the biggest jump with no help. Its problems list also misreports the leaves, saying they were erased, when step 4 is where they wrongly appear.

base.note: B has the same step pictures and words, with the same step 4 magic, the step 12 jump, the step 23 nose and blanket mix-up, and the orange 'Soft pink'. All nine of its diagrams draw, including the slab-and-roll blanket and the fold-shadow sequence for step 12, and they follow the words' order. Its problems list correctly warns about the unmentioned leaves in step 4 and the early nose and whiskers in steps 20 and 21, and tells the painter to mix the pink rosier. Some of the list is internal noise.

ab.note: Everything the painter compares against is the same, so the difference comes only from the diagrams and the warnings. B's diagrams all work, and the ones on the blanket steps give real help at the lesson's biggest jump, where A shows two broken placeholders. B's warnings are also more accurate and more useful, such as mixing the ears pinker and expecting the leaves in step 4. It is a slight preference, not a clear one, because both lessons share the same weak steps.

base.note: The pictures are shared with B and have the same faults. Steps 2 and 3 show no visible leaves, and step 4 (the wall) shows finished leaf clumps plus ghost blotches of the frame and sill and a stray dark mark. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to full knit with stitches, so steps 13 and 14 barely change. Steps 20 and 21 show the nose and whiskers early, and step 23's words paint blanket commas, not the nose its title names. A's Known problems list names these issues and catches step 1's patch-width mismatch, but it mixes in pipeline jargon (merge checks for paints the plan doesn't have) and offers fewer fixes a painter can act on. The diagrams are clear and match the words.

f-lean.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same early leaves, ghosts at step 4, the knit jump at step 12, the early nose and whiskers, and the wrong change at step 23. B's Known problems list is shorter and easier to act on. It says to use step 4 for the leaves, gives a recipe for a rosy pink, and says to paint the nose at step 23 as the title says. It also wrongly claims the paint-name mismatch in the words is fixed. Its diagrams match A's in quality.

ab.note: The step pictures and words are the same, and they decide almost everything here: early leaves, the step 4 ghosts, the knit jump at step 12, and the misplaced nose step hurt both lessons equally. B's notes give a little more practical help at steps 2-3, 19 and 23, and A flags the step 1 width error. Both sets of diagrams are about equally good. It's a toss-up with a slight lean to B, which is too small to call a preference.

f-lean.note: The step pictures read as a real painting in progress until the face. Step 18 shows only a pale streak where the nose should be, and step 19 then delivers the whole nose, muzzle and eye area at once. Several recipes don't mix to the colours shown (Sunlit green, Golden ginger, Sunlit cream, Nose pink), but A's Known problems gives a concrete fix for each one, such as 'add yellow' or 'add white and Sunset gold', so a beginner can still match the pictures. The diagrams for the block-in, shading, horns, locks and nose are clear and fill the step-18 gap.

base.note: B has the same pictures and words as A, with the same nose jump at steps 18–19 and the same recipes that don't match their colours. B's diagrams are slightly fuller: a 'rough up the edges' panel and a third shading panel. But its Known problems only describe the dull Sunlit green and grey Sunlit cream without saying how to fix them, so the meadow, grass and highlights will come out muddier than the pictures. It also includes notes the painter can't act on: the missing card fields, and a 'plan vs words' remark about the horn shine that only adds confusion.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, so this comes down to the add-ons. A's Known problems give an actionable colour fix for every paint that misses its picture. B leaves the two most-used mismatches (Sunlit green and Sunlit cream) without a fix and adds meta notes a beginner can't use. B's diagrams are a little richer but don't outweigh this. Preference is slight.

base.note: From step 15 on, the pictures look like a real half-done birch painting. But step 1's picture already shows three far trunks the words say aren't there yet, which also leaves step 3 with almost nothing to show. Step 10 has a path ghosted in before step 11, and step 6's olive dabs are odd hard blotches no stiff brush would make. A's diagrams match the words closely: a ground line under the boulder, the two small trunks behind it, and a gray strip already on the trunk for the bark marks. Its Known problems list admits the early trunks and the ghost path honestly.

f-lean-sonnet.note: The pictures and words are the same as A's, so B has the same faults: trunks in step 1 before step 3, a ghost path in step 10, and blotchy olive in step 6. Its diagrams are mostly as useful as A's, with a few misses. The bark diagram's first panel outlines a plain pale trunk as 'what to paint', when the trunk is already gray by step 17. The boulder's side pieces bulge below the ground, and the birch diagram leaves out the two small trunks behind the boulder. Its Known problems list is honest too, but files the early-trunk problem under the wrong step and spends a line on missing Load lines, which doesn't help a painter.

ab.note: The two lessons share every picture and word, so the real faults (trunks in step 1, the ghost path in step 10, the blotches in step 6) sink both equally. A's diagrams and notes fit the steps a little better, especially for the bark marks and the boulder, but that is a small edge and not a real difference. Toss-up, leaning slightly to A.

base.note: The shared pictures carry ghosts. Pale far trunks already stand in step 1, whose words say no trees yet, so step 3 barely changes, and a faint path shows in step 10 before step 11. Steps 6 to 9 and 12 to 19 paint well and in a sensible order, but step 20 hardly changes and Path tan and Bark white mix darker than their names. A's diagrams pull against its words in three places: the path diagram is a long full-height wedge where the words ask for a short back stretch, the pines are 'taller behind, small in front' instead of shorter on either side, and the bark diagram puts the foot last where the words start at the foot.

f-lean.note: B has the same pictures and words, with the same early trunks in step 1, a weak step 3, a path showing early in step 10, and paints that mix off their names. B's diagrams match the words: shorter pines on each side, a short path wedge inside the floor band, the dark foot first and then marks across, and the two small trunks behind the boulder named. Its Known problems list also names the step 1 contradiction and the step 5 title mismatch plainly.

ab.note: Everything on the canvas is identical, so the choice rests on the diagrams. A's diagrams contradict its words on three steps (pines, path length, bark order), and a beginner holding a phone would hit those conflicts. B's diagrams agree with the words. The preference is slight: the shared step 1, 3 and 10 problems weigh more than either set of diagrams.

f-lean.note: The shared pictures carry the main faults. Step 1's sky already shows three far trunks while its words say 'no trees yet', and step 2 adds more, so step 3 changes little. Step 16 jumps from flat white trunks to fully speckled bark in one dry-brush pass. A's diagrams match the words: shorter pines on each side, the path as a short strip in the back of the floor, a dark foot first and then marks across the trunk. Its Known problems correctly flag the ghost trunks, the step 5 title mismatch and the paint-colour gaps.

base.note: B has the same pictures and words, so the same faults: ghost far trunks in steps 1 and 2, and the big bark jump at step 16. Two of B's diagrams pull against the words. Step 11's diagram shows one long path triangle running from the front to the dot, but the words say only the back stretch is painted and the front stays leaves. Step 17's diagram puts the marks first and the dark foot second, but the words say to start at the foot. Its Known problems usefully add that a faint path already shows in step 10.

ab.note: The lessons are identical except for the diagrams and notes. A's diagrams agree with the step words, while B's path and bark diagrams would steer a beginner wrong on two steps. The edge is slight but concrete.

base.note: The pictures are the same in both lessons, and they share the same faults. Steps 2 and 3 change almost nothing. Step 4 suddenly shows full leaf clumps plus ghosts of the frame and sill and a stray dark mark, none of which its words cover. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to finished knit, and step 13 then looks the same. The nose and whiskers appear in steps 20 and 21, before the steps that name them. Step 23 is called the nose but paints the blanket, and its 'Soft pink' mixes an orange-brown. A's stitch, stripe and whisker diagrams help a beginner. But its cat diagram starts with the body oval while the words start with the head. Its Known problems flag more of the picture faults (sky width, step 4 leaves, early nose and whiskers), but they are full of pipeline jargon and only say 'mix pinker' for the pink.

f-split.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same magic at steps 4 and 21, the same big jump at step 12, and the same misplaced nose step 23. B's diagrams follow the words' order (head, ears, body, tail) and add useful sill steps. It has no stitch-comma or whisker diagram. Its Known problems give real fixes: mix pink from white and a touch of red, and paint the nose on the muzzle. But it does not warn about the step 1 sky width or the nose and whiskers appearing early in steps 20 and 21.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, and their faults (step 4 leaves and ghosts, step 12 jump, nose and whiskers early, step 23 mislabeled) sink both lessons equally. The pages add different strengths: A has better technique diagrams and flags more faults; B's diagrams match the words and its fixes are more usable. Neither page outweighs the other, so this is a toss-up.

f-lean-sonnet.note: The landscape steps build believably. The cow does not. Step 12 jumps from a flat silhouette to a fully shaggy, modelled cow, and step 19 shows magic: the whole face, the pink nose and a reshaped fringe appear on a step that asks only for liner nostrils and a mouth, after step 18's picture shows just a pale streak. Several recipes don't match their pictures (Nose pink mixes olive gray, Golden ginger is near the rust base, Sunlit green is dull olive), and A's Known problems only admit this without telling the painter how to fix it; one entry about the gold sky reaching the bottom edge doesn't match the words and would confuse.

base.note: Same pictures and words, so the same jump at step 12, the same magic face at step 19 and the same empty nose at step 18. B's Known problems give the beginner workable fixes for the worst recipe mismatches: warm the olive Nose pink with red and white, lighten Golden ginger with yellow and white, and darken a little Hazy violet for the step 5 ridge. They also flag that step 17's picture barely changes. B's nose diagram places the nose under the fringe, which helps a little more than A's.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, so the difference is only the diagrams and the Known problems list. B's list tells a beginner what to do about paints that would otherwise come out olive or muddy, where A's only explains why nothing was changed. It's a slight preference: both lessons share the same serious faults at steps 12, 18 and 19, and neither list mentions the step 12 jump or the step 19 magic.

f-lean.note: The shared pictures carry the main faults. Step 4 shows finished leaf clumps that steps 2 and 3 never painted, plus ghost blotches of the frame and sill and a stray dark triangle that stays until step 14. Step 12 jumps the whole knit from flat to finished, step 21 shows the nose and whiskers early, and step 23's words describe blanket commas under a nose title. A's Known problems describe these accurately and give usable fixes: use step 4's picture for the leaves, mix a real rosy pink, and paint a small pink triangle for the nose at step 23.

base.note: The pictures and words are the same as A's, with the same leaf magic and ghosts in step 4, the knit jump at step 12, the early nose and whiskers, and the wrong words at step 23. B's list catches a few extra real mismatches, such as the sky patch being wider than the words say. It also misdescribes steps 2 and 3 as showing green specks, adds confusing entries about paints that don't exist, and never tells the painter to actually paint the nose. B's face diagram for step 22 matches the words a little better than A's.

ab.note: The step pictures and words are identical, so both lessons share the same serious faults. Neither page's extras change what the painter faces. A's notes are cleaner and fix the nose step outright, while B's diagrams fit the face words slightly better. It's a toss-up, with at most a slight lean to A, which is not enough to prefer it.

f-split.note: The step pictures are shared and mostly read as a real painting in progress, but they have real faults. Step 4 shows full leaf clumps and faint frame and sill ghosts that the words never ask for. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to full knit, and step 23 is named for the nose but paints the blanket. A's Known problems give useful fixes (mix the pink from white and red, add the nose yourself), but they never warn that steps 4, 20 and 21 show things early. Its diagrams follow the words' order (head first, paws first) and cover the sill well.

base.note: Same pictures, words and faults as A. B's Known problems do name the leaf clumps appearing in step 4, the nose and whiskers showing up in steps 20 and 21, and the sky patch being wider than the words say, so a beginner is warned where the pictures mislead. Its diagrams add the comma-V stitch (useful for steps 13, 14, 19 and 23), the nose placement and the whiskers. Against that, a few diagrams run in a different order from the words (body first, muzzle first), and two merge notes about paints that don't exist are noise.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, so the difference is only the extras. B's problem list warns about the places where the pictures run ahead of the words (steps 4, 20, 21), which A leaves silent, and its stitch and face diagrams fill the most technique-heavy steps. A's clearer pink and nose fixes and better diagram ordering keep this slight, not clear.

f-lean-sonnet.note: The step pictures are shared, and so are their faults. Step 1 says 'no trees yet' but already shows three trunks, step 10 already carries a faint path, and step 3 therefore adds little. The middle steps (pines, bushes, floor, boulder, birches) build up believably. A's diagrams agree poorly with the pictures in places: smooth triangle firs, a broad symmetric triangle for a thin winding path, and bark dashes floating mid-trunk. Its Known problems puts the early trunks at step 2, when they first show in step 1.

base.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same early trunks in step 1 and the same path ghost in step 10. Its diagrams match the canvas better: needle-edged tiered pines, a narrow wedge path, bark marks coming in from the trunk edges over a shaded right side, and a ground line under the boulder and birches. Its Known problems correctly flags that trunks already show in steps 1 and 2, so a painter is warned at the right place.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, so the choice rests on the extras. B's diagrams for the pines, path and bark marks look more like what the step pictures show. Its problem list points to the right steps, while A's path and bark diagrams could mislead a beginner a little. Slight preference: the core weaknesses (step 1 trunks, step 10 path ghost) sink both equally.

base.note: The background steps (1-10) are clean and buildable, but the cow breaks down. Step 12 jumps from a flat blob to a hairy, shaded cow. Step 18's picture shows a pale streak, not the pink nose it describes. Step 19, a liner step for nostrils, has the whole face, fringe and head pose re-form at once, which is magic. Several recipes don't match their names or pictures (olive 'Nose pink', dull 'Sunlit green', dark 'Golden ginger', same paint for steps 4 and 5). A's Known problems gives a beginner concrete fixes for each: darken the violet, warm the nose with red and white, lighten the ginger with yellow and white.

f-lean-sonnet.note: B has the same pictures and words, so the same faults: the step 12 jump, the step 18 nose missing, and the step 19 face appearing by magic. Its diagrams are a little tidier than A's (the fringe cap is drawn in step 11, the horns sit on the head in step 13). But its Known problems only report the colour gaps in Lab units, with no mixing fix. It also adds a confusing note claiming the words for steps 1, 7 and 8 put gold sky at the bottom edge, which they don't.

ab.note: The pictures, words and diagrams are essentially a wash. A wins because its Known problems tell a beginner how to fix the wrong recipes (nose, ginger, the darker ridge). B only reports the mismatch and adds one misleading item. This is a slight preference, not a clear one, and the shared problems with the cow at steps 12, 18 and 19 dominate both.

base.note: The step pictures read as a believable half-done acrylic all the way through. But step 1 already shows three far trunks while its words say 'There are no trees yet', and step 2 adds more trunks that its dry-brush words don't cover, so step 3 has little left to do. Step 20 barely changes the canvas. The Known problems list names both the step 1 and 2 ghosts and the faint path in step 10. The extra bark-mark diagram for step 17 is clear, and the boulder diagram matches the flat dome in the picture.

f-split.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same early far trunks in steps 1 and 2 and the same near-invisible last step. Its Known problems list blames step 2 for the trunks, when they are already there in step 1, and it misses the ghost path in step 10. Its diagrams are good on placement: 'mark six feet first' for the birches, and a path drawn in context between the bushes. But its boulder comes out as a cloud of three bumps that the picture doesn't show, and it has no bark diagram.

ab.note: Both lessons share every picture and word, so they share the real faults: trunks on the canvas before step 3, and a step 20 that hardly changes anything. Neither the diagrams nor the problem lists fix those. A has slightly more accurate warnings and a useful bark diagram, and B has a better birch-placement diagram. That is a small edge to A, not a preference, so I call it a toss-up.

base.note: The shared step pictures carry the problems the owner marks down most. In step 4, full leaf clumps and stray ghost marks (a dark box, a dark arrowhead) appear on a step that only names wall paint. Step 12 jumps the blanket from flat to fully knitted in one go, which leaves step 13 nearly empty. Steps 20 and 21 already show the nose and whiskers, which belong to steps 23 and 24. All nine diagrams draw something usable, including where the fold shadows go on step 12. The Known problems list is long and jargon-heavy, but it gives a painter real fixes: mix the ears and nose pinker than the recipe, and the step 1 patch is bigger than its words say.

f-lean-sonnet.note: B has the same step pictures, so it has the same leaf magic in step 4, the same big jump in step 12, and the same nose and whiskers arriving early in steps 20 to 23. Two of its nine diagrams, on steps 11 and 12, show a 'This spec is broken' error instead of a drawing. Those are the blanket steps where a beginner most needs the help. Its Known problems list is shorter, but it wrongly says the step 1 words match the picture.

ab.note: The lessons differ only in their extras. In those extras, A beats B in two places: A's diagrams all work, while B shows error text on the two blanket steps, and A's notes are more accurate and more usable. The underlying step pictures are flawed the same way in both, so this is a slight but real preference, not a toss-up.

f-lean-low.note: The step pictures are shared, so they set the scores. Step 1 already shows far trunks standing in the glow, and step 10 already shows a faint path. That leaves steps 3 and 11 with little to show and makes step 1 the worst kind of early ghost. A's Known problems list does tell the painter, at step 1, to follow the words and not the trunks. Its diagrams match the words (bark marks laid across the trunk, path strokes pulled toward the dot), but they are generic.

base.note: B has the same pictures, so the same ghost trunks in steps 1 and 2 and the same early path in step 10. B's path diagram is lopsided like the real bending path, and its birch diagram shows the ground line and the two small trunks behind the boulder. Its bark diagram shows a half-dark trunk that doesn't match the canvas at step 17. B's Known problems list files the ghost trunks under step 3, so a painter at step 1 gets no warning.

ab.note: The pictures, words and paints are identical, and they decide everything that matters: the ghost trunks in step 1, the early path in step 10, and the small change in step 3. A's warning lands at step 1, while B's diagrams are a little closer to the scene. The two extras pull in opposite directions and are each minor, so this is a toss-up and I have no real preference.

base.note: The canvas is a real half-done painting from the trees on, but step 1 already shows three far trunks while its words say 'no trees yet'. Step 2 adds more, so step 3's 'pull the far trunks' barely changes anything. The path is faintly visible at step 10 before step 11 paints it, and step 16 is titled 'shade the right sides' but covers nearly the whole trunk. The diagrams help on the pines, boulder and birches, but the path sketch is a lopsided right-angle wedge, and the Known problems list is written in pipeline jargon ('chain', 'checker', 'erase') a beginner can't use.

f-lean-low.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same early trunks in steps 1-2, the same flat step 3, the same early path at step 10 and the same title/picture mismatch at step 16. Its path diagram is the cleaner one: three panels matching the three instructions, with a symmetric fan. Its Known problems list gives a little more usable advice ('follow the words, not the trunks', 'mix it a little whiter'), but it also carries jargon, including an item about 'stroke cards'.

ab.note: The paintings, words and paints are identical, and the faults that matter (trunks and path showing early, step 16's mismatch) are the same in both. B's path diagram and its slightly more directive Known problems notes are a small edge, not enough to prefer it, so this is a toss-up leaning faintly to B.

base.note: The pictures read as a real painting building up, but the face is wrong across several steps. Step 18 shows no nose, and step 19 turns the head to face us and finishes the whole face, when its words only ask for nostrils and a mouth line. A's construction diagrams work on every cow step, including the step 11 block-in. Its Known problems list tells the painter how to fix the bad recipes: darken Hazy violet for step 5, warm the nose mix with red and white, lighten the ginger with yellow and white.

f-lean-low.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same face problems at steps 18 and 19. Its step 11 diagram is broken: it shows the message 'This spec is broken: it draws nothing.' That is on the step where a beginner most needs help to build the cow's shape. B's Known problems list names the same wrong recipes but rarely says how to fix them, so the painter is left with a gray 'cream', an olive 'pink' and no darker blue for step 5.

ab.note: A, slightly. The lessons differ only in their extras, and A's extras all work and tell the painter what to do. B has a visibly broken diagram on the key block-in step and Known problems that warn without fixing. B's other diagrams are a little nicer because they start from the previous canvas, but that doesn't make up for the broken one.

f-lean-low.note: The step pictures read as a believable half-done painting. The trouble is that several recipes don't make the colours shown: Sunlit green, Golden ginger and Nose pink all mix dull or olive. Step 5 changes almost nothing, and the paint it names is the same as step 4's. The nose is barely there in step 18, then step 19 shows the whole face; that is magic for a step that only names a liner and dark umber. Lesson A's diagram for step 11, the step that sets the cow's shape, is broken and draws nothing. Its Known problems name each colour mismatch but give no way to fix the mix.

base.note: B has the same pictures and words, so it has the same nose jump between steps 18 and 19 and the same quiet step 5. Its step 11 diagram builds the cow from an oval, a head, legs and ragged edges, which is the hardest shape for a beginner to place. Its Known problems give fixes a painter can use at the palette: darken the violet for the ridge, warm the nose mix with red and white, lighten the ginger with yellow and white. One note about cards missing load fields is jargon, but it does no harm.

ab.note: The pictures and words are identical, so the extras decide it. B has a working diagram for blocking in the cow where A's is broken, and B's problem list tells the painter how to fix the off recipes instead of just naming them. It is a clear preference, though the shared faults (the step 18/19 nose jump and the weak step 5) hold both lessons down.

base.note: The shared steps sink both lessons. Step 4's wall picture shows finished leaf clumps (steps 2 and 3 change nothing) and ghosts of the frame and sill before their steps. Step 12 jumps from flat gold to finished knit. Steps 20 and 21 add the nose, eye lines and whiskers that their words don't mention, and step 23, named for the nose, actually paints the blanket. The diagrams build up from step to step and match the words well, for example the roll laid on the slab. The Known problems list catches the step 20/21 magic and the step 1 width mismatch, but it is long and full of pipeline jargon, including merges of paints that don't exist.

f-lean-low.note: The steps, pictures and words are the same as A's, with the same early leaves and ghosts in step 4, the jump at step 12, and the misplaced nose and whiskers at steps 20 to 23. The diagrams are cleaner but less complete: the blanket skips the roll on top, and the stripe panels don't carry the earlier stripes forward. The Known problems list is shorter and plainer with useful advice ('follow the words', 'mix a rosy pink'). However, it says nothing about the nose and whiskers showing up early in steps 20 and 21.

ab.note: The only differences are the diagrams and the problem notes, and they trade off. A's diagrams are a little fuller and its list warns about more traps. B's list is easier for a beginner to read. Neither fixes the step 4 magic, the step 12 jump or the face appearing early, which hurt both lessons equally. It's a toss-up with at most a hair toward A, which is not enough to prefer it.

f-lean-low.note: The pictures are the same in both lessons. Their faults are what score lowest here. Steps 2 and 3 show nothing, and step 4 then brings in finished leaves, a ghost of the frame and sill, a dark box, and a stray arrowhead that stays for many steps. Step 12 jumps from a flat blanket to finished knit. A's Known problems list is short and covers the leaves, the stitches, the pink recipe and step 23's mismatched words. It says nothing about the nose and whiskers showing early in steps 20 and 21, about step 12's jump, or about step 1's patch being wider than its words. A's diagrams float on blank white, and the face diagram's toe lines hang loose below the head.

base.note: B has the same step pictures, with the same ghosts in step 4, the same jump in step 12 and the same step 23 mix-up. B's diagrams follow the words more closely: the frame next to the glass, the blanket's slab plus roll plus end, the three fold-shadow places, the stitches on mustard, and the face and whiskers drawn on the muzzle and paws. Its Known problems list warns about the nose and whiskers arriving early in steps 20 and 21, step 12's jump and step 1's width. But it is padded with pipeline jargon (chain, cost cap, plan.json, paints that don't exist, stroke cards) that means nothing to a painter.

ab.note: The pictures and words are the same, so the choice comes down to the extras. B's diagrams match the steps better, and its problem list catches the early nose and whiskers that A misses. Against that, B's list is noisy where A's is clean. I would paint from B, but the edge is slight, since the shared picture faults dominate both.

blend-window-sky.start: Start in the canvas's upper left corner. The sky through the window is a small patch: its top is at the top edge, its left side is at the left edge, and it's about 1 1/4 in wide.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke Sky blue side to side across the top of the patch. Without rinsing, pick up Pale sky blue and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The deeper blue sits at the top and the paler blue lower down, the way a sky pales toward the horizon. Let the outer edge of the patch stay soft and ragged.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave a small cloud of bare white canvas inside the blue, touching the left edge. Leave the rest of the canvas white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when you have one small blue corner patch, deeper at the top and paler at its ragged lower edge, with a white cloud in it. If you see a hard line where the blues meet, add a little more Pale sky blue at the join and blend again.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky through the window dry.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start where the blue curls around the white cloud. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap with just the tip of the dry brush, only a few touches. Don't drag the brush.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Put two or three dark taps along the blue rim of the cloud. Add one small tap near the ragged lower edge of the sky through the window. These are shaded leaves just peeking in.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave nearly all of the blue and the white cloud showing.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when a few small Leaf green specks sit in the sky and the corner still reads as blue. If they turn into blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-light-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green specks dry.
dab-light-leaves.start: Start at the ragged lower edge of the sky, near the left edge of the canvas.
dab-light-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the dry brush, a touch at a time.
dab-light-leaves.inside: Most of these taps go in the bottom half of the leaves outside the window, and on its left side, where the sun reaches the leaves.
dab-light-leaves.leave: Leave the Leaf green specks and the blue showing between your taps.
dab-light-leaves.stop: Stop when there are a few small light touches along the lower edge of the patch. The corner still reads mostly blue.

blend-wall.first: Let the sky and leaves dry.
blend-wall.start: Start in the canvas's top right corner with Sky blue, the palest part of the wall.
blend-wall.strokes: Work short strokes that cross like X shapes, moving across the canvas and downward. Pick up Soft wall blue as you go lower. While the paint is wet, go over it with longer side-to-side strokes.
blend-wall.inside: Keep Sky blue at the top and Soft wall blue through the middle and lower canvas. Work a little Deep wall blue in at the right edge of the canvas, the corner farthest from the window light. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the sky through the window showing in the upper left corner. Paint up to its edge, not over it.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the wall covers everything but the window, down to the bottom edge: an even periwinkle with faint X marks.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall and the window view dry.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the tall post: a cream rectangle down from the top edge, along the right side of the sky through the window.
block-in-frame.strokes: Pull long straight strokes down the post. Then lay the crossbar and the window ledge as separate rectangles, each stroke running the length of its bar.
block-in-frame.inside: The post is the wide inner side of the window opening. The crossbar runs across the panes. The ledge slopes down to the left edge at the foot of the window. The whole frame is about 3 in wide and 7 in tall.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two panes, one on each side of the crossbar.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when flat cream bars and a wide cream post frame the window view, with no shading yet.

shade-frame.first: The cream frame must be dry.
shade-frame.start: Start at the top edge, just right of the window frame. Pull a narrow dark band down the wall beside the post.
shade-frame.strokes: Pull long straight strokes down that band. Then turn the brush on its edge and run thin lines along the edges of each bar and the ledge.
shade-frame.inside: The band is the shadowed inner wall of the window recess. Thin lines go along the undersides of the bars and down the inner edge of the post. A soft shadow goes where the window ledge meets the wall. All of these face away from the light outside.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the cream faces of the post and bars wide and clean.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when a blue-gray strip runs down beside the post and every bar has a thin dark edge, so the window looks set into the wall.

light-frame.start: Start at the top edge, on the face of the post nearest the sky.
light-frame.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush. Skim light strokes down the post and along each bar and the ledge. Build up in several light passes.
light-frame.inside: The white goes on the faces that turn toward the window light: the post, the inner faces of the bars and the top of the ledge.
light-frame.leave: Leave the Deep wall blue edges and the dark band beside the post untouched. Let some cream show through the white.
light-frame.stop: Stop when the bars and post look sunlit, broken and near-white, with crisp dark edges. If the white goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush cream back over part of it.

lay-in-sill.start: Start at the left edge, below the window frame. Lay the top line of the sill across to the right edge, sloping gently down. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Fill the ledge with long, level side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.inside: Cover the whole sill evenly in Wood brown, straight through where the blanket will go.
lay-in-sill.leave: Keep the sill's top line clean and straight so the wall and frame stay crisp.
lay-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat warm-brown slab fills the bottom of the canvas from edge to edge, with level streaks.

darken-sill-edge.first: The Wood brown must be dry.
darken-sill-edge.start: Start along the sill's top line, near the foot of the window frame.
darken-sill-edge.strokes: Load the brush lightly. Pull long, level strokes across the whole ledge to the right edge, and let them streak and break.
darken-sill-edge.inside: Streak the back of the ledge, its front along the bottom edge, and its far end. These are the parts the window light doesn't reach.
darken-sill-edge.leave: Leave a long tapering patch of plain Wood brown on the left side of the wooden windowsill, running from the left edge toward the middle. Also leave a thin slanting strip near the left edge. The sun falls there.
darken-sill-edge.stop: Stop when the sill reads as grainy dark wood with one clean patch waiting on its left end.

light-sill.start: Start at the left edge, inside the plain patch you left.
light-sill.strokes: Skim the dry brush from left to right along the patch with light pressure. Let it break up toward the far end. Build up in light passes.
light-sill.inside: Fill the patch and the thin slanting strip beside it. This is the window's sunlight lying on the sill, about 8 1/4 in wide, broad at the left edge and tapering to a ragged point.
light-sill.leave: Leave the dark streak between the strip and the patch; it is the window bar's shadow. Leave all the dark wood around them.
light-sill.stop: Stop when a bright tan wedge of sun lies on the left end of the sill, fading out in broken touches.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with the folded front: a long rounded rectangle on the sill. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Lay the long front shape first. Then add curved pieces on top for the roll, running out to the right edge of the canvas.
block-in-blanket.inside: Fill the whole blanket solid Mustard gold, including where the cat will lie. Round off its left end like a folded roll.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a thin strip of dark wood showing below the mustard knit blanket, and the wall around it.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when a flat, rounded mustard shape lies on the sill, from near the window to the right edge, with no folds yet.

shade-blanket.first: The Mustard gold must be dry.
shade-blanket.start: Start at the left end of the blanket, curling strokes around the rounded fold.
shade-blanket.strokes: Pull short curved strokes in rows along each roll, like twists of rope, bending each one over the roll. Then run one curved line along the groove between the folds.
shade-blanket.inside: Cover the top rim, the inner fold and the front roll with these braided rows. Press darker in the groove between the folds and where the front roll meets the sill, the parts turned away from the light.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave Mustard gold showing between the twists so each stitch reads.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket reads as chunky knit in two soft rolls, with darker grooves.

dark-stitches.start: Start in the groove just inside the blanket's top rim, at its left end.
dark-stitches.strokes: Touch down, press, then pull and lift so each comma ends on a point. Set them in V pairs that follow the curve of the roll.
dark-stitches.inside: Run a nearly solid line of commas along that inner groove. Then scatter V pairs over the front roll and its lower fold, with more of them on the right side of the mustard knit blanket.
dark-stitches.leave: Leave the knit twists and plenty of mustard showing between the marks.
dark-stitches.stop: Stop when dark V stitches dot the front roll and a dark line marks the inner fold. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-stitches.start: Start along the top rim of the blanket at its left end, near the window frame.
light-stitches.strokes: Press and lift short commas in V pairs, following the curve, just like the dark ones.
light-stitches.inside: Put them on the tops of the rolls, the sides facing the window: thickly along the top rim and around the left end, a cluster in the middle of the inner fold, and scattered over the front roll.
light-stitches.leave: Leave the Dark gold stitches and the grooves showing between the bright marks.
light-stitches.stop: Stop when bright stitches glow on the tops of the rolls over darker gaps.

block-in-cat.start: Start with a circle for the head near the window frame, with the ears pointing up. The cat's top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
block-in-cat.strokes: Build it in pieces: the head circle, two triangle ears, a big oval for the curled body, and a curved piece for the tail wrapping along the front. Round the strokes along the back.
block-in-cat.inside: Fill the whole cat flat Cat gray, from the head out to the right edge of the canvas, lying over the top of the blanket.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the front rolls of the blanket showing below the sleeping tabby cat, and the blue wall around its back.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when a flat gray curled-cat shape fills the top of the blanket, with the head and ears near the window and no detail.

shade-cat.start: Start on the forehead, between the ears, with bands sweeping back from the face. This step's left side is about 2 in from the left edge.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend every stroke with the body: from the spine down around the back toward the blanket, and in short arcs across the tail.
shade-cat.inside: These Dark gray bands are the base for the tabby stripes, on the head, back, haunch and tail. Make them wider and more joined on the far end of the body, away from the window. Add a thin line around the paws.
shade-cat.leave: Leave plenty of Cat gray between the bands. Leave the ears, muzzle and chest plain gray.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when soft darker bands curve around the whole cat, following its shape.

white-patches.first: Let the dark gray dry. Let each coat of white dry before the next.
white-patches.start: Start with the two front paws, tucked where the chin meets the blanket. Their left side is about 3 1/2 in from the left edge.
white-patches.strokes: Curve the strokes around each paw's rounded toes. Then work up over the muzzle and chin, and pull a pointed triangle on the chest.
white-patches.inside: White goes on the paws, the muzzle and chin, and the chest patch farther along the body. Use 2 to 3 thin coats so it stays clean and bright.
white-patches.leave: Leave the gray and the bands around the white untouched.
white-patches.stop: Stop when two round white paws, a white muzzle and a white chest triangle stand out clearly.

cat-stripes.start: Start on top of the head, with short bars between the ears.
cat-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush at the spine end of each stripe. Then turn onto the edge and lighten up so the stripe tapers toward the belly. Lay short tapered bands across the tail.
cat-stripes.inside: Lay Charcoal over the dark gray bands on the head, cheeks, back and tail. Make it darkest along the far curl of the body and the tail. Add a dark line along the back of each ear.
cat-stripes.leave: Leave Cat gray between the stripes, and keep off the white patches.
cat-stripes.stop: Stop when bold, dark, tapering stripes wrap around the whole cat and the ears are still gray inside.

pink-ears.start: Start at the base of the ear nearest the window.
pink-ears.strokes: Press the tip near the base of the ear, then pull toward the ear's point and lift. Do the same in the other ear.
pink-ears.inside: Pink fills the inside of both ears, fullest near the base.
pink-ears.leave: Leave a gray rim around each ear.
pink-ears.stop: Stop when both ears glow pink inside with gray rims.

flick-fur.start: Start on top of the head, between the ears.
flick-fur.strokes: Use a lightly loaded fan brush and make quick short flicks, lifting off as you go. Follow the way the fur lies: back from the face over the head, and along the curve of the back.
flick-fur.inside: Flick over the stripe edges on the head and cheeks and along the top of the back, so the edges soften. Add a few flicks on the back's outline against the wall.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the dark stripes showing between the flicks, and keep the white and pink clean.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the stripe edges look soft and furry and the back has a fuzzy outline. Flat blobs mean too much paint.

window-light.start: Start at the rim of the ear nearest the window.
window-light.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush. Skim lightly along each rim, following its curve, in a few light passes.
window-light.inside: Cream catches the ear rims, the top of the head, around the eyes, a few spots along the back, and the stitch tops at the left end of the mustard knit blanket. These are the parts facing the window.
window-light.leave: Leave most of the gray and the stripes untouched.
window-light.stop: Stop when soft, broken glints of light sit on the edges nearest the window, never solid.

eyes-toes.first: Everything underneath must be dry, or the lines will feather.
eyes-toes.start: Start with the eye nearest the window: a thin curve on the cheek, bowed down like a sleepy smile.
eyes-toes.strokes: Use thin paint and hold the liner upright. Pull each curve in one light, steady stroke, thick in the middle and tapering at the ends.
eyes-toes.inside: Make two closed-eye curves, the second one higher up the face. Add a few short dashes on the cheek and small dark touches along the top of the back.
eyes-toes.leave: Keep the white muzzle and the paws clean.
eyes-toes.stop: Stop when the cat clearly has closed, sleeping eyes.

paint-nose.first: Let the blanket and the face dry.
paint-nose.start: Start at the left end of the mustard knit blanket, where the fold rounds near the sill.
paint-nose.strokes: Press and lift small commas into the gaps between stitches, following the curve of the roll.
paint-nose.inside: Tuck them into the gaps of the front roll and along the groove between the folds, to warm the shadows.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the bright stitches on top of the rolls untouched.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when the blanket's gaps look warmer and deeper, with no blobs.

whiskers.start: Start at the side of the white muzzle nearest the window. This step's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
whiskers.strokes: Use thin paint on the liner. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one quick stroke, pressing at the start and lifting so it tapers.
whiskers.inside: Make three or four whiskers on each side. On the window side they sweep over the cheek toward the blanket. On the other side they reach out across the gray of the body.
whiskers.leave: Leave the face lines and the nose untouched.
whiskers.stop: Stop when fine white whiskers fan from both sides of the muzzle. That finishes the painting. If a line skips, add water.

blend-window-sky.text: Start in the canvas's upper left corner. The sky through the window is a small patch: its top is at the top edge, its left side is at the left edge, and it's about 1 1/4 in wide.

Stroke Sky blue side to side across the top of the patch. Then, without rinsing, pick up Pale sky blue and paint the lower part of the patch. Stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
The deeper blue sits at the top and the paler blue lower down, the way a sky pales toward the horizon. Let the outer edge of the patch stay soft and ragged.
Leave a small cloud of bare white canvas partway down the patch, touching the left edge. Leave the rest of the canvas white.

Stop when you have one small blue corner patch, deeper at the top and paler at its ragged lower edge, with a white cloud in it. If you see a hard line where the blues meet, add a little more Pale sky blue at the join and blend again.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky through the window dry.
Start where the blue curls around the white cloud. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge.
Tap with just the tip of the dry brush, only a few touches. Don't drag the brush.
Put two or three dark taps along the blue rim of the cloud. Add one small tap near the ragged lower edge of the sky through the window. These are shaded leaves just peeking in.
Leave nearly all of the blue and the white cloud showing.
Stop when a few small Leaf green specks sit in the sky and the corner still reads as blue. If they turn into blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-light-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green specks dry.
Start at the ragged lower edge of the sky, near the left edge of the canvas.
Tap lightly with the tip of the dry brush, a touch at a time.
Most of these taps go in the bottom half of the leaves outside the window, and on its left side, where the sun reaches the leaves.
Leave the Leaf green specks and the blue showing between your taps.
Stop when there are a few small light touches along the lower edge of the patch. The corner still reads mostly blue.

blend-wall.text: Let the sky and leaves dry.
Start in the canvas's top right corner with Sky blue, the palest part of the wall.
Work short strokes that cross like X shapes, moving across the canvas and downward. Pick up Soft wall blue as you go lower. While the paint is wet, go over it with longer side-to-side strokes.

Keep Sky blue at the top and Soft wall blue through the middle and lower canvas. Work a little Deep wall blue in at the right edge of the canvas, the corner farthest from the window light. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
Leave the sky through the window showing in the upper left corner. Paint up to its edge, not over it.
Stop when the wall covers everything but the window, down to the bottom edge: an even periwinkle with faint X marks.

block-in-frame.text: Let the wall and the window view dry.
Start with the tall post: a cream rectangle down from the top edge, along the right side of the sky through the window.
Pull long straight strokes down the post. Then lay the crossbar and the window ledge as separate rectangles, each stroke running the length of its bar.

The post is the wide inner side of the window opening. The crossbar runs across the panes. The ledge slopes down to the left edge at the foot of the window. The whole frame is about 3 in wide and 7 in tall.
Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two panes, one on each side of the crossbar.
Stop when flat cream bars and a wide cream post frame the window view, with no shading yet.

shade-frame.text: The cream frame must be dry.
Start at the top edge, on the wall where it meets the cream post. Pull a narrow dark band down the wall there.
Pull long straight strokes down that band. Then turn the brush on its edge and run thin lines along the edges of each bar and the ledge.

The band is the shadowed inner wall of the window recess. Thin lines go along the undersides of the bars and down the inner edge of the post. A soft shadow goes where the window ledge meets the wall. All of these face away from the light outside.
Leave the cream faces of the post and bars wide and clean.
Stop when a blue-gray strip runs down the wall where it meets the cream post, and every bar has a thin dark edge, so the window looks set into the wall.

light-frame.text: Let the blue-gray shading dry.
Start at the top edge, on the face of the post nearest the sky.
