Dip only the tip of the dry brush. Skim light strokes down the post and along each bar and the ledge. Build up in several light passes.
The white goes on the faces that turn toward the window light: the post, the inner faces of the bars and the top of the ledge.
Leave the Deep wall blue edges and the dark band on the wall untouched. Let some cream show through the white.
Stop when the bars and post look sunlit, broken and near-white, with crisp dark edges. If the white goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush cream back over part of it.

lay-in-sill.text: Let the frame dry.
Start at the left edge, below the window frame. Lay the top line of the sill across to the right edge, sloping gently down. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Fill the ledge with long, level side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge.
Cover the whole sill evenly in Wood brown, straight through where the blanket will go.
Keep the sill's top line clean and straight so the wall and frame stay crisp.
Stop when a flat warm-brown slab fills the bottom of the canvas from edge to edge, with level streaks.

Leave a long tapering patch of plain Wood brown on the left side of the wooden windowsill, running from the left edge toward the middle. Also leave a thin slanting strip near the left edge. The sun falls there.
Stop when the sill reads as grainy dark wood with one clean patch waiting on its left end.

Start at the left edge, at the broad end of the plain Wood brown patch.

Fill the patch and the thin slanting strip near the left edge. This is the window's sunlight lying on the sill, broad at the left edge and tapering to a ragged point.
Leave the dark streak between the strip and the patch; it is the window bar's shadow. Leave all the dark wood around them.
Stop when a bright tan wedge of sun lies on the left end of the sill, fading out in broken touches.

Start at the left edge, below the window frame. Lay the top line of the sill across to the right edge, sloping gently down. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Fill the ledge with long, level side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge.
Cover the whole sill evenly in Wood brown, straight through where the blanket will go.
Keep the sill's top line clean and straight so the wall and frame stay crisp.
Stop when a flat warm-brown slab fills the bottom of the canvas from edge to edge, with level streaks.

darken-sill-edge.text: The Wood brown must be dry.
Start along the sill's top line, near the foot of the window frame.
The same long, level strokes you laid the sill in with, but now with a lightly loaded brush in the darker brown, letting the strokes streak and break.
Load the brush lightly. Pull long, level strokes across the whole ledge to the right edge, and let them streak and break.
Streak the back of the ledge, its front along the bottom edge, and its far end. These are the parts the window light doesn't reach.

Leave a long tapering patch of plain Wood brown on the left side of the wooden windowsill, running from the left edge toward the middle. Also leave a thin slanting strip near the left edge. The sun falls there.
Stop when the sill reads as grainy dark wood with one clean patch waiting on its left end.

light-sill.text: Let the dark streaks dry.
Start at the left edge, at the broad end of the plain Wood brown patch.
The same dry skim that lit the window bars, now in Sunlit wood, laid where the window's sun falls on the sill.
Skim the dry brush from left to right along the patch with light pressure. Let it break up toward the far end. Build up in light passes.
Fill the patch and the thin slanting strip near the left edge. This is the window's sunlight lying on the sill, broad at the left edge and tapering to a ragged point.
Leave the dark streak between the strip and the patch; it is the window bar's shadow. Leave all the dark wood around them.
Stop when a bright tan wedge of sun lies on the left end of the sill, fading out in broken touches.

block-in-blanket.text: Let the sill dry.
Start with the folded front: a long rounded rectangle on the sill. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
You build the blanket from simple pieces the way you built the window frame, but with the bigger brush and rounded pieces instead of straight bars.
Lay the long front shape first. Then add curved pieces on top for the roll, running out to the right edge of the canvas.
Fill the whole blanket solid Mustard gold, including where the cat will lie. Round off its left end like a folded roll.
Leave a thin strip of dark wood showing below the mustard knit blanket, and the wall around it.
Stop when a flat, rounded mustard shape lies on the sill, from near the window to the right edge, with no folds yet.

shade-blanket.text: The Mustard gold must be dry.
Start at the left end of the blanket, curling strokes around the rounded fold.
Pull short curved strokes in rows along each roll, like twists of rope, bending each one over the roll. Then run one curved line along the groove between the folds.

Cover the top rim, the inner fold and the front roll with these braided rows. Press darker in the groove between the folds and where the front roll meets the sill, the parts turned away from the light.
Leave Mustard gold showing between the twists so each stitch reads.
Stop when the blanket reads as chunky knit in two soft rolls, with darker grooves.

dark-stitches.text: Let the folds dry.
Start in the groove just inside the blanket's top rim, at its left end.
Touch down, press, then pull and lift so each comma ends on a point. Set them in V pairs that follow the curve of the roll.
Run a nearly solid line of commas along that inner groove. Then scatter V pairs over the front roll and its lower fold, with more of them on the right side of the mustard knit blanket.
Leave the knit twists and plenty of mustard showing between the marks.
Stop when dark V stitches dot the front roll and a dark line marks the inner fold. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-stitches.text: Let the dark stitches dry.
Start along the top rim of the blanket at its left end, near the window frame.
The same press-and-lift commas as the dark stitches, in V pairs again, now in Bright gold and mostly on the sides facing the window.
Press and lift short commas in V pairs, following the curve, just like the dark ones.
Put them on the tops of the rolls, the sides facing the window: thickly along the top rim and around the left end, a cluster in the middle of the inner fold, and scattered over the front roll.
Leave the Dark gold stitches and the grooves showing between the bright marks.
Stop when bright stitches glow on the tops of the rolls over darker gaps.

block-in-cat.text: The blanket must be dry.
Start with a circle for the head near the window frame, with the ears pointing up. The cat's top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Like the blanket, the cat starts as a few simple pieces laid flat with the big brush: this time a circle, two triangles and an oval.
Build it in pieces: the head circle, two triangle ears, a big oval for the curled body, and a curved piece for the tail wrapping along the front. Round the strokes along the back.
Fill the whole cat flat Cat gray, from the head out to the right edge of the canvas, lying over the top of the blanket.
Leave the front rolls of the blanket showing below the sleeping tabby cat, and the blue wall around its back.
Stop when a flat gray curled-cat shape fills the top of the blanket, with the head and ears near the window and no detail.

shade-cat.text: Let the Cat gray dry.
Start on the forehead, between the ears, with bands sweeping back from the face. This step's left side is about 2 in from the left edge.
The same curved strokes that shaded the blanket's folds, with the same brush, now in Dark gray bending around the cat's round body.
Bend every stroke with the body: from the spine down around the back toward the blanket, and in short arcs across the tail.

These Dark gray bands are the base for the tabby stripes, on the head, back, haunch and tail. Make them wider and more joined on the far end of the body, away from the window. Add a thin line around the paws.
Leave plenty of Cat gray between the bands. Leave the ears, muzzle and chest plain gray.
Stop when soft darker bands curve around the whole cat, following its shape.

white-patches.text: Let the dark gray dry. Let each coat of white dry before the next.
Start with the two front paws, tucked where the chin meets the blanket. Their left side is about 3 1/2 in from the left edge.
The Pure white that lit the window bars, but this time it goes on in thin, full coats with a round brush, not dry-brushed.
Curve the strokes around each paw's rounded toes. Then work up over the muzzle and chin, and pull a pointed triangle on the chest.
White goes on the paws, the muzzle and chin, and the chest patch farther along the body. Use 2 to 3 thin coats so it stays clean and bright.
Leave the gray and the bands around the white untouched.
Stop when two round white paws, a white muzzle and a white chest triangle stand out clearly.

cat-stripes.text: Let the white dry.
Start on top of the head, with short bars between the ears.
Press the full width of the angle brush at the spine end of each stripe. Then turn onto the edge and lighten up so the stripe tapers toward the belly. Lay short tapered bands across the tail.
Lay Charcoal over the dark gray bands on the head, cheeks, back and tail. Make it darkest along the far curl of the body and the tail. Add a dark line along the back of each ear.
Leave Cat gray between the stripes, and keep off the white patches.
Stop when bold, dark, tapering stripes wrap around the whole cat and the ears are still gray inside.

pink-ears.text: Let the stripes dry.
Start at the base of the ear nearest the window.
The press-and-lift comma from the blanket stitches, with the same round brush, now one stroke pulled toward each ear's point in Soft pink.
Press the tip near the base of the ear, then pull toward the ear's point and lift. Do the same in the other ear.
Pink fills the inside of both ears, fullest near the base.
Leave a gray rim around each ear.
Stop when both ears glow pink, each with a gray rim.

flick-fur.text: Let the pink ears dry.
Start on top of the head, between the ears.
The same Cat gray you blocked the cat in with, now flicked on lightly with the fan brush so the darker bands show between the marks.
Use a lightly loaded fan brush and make quick short flicks, lifting off as you go. Follow the way the fur lies: back from the face over the head, and along the curve of the back.
Flick over the stripe edges on the head and cheeks and along the top of the back, so the edges soften. Add a few flicks on the back's outline against the wall.
Leave the dark stripes showing between the flicks, and keep the white and pink clean.
Stop when the stripe edges look soft and furry and the back has a fuzzy outline. Flat blobs mean too much paint.

window-light.text: Let the fur dry.
Start at the rim of the ear nearest the window.
The same dry skim that put sunlight on the sill, now in Warm cream along the cat's lit rims and the blanket's stitch tops.
Dip only the tip of the dry brush. Skim lightly along each rim, following its curve, in a few light passes.
Cream catches the ear rims, the top of the head, around the eyes, a few spots along the back, and the stitch tops at the left end of the mustard knit blanket. These are the parts facing the window.
Leave most of the gray and the stripes untouched.
Stop when soft, broken glints of light sit on the edges nearest the window, never solid.

eyes-toes.text: Everything underneath must be dry, or the lines will feather.
Start with the eye nearest the window: a thin curve on the cheek, bowed down like a sleepy smile.
The Charcoal from the stripes, now thinned with water so the liner pulls a fine, steady line.
Use thin paint and hold the liner upright. Pull each curve in one light, steady stroke, thick in the middle and tapering at the ends.
Make two closed-eye curves, the second one higher up the face. Add a few short dashes on the cheek and small dark touches along the top of the back.
Keep the white muzzle and the paws clean.
Stop when the cat clearly has closed, sleeping eyes.

paint-nose.text: Let the blanket and the face dry.
Start at the left end of the mustard knit blanket, where the fold rounds near the sill.
Press and lift small commas into the gaps between stitches, following the curve of the roll.
Tuck them into the gaps of the front roll and along the groove between the folds, to warm the shadows.
Leave the bright stitches on top of the rolls untouched.
Stop when the blanket's gaps look warmer and deeper, with no blobs.

whiskers.text: The face must be dry.
Start at the side of the white muzzle nearest the window. This step's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
The same liner and thin paint as the eye lines, now in Pure white, pulled out in quick strokes that taper.
Use thin paint on the liner. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one quick stroke, pressing at the start and lifting so it tapers.
Make three or four whiskers on each side. On the window side they sweep over the cheek toward the blanket. On the other side they reach out across the gray of the body.
Leave the face lines and the nose untouched.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan from both sides of the muzzle. That finishes the painting. If a line skips, add water.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a gray tabby kitten fast asleep, curled on a folded mustard knit blanket on a wooden windowsill by a sunny window. The heart of the painting is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white paws tucked against the chin. Soft daylight and warm colors make it feel cozy and quiet, so keep your marks gentle and let the light do the singing.
opening.light: The soft daylight comes in through the window and falls on the things nearest the glass: the cat's head and ears, the near end of the blanket and the end of the sill. The far curl of the cat, the deep folds of the blanket and the front edge of the sill turn away from the window, so they stay darker.

skills.how: You start a shape with one simple piece, a rectangle, an oval or a circle, and add the rest in smaller pieces around it. Here it builds the straight window bars, the rolled blanket and the curled cat. Only soften the joins where the shape should look smooth; otherwise let the pieces show.

You touch down with the tip, press so the brush spreads, then pull and lift so the mark ends in a point. It stamps every knit stitch on the blanket and fills the pink of the ears. If you get blobs instead of teardrops, use less paint and lift faster.

Only the tip of a dry brush touches the paint, and you skim the canvas with light pressure so the marks break up. It is how the window light lands on the frame, the sill, the cat's rims and the blanket's stitches. It should never go on solid, so build it in several light passes.

opening.road: We paint from the farthest thing to the nearest. The view through the window opens the painting: a soft blended sky with dabbed leaves. The blue wall goes on next, straight through where everything else will sit, and then the cream window frame is built, shaded and lit so it looks set into the wall. The wooden sill follows, a warm ledge with a dark front edge and a wedge of sunlight. The blanket comes next, built from a flat gold shape up to chunky stitches, because the cat lies in it. The cat comes last and gets the most care: a flat gray shape, then shading, white patches, stripes and ears, and finally the fur, the window light and the sleeping face.

the-window-view.for: Paint the farthest thing in the picture, the sky and leaves seen through the window.
the-window-view.end: A small patch of soft blue sky with a bare white cloud and a few tiny touches of green sits in one corner of the white canvas.

the-wall.for: Cover the rest of the canvas with the smooth periwinkle wall, painted straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
the-wall.end: Soft periwinkle blue covers the whole canvas except the window view, where sky and leaf clumps still show.

the-window-frame.for: Build the cream window frame, then give it a shadow side and sunlit faces so it looks set into the wall.
the-window-frame.end: Sunlit cream bars and a deep blue-gray inner wall frame the sky and leaves, with plain blue wall everywhere else.

the-sill.for: Lay the wooden ledge that the blanket and cat will rest on, with a dark front edge and sunlight from the window.
the-sill.end: A warm brown sill runs across the canvas, dark along its front edge, with a bright wedge of sunlight on the end nearest the window.

the-blanket.for: Build the folded knit blanket from a flat gold shape to chunky stitches before the cat lies on it.
the-blanket.end: A chunky mustard blanket in soft rolls lies on the sill, its bright stitches glowing over darker gaps, with no cat yet.

the-cat.for: Shape the cat in layers: a flat gray form, then its shading, white patches, stripes and pink ears.
the-cat.end: A striped gray cat lies curled on the blanket with a white muzzle, chest and paws and pink ears, but its face is still blank.

the-light-and-face.for: Bring the cat to life with soft fur, the window light and the sleeping face.
the-light-and-face.end: The painting is finished: a furry tabby asleep on its knit blanket, light on its head and back, with closed eyes, a pink nose and fine white whiskers.

back.text: The same dry tapping you used for the shaded leaves, with the same brush, now in the lighter green and only where the sun reaches.
The Deep wall blue you worked into the wall's far corner comes back here, now in narrow bands and edges that set the window into the wall.
The same long, level strokes you laid the sill in with, but now with a lightly loaded brush in the darker brown, letting the strokes streak and break.
The same dry skim that lit the window bars, now in Sunlit wood, laid where the window's sun falls on the sill.
You build the blanket from simple pieces the way you built the window frame, but with the bigger brush and rounded pieces instead of straight bars.
The same press-and-lift commas as the dark stitches, in V pairs again, now in Bright gold and mostly on the sides facing the window.
Like the blanket, the cat starts as a few simple pieces laid flat with the big brush: this time a circle, two triangles and an oval.
The same curved strokes that shaded the blanket's folds, with the same brush, now in Dark gray bending around the cat's round body.
The Pure white that lit the window bars, but this time it goes on in thin, full coats with a round brush, not dry-brushed.
The press-and-lift comma from the blanket stitches, with the same round brush, now one stroke pulled toward each ear's point in Soft pink.
The same Cat gray you blocked the cat in with, now flicked on lightly with the fan brush so the darker bands show between the marks.
The same dry skim that put sunlight on the sill, now in Warm cream along the cat's lit rims and the blanket's stitch tops.
The Charcoal from the stripes, now thinned with water so the liner pulls a fine, steady line.
The same liner and thin paint as the eye lines, now in Pure white, pulled out in quick strokes that taper.

blend-the-sky.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue. Lay long side-to-side strokes all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-the-sky.strokes: Work down the canvas in bands. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold for the next band lower down, then stroke back up over the join several times while both colors are wet. Go back to Sky blue for the lower sky and blend it into the gold the same way.
blend-the-sky.inside: The gold sits in a broad glowing band across the upper middle of the sky, brightest at the right edge of the canvas, where the sun sets behind the hills. Let a few soft gold streaks trail into the blue lower down.
blend-the-sky.leave: Leave no white canvas. The sky runs to every edge because everything else is painted over it.
blend-the-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is soft sky: blue at the top, a warm gold band, then blue again lower down. If you see a hard line where the colors meet, add a little more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.first: Let the sky dry completely so the cloud edges stay clean.
lay-in-clouds.start: Start with the biggest cloud masses in a band about 5 in tall across the top of the canvas, beginning at the left edge.
lay-in-clouds.strokes: Work small circles with the tip of the round so each cloud gets a soft, bumpy edge. Keep each streak long and flat, level or sloping gently toward the right edge of the canvas.
lay-in-clouds.inside: Most of the cloud paint goes on the left side of the sky and in its top half, where the big masses join up. Lower down, make the streaks smaller, thinner and farther apart, like wisps catching the sunset.
lay-in-clouds.leave: Leave plenty of blue showing between the streaks and in gaps inside the big masses.
lay-in-clouds.stop: Stop when ragged gold clouds fill the upper sky and thin gold wisps float in the blue lower down. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with lighter circles.

light-cloud-tops.first: Let the gold cloud streaks dry first.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start along the top edge of the canvas, in a strip about 1 3/4 in tall that begins at the left edge.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Sunlit cream, wipe it, and skim lightly side to side so the paint breaks up on the canvas. Lower in the sky, skim it along long wavy lines that rise and dip, sloping down toward the right edge of the canvas.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Most of the cream goes in the bottom half of the sky, along the wavy edges of the low cloud bands that catch the setting sun. Up high it only touches the edges of the gold clouds.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave blue and gold showing through every mark. This paint never covers an area solidly.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when soft cream glows along the top clouds and traces a few wavy lines across the lower sky. If a mark went on solid, your brush was too loaded, so wipe it more before the next pass.

lay-in-far-hills.first: Let the sky dry completely before the hills go over it.
lay-in-far-hills.start: Start with the farthest ridge line, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, running all the way across from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-in-far-hills.strokes: Bend each stroke with the hills: start at the top of each rounded bump and pull down along its curve. Lay ridge after ridge, each one a little lower, down to the bottom edge of the canvas.
lay-in-far-hills.inside: Hazy violet covers everything from that first ridge line down, flat and soft with no texture, because these hills are far away in the haze.
lay-in-far-hills.leave: Leave the sky and clouds showing in the top 2 in of the canvas. Let a thin glint of gold sky show along each ridge line so the ranges separate.
lay-in-far-hills.stop: Stop when the canvas from about 2 in down is soft, layered violet ridges with faint gold glints between them. There are no darker ridges or lake yet.

shade-near-ridges.first: Let the far hills dry first.
shade-near-ridges.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, just in front of the farthest range, and work toward the left edge.
shade-near-ridges.strokes: Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Lay one band that slopes gently down toward the right edge of the canvas.
shade-near-ridges.inside: Down the middle of the ridges, the band runs from about 3 in to about 4 in from the top edge. Most of it is on the right side of the ridges, where it is widest, and it narrows to a thin line toward the left edge of the canvas.
shade-near-ridges.leave: Leave the pale back range showing along the sky, and leave the lower violet ridges untouched.
shade-near-ridges.stop: Stop when one darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range, soft and without texture. There is no lake yet.

paint-lake.first: Let the ridges dry first so the pale paint stays clean.
paint-lake.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, with the lake's top about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
paint-lake.strokes: Bend each small stroke with the shoreline. Pull it in from the right edge of the canvas along the foot of the darker ridge, and let it end in a point.
paint-lake.inside: The lake is one flat sliver of Pale sky, about 1 1/4 in wide and 1/2 in tall, lying in the valley where the water reflects the sky.
paint-lake.leave: Leave the darker slate ridge untouched around it, so the water sits in a notch of the hills.
paint-lake.stop: Stop when a small pale wedge of water shines at the right edge of the canvas, wide at the edge and tapering to a point.

lay-in-hillside.first: Let the ridges and the lake dry first.
lay-in-hillside.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, with the hillside's top about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-in-hillside.strokes: Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Lay the top line of the slope first, letting it fall gently toward the lake, then fill in downward with long level strokes.
lay-in-hillside.inside: Olive green covers the whole lower canvas flat and even, from that sloping line to the bottom edge of the canvas. It is the shaded base that the sunlit patches go over.
lay-in-hillside.leave: Leave the back ranges, the darker ridge and the lake showing. The slope's edge only just meets the lake's lower shore.
lay-in-hillside.stop: Stop when the lower canvas is one flat olive-green slope falling gently toward the lake, with no sunlit patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.first: Let the olive green dry first, or the taps will smear into it.
tap-sunlit-slope.start: Start along the top of the green hillside at the left edge of the canvas, and work down in a zigzag.
tap-sunlit-slope.strokes: Stroke the fan on the palette until it spreads, then stamp only the middle tips. Tap short marks in different directions, pressing harder as you go down so the patches grow heavier toward the bottom edge of the canvas.
tap-sunlit-slope.inside: Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside in long soft drifts that slope down toward the right edge of the canvas, the way the low sun rakes across the hill.
tap-sunlit-slope.leave: Leave olive green showing in diagonal streaks and small round clumps between the taps, because those are the bushes and shadows. Keep the thin strip just in front of the ridges mostly olive.
tap-sunlit-slope.stop: Stop when the hillside is dappled yellow-green, with dark olive bushes running through it. If the marks look clumpy, thin the paint a little and spread the fan.

lay-in-meadow.start: Start at the meadow's top line, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas at the left edge, and work down.
lay-in-meadow.strokes: Use short strokes that cross each other like overlapping X shapes to build one even fill. Let the top line slope gently down toward the right edge of the canvas.
lay-in-meadow.inside: Sunlit green covers everything from that line to the bottom edge of the canvas, all the way across. This is the sunny meadow in front of the hill.
lay-in-meadow.leave: Leave the dappled hillside showing in the upper canvas, with a soft, slightly ragged edge where the grass meets it.
lay-in-meadow.stop: Stop when the lower canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow with faint criss-cross marks. There is no dark front and there are no grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.first: Let the meadow dry first, so the dark green skims over it instead of mixing in.
darken-meadow-front.start: Start low in the meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas. Work upward until the dark reaches about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
darken-meadow-front.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Deep grass green and skim it lightly in short, upward slanting strokes, like grass leaning in the breeze. Build it up in several light passes.
darken-meadow-front.inside: Most of the dark goes in the lower meadow, the shadowed front. Higher up it thins to scattered streaks, where the sun still lights the grass.
darken-meadow-front.leave: Leave plenty of yellow-green showing between the strokes, most of all in the upper meadow.
darken-meadow-front.stop: Stop when the meadow is streaky, sunny at the back and darker toward the bottom edge of the canvas. If it went on solid, your brush was too loaded.

block-in-cow.first: Let the meadow and the hillside dry first.
block-in-cow.start: Start with the big oval of the body, its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas.
block-in-cow.strokes: Lay the body as one oval. Add the head as a smaller rounded piece at its upper front and the fringe as a curved cap over the head. Then add the legs as short pieces down into the grass, and keep every outer edge ragged, like long hair.
block-in-cow.inside: Rust brown fills the whole cow solidly. The cow is about 7 1/2 in wide and 8 1/2 in tall, with its bottom about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave the meadow showing between the legs, in two small notches of grass.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop when a flat rust-brown shaggy shape stands in the meadow with a round body, a head and stubby legs. There is no shading, horns or face yet.

shade-cow.first: Let the rust brown dry first.
shade-cow.start: Start high on the cow's back, where the head meets the body, and work down.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull long curved strokes down the body, bending them with the hair as it falls toward the legs. Curve shorter strokes around the fringe and the head.
shade-cow.inside: Most of the dark goes on the left side of the cow, the side turned away from the sun. Lay it in long hanging streaks down the body, in the hollow where the fringe hangs over the face, at the throat, and between the legs.
shade-cow.leave: Leave rust showing on the sunlit side of the cow, on the fringe and the front of the face, and in stripes between the dark streaks.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks round and hairy, with dark streaks on its shadow side and warm rust glowing toward the sun.

block-in-horns.start: Start the bigger horn at its root, where it leaves the crown of the head. Its tip reaches about 2 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas.
block-in-horns.strokes: Build each horn from tapering curved pieces. Make each thick at the root, sweep it out and up, and narrow it to a point that turns upward.
block-in-horns.inside: The bigger horn is about 2 1/4 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall and sweeps up and out against the hills. The smaller horn is about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall and curves up from the far side of the head.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the fringe untouched between the two roots.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop when two flat, smooth bone-colored horns curve up from the head, each ending in an upturned point. There is no shading yet.

shade-horns.start: Start at the tip of the bigger horn and work back toward its root.
shade-horns.strokes: Follow each horn's curve with the round, pulling thin strokes along its length and never across it.
shade-horns.inside: Most of the Nose pink goes along the lower, inner curve of each horn and darkens the tips, which are the parts turned away from the light. Carry it a little onto the roots where they meet the hair.
shade-horns.leave: Leave a stripe of Horn bone showing along the upper curve of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when each horn looks round: darker along its inner curve and tip, and pale bone along its outer curve.

pull-ginger-locks.first: Let the cow's shading dry first so the locks stay clean on top of it.
pull-ginger-locks.start: Start at the fringe, at the top of the cow, pulling locks down over the face.
pull-ginger-locks.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush at the root of each lock. Then lighten and turn onto its edge as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point the way the hair hangs.
pull-ginger-locks.inside: Pull long ginger locks down the body, most of them on the left side of the cow, where they streak over the dark umber. Hang a few short ones from the fringe over the face.
pull-ginger-locks.leave: Leave dark umber gaps between the locks. Also leave the dark face where the fringe shades it, and the rust along the cow's sunlit edge.
pull-ginger-locks.stop: Stop when long ginger locks hang down the body and fringe with dark coat showing between them. There are no pale straw locks yet.

pull-straw-locks.first: Let the ginger locks dry first.
pull-straw-locks.start: Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
pull-straw-locks.strokes: Press the small angle brush flat at the root of each lock. Then lift it onto its edge as you pull down, tapering each lock to a point.
pull-straw-locks.inside: Most of the straw gold goes on the right side of the cow, where the sun hits, as a long run of locks down the sunlit edge of the face and chest to the front leg. Add a few locks on the upper back toward the left edge of the canvas, and a few short touches at the feet.
pull-straw-locks.leave: Leave most of the ginger locks and dark gaps showing. This paint only catches the sunlit edges.
pull-straw-locks.stop: Stop when a bright straw-gold edge runs down the sunlit outline of the cow and the fringe glows along its crown.

light-the-rims.first: Let the straw locks and the horns dry first.
light-the-rims.start: Start on the bigger horn, near its root.
light-the-rims.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry flat in Sunlit cream and skim it lightly along the curve, so the shine breaks up.
light-the-rims.inside: Lay a thin broken shine along the inner curve of the bigger horn and small touches where each horn meets the hair. Add a few tiny feathery touches along the crown of the fringe, between the horns, where the low sun catches the hair tips.
light-the-rims.leave: Leave the horn color showing through the shine, and leave the rest of the coat as it is.
light-the-rims.stop: Stop when a few small, bright glints sit at the horns and along the crown of the fringe, with no solid line anywhere. If one went on solid, your brush was too loaded.

paint-nose.first: Let the coat and the fringe dry first.
paint-nose.start: Start where the fringe meets the face. The nose's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Use small curved strokes that wrap around the rounded nose, like the end of a soft cylinder.
paint-nose.inside: The nose is a broad, rounded pink pad about 1 in wide and 3/4 in tall, peeking out of the hair at the front of the face.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the ginger hair framing the nose all round, and let a few hair tips overlap its edge.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a plain dusty-pink nose sits at the front of the face. There are no nostrils or mouth yet.

line-nostrils-mouth.first: Let the nose dry completely, or the lines will spread and feather.
line-nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the two nostrils, low on the pink nose.
line-nostrils-mouth.strokes: Swirl the liner in water and then in Dark umber, hold it upright, and use light, steady pressure. Make each nostril a short curved comma, then add a short faint mouth line that wobbles a little. Reload often.
line-nostrils-mouth.inside: The nostrils sit at the lower corners of the nose, and the mouth line runs across the chin a little lower down. Run a fine dark line around the edge of the nose so it stands out from the hair.
line-nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave most of the pink showing, because these are only thin lines.
line-nostrils-mouth.stop: Stop when the nose has two dark nostrils and a short mouth line, and the face reads clearly. If a line skips, add a little water.

flick-dark-grass.first: Let the cow and the meadow dry first.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, about 1/2 in from the left edge, and work across.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush. Flick quick upward strokes that thin out as you lift off, leaning a little like grass blades.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Most of the blades go in the lower meadow, thickest at the bottom edge of the canvas. Carry them up over the cow's legs and the bottom of its belly, so the legs disappear into the grass.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave plenty of meadow showing between the blades, and keep them off the cow's upper body and face.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Stop when dark green blades rise across the front of the meadow and over the cow's legs. There are no lighter blades yet.

flick-light-grass.first: Let the dark blades dry first.
flick-light-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work up and across. The light blades reach up to about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
flick-light-grass.strokes: Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush and flick quick upward strokes that thin out as you lift off.
flick-light-grass.inside: Lay the blades over the dark ones, most of them on the right side of the grass in front of the cow, where the sun reaches past the cow. Put a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.
flick-light-grass.leave: Leave dark green showing between every light blade so the grass has depth.
flick-light-grass.stop: Stop when yellow-green blades sit over the dark ones across the front, with dark still showing between them. There are no gold tips yet.

flick-gold-tips.first: Let the green blades dry first.
flick-gold-tips.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, near the left edge, and work up and across.
flick-gold-tips.strokes: Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush and flick short upward marks. Each one is a small seed head.
flick-gold-tips.inside: Make the tips bigger and farther apart near the bottom edge, and smaller toward the hillside. The highest ones reach about 6 3/4 in from the top edge. Scatter a few over the cow's front legs and along the far edge of the meadow, where the sun lights the grass.
flick-gold-tips.leave: Leave most of the green blades showing. These are sparkles, not a coat.
flick-gold-tips.stop: Stop when golden tips sparkle across the whole meadow and in front of the cow. The painting is finished.

blend-the-sky.text: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue. Lay long side-to-side strokes all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge.

Work down the canvas in bands. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold for the next band lower down, then stroke back up over the join several times while both colors are wet. Go back to Sky blue for the lower sky and blend it into the gold the same way.

The gold sits in a broad glowing band across the upper middle of the sky, brightest at the right edge of the canvas, where the sun sets behind the hills. Let a few soft gold streaks trail into the blue lower down.
Leave no white canvas. The sky runs to every edge because everything else is painted over it.

Stop when the whole canvas is soft sky: blue at the top, a warm gold band, then blue again lower down. If you see a hard line where the colors meet, add a little more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.text: Let the sky dry completely so the cloud edges stay clean.
Start with the biggest cloud masses in a band about 5 in tall across the top of the canvas, beginning at the left edge.
Work small circles with the tip of the round so each cloud gets a soft, bumpy edge. Keep each streak long and flat, level or sloping gently toward the right edge of the canvas.

Most of the cloud paint goes on the left side of the sky and in its top half, where the big masses join up. Lower down, make the streaks smaller, thinner and farther apart, like wisps catching the sunset.
Leave plenty of blue showing between the streaks.
Stop when ragged gold clouds fill the upper sky and thin gold wisps float in the blue lower down. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with lighter circles.

light-cloud-tops.text: Let the gold cloud streaks dry first.
Start along the top edge of the canvas, in a strip about 1 3/4 in tall that begins at the left edge.

Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Sunlit cream, wipe it, and skim lightly side to side so the paint breaks up on the canvas. Lower in the sky, skim it along long wavy lines that rise and dip, sloping down toward the right edge of the canvas.
Most of the cream goes in the bottom half of the sky, along the wavy edges of the low cloud bands that catch the setting sun. Up high it only touches the edges of the gold clouds.
Leave blue and gold showing through every mark. This paint never covers an area solidly.
Stop when soft cream glows along the top clouds and traces a few wavy lines across the lower sky. If a mark went on solid, your brush was too loaded, so wipe it more before the next pass.

lay-in-far-hills.text: Let the sky dry completely before the hills go over it.
Start with the farthest ridge line, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, running all the way across from the left edge to the right edge.
Bend each stroke with the hills: start at the top of each rounded bump and pull down along its curve. Lay ridge after ridge, each one a little lower, down to the bottom edge of the canvas.
Hazy violet covers everything from that first ridge line down, flat and soft with no texture, because these hills are far away in the haze.
Leave the sky and clouds showing along the top of the canvas, down to that first ridge line. Let a thin glint of gold sky show along each ridge line so the ranges separate.
Stop when everything from the first ridge line to the bottom edge of the canvas is soft, layered violet ridges with faint gold glints between them. There are no darker ridges or lake yet.

shade-near-ridges.text: Let the far hills dry first.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, just in front of the farthest range, and work toward the left edge.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Lay one band that slopes gently down toward the right edge of the canvas.
Most of the band is on the right side of the ridges, where it is widest, and it narrows to a thin line toward the left edge of the canvas.
Leave the pale back range showing along the sky, and leave the lower violet ridges untouched.
Stop when one darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range, soft and without texture. There is no lake yet.

paint-lake.text: Let the ridges dry first so the pale paint stays clean.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, with the lake's top about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Bend each small stroke with the shoreline. Pull it in from the right edge of the canvas along the foot of the darker ridge, and let it end in a point.
The lake is one flat sliver of Pale sky, about 1 1/4 in wide and 1/2 in tall, lying in the valley where the water reflects the sky.
Leave the darker slate ridge untouched around it, so the water sits in a notch of the hills.
Stop when a small pale wedge of water shines at the right edge of the canvas, wide at the edge and tapering to a point.

lay-in-hillside.text: Let the ridges and the lake dry first.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, with the hillside's top about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Lay the top line of the slope first, letting it fall gently toward the lake, then fill in downward with long level strokes.
Olive green covers the whole lower canvas flat and even, from that sloping line to the bottom edge of the canvas. It is the shaded base that the sunlit patches go over.
Leave the back ranges, the darker ridge and the lake showing. The slope's edge only just meets the lake's lower shore.
Stop when the lower canvas is one flat olive-green slope falling gently toward the lake, with no sunlit patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: Let the olive green dry first, or the taps will smear into it.
Start along the top of the green hillside at the left edge of the canvas, and work down in a zigzag.

Stroke the fan on the palette until it spreads, then stamp only the middle tips. Tap short marks in different directions, pressing harder as you go down so the patches grow heavier toward the bottom edge of the canvas.
Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside in long soft drifts that slope down toward the right edge of the canvas, the way the low sun rakes across the hill.
Leave olive green showing in diagonal streaks and small round clumps between the taps, because those are the bushes and shadows. Keep the thin strip just in front of the ridges mostly olive.
Stop when the hillside is dappled yellow-green, with dark olive bushes running through it. If the marks look clumpy, thin the paint a little and spread the fan.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside dry first.
Start at the meadow's top line, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas at the left edge, and work down.
Use short strokes that cross each other like overlapping X shapes to build one even fill. Let the top line slope gently down toward the right edge of the canvas.
The meadow's Sunlit green runs from that line to the bottom edge of the canvas and reaches both the left and right edges. This is the sunny meadow in front of the hill.
Leave the dappled hillside showing in the upper canvas, with a soft, slightly ragged edge where the grass meets it.
Stop when the lower canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow with faint criss-cross marks. There is no dark front and there are no grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry first, so the dark green skims over it instead of mixing in.
Start low in the meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas. Work upward until the dark reaches about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Deep grass green and skim it lightly in short, upward slanting strokes, like grass leaning in the breeze. Build it up in several light passes.
Most of the dark goes in the lower meadow, the shadowed front. Higher up it thins to scattered streaks, where the sun still lights the grass.
Leave plenty of yellow-green showing between the strokes, most of all in the upper meadow.
Stop when the meadow is streaky, sunny at the back and darker toward the bottom edge of the canvas. If it went on solid, your brush was too loaded.

Lay the body as one oval. Add the head as a smaller rounded piece at its upper front and the fringe as a curved cap over the head. Then add the legs as short pieces down into the grass, and keep every outer edge ragged, like long hair.
Rust brown fills the whole cow solidly. The cow is about 7 1/2 in wide and 8 1/2 in tall, with its bottom about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
Leave the meadow showing between the legs, in two small notches of grass.
Stop when a flat rust-brown shaggy shape stands in the meadow with a round body, a head and stubby legs. There is no shading, horns or face yet.

Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush and flick quick upward strokes that thin out as you lift off.
Lay the blades over the dark ones, most of them on the right side of the grass in front of the cow, where the sun reaches past the cow. Put a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.

Leave the pale back range showing along the sky, and leave the lower violet ridges untouched.
Stop when one darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range, soft and without texture. There is no lake yet.

Start at the right edge of the canvas, with the lake's top about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
These are the same curved strokes you bent along the hills, now tiny, with a small round, following the shoreline.

Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside in long soft drifts that slope down toward the right edge of the canvas, the way the low sun rakes across the hill.
Leave olive green showing in diagonal streaks and small round clumps between the taps, because those are the bushes and shadows. Keep the thin strip just in front of the ridges mostly olive.
Stop when the hillside is dappled yellow-green, with dark olive bushes running through it. If the marks look clumpy, thin the paint a little and spread the fan.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside dry first.
Start at the meadow's top line, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas at the left edge, and work down.
This is the same Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, now laid as a solid fill with crossing strokes instead of fan taps.
Use short strokes that cross each other like overlapping X shapes to build one even fill. Let the top line slope gently down toward the right edge of the canvas.
The meadow's Sunlit green runs from that line to the bottom edge of the canvas and reaches both the left and right edges. This is the sunny meadow in front of the hill.
Leave the dappled hillside showing in the upper canvas, with a soft, slightly ragged edge where the grass meets it.
Stop when the lower canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow with faint criss-cross marks. There is no dark front and there are no grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry first, so the dark green skims over it instead of mixing in.
Start low in the meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas. Work upward until the dark reaches about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
This is the same dry brush you skimmed along the cloud tops, now with the big flat and dark green, in short upward strokes.
Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Deep grass green and skim it lightly in short, upward slanting strokes, like grass leaning in the breeze. Build it up in several light passes.
Most of the dark goes in the lower meadow, the shadowed front. Higher up it thins to scattered streaks, where the sun still lights the grass.
Leave plenty of yellow-green showing between the strokes, most of all in the upper meadow.
Stop when the meadow is streaky, sunny at the back and darker toward the bottom edge of the canvas. If it went on solid, your brush was too loaded.

block-in-cow.text: Let the meadow and the hillside dry first.
Start with the big oval of the body, its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas.

Lay the body as one oval. Add the head as a smaller rounded piece at its upper front and the fringe as a curved cap over the head. Then add the legs as short pieces down into the grass, and keep every outer edge ragged, like long hair.
Rust brown fills the whole cow solidly. The cow is about 7 1/2 in wide and 8 1/2 in tall, with its bottom about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
Leave the meadow showing between the legs, in two small notches of grass.
Stop when a flat rust-brown shaggy shape stands in the meadow with a round body, a head and stubby legs. There is no shading, horns or face yet.

shade-cow.text: Let the rust brown dry first.
Start high on the cow's back, where the head meets the body, and work down.
Bend the strokes the way you did on the hills, but now they hang down the cow's body like falling hair.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, bending them with the hair as it falls toward the legs. Curve shorter strokes around the fringe and the head.

Most of the dark goes on the left side of the cow, the side turned away from the sun. Lay it in long hanging streaks down the body, in the hollow where the fringe hangs over the face, at the throat, and between the legs.
Leave rust showing on the sunlit side of the cow, on the fringe and the front of the face, and in stripes between the dark streaks.
Stop when the cow looks round and hairy, with dark streaks on its shadow side and warm rust glowing toward the sun.

block-in-horns.text: Let the cow dry first.
Start the bigger horn at its root, where it leaves the crown of the head. Its tip reaches about 2 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas.
This is the same small round and curved strokes you used for the lake, now built into tapering pieces that sweep up into horns.
Build each horn from tapering curved pieces. Make each thick at the root, sweep it out and up, and narrow it to a point that turns upward.
The bigger horn is about 2 1/4 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall and sweeps up and out against the hills. The smaller horn is about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall and curves up from the far side of the head.
Leave the fringe untouched between the two roots.
Stop when two flat, smooth bone-colored horns curve up from the head, each ending in an upturned point. There is no shading yet.

shade-horns.text: Let the horns dry first.
Start at the tip of the bigger horn and work back toward its root.
Follow each horn's curve with the round, pulling thin strokes along its length and never across it.
Most of the Nose pink goes along the lower, inner curve of each horn and darkens the tips, which are the parts turned away from the light. Carry it a little onto the roots where they meet the hair.
Leave a stripe of Horn bone showing along the upper curve of each horn.
Stop when each horn looks round: darker along its inner curve and tip, and pale bone along its outer curve.

pull-ginger-locks.text: Let the cow's shading dry first so the locks stay clean on top of it.
Start at the fringe, at the top of the cow, pulling locks down over the face.
Press the full width of the angle brush at the root of each lock. Then lighten and turn onto its edge as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point the way the hair hangs.
Pull long ginger locks down the body, most of them on the left side of the cow, where they streak over the dark umber. Hang a few short ones from the fringe over the face.
Leave dark umber gaps between the locks. Also leave the dark face where the fringe shades it, and the rust along the cow's sunlit edge.
Stop when long ginger locks hang down the body and fringe with dark coat showing between them. There are no pale straw locks yet.

pull-straw-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry first.
Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
This is the same thick-to-thin pull as the ginger locks, now with the smaller angle brush, with shorter locks and only where the sun hits.
Press the small angle brush flat at the root of each lock. Then lift it onto its edge as you pull down, tapering each lock to a point.

Most of the straw gold goes on the right side of the cow, where the sun hits, as a long run of locks down the sunlit edge of the face and chest to the front leg. Add a few locks on the upper back toward the left edge of the canvas, and a few short touches at the feet.
Leave most of the ginger locks and dark gaps showing. This paint only catches the sunlit edges.
Stop when a bright straw-gold edge runs down the sunlit outline of the cow and the fringe glows along its crown.

light-the-rims.text: Let the straw locks and the horns dry first.
Start on the bigger horn, near its root.
This is the same Sunlit cream and dry skim that lit the cloud tops, now with a tiny flat, for small glints on the horns and fringe.
Dip only the tip of the dry flat in Sunlit cream and skim it lightly along the curve, so the shine breaks up.

Lay a thin broken shine along the inner curve of the bigger horn and small touches where each horn meets the hair. Add a few tiny feathery touches along the crown of the fringe, between the horns, where the low sun catches the hair tips.
Leave the horn color showing through the shine, and leave the rest of the coat as it is.
Stop when a few small, bright glints sit at the horns and along the crown of the fringe, with no solid line anywhere. If one went on solid, your brush was too loaded.

paint-nose.text: Let the coat and the fringe dry first.
Start where the fringe meets the face. The nose's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
This is the Nose pink you shaded the horns with, now wrapped in small curves around the rounded nose.
Use small curved strokes that wrap around the rounded nose, like the end of a soft cylinder.
The nose is a broad, rounded pink pad about 1 in wide and 3/4 in tall, peeking out of the hair at the front of the face.
Leave the ginger hair framing the nose all round, and let a few hair tips overlap its edge.
Stop when a plain dusty-pink nose sits at the front of the face. There are no nostrils or mouth yet.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: Let the nose dry completely, or the lines will spread and feather.
Start with the two nostrils, low on the pink nose.
This is the Dark umber that shaded the cow's dark side, now thinned with water in the liner for fine lines.

Swirl the liner in water and then in Dark umber, hold it upright, and use light, steady pressure. Make each nostril a short curved comma, then add a short faint mouth line that wobbles a little. Reload often.
The nostrils sit at the lower corners of the nose, and the mouth line runs across the chin a little lower down. Run a fine dark line around the edge of the nose so it stands out from the hair.
Leave most of the pink showing, because these are only thin lines.
Stop when the nose has two dark nostrils and a short mouth line, and the face reads clearly. If a line skips, add a little water.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the cow and the meadow dry first.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, about 1/2 in from the left edge, and work across.
This is the same Deep grass green you dry-brushed on the front of the meadow, now flicked as single upward blades with a stiff brush.
Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush. Flick quick upward strokes that thin out as you lift off, leaning a little like grass blades.
Most of the blades go in the lower meadow, thickest at the bottom edge of the canvas. Carry them up over the cow's legs and the bottom of its belly, so the legs disappear into the grass.
Leave plenty of meadow showing between the blades, and keep them off the cow's upper body and face.
Stop when dark green blades rise across the front of the meadow and over the cow's legs. There are no lighter blades yet.

flick-light-grass.text: Let the dark blades dry first.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work up and across, keeping the light blades lower than the tallest dark ones.
This is the Sunlit green of the meadow's base, now flicked as single blades over the dark ones.
Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush and flick quick upward strokes that thin out as you lift off.
Lay the blades over the dark ones, most of them on the right side of the grass in front of the cow, where the sun reaches past the cow. Put a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.
Leave dark green showing between every light blade so the grass has depth.
Stop when yellow-green blades sit over the dark ones across the front, with dark still showing between them. There are no gold tips yet.

flick-gold-tips.text: Let the green blades dry first.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, near the left edge, and work up and across.
This is the Straw gold of the cow's sunlit locks, now in short flicks for seed tips.
Dip only the tip of the stiff dry brush and flick short upward marks. Each one is a small seed head.

Make the tips bigger and farther apart near the bottom edge, and smaller toward the hillside. The highest ones reach about 6 3/4 in from the top edge. Scatter a few over the cow's front legs and along the far edge of the meadow, where the sun lights the grass.
Leave most of the green blades showing. These are sparkles, not a coat.
Stop when golden tips sparkle across the whole meadow and in front of the cow. The painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall sunlit grass on a hillside at sunset, with hazy blue hills and a glimpse of a lake far away. The heart of the painting is the cow's face: its dusty pink nose peeking out of the glowing fringe, framed by its curved horns. Warm gold light against soft hazy blues gives the whole scene a calm, glowing evening mood.
opening.light: The light comes from the low sun setting past the far hills, and it warms the sky nearest it to its palest gold. It catches the edges of the cow's hair, its fringe, the horns and the grass tips on the side facing it, while the side turned away stays deep and dark.

skills.how: Only the tip of a dry brush goes in the paint, and you skim it lightly so it breaks into feathery, see-through marks. Here it lights the cloud edges, darkens the meadow, catches the sun on the fringe and horns, and flicks every blade of grass. Watch that it never goes on solid; if it does, the brush was too loaded.

Every stroke bends with the shape, pulling along a curve or wrapping around something round. It rounds the far hills, the lake's shore, the cow's shaded coat, the horns and the nose. Lay the darker paint along the shadow side and keep each stroke following the curve.

Press the full width of the angle brush, then turn onto its edge and ease off as you pull, so each mark starts wide and tapers to a point. That taper is every lock of the cow's hair, in ginger and then in straw gold. The lighter you press, the thinner the line, so lighten steadily through the pull.

opening.road: We begin with the sunset sky blended across the whole canvas, then float soft clouds in it and light their edges. Next come the hazy far hills and the small pale lake, the most distant things in the scene. The green hillside and the meadow follow, laid from far to near, so you have a whole landscape before the cow arrives. The cow goes on as a single rust-brown shape, gets its shading and its horns, then its long shaggy locks and a sunlit rim. Its face comes at the end of the cow, a pink nose with nostrils and a mouth. Grass is flicked over the cow's legs to finish, so the cow stands inside the meadow rather than pasted onto it.

the-sky.for: This stage covers the whole canvas in a glowing sunset sky with soft clouds, the ground that everything else is painted over.
the-sky.end: The canvas is all sky, soft blue warming into gold, with cream-gold clouds glowing along their lit edges.

the-distance.for: This stage lays the hazy far hills and the small pale lake, the most distant land in the painting.
the-distance.end: Soft violet ridges fill the canvas from the horizon down, with gold sky glinting between them and a pale sliver of lake shining at the foot of the darker ridge.

the-green-land.for: This stage brings the land close, with a sunlit green hillside and a grassy meadow laid from far to near.
the-green-land.end: A dappled green hillside rolls toward the lake, and a streaky yellow-green meadow fills the foreground, empty and waiting for the cow.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage builds the cow as a simple rust-brown shape, shades it so it looks round, and gives it its curved horns.
the-cow-shape.end: A shaded rust-brown cow stands in the meadow with its bone-colored horns curving against the hills, with no locks or face yet.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the flat cow shaggy with long tapering locks and lets the low sun catch its hair and horns.
the-shaggy-coat.end: Ginger and straw-gold locks hang all over the cow, its fringe and sunlit edges glow, and the face still has no nose.

the-face.for: This stage gives the cow its face, the focal point of the painting, with a dusty pink nose peeking out of the hair.
the-face.end: A pink nose with dark nostrils and a faint mouth sits in the fringe of hair, and the cow is finished except for the grass at its legs.

the-grass-in-front.for: This stage flicks grass across the meadow and over the cow's legs so the cow stands inside the grass.
the-grass-in-front.end: Dark, sunlit and golden grass blades rise across the meadow and hide the cow's legs, and the painting is finished.
