back.text: These are the same curved strokes you bent along the hills, now tiny, with a small round, following the shoreline.
These are the same long level strokes as the darker blue ridge, now with the big flat and in olive green, covering the whole lower canvas.
This is the same Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, now laid as a solid fill with crossing strokes instead of fan taps.
This is the same dry brush you skimmed along the cloud tops, now with the big flat and dark green, in short upward strokes.
Bend the strokes the way you did on the hills, but now they hang down the cow's body like falling hair.
This is the same small round and curved strokes you used for the lake, now built into tapering pieces that sweep up into horns.
This is the same thick-to-thin pull as the ginger locks, now with the smaller angle brush, with shorter locks and only where the sun hits.
This is the same Sunlit cream and dry skim that lit the cloud tops, now with a tiny flat, for small glints on the horns and fringe.
This is the Nose pink you shaded the horns with, now wrapped in small curves around the rounded nose.
This is the Dark umber that shaded the cow's dark side, now thinned with water in the liner for fine lines.
This is the same Deep grass green you dry-brushed on the front of the meadow, now flicked as single upward blades with a stiff brush.
This is the Sunlit green of the meadow's base, now flicked as single blades over the dark ones.
This is the Straw gold of the cow's sunlit locks, now in short flicks for seed tips.

blend-sky.start: Start with Sun cream where the sun glows, high up at the left edge of the canvas, then work outward from it.
blend-sky.strokes: Criss-cross short X strokes in two directions, letting each color run into the next while everything is wet. Where you want it smooth, go over it lightly with longer side-to-side strokes. Don't overwork it, or the gold and blue turn a muddy green-gray.
blend-sky.inside: Sun cream makes the small sun spot, Warm gold spreads out from it, and Haze blue takes over toward the right edge and along the top, because all the light comes from the sun. Low down, let gold and blue mottle together like mist lying on the ground.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas should show anywhere. This glow is under everything.
blend-sky.stop: The whole canvas, 16 in wide and all the way to the bottom edge, is a soft misty glow: cream and gold around the sun, blue everywhere else. There are no trees yet.

brush-far-treeline.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will drag it.
brush-far-treeline.start: Begin near the right edge of the canvas at the tops of the far trees, and work back toward the middle. The far tree line's left end is about 6 3/4 in from the left edge.
brush-far-treeline.strokes: Load only the tip and use no water. Skim the brush lightly up and down so the marks break into ragged treetops and a few upright trunk shapes. Build it up in light passes.
brush-far-treeline.inside: Most of the paint goes in the right half of the far tree line, where the wood is deepest. Toward its left end, over the gold, keep it thin and faint. Let the bottoms of the trees fade into the mist.
brush-far-treeline.leave: Keep the sun glow clear, and the sky over the treetops. Leave the misty ground untouched.
brush-far-treeline.stop: You have a soft, broken blue band of far trees, ragged on top and fading out at the bottom. It is never solid.

pull-far-trunks.first: The far tree line must be dry.
pull-far-trunks.start: Start with the tallest far trunk, its middle about 4 1/2 in from the left edge, at the top edge of the canvas.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Pull each trunk straight down. Press the full width where the trunk is thickest, then lighten onto the edge so it tapers and fades into the mist. Keep every trunk upright, never leaning.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Besides the tall trunk, pull one short trunk down from the top edge near the middle of the canvas. Add a few short pale stubs that cross the tall trunk's middle, and a dark cluster of short trunks lower down near the middle of the canvas, where the wood is thickest.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the blue tree line and the gold glow showing around and between the trunks.
pull-far-trunks.stop: A few soft, pale trunks stand in the haze, plain with no bark marks. They should look far away, not crisp.

stamp-pines.first: The far trunks must be dry.
stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tallest pine, in the middle of the group. The group runs from about 10 in from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas.
stamp-pines.strokes: Stamp with the middle tips of the fan. Work down from each tip in a zigzag and press harder as you go, so each tree widens toward its bottom. Then do the shorter pines on either side, and one at the right edge. If the marks go clumpy, the paint is too thick: thin it and spread the fan.
stamp-pines.inside: Each pine is flat and dark all over for now, and their bottoms join into one dark mass.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the misty sky showing between the pointed tips.
stamp-pines.stop: A group of dark blue-green pines with needle-textured edges. The bottom of the group is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

tap-pine-light.first: Let the dark pines dry, or the teal will mix into them.
tap-pine-light.start: Start at the left edge of the pine group, in a soft patch about 8 3/4 in to 10 1/2 in from the left edge of the canvas.
tap-pine-light.strokes: Tap lightly with the fan's middle tips, using short strokes in different directions. Then work along the gaps between the pine tips and along their feet.
tap-pine-light.inside: The teal goes around the pines, not on them. Put it in the sky between their tips, in that patch at the left edge of the group, and in a band along their feet. This sinks the pines into blue haze, the way mist does when the sun shines through it.
tap-pine-light.leave: Leave the dark bodies of the pines untouched. A common mistake is tapping into them and turning them gray.
tap-pine-light.stop: Teal mist softens the pines' outline everywhere, and their bottoms fade into it.

dab-bush-darks.first: The pines and their haze must be dry.
dab-bush-darks.start: Start at the feet of the pines, where the undergrowth is thickest, then carry the dabs across the canvas toward the left edge.
dab-bush-darks.strokes: Use a dry, lightly loaded brush and tap with the tip. Tap a spot more for a solid patch, less for dots. If you get blobs, wipe paint off on a paper towel.
dab-bush-darks.inside: Make a broken band of dark dabs along the pines' feet and across the low mist. Then scatter looser dabs over the misty ground down to the bottom edge. Add a few thin sprays high in the sky, starting about 3 3/4 in from the left edge, as twigs for the canopy. Most of it goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy.
dab-bush-darks.leave: Leave plenty of mist showing between the dabs, and keep the sun glow clear.
dab-bush-darks.stop: Loose dark olive masses cross the lower canvas, more broken toward the bottom, with a few thin sprays up high.

dab-canopy-darks.start: Start with the bush band at the left edge of the canvas. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge.
dab-canopy-darks.strokes: Tap with the brush tip to build the band across the canvas. Then dab loose clusters that hang down from the top edge of the canvas.
dab-canopy-darks.inside: Most of the orange goes in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy: the thick bush band and the canopy clusters along the top. Toward the right edge, add only a few clusters near the top edge and a few small patches at the feet of the pines.
dab-canopy-darks.leave: Leave sky showing through the canopy clusters, and leave the misty ground where the floor will go.
dab-canopy-darks.stop: You have a dense orange bush band with ragged holes, and loose orange clusters with sky between them.

dab-golden-leaves.first: Let the orange dry so the gold sits on top.
dab-golden-leaves.start: Start in the canopy at the top edge of the canvas, near the left edge, and work across.
dab-golden-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip, each dab about leaf-sized. Build each cluster from its sunny edge.
dab-golden-leaves.inside: Gold covers most of each canopy cluster and the top of the bush band, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, because the sun lights the tops. Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy, nearest the sun. Let a few loose leaves drift lower.
dab-golden-leaves.leave: Leave orange showing in the shadowed bottoms of the clusters, olive showing low in the bush band, and sky between the clusters.
dab-golden-leaves.stop: The canopy and bushes glow gold, with orange and olive still in the shadows.

dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start with a few taps on the canopy nearest the sun, at the left edge of the canvas.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap with the round's tip: small light taps on the leaves, then bigger dappled patches on the misty ground. Tap more where you want a patch solid.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Light the sunny edges of the canopy and the tops of the bush band. Then dab broad golden patches over the misty ground, starting about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, as if sunlight lay on the mist. Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the gold and orange leaves showing around the taps, and blue mist between the ground patches.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Small pale sparkles sit on the leaves, and a warm, dappled glow lies across the lower canvas.

dab-floor-darks.start: Start along the feet of the bushes, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, and work down to the bottom edge.
dab-floor-darks.strokes: Tap dense dabs with the tip, each one leaf-sized and a little bigger toward the bottom edge. Overlap them until no mist shows.
dab-floor-darks.inside: Cover the whole floor from edge to edge, dabbing up into the bottoms of the bushes so they sit in the leaves. In the gap between the bushes, let the floor run back where the path will vanish.
dab-floor-darks.leave: Leave the bush tops and the pines' feet showing along the top of the leaf-covered ground.
dab-floor-darks.stop: The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor, with no mist showing. There is no path or boulder yet.

pull-path.start: Mark one dot where the path vanishes into the gap between the bushes. Then draw a few faint chalk lines fanning down from it.
pull-path.strokes: Pull each stroke along a chalk line, from the front toward the dot: wide in front and thin near the dot.
pull-path.inside: This is only the back stretch of the path, where it bends into the grove. At its widest it runs from about 8 3/4 in to 10 1/4 in from the left edge, and it narrows to a thread at the dot. Let its far end go dark in the shade of the bushes.
pull-path.leave: Leave the rust floor all around the path. The front of the path stays as the leaves you have already dabbed.
pull-path.stop: A short pale tan strip narrows and disappears into the bushes. It is plain, with no leaves on it yet.

block-in-boulder.start: Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove. Its left side is about 10 1/2 in from the left edge.
block-in-boulder.strokes: Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.
block-in-boulder.inside: Fill the whole shape with one flat, even olive. It is about 2 1/2 in wide, and its flat bottom sits on the leaves.
block-in-boulder.leave: Leave the bushes and the leaf floor around it as they are.
block-in-boulder.stop: You have one flat olive dome, wider than it is tall, with no shading yet.

shade-boulder.start: Start at the top of the boulder, on the right side of the mossy boulder, and work down.
shade-boulder.strokes: Bend every stroke with the dome: from the top down along its curve, and around its bottom.
shade-boulder.inside: The dark olive covers most of the boulder, mostly on the right side of the mossy boulder and along its bottom. That is where the sun can't reach and where the boulder sits on the leaves.
shade-boulder.leave: Leave a thin strip of the olive showing along the boulder's upper left edge, facing the sun.
shade-boulder.stop: The boulder is mostly dark and looks round, with a sliver of lighter olive at its upper left.

light-boulder.first: Let the dark olive dry, or the dry brush will smear into it.
light-boulder.start: Start at the boulder's upper left curve, about 10 3/4 in from the left edge.
light-boulder.strokes: Load only the tip and use no water. Skim lightly along the curve of the top, in a few light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.
light-boulder.inside: The pale moss makes a broken cap along the top and upper left of the boulder, facing the sun. Almost all of it is on the left side of the mossy boulder.
light-boulder.leave: Leave the dark right side and the dark lower body showing.
light-boulder.stop: A feathery pale mossy cap sits on the upper left, and the boulder now looks round.

pull-birches.first: The floor, path and boulder must be dry.
pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of a big leaning trunk, in the leaves, and pull up past the top edge.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full width of the brush at each foot and pull up, flaring the foot a little. For branches, press, then lift onto the edge so they taper.
pull-birches.inside: There are six trunks: a thin one at the left edge of the canvas, two big leaning ones, a thin one near the path with its middle about 8 in from the left edge, and two starting about 12 3/4 in from the left edge, the one at the right edge widest. Add a few thick branches high up, and two small trunks standing behind the boulder.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves, bushes and sky showing between the trunks.
pull-birches.stop: Flat pale gray-white trunks stand over everything, with no shading yet.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas on each trunk and work down.
shade-birches.strokes: Load only the tip and use no water. Skim the gray lightly down the trunk and out along each branch, in light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush is too loaded.
shade-birches.inside: The gray covers most of each trunk so it reads as bark. The skimming brush leaves broken pale patches behind.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged pale patches all the way down each trunk, and keep the lowest part of each trunk pale. On the trunk at the right edge of the canvas, the gray stops about 1 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
shade-birches.stop: The trunks are gray and speckled with pale birch patches, still pale near the ground, with no dark marks yet.

mark-birch-bark.start: Start at the foot of each trunk, where it meets the leaves.
mark-birch-bark.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush and lift, so each mark starts wide and tapers. Lay the marks across the trunk, not along it.
mark-birch-bark.inside: Paint a solid dark foot on each trunk. Then add short broken marks up the trunk, more lower down and fewer higher up, and a dark line along each branch. Most of it is in the bottom half of the birches' shading and bark marks.
mark-birch-bark.leave: Leave plenty of gray and pale patches between the marks. Don't space the marks evenly like stripes.
mark-birch-bark.stop: The trunks read clearly as birches, with dark feet, scattered dark marks and dark branches.

dab-orange-leaves.start: Start where the path vanishes into the bushes, and work forward toward the bottom edge.
dab-orange-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip, making the dabs small near the back and bigger toward the bottom edge.
dab-orange-leaves.inside: Cover most of the floor from edge to edge, from about 7 3/4 in from the top edge down, path included. Tuck dabs against the trunks' dark feet so they sit in the leaves.
dab-orange-leaves.leave: Leave many small gaps of rust brown between the dabs, and keep the trunks and boulder clear.
dab-orange-leaves.stop: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust peeking through, and leaves lie scattered on the path.

dab-gold-leaves.start: Start at the far end of the path, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, and work forward.
dab-gold-leaves.strokes: Tap with the round's tip, one leaf-sized dab at a time.
dab-gold-leaves.inside: Make a trail of golden dabs down the path that spreads toward the right edge where the sun falls across it, most of it in the right half of the fallen leaves. Add a few dabs at the trunks' feet near the left edge, and a few loose ones toward the bottom edge.
dab-gold-leaves.leave: Leave most of the orange and rust showing. The gold dabs should be far fewer than the orange ones.
dab-gold-leaves.stop: A glowing trail of golden leaves crosses the floor.

light-birch-bark.first: Make sure the bark marks are dry.
light-birch-bark.start: Start on each trunk near the top edge, on the side facing the sun.
light-birch-bark.strokes: Load only the tip and use no water. Skim lightly down the trunk in a few passes so the white breaks over the dark marks.
light-birch-bark.inside: The near-white goes down the left side of each birch trunk and over its middle, since the sun is low and to the left. On the trunk at the right edge, the white runs about 10 3/4 in tall.
light-birch-bark.leave: Leave a gray strip down the right side of each birch trunk, and keep the dark feet untouched.
light-birch-bark.stop: The birches glow with bright, broken sunlit bark over the dark marks, and the painting is finished.

blend-sky.text: Start with Sun cream where the sun glows, high up at the left edge of the canvas, then work outward from it.

Criss-cross short X strokes in two directions, letting each color run into the next while everything is wet. Where you want it smooth, go over it lightly with longer side-to-side strokes. Don't overwork it, or the gold and blue turn a muddy green-gray.

Sun cream makes the small sun spot, Warm gold spreads out from it, and Haze blue takes over toward the right edge and along the top, because all the light comes from the sun. Low down, let gold and blue mottle together like mist lying on the ground.
No white canvas should show anywhere. This glow is under everything.
The whole canvas, 16 in wide and all the way to the bottom edge, is a soft misty glow: cream and gold around the sun, blue everywhere else. There are no trees yet.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will drag it.
Begin near the right edge of the canvas at the tops of the far trees, and work back toward the middle. The far tree line's left end is about 6 3/4 in from the left edge.
Load only the tip and use no water. Skim the brush lightly up and down so the marks break into ragged treetops and a few upright trunk shapes. Build it up in light passes.
Most of the paint goes in the right half of the far tree line, where the wood is deepest. Toward its left end, over the gold, keep it thin and faint. Let the bottoms of the trees fade into the mist.
Keep the sun glow clear, and the sky over the treetops. Leave the misty ground untouched.
You have a soft, broken blue band of far trees, ragged on top and fading out at the bottom. It is never solid.

pull-far-trunks.text: The far tree line must be dry.
Start with the tallest far trunk, its middle about 4 1/2 in from the left edge, at the top edge of the canvas.
Pull each trunk straight down. Press the full width where the trunk is thickest, then lighten onto the edge so it tapers and fades into the mist. Keep every trunk upright, never leaning.

Besides the tall trunk, pull one short trunk down from the top edge near the middle of the canvas. Add a few short pale stubs that cross the tall trunk's middle, and a dark cluster of short trunks lower down near the middle of the canvas, where the wood is thickest.
Leave the blue tree line and the gold glow showing around and between the trunks.
A few soft, pale trunks stand in the haze, plain with no bark marks. They should look far away, not crisp.

stamp-pines.text: The far trunks must be dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine, in the middle of the group. The group runs from about 10 in from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas.

Stamp with the middle tips of the fan. Work down from each tip in a zigzag and press harder as you go, so each tree widens toward its bottom. Then do the shorter pines on either side, and one at the right edge. If the marks go clumpy, the paint is too thick: thin it and spread the fan.
Each pine is flat and dark all over for now, and their bottoms join into one dark mass.
Leave the misty sky showing between the pointed tips.
A group of dark blue-green pines with needle-textured edges. The bottom of the group is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the dark pines dry, or the teal will mix into them.

Tap lightly with the fan's middle tips, using short strokes in different directions. Then work along the gaps between the pine tips and along their feet.

The teal goes around the pines, not on them. Put it in the sky between their tips, in a soft patch at the sunny end of the group, and in a band along their feet. This sinks the pines into blue haze, the way mist does when the sun shines through it.
Leave the dark bodies of the pines untouched. A common mistake is tapping into them and turning them gray.

Make a broken band of dark dabs along the pines' feet and across the low mist. Then scatter looser dabs over the misty ground down to the bottom edge. Add a few thin sprays high in the sky, starting about 3 3/4 in from the left edge, as twigs for the canopy. Most of it goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy.
Leave plenty of mist showing between the dabs, and keep the sun glow clear.
Loose dark olive masses cross the lower canvas, more broken toward the bottom, with a few thin sprays up high.

Most of the orange goes in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy: the thick bush band and the canopy clusters along the top. Toward the right edge, add only a few clusters near the top edge and a few small patches at the feet of the pines.
Leave sky showing through the canopy clusters, and leave the misty ground where the floor will go.

Gold covers most of each canopy cluster and the top of the bush band, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, because the sun lights the tops. Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy, nearest the sun. Let a few loose leaves drift lower.
Leave orange showing in the shadowed bottoms of the clusters, olive showing low in the bush band, and sky between the clusters.
The canopy and bushes glow gold, with orange and olive still in the shadows.

The pale moss makes a broken cap along the top and upper left of the boulder, facing the sun. Almost all of it is on the left side of the mossy boulder.

light-boulder.text: Let the dark olive dry, or the dry brush will smear into it.
Start at the boulder's upper left curve, about 10 3/4 in from the left edge.
The same dry skim you used for the misty far trees, now with a smaller brush and pale moss on the boulder's sunny cap.
Load only the tip and use no water. Skim lightly along the curve of the top, in a few light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.
The pale moss makes a broken cap along the top and upper left of the boulder, facing the sun. Almost all of it is on the left side of the mossy boulder.
Leave the dark right side and the dark lower body showing.
A feathery pale mossy cap sits on the upper left, and the boulder now looks round.

pull-birches.text: The floor, path and boulder must be dry.
Start at the foot of a big leaning trunk, in the leaves, and pull up past the top edge.
The same press-and-lift as the far trunks, now with a wider brush, pulling up from the foot so the near trunks stand bold.
Press the full width of the brush at each foot and pull up, flaring the foot a little. For branches, press, then lift onto the edge so they taper.

Pull six birches: a thin one nearest the sun, two big leaning ones, a thin one near the path into the grove, and two on the right side of the near birch trunks, the outer one widest. Add a few thick branches high up, and two small trunks standing behind the boulder.
Leave the leaves, bushes and sky showing between the trunks.
Flat pale gray-white trunks stand over everything, with no shading yet.

shade-birches.text: Let the trunks dry completely.
Start at the top edge of the canvas on each trunk and work down.
The same dry skim and brush you used for the moss on the boulder, now drawn down each trunk in gray.
Load only the tip and use no water. Skim the gray lightly down the trunk and out along each branch, in light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush is too loaded.
The gray covers most of each trunk so it reads as bark. The skimming brush leaves broken pale patches behind.
Leave ragged pale patches all the way down each trunk, and keep the lowest part of each trunk pale. On the trunk at the right edge of the canvas, the gray stops about 1 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
The trunks are gray and speckled with pale birch patches, still pale near the ground, with no dark marks yet.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the gray dry.
Start at the foot of each trunk, where it meets the leaves.
The same angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke as the far trunks, but now short dark marks laid across the trunk.
Press the full width of the angle brush and lift, so each mark starts wide and tapers. Lay the marks across the trunk, not along it.

Paint a solid dark foot on each trunk. Then add short broken marks up the trunk, more lower down and fewer higher up, and a dark line along each branch. Most of it is in the bottom half of the birches' shading and bark marks.
Leave plenty of gray and pale patches between the marks. Don't space the marks evenly like stripes.
The trunks read clearly as birches, with dark feet, scattered dark marks and dark branches.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start where the path vanishes into the bushes, and work forward toward the bottom edge.
The same Leaf orange you dabbed into the canopy, now on the ground, small at the back and bigger toward the front.
Tap with the tip, making the dabs small near the back and bigger toward the bottom edge.
Cover most of the floor from edge to edge, from about 7 3/4 in from the top edge down, path included. Tuck dabs against the trunks' dark feet so they sit in the leaves.
Leave many small gaps of rust brown between the dabs, and keep the trunks and boulder clear.
The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust peeking through, and leaves lie scattered on the path.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the orange dry.
Start at the far end of the path, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, and work forward.
The same Golden yellow you tapped on the canopy, now with the small round, one leaf at a time down the path.
Tap with the round's tip, one leaf-sized dab at a time.

Make a trail of golden dabs down the path that spreads toward the right edge where the sun falls across it, most of it in the right half of the fallen leaves. Add a few dabs at the trunks' feet near the left edge, and a few loose ones toward the bottom edge.
Leave most of the orange and rust showing. The gold dabs should be far fewer than the orange ones.
A glowing trail of golden leaves crosses the floor.

light-birch-bark.text: Make sure the bark marks are dry.
Start on each trunk near the top edge, on the side facing the sun.
The same dry skim you used to shade the trunks, now in near-white on the sunny side, leaving the gray strip showing.
Load only the tip and use no water. Skim lightly down the trunk in a few passes so the white breaks over the dark marks.
The near-white goes down the left side of each birch trunk and over its middle, since the sun is low and to the left. On the trunk at the right edge, the white runs about 10 3/4 in tall.
Leave a gray strip down the right side of each birch trunk, and keep the dark feet untouched.
The birches glow with bright, broken sunlit bark over the dark marks, and the painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint an autumn birch grove: white trunks leaning over a leaf-covered path that runs off into a misty blue wood. The heart of the picture is the spot where the path disappears into the mist, framed by the big birches. What makes it sing is the contrast between the warm gold of the leaves and sun and the cool blue haze of the deep wood.
opening.light: The low sun glows through the mist, so every trunk, leaf and rock is brightest on the side that faces it. Away from the sun the wood turns cool and blue, and the shadows of the trunks and the boulder fall on the side the sun can't reach.

skills.how: Dabbing means tapping with the tip of a dry, lightly loaded brush, so you get dots that grow more solid the more you tap. Here it builds every leaf in the painting: the bushes, the golden canopy and the whole carpet on the ground, always dark before light. Watch for blobs, which mean the brush is too wet or too full, so wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.

Dry brushing means loading only the tip with no water and skimming lightly, so the paint breaks into feathery marks that catch the canvas texture. It makes the soft far trees in the mist, the mossy cap on the boulder, and the gray shading and sunlit edges on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded, so let it dry and build in light passes instead.

Thick to thin means pressing the full width of the brush, then turning onto its edge and easing off so the line tapers to a point. It pulls the pale far trunks, the big birch trunks and their branches, and the dark bark marks. Keep the press and the lift in a smooth stroke, so each mark starts wide and ends fine.

opening.road: We begin with a wet glow of sun and mist over the whole canvas, because everything else in the painting sits inside that light. Then the far wood goes in: soft blue trees, pale far trunks and dark pines wrapped in haze. Next come the golden leaves of the undergrowth and canopy, dabbed dark to light, followed by the leaf floor and the path running into the grove. The mossy boulder is built and shaded by the path before the birches arrive, because the birches are the nearest things and are painted over everything else. Finally the fallen leaves are dabbed in warm orange and gold, and the sun catches the bark to finish the picture.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the soft glow of sun and mist that every later layer sits in.
the-misty-sky.end: The whole canvas is a soft misty glow, cream and gold around the sun and haze blue across the rest, with no trees yet.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the deep, hazy wood that gives the painting its distance.
the-far-wood.end: Soft blue tree shapes and pale far trunks stand in the haze, with a group of dark pines softened by teal mist.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage brings in the warm autumn color of the undergrowth and the canopy, dabbed from dark to light.
the-golden-leaves.end: Golden leaf clusters and glowing undergrowth hang in the mist, with olive and orange in their shadows and a warm dappled glow across the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage covers the ground in fallen leaves and opens the path that leads the eye into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor fills the ground, and a pale tan path narrows away into the misty grove.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder and makes it look round with shade and light.
the-boulder.end: A round mossy boulder sits by the path, pale moss on its sunny cap and dark where it rests on the leaves.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the nearest trees, the white birches, over everything painted so far.
the-birches.end: Pale birches with gray shading, dark broken bark marks and dark feet stand over the leaves and mist.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage turns the dark floor into a warm, sunlit carpet of fallen leaves.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust in the gaps and a trail of golden leaves down the path.

the-last-lights.for: This stage catches the sun on the birch bark to finish the painting.
the-last-lights.end: The finished painting: sunlit white birches lean over the golden path that runs into the misty blue grove.

back.text: This is the Haze blue you blended into the sky, now pulled into thin trunks so they melt into the mist.
The same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines, now with the lighter teal and tapped around them, not on them.
The same dry tap you used for the dark undergrowth, now in gold and only on the sunny tops, so the darks still show.
The same tap as the golden leaves, but with the small round and the palest mix, and far fewer dabs.
The same dabbing as the undergrowth, but this time keep tapping and overlap until no mist shows through.
This is the Olive moss from the undergrowth, but now laid as a flat, even shape instead of broken dabs.
The same dry skim you used for the misty far trees, now with a smaller brush and pale moss on the boulder's sunny cap.
The same press-and-lift as the far trunks, now with a wider brush, pulling up from the foot so the near trunks stand bold.
The same dry skim and brush you used for the moss on the boulder, now drawn down each trunk in gray.
The same angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke as the far trunks, but now short dark marks laid across the trunk.
The same Leaf orange you dabbed into the canopy, now on the ground, small at the back and bigger toward the front.
The same Golden yellow you tapped on the canopy, now with the small round, one leaf at a time down the path.
The same dry skim you used to shade the trunks, now in near-white on the sunny side, leaving the gray strip showing.

blend-the-sky.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue. Lay it right across, from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-the-sky.strokes: Use long side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold and lay a wide band of it into the wet blue in the upper middle of the canvas. Then go back to Sky blue for the lower half, all the way to the bottom edge. Stroke back over each join while it is still wet.
blend-the-sky.inside: The gold is warmest and brightest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the sun is setting. The blue at the bottom only has to be a soft base, because hills and grass will cover it.
blend-the-sky.leave: No white canvas should show anywhere. The paint reaches all four edges.
blend-the-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is sky: blue at the top, a glowing gold band through the upper middle, then soft blue again lower down, with gentle sideways streaks. A hard line where two colours meet is the usual mistake. Add more of the lighter colour at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.start: Start at the top edge of the sky with a long ragged cloud across the upper part of the canvas. Then add the smaller streaks lower down, starting at the left edge.
lay-in-clouds.strokes: Work in small circles with the tip of the round brush, so each cloud gets a bumpy, soft edge. Draw each streak out sideways, following the slant of the sky's own streaks.
lay-in-clouds.inside: Most of the gold goes on the left side of the sky and in the top half, where the big cloud bank sits. Lower down it breaks into thin, flat-bottomed slivers scattered across the blue.
lay-in-clouds.leave: Let blue sky show in the gaps inside the top cloud and all around the lower slivers.
lay-in-clouds.stop: Stop when there is a broken gold cloud bank at the top and a scatter of thin gold streaks lower down. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with a lighter pass.

light-cloud-tops.first: The cloud streaks must be dry.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start with the low streaks in the bottom half of the sky, near the left edge of the canvas. Then add a few touches along the top edge.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Use a dry brush with only the tip in the paint. Skim lightly sideways along the edges of the streaks, so the cream catches the canvas texture in feathery, wavy bands.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Most of the cream goes on the left side and in the lower sky. There it turns the low streaks into soft, wavy warm ridges. Only a little goes on the clouds at the top.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the Sunset gold and the blue showing through and between the cream. It should never become a solid band.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when the lower sky shows layered, wavy warm-edged streaks over the blue. If a patch went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the sky colour back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.first: The sky and clouds must be dry.
lay-in-far-hills.start: Start with the top line of the farthest range, about 2 in from the top edge, from the left edge across to the right edge.
lay-in-far-hills.strokes: Pull curved strokes from the top of each soft hump down along its curve. Then work down the canvas in layered rolling ranges, each one curving like the one above it.
lay-in-far-hills.inside: Hazy violet covers everything from that top line down to the bottom edge. Let a little of the warm sky glow through along the crest of each lower range.
lay-in-far-hills.leave: Keep the gold sky and clouds clear above the top range.
lay-in-far-hills.stop: Stop when the far blue hills fill the canvas from the top range to the bottom edge, as soft overlapping violet ridges with no texture.

shade-near-ridges.first: The far blue hills must be dry.
shade-near-ridges.start: Start just under the crest of the top range, at the left edge of the canvas.
shade-near-ridges.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Let the band slope down gently toward the right edge.
shade-near-ridges.inside: This is a darker band in front of the palest back range, from about 3 in to 4 in from the top edge, with more of it on the right side. That makes the back range look farther away.
shade-near-ridges.leave: Leave the pale violet back range showing along the top, and all the lower ranges as they are.
shade-near-ridges.stop: Stop when one darker slate ridge crosses the canvas in front of the pale back range. Don't carry it down over the lower hills.

paint-lake.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the darker ridge ends, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
paint-lake.strokes: Pull a few curved strokes in from the right edge, following the bottom of the ridge and coming to a point at the far end.
paint-lake.inside: The lake is a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, sitting at the foot of the far blue hills.
paint-lake.leave: Leave all the hills around it untouched.
paint-lake.stop: Stop when a small pale silvery wedge of water sits at the right edge. Beginners tend to make it too big; keep it a glimpse.

lay-in-hillside.first: The lake and the hills must be dry.
lay-in-hillside.start: Start with the top edge of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-in-hillside.strokes: Keep the brush level and use long left-and-right strokes. Work down from the ridge line to the bottom edge.
lay-in-hillside.inside: The top of the slope runs down toward the right edge, passing just under the lake. Olive green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
lay-in-hillside.leave: Keep the lake, the dark ridge and the back range showing above the green hillside.
lay-in-hillside.stop: Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the canvas from its sloping top line to the bottom edge, with no patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.first: The olive green must be dry.
tap-sunlit-slope.start: Start at the top of the green hillside, at the left edge of the canvas.
tap-sunlit-slope.strokes: Tap with the middle tips of the fanned brush, working down in a zigzag. Let the clusters follow the slope down toward the right.
tap-sunlit-slope.inside: Tap over the whole green hillside, top to bottom and edge to edge. Make long sunny drifts with the olive between them.
tap-sunlit-slope.leave: Leave plenty of olive clumps and streaks showing between the taps. These become the bushes.
tap-sunlit-slope.stop: Stop when the green hillside is dappled yellow-green with dark olive bushes scattered all through it. Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick or you stamped with the side of the fan.

lay-in-meadow.first: The green hillside must be dry.
lay-in-meadow.start: Start with the top edge of the meadow at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge.
lay-in-meadow.strokes: Fill the meadow with short criss-crossing X strokes. Work down to the bottom edge.
lay-in-meadow.inside: The top edge of the meadow runs gently down toward the right edge. Sunlit green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
lay-in-meadow.leave: Keep the dappled green hillside showing above the meadow.
lay-in-meadow.stop: Stop when the lower part of the canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow, edge to edge, down to the bottom edge.

darken-meadow-front.start: Start at the bottom edge of the meadow, and work up from there.
darken-meadow-front.strokes: Use a dry brush and skim it lightly upward and slightly sideways, so the green breaks into streaky grass-like marks.
darken-meadow-front.inside: It covers the whole meadow from its top edge to the bottom edge, heaviest toward the bottom of the canvas. Higher up, the strokes thin out into separate streaks.
darken-meadow-front.leave: Leave the yellow-green showing between the strokes, most of all along the top of the meadow. There it should read as sunny tufts.
darken-meadow-front.stop: Stop when the meadow looks like windblown grass: sunny at the back, darker and streakier at the front. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the yellow-green back over part of it.

block-in-cow.start: Start with the big round body. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
block-in-cow.strokes: Build from pieces. Lay the main body shape first, then add the shaggy head and fringe in rounded pieces up toward the right. Then add the two short legs into the grass.
block-in-cow.inside: The whole Highland cow is one flat rust-brown shape, about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall. Let the edges stay ragged like hair.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave a gap of grass between the two legs, and keep the hills and grass clear all around the outline.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop when a flat, solid rust-brown cow shape stands in the meadow.

shade-cow.first: The Rust brown must be dry.
shade-cow.start: Start at the top of the back, near the left side of the Highland cow.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs, bending with the round shape. Under the fringe, curve them down and around the head.
shade-cow.inside: It covers most of the cow in long streaks, densest on the left side of the body, under the fringe and between the legs. The sun is low behind the hills, so the side away from it goes dark.
shade-cow.leave: Leave rust-brown showing between the streaks, most of all down the chest and the right edge of the face.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks round and furry, dark on its shadowed side, with rust streaks still glowing toward the chest.

block-in-horns.start: Start where each horn grows out of the top of the head. The left horn reaches up to about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
block-in-horns.strokes: Pull each horn in curved, tapering strokes from its thick root out and up to a point.
block-in-horns.inside: The left horn sweeps out and up from the left side of the head. The shorter right horn curves out and hooks upward at its tip. Both are flat Horn bone.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the hills showing around the horns, and don't paint over the fringe.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop when two smooth, flat, pale horns curve up out of the head. A common mistake is making them the same thickness all along; let each one thin to a point.

shade-horns.first: The Horn bone must be dry.
shade-horns.start: Start at the tip of the left horn.
shade-horns.strokes: Pull curved strokes along each horn, following its bend, from the tip back toward the root.
shade-horns.inside: Most of it goes along the lower, shaded curve of each horn and at both ends: the dark tips and the roots where they enter the hair.
shade-horns.leave: Leave a strip of Horn bone showing along the top curve of each horn, the side facing the sky.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when each horn has a dark tip, a darker underside and a pale top edge, so it looks round.

pull-ginger-locks.first: The cow's shading must be dry.
pull-ginger-locks.start: Start at the top of the fringe, where the hair falls between the horns.
pull-ginger-locks.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush at the top of each lock. Then pull down and turn onto the edge, so the lock tapers to a point. Pull locks down the fringe, the back and the sides of the body.
pull-ginger-locks.inside: Most of the ginger goes on the left side of the Highland cow, over the back, fringe and flanks, in long hanging locks. They fall downward the way long hair hangs.
pull-ginger-locks.leave: Leave plenty of the dark streaks showing between the locks. Leave the chest and the face under the fringe mostly as they are.
pull-ginger-locks.stop: Stop when the cow is covered in long, separate ginger locks with dark gaps between them. A common mistake is filling the gaps until the coat goes flat.

pull-straw-locks.first: The ginger locks must be dry.
pull-straw-locks.start: Start at the top of the fringe, then move to the outline of the face and chest, toward the right side of the Highland cow.
pull-straw-locks.strokes: Use the same thick-to-thin pull: press, then lift onto the edge so each lock ends in a point. Pull downward along the outline of the face and chest.
pull-straw-locks.inside: Most of it goes on the right side of the cow, along the edge of the fringe, face and chest where the sunset light hits. A few short locks go on the back and the legs.
pull-straw-locks.leave: Leave the ginger and the dark streaks showing between the straw locks. Leave the shaded middle of the body alone.
pull-straw-locks.stop: Stop when the cow's outline facing the sun glows with straw-gold hair and only a few light locks sit on the body.

light-the-rims.first: The straw-gold locks must be dry.
light-the-rims.start: Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
light-the-rims.strokes: Use a dry brush and skim tiny, light touches along the edge, letting them break up.
light-the-rims.inside: This is only a few small sparks of light along the top of the fringe and where each horn meets the hair, plus a couple on the outline of the back. All of it is in the top half of the Highland cow.
light-the-rims.leave: Leave the rest of the coat and the horns as they are.
light-the-rims.stop: Stop when the top of the fringe catches a few small glints. Too much cream is the usual mistake; a few touches are enough.

paint-nose.start: Start just below the fringe, in the face. The nose's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Pull small curved strokes around the rounded muzzle, following its shape.
paint-nose.inside: The nose is a small broad oval, about 1 in wide, peeking out under the hair.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the hair of the face showing all around it.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a plain dusty-pink nose sits under the fringe, with no nostrils yet. Beginners often paint it too big; keep it small.

line-nostrils-mouth.first: The nose must be dry, or the lines will spread.
line-nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the two nostrils on the front of the nose.
line-nostrils-mouth.strokes: Hold the liner upright and use light, steady pressure with thin paint. Draw two small curved nostrils, then a short line for the mouth under the nose. Darken the hair around the muzzle with a few fine strokes.
line-nostrils-mouth.inside: The dark goes in the nostrils, the mouth and the shadow ring around the muzzle, so the nose stands out of the hair. A few dark touches also go in the coat.
line-nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave the pink showing on top of the nose and between the nostrils.
line-nostrils-mouth.stop: Stop when the face reads clearly: two nostrils, a mouth line and a shadowed muzzle. Skippy lines mean the paint is too thick; add water.

flick-dark-grass.first: The cow and meadow must be dry.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, then move up over the cow's legs.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Use the old stiff brush nearly dry. Flick quick strokes upward so each blade ends in a point, leaning a little different ways.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Blades rise across the whole front of the meadow, thickest in the bottom half of the canvas. They run up over the Highland cow's legs and lower belly so it stands in the grass.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave the meadow's lighter green showing between the blades, and keep the cow's chest and face clear.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Stop when dark blades fill the front of the meadow and hide the cow's legs. A common mistake is a solid dark band; keep the blades separate.

flick-light-grass.first: The dark blades must be dry.
flick-light-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, toward the right side of the meadow.
flick-light-grass.strokes: Use the same quick, nearly dry upward flicks, each blade tapering to a point.
flick-light-grass.inside: These blades are fewer and sit over the dark ones across the meadow, more on the right side, where the sun is. A few go over the bottom of the Highland cow.
flick-light-grass.leave: Leave plenty of the dark blades showing between them.
flick-light-grass.stop: Stop when sunny blades stand in front of the dark ones and the grass looks layered.

flick-gold-tips.first: The sunlit blades must be dry.
flick-gold-tips.start: Start in the meadow at the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-gold-tips.strokes: Use the same nearly dry brush and make short upward flicks, each a small seed head.
flick-gold-tips.inside: Scatter them across the meadow, larger and farther apart at the bottom, smaller toward the back, and more on the right side. Put a few in front of the Highland cow's legs.
flick-gold-tips.leave: Leave the dark and light blades showing around every tip.
flick-gold-tips.stop: Stop when golden tips sparkle across the grass and the painting is finished. Too many tips is the usual mistake; leave space between them.

blend-the-sky.text: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue. Lay it right across, from the left edge to the right edge.

Use long side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold and lay a wide band of it into the wet blue in the upper middle of the canvas. Then go back to Sky blue for the lower half, all the way to the bottom edge. Stroke back over each join while it is still wet.
The gold is warmest and brightest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the sun is setting. The blue at the bottom only has to be a soft base, because hills and grass will cover it.
No white canvas should show anywhere. The paint reaches all four edges.

Stop when the whole canvas is sky: blue at the top, a glowing gold band through the upper middle, then soft blue again lower down, with gentle sideways streaks. A hard line where two colours meet is the usual mistake. Add more of the lighter colour at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.text: Let the sky dry completely.
Start at the top edge of the sky with a long ragged cloud across the upper part of the canvas. Then add the smaller streaks lower down, starting at the left edge.
Work in small circles with the tip of the round brush, so each cloud gets a bumpy, soft edge. Draw each streak out sideways, following the slant of the sky's own streaks.
Most of the gold goes on the left side of the sky and in the top half, where the big cloud bank sits. Lower down it breaks into thin, flat-bottomed slivers scattered across the blue.
Let blue sky show through the gaps in the big cloud bank and all around the lower slivers.
Stop when there is a broken gold cloud bank at the top and a scatter of thin gold streaks lower down. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with a lighter pass.

light-cloud-tops.text: The cloud streaks must be dry.
Start with the low streaks in the bottom half of the sky, near the left edge of the canvas. Then add a few touches along the top edge.
Use a dry brush with only the tip in the paint. Skim lightly sideways along the edges of the streaks, so the cream catches the canvas texture in feathery, wavy bands.
Most of the cream goes on the left side and in the lower sky. There it turns the low streaks into soft, wavy warm ridges. Only a little goes on the clouds at the top.
Leave the Sunset gold and the blue showing through and between the cream. It should never become a solid band.
Stop when the lower sky shows layered, wavy warm-edged streaks over the blue. If a patch went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the sky colour back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.text: The sky and clouds must be dry.
Start with the top line of the farthest range, about 2 in from the top edge, from the left edge across to the right edge.
Pull curved strokes from the top of each soft hump down along its curve. Then work down the canvas in layered rolling ranges, each one curving like the last.
Hazy violet covers everything from that top line down to the bottom edge. Let a little of the warm sky glow through along the crest of each lower range.
Stop the violet at the crest of the farthest range, and don't paint into the gold sky or the golden clouds.
Stop when the far blue hills fill the canvas from the top range to the bottom edge, as soft overlapping violet ridges with no texture.

shade-near-ridges.text: The far blue hills must be dry.
Start just under the crest of the top range, at the left edge of the canvas.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Let the band slope down gently toward the right edge.
This is a darker band in front of the palest back range. Its middle is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and more of it is on the right side. That makes the back range look farther away.
Leave the pale violet back range showing along the top, and all the lower ranges as they are.
Stop when one darker slate ridge crosses the canvas in front of the pale back range. Don't carry it down over the lower hills.

paint-lake.text: The ridges must be dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the darker ridge ends, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
Pull a few curved strokes in from the right edge, following the bottom of the ridge and coming to a point at the far end.
The lake is a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, sitting at the foot of the far blue hills.
Leave all the hills around it untouched.
Stop when a small pale silvery wedge of water sits at the right edge. Beginners tend to make it too big; keep it a glimpse.

lay-in-hillside.text: The lake and the hills must be dry.
Start with the top edge of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
Keep the brush level and use long left-and-right strokes. Work down from the ridge line to the bottom edge.
The top of the slope runs down toward the right edge, passing just under the lake. Olive green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
Keep the lake, the dark ridge and the back range showing above the green hillside.
Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the canvas from its sloping top line to the bottom edge, with no patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: The olive green must be dry.
Start at the top of the green hillside, at the left edge of the canvas.
Tap with the middle tips of the fanned brush, working down in a zigzag. Let the clusters follow the slope down toward the right.
Tap over the whole green hillside, top to bottom and edge to edge. Make long sunny drifts with the olive between them.
Leave plenty of olive clumps and streaks showing between the taps. These become the bushes.
Stop when the green hillside is dappled yellow-green with dark olive bushes scattered all through it. Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick or you stamped with the side of the fan.

lay-in-meadow.text: The green hillside must be dry.
Start with the top edge of the meadow at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge.
Fill the meadow with short criss-crossing X strokes. Work down to the bottom edge.
The top edge of the meadow runs gently down toward the right edge. Sunlit green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
Keep the dappled green hillside showing above the meadow.
Stop when the lower part of the canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow, edge to edge, down to the bottom edge.

darken-meadow-front.text: The meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the meadow, and work up from there.
Use a dry brush and skim it lightly upward and slightly sideways, so the green breaks into streaky grass-like marks.

Its top is about 8 1/4 in from the top edge, and it runs right out to the bottom edge of the canvas. It is heaviest toward the bottom of the canvas. Higher up, the strokes thin out into separate streaks.
Leave the yellow-green showing between the strokes, most of all along the top of the meadow. There it should read as sunny tufts.
Stop when the meadow looks like windblown grass: sunny at the back, darker and streakier at the front. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the yellow-green back over part of it.

block-in-cow.text: The meadow must be dry.
Start with the big round body. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
Build from pieces. Lay the main body shape first, then add the shaggy head and fringe in rounded pieces up toward the right. Then add the two short legs into the grass.
The whole Highland cow is one flat rust-brown shape, about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall. Let the edges stay ragged like hair.
Leave a gap of grass between the two legs, and keep the hills and grass clear all around the outline.
Stop when a flat, solid rust-brown cow shape stands in the meadow.

shade-cow.text: The Rust brown must be dry.
Start at the top of the back, near the left side of the Highland cow.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs, bending with the round shape. Under the fringe, curve them down and around the head.
It covers most of the cow in long streaks, densest on the left side of the body, under the fringe and between the legs. The sun is low behind the hills, so the side away from it goes dark.
Leave rust-brown showing between the streaks, most of all down the chest and the right edge of the face.
Stop when the cow looks round and furry, dark on its shadowed side, with rust streaks still glowing toward the chest.

block-in-horns.text: The cow must be dry.
Start where each horn grows out of the top of the head. The top of the horns is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
Pull each horn in curved, tapering strokes from its thick root out and up to a point.
The left horn sweeps out and up from the left side of the head. The shorter right horn curves out and hooks upward at its tip. Both are flat Horn bone.
Leave the hills showing around the horns, and don't paint over the fringe.
Stop when two smooth, flat, pale horns curve up out of the head. A common mistake is making them the same thickness all along; let each one thin to a point.

shade-horns.text: The Horn bone must be dry.
Start at the tip of the left horn.
Pull curved strokes along each horn, following its bend, from the tip back toward the root.
Most of it goes along the lower, shaded curve of each horn and at both ends: the dark tips and the roots where they enter the hair.
Leave a strip of Horn bone showing along the top curve of each horn, the side facing the sky.
Stop when each horn has a dark tip, a darker underside and a pale top edge, so it looks round.

pull-ginger-locks.text: The cow's shading must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, where the hair falls between the horns.
Press the full width of the angle brush at the top of each lock. Then pull down and turn onto the edge, so the lock tapers to a point. Pull locks down the fringe, the back and the sides of the body.
Most of the ginger goes on the left side of the Highland cow, over the back, fringe and flanks, in long hanging locks. They fall downward the way long hair hangs.
Leave plenty of the dark streaks showing between the locks. Leave the chest and the face under the fringe mostly as they are.
Stop when the cow is covered in long, separate ginger locks with dark gaps between them. A common mistake is filling the gaps until the coat goes flat.

pull-straw-locks.text: The ginger locks must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, then move to the outline of the face and chest, toward the right side of the Highland cow.
Use the same thick-to-thin pull: press, then lift onto the edge so each lock ends in a point. Pull downward along the outline of the face and chest.
Most of it goes on the right side of the cow, along the edge of the fringe, face and chest where the sunset light hits. A few short locks go on the back and the legs.
Leave the ginger and the dark streaks showing between the straw locks. Leave the shaded middle of the body alone.
Stop when the cow's outline facing the sun glows with straw-gold hair and only a few light locks sit on the body.

light-the-rims.text: The straw-gold locks must be dry.
Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
Use a dry brush and skim tiny, light touches along the edge, letting them break up.
This is only a few small sparks of light along the top of the fringe and where each horn meets the hair, plus a couple on the outline of the back. All of it is in the top half of the Highland cow.
Leave the rest of the coat and the horns as they are.
Stop when the top of the fringe catches a few small glints. Too much cream is the usual mistake; a few touches are enough.

paint-nose.text: The coat must be dry.
Start in the middle of the cow's face, where the hanging hair parts. The nose's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
Pull small curved strokes around the rounded muzzle, following its shape.
The nose is a small broad oval, about 1 in wide, peeking out of the hair.
Leave the hair of the face showing all around it.
Stop when a plain dusty-pink nose sits in the face, with no nostrils yet. Beginners often paint it too big; keep it small.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: The nose must be dry, or the lines will spread.
Start with the two nostrils on the front of the nose.

Hold the liner upright and use light, steady pressure with thin paint. Draw two small curved nostrils, then a short line for the mouth under the nose. Darken the hair around the muzzle with a few fine strokes.
The dark goes in the nostrils, the mouth and the shadow ring around the muzzle, so the nose stands out of the hair. A few dark touches also go in the coat.
Leave the pink showing on top of the nose and between the nostrils.
Stop when the face reads clearly: two nostrils, a mouth line and a shadowed muzzle. Skippy lines mean the paint is too thick; add water.

flick-dark-grass.text: The cow and meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, then move up over the cow's legs.
Use the old stiff brush nearly dry. Flick quick strokes upward so each blade ends in a point, leaning a little different ways.
Blades rise across the whole front of the meadow, thickest in the bottom half of the canvas. They run up over the Highland cow's legs and lower belly so it stands in the grass.
Leave the meadow's lighter green showing between the blades, and keep the cow's chest and face clear.
Stop when dark blades fill the front of the meadow and hide the cow's legs. A common mistake is a solid dark band; keep the blades separate.

flick-light-grass.text: The dark blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, toward the right side of the meadow.
Use the same quick, nearly dry upward flicks, each blade tapering to a point.
These blades are fewer and sit over the dark ones across the meadow, more on the right side, where the sun is. A few go over the bottom of the Highland cow.
Leave plenty of the dark blades showing between them.
Stop when sunny blades stand in front of the dark ones and the grass looks layered.

Use the same nearly dry brush and make short upward flicks, each a small seed head.

shade-near-ridges.text: The far blue hills must be dry.
Start just under the crest of the top range, at the left edge of the canvas.
This is the same Hazy violet you used for the far hills. This time you lay it in level strokes as one darker band, not curving humps.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Let the band slope down gently toward the right edge.
This is a darker band in front of the palest back range. Its middle is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and more of it is on the right side. That makes the back range look farther away.
Leave the pale violet back range showing along the top, and all the lower ranges as they are.
Stop when one darker slate ridge crosses the canvas in front of the pale back range. Don't carry it down over the lower hills.

paint-lake.text: The ridges must be dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the darker ridge ends, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
These are the same curved strokes you used on the hill humps, now made with a small round brush and kept to one tiny sliver.
Pull a few curved strokes in from the right edge, following the bottom of the ridge and coming to a point at the far end.
The lake is a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, sitting at the foot of the far blue hills.
Leave all the hills around it untouched.
Stop when a small pale silvery wedge of water sits at the right edge. Beginners tend to make it too big; keep it a glimpse.

lay-in-hillside.text: The lake and the hills must be dry.
Start with the top edge of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
These are the same long, level strokes you used for the darker ridge, now made with the big flat brush across the whole slope.
Keep the brush level and use long left-and-right strokes. Work down from the ridge line to the bottom edge.
The top of the slope runs down toward the right edge, passing just under the lake. Olive green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
Keep the lake, the dark ridge and the back range showing above the green hillside.
Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the canvas from its sloping top line to the bottom edge, with no patches yet.

lay-in-meadow.text: The green hillside must be dry.
Start with the top edge of the meadow at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside. This time you lay it flat and solid with criss-cross strokes.
Fill the meadow with short criss-crossing X strokes. Work down to the bottom edge.
The top edge of the meadow runs gently down toward the right edge. Sunlit green covers everything from that line to the bottom of the canvas.
Keep the dappled green hillside showing above the meadow.
Stop when the lower part of the canvas is one flat yellow-green meadow, edge to edge, down to the bottom edge.

darken-meadow-front.text: The meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the meadow, and work up from there.
This is the dry brush you used for the cream in the sky, now with Deep grass green and a bigger brush. This time skim it upward like grass.
Use a dry brush and skim it lightly upward and slightly sideways, so the green breaks into streaky grass-like marks.

Its top is about 8 1/4 in from the top edge, and it runs right out to the bottom edge of the canvas. It is heaviest toward the bottom of the canvas. Higher up, the strokes thin out into separate streaks.

shade-cow.text: The Rust brown must be dry.
Start at the top of the back, near the left side of the Highland cow.
These are the curved strokes you used on the hills, now bending around the cow's round body and down toward its belly.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs, bending with the round shape. Under the fringe, curve them down and around the head.
It covers most of the cow in long streaks, densest on the left side of the body, under the fringe and between the legs. The sun is low behind the hills, so the side away from it goes dark.
Leave rust-brown showing between the streaks, most of all down the chest and the right edge of the face.
Stop when the cow looks round and furry, dark on its shadowed side, with rust streaks still glowing toward the chest.

block-in-horns.text: The cow must be dry.
Start where each horn grows out of the top of the head. The top of the horns is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
This is the same small round brush and the same curved pull you used for the lake, now sweeping out into a long tapering horn.
Pull each horn in curved, tapering strokes from its thick root out and up to a point.
The left horn sweeps out and up from the left side of the head. The shorter right horn curves out and hooks upward at its tip. Both are flat Horn bone.
Leave the hills showing around the horns, and don't paint over the fringe.
Stop when two smooth, flat, pale horns curve up out of the head. A common mistake is making them the same thickness all along; let each one thin to a point.

shade-horns.text: The Horn bone must be dry.
Start at the tip of the left horn.
Pull curved strokes along each horn, following its bend, from the tip back toward the root.
Most of it goes along the lower, shaded curve of each horn and at both ends: the dark tips and the roots where they enter the hair.
Leave a strip of Horn bone showing along the top curve of each horn, the side facing the sky.
Stop when each horn has a dark tip, a darker underside and a pale top edge, so it looks round.

Start at the top of the fringe, where the hair falls between the horns.
Press the full width of the angle brush at the top of each lock. Then pull down and turn onto the edge, so the lock tapers to a point. Pull locks down the fringe, the back and the sides of the body.

pull-straw-locks.text: The ginger locks must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, then move to the outline of the face and chest, toward the right side of the Highland cow.
This is the same press-and-lift you used for the ginger locks, with a smaller brush. These locks are shorter, and most go along the edge the sun hits.
Use the same thick-to-thin pull: press, then lift onto the edge so each lock ends in a point. Pull downward along the outline of the face and chest.
Most of it goes on the right side of the cow, along the edge of the fringe, face and chest where the sunset light hits. A few short locks go on the back and the legs.
Leave the ginger and the dark streaks showing between the straw locks. Leave the shaded middle of the body alone.
Stop when the cow's outline facing the sun glows with straw-gold hair and only a few light locks sit on the body.

light-the-rims.text: The straw-gold locks must be dry.
Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
This is the same Sunlit cream and the same dry skim you used to light the sky. Now it goes on in a few tiny touches on the fringe.
Use a dry brush and skim tiny, light touches along the edge, letting them break up.
This is only a few small sparks of light along the top of the fringe and where each horn meets the hair, plus a couple on the outline of the back. All of it is in the top half of the Highland cow.

paint-nose.text: The coat must be dry.
Start in the middle of the cow's face, where the hanging hair parts. The nose's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
This is the Nose pink you shaded the horns with. Now it goes on the nose itself, in small curved strokes around the muzzle.
Pull small curved strokes around the rounded muzzle, following its shape.
The nose is a small broad oval, about 1 in wide, peeking out of the hair.
Leave the hair of the face showing all around it.
Stop when a plain dusty-pink nose sits in the face, with no nostrils yet. Beginners often paint it too big; keep it small.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: The nose must be dry, or the lines will spread.
Start with the two nostrils on the front of the nose.
This is the Dark umber that shaded the cow. Thin it with water and use the liner for small, fine lines.

Hold the liner upright and use light, steady pressure with thin paint. Draw two small curved nostrils, then a short line for the mouth under the nose. Darken the hair around the muzzle with a few fine strokes.

flick-dark-grass.text: The cow and meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, then move up over the cow's legs.
This is the same Deep grass green and dry brush you used to darken the meadow. This time, flick it up into separate, pointed blades with the stiff brush.
Use the old stiff brush nearly dry. Flick quick strokes upward so each blade ends in a point, leaning a little different ways.
Blades rise across the whole front of the meadow, thickest in the bottom half of the canvas. They run up over the Highland cow's legs and lower belly so it stands in the grass.

flick-light-grass.text: The dark blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, toward the right side of the meadow.
This is the same upward flick you used for the dark blades, now in Sunlit green and with fewer of them.
Use the same quick, nearly dry upward flicks, each blade tapering to a point.
These blades are fewer and sit over the dark ones across the meadow, more on the right side, where the sun is. A few go over the bottom of the Highland cow.

Stop when sunny blades stand in front of the dark ones and the grass looks layered.

flick-gold-tips.text: The sunlit blades must be dry.
Start in the meadow at the bottom edge of the canvas.
This is the Straw gold that lit the cow's hair. This time it goes on as short flicks for the seed heads in the grass.
Use the same nearly dry brush and make short upward flicks, each a small seed head.
Scatter them across the meadow, larger and farther apart at the bottom, smaller toward the back, and more on the right side. Put a few in front of the Highland cow's legs.
Leave the dark and light blades showing around every tip.
Stop when golden tips sparkle across the grass and the painting is finished. Too many tips is the usual mistake; leave space between them.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass on a hillside at sunset, with blue hills and a glimpse of a lake far behind. The heart of the painting is the cow's face and pink nose, peeking out from the glowing fringe between the two horns. Warm sunset light caught in all that long hair is what will make it sing.
opening.light: The low sun is setting behind the hills, so the sky glows gold near it and the hills fade to soft violet. The same sun catches the edges of the cow's hair, its fringe, the horns and the tips of the grass, while the side of the cow turned away from it falls into deep shadow.

skills.how: Dry brushing means only the tip of the brush touches the paint, with no water, so the mark breaks up and lets the colour already on the canvas show through. Here it lights the clouds, roughens the meadow, sparks the fringe with light and flicks up every blade of grass in front of the cow. Watch for paint going on solid: that means too much on the brush, and you can fix it by dry-brushing the base colour back over part of it once dry.

Every stroke bends with the shape it describes, which is what makes a thing look round or rolling. You use it for the soft humps of the far hills, the round body of the cow, the sweep of each horn and the little nose. Keep the darker paint on the shadow side and let it follow the same curve as the lit side.

Press the full width of the angle brush, then lift onto its edge so the mark tapers to a point. This is how the cow's long, hanging locks are made, first in ginger and then in straw gold. Leave gaps between the locks so the darker coat shows; filling them in makes the coat go flat.

opening.road: You start with the sky, blended wet in one go and carried across the whole canvas so it sits behind everything. Then come the far hills and the little lake, painted from the farthest range forward, so each layer sits in front of the one behind it. Next the green hillside and the meadow go over them, so you have a whole empty landscape before the cow arrives. The cow is built as one rust-brown shape, shaded, given its horns, then its long locks and sunlit edges. The face goes on near the end, because it is the focus and needs everything around it in place. Last of all, grass is flicked up over the cow's legs so it stands inside the meadow rather than on it.

the-sky.for: This stage lays the glowing sunset sky that every other part of the painting sits in front of.
the-sky.end: The canvas is a sunset sky of soft blue and glowing gold, with ragged gold clouds and warm wavy streaks.

the-distance.for: This stage builds the far hills in soft hazy layers and tucks a small lake into the valley, so the painting gains distance.
the-distance.end: Soft violet ranges roll across the canvas in front of the golden sky, with a darker ridge and a small silvery lake.

the-green-land.for: This stage brings the land forward, first a sunlit green hillside and then a grassy meadow, so the cow has somewhere to stand.
the-green-land.end: A dappled green hillside slopes away behind a windblown meadow, and the landscape is complete but empty.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage puts the cow in as one simple shape, gives it shadow so it looks round, and adds the two horns.
the-cow-shape.end: A furry, rounded rust-brown cow stands in the meadow, dark on its shadow side, with two shaded horns curving out of its head.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the plain coat into long shaggy hair and lets the sunset catch it.
the-shaggy-coat.end: The cow is covered in long ginger and straw-gold locks, glowing along the edges that face the sun.

the-face.for: This stage paints the nose and its small details, the focal point of the whole painting.
the-face.end: A dusty-pink nose with dark nostrils and a mouth line peeks out from the fringe, and the cow is finished except for the grass in front of it.

the-grass-in-front.for: This stage flicks grass up across the meadow and over the cow's legs, dark first and lightest last, so the cow stands in the grass.
the-grass-in-front.end: Layered dark, sunny and golden grass fills the meadow and hides the cow's legs, and the painting is finished.
