back.text: This is the same Hazy violet you used for the far hills. This time you lay it in level strokes as one darker band, not curving humps.
These are the same curved strokes you used on the hill humps, now made with a small round brush and kept to one tiny sliver.
These are the same long, level strokes you used for the darker ridge, now made with the big flat brush across the whole slope.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside. This time you lay it flat and solid with criss-cross strokes.
This is the dry brush you used for the cream in the sky, now with Deep grass green and a bigger brush. This time skim it upward like grass.
These are the curved strokes you used on the hills, now bending around the cow's round body and down toward its belly.
This is the same small round brush and the same curved pull you used for the lake, now sweeping out into a long tapering horn.
This is the same press-and-lift you used for the ginger locks, with a smaller brush. These locks are shorter, and most go along the edge the sun hits.
This is the same Sunlit cream and the same dry skim you used to light the sky. Now it goes on in a few tiny touches on the fringe.
This is the Nose pink you shaded the horns with. Now it goes on the nose itself, in small curved strokes around the muzzle.
This is the Dark umber that shaded the cow. Thin it with water and use the liner for small, fine lines.
This is the same Deep grass green and dry brush you used to darken the meadow. This time, flick it up into separate, pointed blades with the stiff brush.
This is the same upward flick you used for the dark blades, now in Sunlit green and with fewer of them.
This is the Straw gold that lit the cow's hair. This time it goes on as short flicks for the seed heads in the grass.

blend-sky.start: Begin with Sun cream in a small round glow close to the left edge of the canvas, high up, where the sun sits.
blend-sky.strokes: Work outward from the glow in short crossing X strokes, picking up Warm gold as you move away from the sun, then Haze blue. While it is all wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes to soften the joins.
blend-sky.inside: The light comes from the sun, so the cream and gold stay around it. The blue takes over toward the right edge and across the top. Carry the same soft glow all the way down: the lower part is a dappled mist of gold and blue patches, not a flat colour.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas. Common mistake: scrubbing gold into blue too long until it turns green. Stop blending once the colours meet softly.
blend-sky.stop: The paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The whole canvas reads as one hazy glow, brightest around the sun.

brush-far-treeline.first: Let the sky dry fully; dry-brush on wet paint just smears it.
brush-far-treeline.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas near the top, with the tips of the tallest far trees.
brush-far-treeline.strokes: Load only the tip, wipe it nearly dry, and skim light up-and-down strokes. Rough out tree tops of uneven heights and pull them down into the mist.
brush-far-treeline.inside: Most of it goes in the right half of the misty far tree line, where the shapes are bluest and closest together. Toward the sun they thin to a faint ragged band that lets the gold glow through.
brush-far-treeline.leave: Leave the sun glow and the misty ground clear, and let the sky show through the strokes everywhere.
brush-far-treeline.stop: Its paint reaches the right edge and the top edge of the canvas. It reads as soft, see-through blue tree shapes with flat-ish feet fading into haze. No hard edges.

pull-far-trunks.first: The far tree line must be dry.
pull-far-trunks.start: Start at the foot of the tallest far trunk, in the mist on the left. Its middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge, and it runs up to the top edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the angle brush flat at the foot, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull straight up, so the trunk tapers. Add a short trunk top coming down from the top edge, its middle about 8 1/4 in from the left edge. Add a cluster of short pale stubs in the mist, near the middle of the canvas.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Keep them pale and plain. They are far away in the haze, so no bark marks and no light side.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the sky and the far tree line around each trunk untouched.
pull-far-trunks.stop: A few thin, soft blue-gray trunks stand faintly in the mist. If one looks crisp and dark, the paint was too thick.

stamp-pines.first: The far trunks and far tree line must be dry.
stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tallest pine. The group's top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Spread the fan on the palette and stamp only its middle tips. Work each pine from its tip down in a zigzag, pressing harder as you go lower so it widens toward the bottom.
stamp-pines.inside: Make a group of overlapping pines from about 10 in from the left edge out to the right edge of the canvas. Keep them flat and dark all over for now.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave sky and far trunks showing between the pine tips. Keep the bottom edge ragged, with mist below it.
stamp-pines.stop: A dark blue-green group of firs with needle-like edges, no lighter side yet. Mistake: stamping with the side of the fan gives heavy clumps, so spread the bristles and use the tips.

tap-pine-light.first: The Pine dark has to be dry.
tap-pine-light.start: Start in the haze left of the dark pines on the right, where the paint crosses about 8 3/4 in to 10 1/2 in from the left edge.
tap-pine-light.strokes: Tap the middle tips of the fan in short strokes going different ways, rough and broken like needles.
tap-pine-light.inside: The teal goes around the pines rather than on them: a soft band of it at their left, more tucked between their tips near the right edge of the canvas, and a ragged strip along their base. It makes the dark firs stand out from a cool, misty-teal wood.
tap-pine-light.leave: Leave the Pine dark trees themselves dark and untouched.
tap-pine-light.stop: The pines sit in a ring of dusty teal mist, still dark inside, with the teal reaching the right edge of the canvas.

dab-bush-darks.first: The pines and teal must be dry.
dab-bush-darks.start: Begin at the foot of the dark pines and dab outward across the middle of the canvas.
dab-bush-darks.strokes: Tap with the tip of the stiff flat, light load and no water. Turn the brush between taps so the dabs look like loose leaf clumps.
dab-bush-darks.inside: Most of it goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Lay a broad band of bushes from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, with scattered clumps lower down over the misty ground. Add a few loose sprigs up near the top edge, between the trunk tops, for the canopy's shadows.
dab-bush-darks.leave: Leave plenty of mist showing in gaps between the dabs, and leave the pines clear.
dab-bush-darks.stop: Dull olive masses run across the canvas, broken and airy, not solid. Blobs mean too much paint: wipe the brush on a towel.

dab-canopy-darks.first: The Olive moss dabs must be dry.
dab-canopy-darks.start: Start with the big bush at the left edge of the canvas. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
dab-canopy-darks.strokes: Tap the brush tip in small leaf-sized dabs, tapping more where you want it denser.
dab-canopy-darks.inside: Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Fill that bush thickly over the Olive moss. Then hang loose clusters of leaves down from the top edge of the canvas, and add a few clumps along the base of the pines.
dab-canopy-darks.leave: Leave Olive moss showing along the bottom of the big bush and sky between the hanging clusters.
dab-canopy-darks.stop: One full orange bush on the left and airy orange leaf clusters along the top. The ground is still misty.

dab-golden-leaves.first: The Leaf orange must be dry, or the yellow will turn muddy.
dab-golden-leaves.start: Start in the canopy at the top edge of the canvas, toward its upper left.
dab-golden-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the stiff flat, one leaf shape at a time, a little lighter than the orange taps.
dab-golden-leaves.inside: Most of it is in the left half and the top half of the golden undergrowth and canopy, the side nearest the sun. Cover the canopy clusters and the top of the big bush, whose top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge. Scatter only a few dabs lower down.
dab-golden-leaves.leave: Leave orange showing in the undersides of the clusters and at the bottom of the bush, so they keep their shadows.
dab-golden-leaves.stop: The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange and olive still showing in their shade.

dab-sunlit-leaves.first: The Golden yellow must be dry.
dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas near the sun, on the canopy leaves nearest it.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the round, small soft dabs, building up where the light is strongest.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: A light veil of taps lifts the canopy around the sun. Most of the paint goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy: warm sunlit patches over the misty ground and along the foot of the bushes, as if light is pooling on the ground.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the gold and orange leaves showing through, and leave blue mist between the sunlit patches.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Its paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The sunny side glows and the lower misty ground carries soft lemon patches of light.

dab-floor-darks.first: The undergrowth and sunlit taps must be dry.
dab-floor-darks.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work upward.
dab-floor-darks.strokes: Tap the stiff flat on its corner and flat face in short, slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, tapping often so the patches go nearly solid.
dab-floor-darks.inside: Cover the whole leaf-covered ground from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Its top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, running over the bottom of the bushes. Let a few darker and lighter dabs vary the brown so it reads as fallen leaves.
dab-floor-darks.leave: Leave a ragged golden-olive rim of the bushes showing where they meet the floor.
dab-floor-darks.stop: The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf carpet, with no mist left in it.

pull-path.first: The Rust brown must be dry.
pull-path.start: Mark a dot where the path meets the bushes, and lay the first stroke there. Its middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge and 8 in from the top edge.
pull-path.strokes: Draw three faint lines fanning down from the dot. Pull each stroke along them, thin near the dot and widening as you come forward.
pull-path.inside: This is only the far part of the path, a short curving strip disappearing into the grove between the bushes.
pull-path.leave: Leave the rust leaf floor around it.
pull-path.stop: A small pale tan strip leads back into the trees. Mistake: strokes running side to side make it stand up instead of lie down.

block-in-boulder.first: The path and leaf floor must be dry.
block-in-boulder.start: Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove. Its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 1/2 in wide.
block-in-boulder.strokes: Lay the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side, like ( ), slightly smaller toward the edges.
block-in-boulder.inside: Fill the whole boulder flat with Olive moss. Its flat bottom sits on the leaves.
block-in-boulder.leave: Leave the leaf floor and bushes crisp around it.
block-in-boulder.stop: One flat olive mound, wider than tall, with no shading yet.

shade-boulder.first: The Olive moss must be dry.
shade-boulder.start: Start on the right side of the boulder, at the top of its curve.
shade-boulder.strokes: Bend each stroke with the rock: from the top of the bump down and around its curve toward where it sits on the leaves.
shade-boulder.inside: The sun is far to the left, so the shadow is on the right side of the boulder and heaviest along its base. Most of it is in the bottom half of the boulder. Carry it lightly over most of the rock so it reads as stone.
shade-boulder.leave: Leave a little Olive moss showing on the sunny upper edge facing the sun.
shade-boulder.stop: The boulder is dark and round, darkest on its right and base.

light-boulder.first: The Dark olive must be dry.
light-boulder.start: Start on the upper left of the boulder, the part facing the sun.
light-boulder.strokes: Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim short curved strokes along the top of the rock, light pressure only.
light-boulder.inside: Nearly all of it goes on the left side of the boulder, mostly near its top, where moss catches the sun. Its middle is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
light-boulder.leave: Leave the dark shading showing on the rest of the rock.
light-boulder.stop: A broken, feathery patch of pale moss on the top left. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

pull-birches.first: The leaf floor, bushes and boulder must be dry; the trunks go over all of them.
pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of each trunk on the leaves, beginning with the one nearest the left edge, its middle about 1 in from the left edge.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full width of the flat at the foot, then pull up to the top edge of the canvas, easing the pressure so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out and up from the upper trunks the same way.
pull-birches.inside: Make six trunks. One is thin near the left edge, two are big and lean right, one is thin beside the path, and two are on the right, the outer one widest at the right edge. Fill each one flat.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves and mist clear between the trunks.
pull-birches.stop: Flat pale gray-white trunks and branches, no shading or marks.

shade-birches.first: The Birch gray must be dry.
shade-birches.start: Start at the top of each trunk, at the top edge of the canvas.
shade-birches.strokes: Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim down each trunk and branch with light pressure, so the gray breaks up on the texture.
shade-birches.inside: Gray covers most of each trunk, heaviest on its shady side, away from the sun. Most of it is in the top half of the birches' shading and bark marks.
shade-birches.leave: Leave broken flecks of Birch gray showing all along the trunks, and leave each trunk's foot pale.
shade-birches.stop: The trunks read gray and rounded, with pale flecks and light feet. Gone solid? Too much paint; dry-brush Birch gray back over.

mark-birch-bark.first: The Bark gray must be dry.
mark-birch-bark.start: Start at the foot of the trunk near the left edge of the canvas, where it meets the leaves.
mark-birch-bark.strokes: Press the angle brush flat, then lift onto its edge. Make short sideways dashes across each trunk that start thick and taper.
mark-birch-bark.inside: Most marks go in the bottom half of the birches' shading and bark marks. Make each foot dark and solid, then put the dashes closer together low down and sparser higher up. Darken the branches the same way.
mark-birch-bark.leave: Leave plenty of gray and pale bark between the marks.
mark-birch-bark.stop: Clear birches with broken dark marks and dark feet. Mistake: even, evenly spaced stripes look like a zebra.

dab-orange-leaves.first: The bark marks and leaf floor must be dry.
dab-orange-leaves.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work back toward the path.
dab-orange-leaves.strokes: Tap the stiff flat in slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, smaller as you go farther back.
dab-orange-leaves.inside: Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge down. Let the dabs spill across the path and over the dark trunk feet, so the trees sit in the leaves.
dab-orange-leaves.leave: Leave rust brown showing in gaps between the dabs.
dab-orange-leaves.stop: A warm orange leaf carpet with darker gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.first: The Leaf orange must be dry.
dab-gold-leaves.start: Start on the path, where it comes out of the grove near the boulder.
dab-gold-leaves.strokes: Tap the round in small single leaves, laid slightly sideways.
dab-gold-leaves.inside: Most of it is in the right half and the top half of the fallen leaves. It trails down along the path and across the floor where the light falls, about 11 in from the left edge in its biggest patch. Scatter a few near the left edge of the canvas.
dab-gold-leaves.leave: Leave orange and rust showing between the golden leaves; use far fewer than the orange.
dab-gold-leaves.stop: A trail of golden leaves catches the light along the path.

light-birch-bark.first: The bark marks must be dry, so the white doesn't turn gray.
light-birch-bark.start: Start at the top of the big trunk nearest the sun, and work down.
light-birch-bark.strokes: Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim lightly down each trunk and branch, letting it break on the texture.
light-birch-bark.inside: Keep it to the edge of each trunk facing the sun, catching across some dark marks. Its paint reaches the left edge and the top edge of the canvas.
light-birch-bark.leave: Leave the shady edge gray and most dark marks showing.
light-birch-bark.stop: Sunlit white birches. Too much white flattens the trunks again.

blend-sky.text: Begin with Sun cream in a small round glow close to the left edge of the canvas, high up, where the sun sits.

Work outward from the glow in short crossing X strokes, picking up Warm gold as you move away from the sun, then Haze blue. While it is all wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes to soften the joins.

The light comes from the sun, so the cream and gold stay around it. The blue takes over toward the right edge and across the top. Carry the same soft glow all the way down: the lower part is a dappled mist of gold and blue patches, not a flat colour.
No white canvas. Common mistake: scrubbing gold into blue too long until it turns green. Stop blending once the colours meet softly.
The paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The whole canvas reads as one hazy glow, brightest around the sun.

Start at the right edge of the canvas near the top, with the tips of the tallest far trees.
Load only the tip, wipe it nearly dry, and skim light up-and-down strokes. Rough out tree tops of uneven heights and pull them down into the mist.
Most of it goes in the right half of the misty far tree line, where the shapes are bluest and closest together. Toward the sun they thin to a faint ragged band that lets the gold glow through.
Leave the sun glow and the misty ground clear, and let the sky show through the strokes everywhere.
Its paint reaches the right edge and the top edge of the canvas. It reads as soft, see-through blue tree shapes with flat-ish feet fading into haze. No hard edges.

pull-far-trunks.text: The far tree line must be dry.
Start at the foot of the tallest far trunk, in the mist on the left. Its middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge, and it runs up to the top edge.

Press the angle brush flat at the foot, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull straight up, so the trunk tapers. Add a short trunk top coming down from the top edge, its middle about 8 1/4 in from the left edge. Add a cluster of short pale stubs in the mist, near the middle of the canvas.
Keep them pale and plain. They are far away in the haze, so no bark marks and no light side.
Leave the sky and the far tree line around each trunk untouched.
A few thin, soft blue-gray trunks stand faintly in the mist. If one looks crisp and dark, the paint was too thick.

stamp-pines.text: The far trunks and far tree line must be dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine. The group's top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Spread the fan on the palette and stamp only its middle tips. Work each pine from its tip down in a zigzag, pressing harder as you go lower so it widens toward the bottom.
Make a group of overlapping pines from about 10 in from the left edge out to the right edge of the canvas. Keep them flat and dark all over for now.
Leave sky and far trunks showing between the pine tips. Keep the pines' feet ragged, with mist showing where they end.
A dark blue-green group of firs with needle-like edges, no lighter side yet. Mistake: stamping with the side of the fan gives heavy clumps, so spread the bristles and use the tips.

tap-pine-light.text: The Pine dark has to be dry.
Start in the haze along the left side of the dark pines on the right; this step's left side is about 10 in from the left edge.
Tap the middle tips of the fan in short strokes going different ways, rough and broken like needles.

The teal goes around the pines rather than on them: a soft band of it at their left, more tucked between their tips near the right edge of the canvas, and a ragged strip along their base. It makes the dark firs stand out from a cool, misty-teal wood.
Leave the Pine dark trees themselves dark and untouched.
The pines sit in a ring of dusty teal mist, still dark inside, with the teal reaching the right edge of the canvas.

dab-bush-darks.text: The pines and teal must be dry.
Begin at the foot of the dark pines and dab outward across the middle of the canvas.
Tap with the tip of the stiff flat, light load and no water. Turn the brush between taps so the dabs look like loose leaf clumps.

Most of it goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Lay a broad band of bushes from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, with scattered clumps lower down over the misty ground. Add a few loose sprigs up near the top edge, between the trunk tops, for the canopy's shadows.
Leave plenty of mist showing in gaps between the dabs, and leave the pines clear.
Dull olive masses run across the canvas, broken and airy, not solid. Blobs mean too much paint: wipe the brush on a towel.

dab-canopy-darks.text: The Olive moss dabs must be dry.
Start with the big bush at the left edge of the canvas. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
Tap the brush tip in small leaf-sized dabs, tapping more where you want it denser.

Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Fill that bush thickly over the Olive moss. Then hang loose clusters of leaves down from the top edge of the canvas, and add a few clumps along the base of the pines.
Leave Olive moss showing along the bottom of the big bush and sky between the hanging clusters.
One full orange bush on the left and airy orange leaf clusters along the top. The ground is still misty.

dab-golden-leaves.text: The Leaf orange must be dry, or the yellow will turn muddy.
Start in the canopy at the top edge of the canvas, toward its upper left.
Tap lightly with the tip of the stiff flat, one leaf shape at a time, a little lighter than the orange taps.

Most of it is in the left half and the top half of the golden undergrowth and canopy, the side nearest the sun. Cover the canopy clusters and the top of the big bush, whose top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge. Scatter only a few dabs lower down.
Leave orange showing in the undersides of the clusters and at the bottom of the bush, so they keep their shadows.
The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange and olive still showing in their shade.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: The Golden yellow must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas near the sun, on the canopy leaves nearest it.
Tap with the tip of the round, small soft dabs, building up where the light is strongest.

A light veil of taps lifts the canopy around the sun. Most of the paint goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy: warm sunlit patches over the misty ground and along the foot of the bushes, as if light is pooling on the ground.
Leave the gold and orange leaves showing through, and leave blue mist between the sunlit patches.
Its paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The sunny side glows and the lower misty ground carries soft lemon patches of light.

dab-floor-darks.text: The undergrowth and sunlit taps must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work upward.
Tap the stiff flat on its corner and flat face in short, slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, tapping often so the patches go nearly solid.

Cover the whole leaf-covered ground from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Its top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, running over the bottom of the bushes. Let a few darker and lighter dabs vary the brown so it reads as fallen leaves.
Leave a ragged golden-olive rim of the bushes showing where they meet the floor.
The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf carpet, with no mist left in it.

pull-path.text: The Rust brown must be dry.
Mark a dot where the path meets the bushes, and lay the first stroke there. Its middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge and 8 in from the top edge.
Draw three faint lines fanning down from the dot. Pull each stroke along them, thin near the dot and widening as you come forward.
This is only the far part of the path, a short curving strip disappearing into the grove between the bushes.
Leave the rust leaf floor around it.
A small pale tan strip leads back into the trees. Mistake: strokes running side to side make it stand up instead of lie down.

block-in-boulder.text: The path and leaf floor must be dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove. Its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 1/2 in wide.
Lay the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side, like ( ), slightly smaller toward the edges.
Fill the whole boulder flat with Olive moss. Its flat bottom sits on the leaves.
Leave the leaf floor and bushes crisp around it.
One flat olive mound, wider than tall, with no shading yet.

shade-boulder.text: The Olive moss must be dry.
Start on the right side of the boulder, at the top of its curve.
Bend each stroke with the rock: from the top of the bump down and around its curve toward where it sits on the leaves.

The sun is far to the left, so the shadow is on the right side of the boulder and heaviest along its base. Most of it is in the bottom half of the boulder. Carry it lightly over most of the rock so it reads as stone.
Leave a little Olive moss showing on the sunny upper edge facing the sun.
The boulder is dark and round, darkest on the right side of the boulder and where it sits on the leaves.

light-boulder.text: The Dark olive must be dry.
Start on the upper left of the boulder, the part facing the sun.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim short curved strokes along the top of the rock, light pressure only.
Nearly all of it goes on the left side of the boulder, mostly near its top, where moss catches the sun. Its middle is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the dark shading showing on the rest of the rock.
A broken, feathery patch of pale moss on the top left. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

pull-birches.text: The leaf floor, bushes and boulder must be dry; the trunks go over all of them.
Start at the foot of each trunk on the leaves, beginning with the one nearest the left edge, its middle about 1 in from the left edge.

Press the full width of the flat at the foot, then pull up to the top edge of the canvas, easing the pressure so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out and up from the upper trunks the same way.
Fill each one flat.
Leave the leaves and mist clear between the trunks.
Flat pale gray-white trunks and branches, no shading or marks.

shade-birches.text: The Birch gray must be dry.
Start at the top of each trunk, at the top edge of the canvas.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim down each trunk and branch with light pressure, so the gray breaks up on the texture.
Gray covers most of each trunk, heaviest on its shady side, away from the sun. Most of it is in the top half of the birches' shading and bark marks.
Leave broken flecks of Birch gray showing all along the trunks, and leave each trunk's foot pale.
The trunks read gray and rounded, with pale flecks and light feet. Gone solid? Too much paint; dry-brush Birch gray back over.

mark-birch-bark.text: The Bark gray must be dry.
Start at the foot of the trunk near the left edge of the canvas, where it meets the leaves.
Press the angle brush flat, then lift onto its edge. Make short sideways dashes across each trunk that start thick and taper.

Most marks go in the bottom half of the birches' shading and bark marks. Make each foot dark and solid, then put the dashes closer together low down and sparser higher up. Darken the branches the same way.
Leave plenty of gray and pale bark between the marks.
Clear birches with broken dark marks and dark feet. Mistake: even, evenly spaced stripes look like a zebra.

dab-orange-leaves.text: The bark marks and leaf floor must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work back toward the path.
Tap the stiff flat in slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, smaller as you go farther back.

Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge down. Let the dabs spill across the path and over the dark trunk feet, so the trees sit in the leaves.
Leave rust brown showing in gaps between the dabs.
A warm orange leaf carpet with darker gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.text: The Leaf orange must be dry.
Start on the path, where it comes out of the grove near the boulder.
Tap the round in small single leaves, laid slightly sideways.

Most of it is in the right half and the top half of the fallen leaves. It trails down along the path and across the floor where the light falls, about 11 in from the left edge in its biggest patch. Scatter a few near the left edge of the canvas.
Leave orange and rust showing between the golden leaves; use far fewer than the orange.
A trail of golden leaves catches the light along the path.

light-birch-bark.text: The bark marks must be dry, so the white doesn't turn gray.
Start at the top of the big trunk nearest the sun, and work down.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim lightly down each trunk and branch, letting it break on the texture.
Keep it to the edge of each trunk facing the sun, catching across some dark marks. Its paint reaches the top edge and the right edge of the canvas.
Leave the shady edge gray and most dark marks showing.
Sunlit white birches. Too much white flattens the trunks again.

blend-sky.text: Begin with Sun cream in a small round glow close to the left edge of the canvas, high up, where the sun sits.

Work outward from the glow in short crossing X strokes, picking up Warm gold as you move away from the sun, then Haze blue. While it is all wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes to soften the joins.

The light comes from the sun, so the cream and gold stay around it. The blue takes over toward the right edge and across the top. Carry the same soft glow all the way down: the lower part is a dappled mist of gold and blue patches, not a flat colour.
No white canvas. Common mistake: scrubbing gold into blue too long until it turns green. Stop blending once the colours meet softly.
The paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The whole canvas reads as one hazy glow, brightest around the sun.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry fully; dry-brush on wet paint just smears it.
Start at the right edge of the canvas near the top, with the tips of the tallest far trees.
Load only the tip, wipe it nearly dry, and skim light up-and-down strokes. Rough out tree tops of uneven heights and pull them down into the mist.
Most of it goes in the right half of the misty far tree line, where the shapes are bluest and closest together. Toward the sun they thin to a faint ragged band that lets the gold glow through.
Leave the sun glow and the misty ground clear, and let the sky show through the strokes everywhere.
Its paint reaches the right edge and the top edge of the canvas. It reads as soft, see-through blue tree shapes with flat-ish feet fading into haze. No hard edges.

pull-far-trunks.text: The far tree line must be dry.
Start at the foot of the tallest far trunk, in the mist on the left. Its middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge, and it runs up to the top edge.
This is the same Haze blue you blended into the sky in step 1. This time you pull it as thin trunks with the angle brush, so they melt into the mist.

Press the angle brush flat at the foot, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull straight up, so the trunk tapers. Add a short trunk top coming down from the top edge, its middle about 8 1/4 in from the left edge. Add a cluster of short pale stubs in the mist, near the middle of the canvas.
Keep them pale and plain. They are far away in the haze, so no bark marks and no light side.
Leave the sky and the far tree line around each trunk untouched.
A few thin, soft blue-gray trunks stand faintly in the mist. If one looks crisp and dark, the paint was too thick.

stamp-pines.text: The far trunks and far tree line must be dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine. The group's top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Spread the fan on the palette and stamp only its middle tips. Work each pine from its tip down in a zigzag, pressing harder as you go lower so it widens toward the bottom.
Make a group of overlapping pines from about 10 in from the left edge out to the right edge of the canvas. Keep them flat and dark all over for now.
Leave sky and far trunks showing between the pine tips. Keep the pines' feet ragged, with mist showing where they end.
A dark blue-green group of firs with needle-like edges, no lighter side yet. Mistake: stamping with the side of the fan gives heavy clumps, so spread the bristles and use the tips.

tap-pine-light.text: The Pine dark has to be dry.
Start in the haze along the left side of the dark pines on the right; this step's left side is about 10 in from the left edge.
It is the same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines in step 4, with the bristles spread and only the middle tips touching. The difference is the lighter Pine teal and a softer touch.
Tap the middle tips of the fan in short strokes going different ways, rough and broken like needles.

The teal goes around the pines rather than on them: a soft band of it at their left, more tucked between their tips near the right edge of the canvas, and a ragged strip along their base. It makes the dark firs stand out from a cool, misty-teal wood.
Leave the Pine dark trees themselves dark and untouched.
The pines sit in a ring of dusty teal mist, still dark inside, with the teal reaching the right edge of the canvas.

dab-bush-darks.text: The pines and teal must be dry.
Begin at the foot of the dark pines and dab outward across the middle of the canvas.
Tap with the tip of the stiff flat, light load and no water. Turn the brush between taps so the dabs look like loose leaf clumps.

Most of it goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Lay a broad band of bushes from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, with scattered clumps lower down over the misty ground. Add a few loose sprigs up near the top edge, between the trunk tops, for the canopy's shadows.
Leave plenty of mist showing in gaps between the dabs, and leave the pines clear.
Dull olive masses run across the canvas, broken and airy, not solid. Blobs mean too much paint: wipe the brush on a towel.

dab-canopy-darks.text: The Olive moss dabs must be dry.
Start with the big bush at the left edge of the canvas. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
You dabbed the undergrowth the same way in step 6, with the same stiff flat. Now the Leaf orange goes over it in fuller, leaf-sized clumps.
Tap the brush tip in small leaf-sized dabs, tapping more where you want it denser.

Most of it is in the left half of the golden undergrowth and canopy. Fill that bush thickly over the Olive moss. Then hang loose clusters of leaves down from the top edge of the canvas, and add a few clumps along the base of the pines.
Leave Olive moss showing along the bottom of the big bush and sky between the hanging clusters.
One full orange bush on the left and airy orange leaf clusters along the top. The ground is still misty.

dab-golden-leaves.text: The Leaf orange must be dry, or the yellow will turn muddy.
Start in the canopy at the top edge of the canvas, toward its upper left.
Tap lightly with the tip of the stiff flat, one leaf shape at a time, a little lighter than the orange taps.

Most of it is in the left half and the top half of the golden undergrowth and canopy, the side nearest the sun. Cover the canopy clusters and the top of the big bush, whose top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge. Scatter only a few dabs lower down.
Leave orange showing in the undersides of the clusters and at the bottom of the bush, so they keep their shadows.
The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange and olive still showing in their shade.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: The Golden yellow must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas near the sun, on the canopy leaves nearest it.
This is the same dabbing as the golden leaves in step 8, but with the round brush and much smaller, softer taps.
Tap with the tip of the round, small soft dabs, building up where the light is strongest.

A light veil of taps lifts the canopy around the sun. Most of the paint goes in the bottom half of the golden undergrowth and canopy: warm sunlit patches over the misty ground and along the foot of the bushes, as if light is pooling on the ground.
Leave the gold and orange leaves showing through, and leave blue mist between the sunlit patches.
Its paint reaches all four edges of the canvas. The sunny side glows and the lower misty ground carries soft lemon patches of light.

dab-floor-darks.text: The undergrowth and sunlit taps must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work upward.
It is the same stiff-flat dabbing you used on the undergrowth in step 6. This time keep tapping until the patches are nearly solid.
Tap the stiff flat on its corner and flat face in short, slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, tapping often so the patches go nearly solid.

Cover the whole leaf-covered ground from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Its top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, running over the bottom of the bushes. Let a few darker and lighter dabs vary the brown so it reads as fallen leaves.
Leave a ragged golden-olive rim of the bushes showing where they meet the floor.
The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf carpet, with no mist left in it.

pull-path.text: The Rust brown must be dry.
Mark a dot where the path meets the bushes, and lay the first stroke there. Its middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge and 8 in from the top edge.
Draw three faint lines fanning down from the dot. Pull each stroke along them, thin near the dot and widening as you come forward.
This is only the far part of the path, a short curving strip disappearing into the grove between the bushes.
Leave the rust leaf floor around it.
A small pale tan strip leads back into the trees. Mistake: strokes running side to side make it stand up instead of lie down.

block-in-boulder.text: The path and leaf floor must be dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove. Its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 1/2 in wide.
The Olive moss you dabbed for the undergrowth in step 6 comes back here. This time it is laid flat in curved pieces with the smaller flat brush.
Lay the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side, like ( ), slightly smaller toward the edges.
Fill the whole boulder flat with Olive moss. Its flat bottom sits on the leaves.
Leave the leaf floor and bushes crisp around it.
One flat olive mound, wider than tall, with no shading yet.

shade-boulder.text: The Olive moss must be dry.
Start on the right side of the boulder, at the top of its curve.
Bend each stroke with the rock: from the top of the bump down and around its curve toward where it sits on the leaves.

The sun is far to the left, so the shadow is on the right side of the boulder and heaviest along its base. Most of it is in the bottom half of the boulder. Carry it lightly over most of the rock so it reads as stone.
Leave a little Olive moss showing on the sunny upper edge facing the sun.
The boulder is dark and round, darkest on the right side of the boulder and where it sits on the leaves.

light-boulder.text: The Dark olive must be dry.
Start on the upper left of the boulder, the part facing the sun.
You used this nearly dry skim on the far trees in step 2. Now it is a smaller stiff flat, and only a little patch of moss catching the sun.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim short curved strokes along the top of the rock, light pressure only.
Nearly all of it goes on the left side of the boulder, mostly near its top, where moss catches the sun. Its middle is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the dark shading showing on the rest of the rock.
A broken, feathery patch of pale moss on the top left. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

pull-birches.text: The leaf floor, bushes and boulder must be dry; the trunks go over all of them.
Start at the foot of each trunk on the leaves, beginning with the one nearest the left edge, its middle about 1 in from the left edge.
This is the same press-then-ease stroke you used for the far trunks in step 3. Now it is with the wider flat and much more paint, so the trunks come out bold and solid.

Press the full width of the flat at the foot, then pull up to the top edge of the canvas, easing the pressure so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out and up from the upper trunks the same way.
Fill each one flat.
Leave the leaves and mist clear between the trunks.
Flat pale gray-white trunks and branches, no shading or marks.

shade-birches.text: The Birch gray must be dry.
Start at the top of each trunk, at the top edge of the canvas.
This is the same dry skim you used for the moss in step 14, with the same stiff flat. Now it runs the length of each trunk in gray.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim down each trunk and branch with light pressure, so the gray breaks up on the texture.
Gray covers most of each trunk, heaviest on its shady side, away from the sun. Most of it is in the top half of the birches' shading and bark marks.
Leave broken flecks of Birch gray showing all along the trunks, and leave each trunk's foot pale.
The trunks read gray and rounded, with pale flecks and light feet. Gone solid? Too much paint; dry-brush Birch gray back over.

mark-birch-bark.text: The Bark gray must be dry.
Start at the foot of the trunk near the left edge of the canvas, where it meets the leaves.
This is the angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke from the far trunks in step 3. Here they make short dashes across each trunk instead of long pulls up it.
Press the angle brush flat, then lift onto its edge. Make short sideways dashes across each trunk that start thick and taper.

Most marks go in the bottom half of the birches' shading and bark marks. Make each foot dark and solid, then put the dashes closer together low down and sparser higher up. Darken the branches the same way.
Leave plenty of gray and pale bark between the marks.
Clear birches with broken dark marks and dark feet. Mistake: even, evenly spaced stripes look like a zebra.

dab-orange-leaves.text: The bark marks and leaf floor must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work back toward the path.
This is the same Leaf orange and the same brush you dabbed into the canopy in step 7. Now the dabs lie slightly sideways as fallen leaves on the ground.
Tap the stiff flat in slightly sideways leaf-shaped dabs, smaller as you go farther back.

Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge down. Let the dabs spill across the path and over the dark trunk feet, so the trees sit in the leaves.
Leave rust brown showing in gaps between the dabs.
A warm orange leaf carpet with darker gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.text: The Leaf orange must be dry.
Start on the path, where it comes out of the grove near the boulder.
Use the round brush the way you did for the sunlit taps in step 9. This time the paint is the Golden yellow from the canopy, laid down as single leaves along the path.
Tap the round in small single leaves, laid slightly sideways.

Most of it is in the right half and the top half of the fallen leaves. It trails down along the path and across the floor where the light falls, about 11 in from the left edge in its biggest patch. Scatter a few near the left edge of the canvas.
Leave orange and rust showing between the golden leaves; use far fewer than the orange.
A trail of golden leaves catches the light along the path.

light-birch-bark.text: The bark marks must be dry, so the white doesn't turn gray.
Start at the top of the big trunk nearest the sun, and work down.
It is the same brush and dry skim you used to shade the trunks in step 16. Now the paint is the near-white Bark white, kept to the edge facing the sun.
Wipe the stiff flat nearly dry and skim lightly down each trunk and branch, letting it break on the texture.
Keep it to the edge of each trunk facing the sun, catching across some dark marks. Its paint reaches the top edge and the right edge of the canvas.
Leave the shady edge gray and most dark marks showing.
Sunlit white birches. Too much white flattens the trunks again.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a quiet autumn wood: white birches leaning over a leaf-covered path that runs back into a misty blue grove. What makes it sing is the contrast between warm golden leaves and cool blue haze, and the path pulling your eye deep into the trees. Keep that path and its glowing mist as the heart of the picture.
opening.light: A low sun shines through the mist, so everything near it glows cream and gold while the far wood fades cool and blue. Every highlight in this painting sits on the side of a thing facing that low sun, and every shadow on the side turned away from it.

skills.how: Dabbing means tapping the brush tip lightly, with no water, so the paint lands as small leaf-like dots. Here it builds every leaf in the painting: the bushes, the hanging canopy, the dark leaf floor and the fallen leaves on the path. You always dab the dark colour first and the lighter ones over it. Watch for blobs; they mean the brush is too wet or too full, so wipe it on a towel and tap again.

Dry brushing is skimming a nearly dry brush lightly over the surface so the paint breaks up into feathery, see-through marks. It makes the hazy far trees, the sunlit moss on the boulder, and the shading and sunlight on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim the earlier colour back over.

You press the brush's full width for the thick part, then turn onto its edge and ease off so the mark tapers. It draws every trunk, from the faint far ones to the big birches, and then the short broken bark marks. Keep the pressure changing through the stroke, or the trunks look like flat poles.

opening.road: We begin with the misty sky, a single wet glow that sets where all the light comes from. Next comes the far wood: hazy trees, faint trunks and dark pines, painted pale and soft because they sit deep in the mist. Then the golden leaves of the bushes and canopy go on, dark dabs first and the sunlit ones last. The leaf floor and the path come next, then the mossy boulder, each a step nearer to you. The birches go on over everything because they are the nearest things of all. Last, the fallen leaves and the sun on the bark finish the painting.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the soft glow of sun and mist that everything else sits in.
the-misty-sky.end: The whole canvas is a hazy glow of cream, gold and blue, brightest around the sun, with faint pale trunks and a dappled misty ground.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the distant wood in the haze, from soft far trees to dark pines.
the-far-wood.end: Faint blue trees and pale trunks stand in the mist, with a group of dark pines wrapped in dusty teal haze.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage dabs in the golden bushes and the canopy of leaves, dark to light.
the-golden-leaves.end: A golden bush and hanging leaf clusters glow in the sunlight, with soft lemon light pooling on the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage covers the ground in dark fallen leaves and opens a path into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor fills the ground, with a small pale path leading back between the bushes.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder by the path and makes it look round.
the-boulder.end: A rounded boulder sits by the path, shadowed away from the sun with pale moss where the light falls.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the near birch trunks over everything and gives them shading and bark marks.
the-birches.end: Tall birches with gray shading, dark broken bark marks and dark feet lean over the golden wood.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage scatters bright fallen leaves over the dark floor and along the path.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet, with golden leaves trailing along the path into the grove.

the-last-lights.for: This stage catches the sun on the birch bark to finish the painting.
the-last-lights.end: Sunlit white birches lean over the golden leaf-covered path that runs into the misty blue grove.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage dabs in the golden bushes and the canopy of leaves, dark to light.
the-golden-leaves.end: A golden bush and hanging leaf clusters glow in the sunlight, with soft lemon light pooling on the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage covers the ground in dark fallen leaves and opens a path into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor fills the ground, with a small pale path leading back between the bushes.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder by the path and makes it look round.
the-boulder.end: A rounded boulder sits by the path, shadowed away from the sun with pale moss where the light falls.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the near birch trunks over everything and gives them shading and bark marks.
the-birches.end: Tall birches with gray shading, dark broken bark marks and dark feet lean over the golden wood.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage scatters bright fallen leaves over the dark floor and along the path.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet, with golden leaves trailing along the path into the grove.

the-last-lights.for: This stage catches the sun on the birch bark to finish the painting.
the-last-lights.end: Sunlit white birches lean over the golden leaf-covered path that runs into the misty blue grove.

back.text: This is the same Haze blue you blended into the sky in step 1. This time you pull it as thin trunks with the angle brush, so they melt into the mist.
It is the same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines in step 4, with the bristles spread and only the middle tips touching. The difference is the lighter Pine teal and a softer touch.
You dabbed the undergrowth the same way in step 6, with the same stiff flat. Now the Leaf orange goes over it in fuller, leaf-sized clumps.
This is the same dabbing as the golden leaves in step 8, but with the round brush and much smaller, softer taps.
It is the same stiff-flat dabbing you used on the undergrowth in step 6. This time keep tapping until the patches are nearly solid.
The Olive moss you dabbed for the undergrowth in step 6 comes back here. This time it is laid flat in curved pieces with the smaller flat brush.
You used this nearly dry skim on the far trees in step 2. Now it is a smaller stiff flat, and only a little patch of moss catching the sun.
This is the same press-then-ease stroke you used for the far trunks in step 3. Now it is with the wider flat and much more paint, so the trunks come out bold and solid.
This is the same dry skim you used for the moss in step 14, with the same stiff flat. Now it runs the length of each trunk in gray.
This is the angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke from the far trunks in step 3. Here they make short dashes across each trunk instead of long pulls up it.
This is the same Leaf orange and the same brush you dabbed into the canopy in step 7. Now the dabs lie slightly sideways as fallen leaves on the ground.
Use the round brush the way you did for the sunlit taps in step 9. This time the paint is the Golden yellow from the canopy, laid down as single leaves along the path.
It is the same brush and dry skim you used to shade the trunks in step 16. Now the paint is the near-white Bark white, kept to the edge facing the sun.

taken_out.sentence: Make six trunks: a thin one near the left edge, two big ones leaning toward the path, a thin one with its middle about 8 in from the left edge, and two near the right edge of the canvas, the outer one widest.
taken_out.why: step 15 (pull-birches), line 4 (inside): "about 8 in from the left edge" says 8 in from the left edge; sheet: The far misty trunks, its middle: nearest from the left edge 4 1/8 in

blend-window-sky.start: Start in the very corner where the top edge and the left edge of the canvas meet, with Sky blue.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side in short rows, working down. Without rinsing, pick up Pale sky blue for the lowest rows, then stroke back up over the join a few times while it is wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The deepest blue sits along the top edge; it pales as you go down, the way a sky lightens toward the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave a ragged white gap inside the blue like a cloud, and let the patch end in a soft, broken fringe. The rest of the canvas stays white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the patch is about 1 1/4 in wide and 3 1/4 in tall: a small, soft sky with no hard line between the two blues.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky through the window dry, or the green will turn to mud in the blue.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start where the blue meets the white cloud gap, about 1 in from the top edge.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Wipe most of the Leaf green off the brush, then tap with just its tips. Don't drag it.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: These are only a few tiny taps, the first hint of shaded leaves peeping in at the edge of the cloud.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave almost all of the blue and the white gap untouched.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop after a handful of small dots. From across the room you should barely see them; if you get blobs, the brush is too wet.

dab-light-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green taps dry first.
dab-light-leaves.start: Start at the ragged blue fringe where the sky patch fades out, near the left edge of the canvas.
dab-light-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tips of the dry, stiff brush, just as before, with very little paint.
dab-light-leaves.inside: The Light leaf green goes on as a few sunny taps where the sky thins out, catching the light from the window side.
dab-light-leaves.leave: Leave the Leaf green dots and the blue sky showing.
dab-light-leaves.stop: Stop after a few small light dots. It is a tiny touch, not a full tree.

blend-wall.first: Let the window sky and leaf taps dry completely before you paint next to them.
blend-wall.start: Start just right of the sky through the window, near the top edge, with Sky blue.
blend-wall.strokes: Make short criss-cross X strokes, mixing in Soft wall blue as you work down and across. Go back over it while wet with longer, lighter side-to-side strokes to smooth it.
blend-wall.inside: The wall is palest near the top edge. Work a little Deep wall blue in toward the right edge of the canvas and in a soft upright band where the window post will stand.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the corner where the top edge and left edge of the canvas meet. Paint straight through where the sill, blanket and cat will go.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the soft blue reaches all four edges of the canvas, smooth with faint criss-cross marks.

block-in-frame.first: The wall must be dry, or the cream will pick up blue.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the tall upright post, a long rectangle standing right of the sky through the window.
block-in-frame.strokes: Build the frame from flat Warm cream rectangles: the post, a crossbar across the glass, and a slanting ledge at the foot of the window. Keep each edge straight by pulling the flat brush along it.
block-in-frame.inside: The cream is flat everywhere for now, with no shading.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing as two panes, one above the crossbar and one beneath it.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when the frame is about 3 in wide and 7 in tall, its middle about 1 3/4 in from the left edge, standing clean against the blue wall.

shade-frame.first: Let the cream frame dry completely so your shadow edges stay crisp.
shade-frame.start: Start at the top edge with a long dark strip running down the outer side of the post, where the window opening turns back into the wall.
shade-frame.strokes: Pull long straight strokes of Deep wall blue down the post, then lay thin lines along the edges of the bars and beneath the slanting ledge, as small separate pieces.
shade-frame.inside: The shadow sits on the sides of the bars turned away from the light outside, and fades out low on the wall at the foot of the post.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the cream faces of the bars and post clear, and the panes untouched.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when the frame has crisp blue-gray edges and a deep strip down the post about 7 3/4 in tall, so it reads as a real opening.

light-frame.first: The blue-gray shadows must be dry before you skim over the frame.
light-frame.start: Start on the face of the crossbar nearest the light, close to the left edge of the canvas.
light-frame.strokes: Dip just the tip of the stiff brush, wipe it nearly dry, and skim lightly along the length of each bar and post.
light-frame.inside: The Pure white catches the faces that look into the light: the bars, the slanting ledge and the inner post.
light-frame.leave: Leave the cream showing through the broken marks, and every blue-gray shadow edge untouched.
light-frame.stop: Stop when the frame glows a little brighter, about 2 1/4 in wide in all. It should look sunlit, never painted solid white.

lay-in-sill.first: Let the window frame and wall dry first.
lay-in-sill.start: Start where the ledge meets the foot of the window, about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, and lay its far edge as one slanting line across to the right edge of the canvas.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right across the ledge, working down to the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.inside: Wood brown covers the whole ledge flat, straight through where the blanket and cat will lie.
lay-in-sill.leave: Leave the wall and window frame clean along the far edge of the ledge.
lay-in-sill.stop: Stop when warm brown fills the lowest part of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, flat and smooth with faint level streaks.

darken-sill-edge.first: The Wood brown must be dry so the streaks stay separate.
darken-sill-edge.start: Start along the far edge of the ledge, where it meets the wall, near the left edge of the canvas.
darken-sill-edge.strokes: Pull long, level strokes of Dark wood brown across the ledge, letting them break into streaks like wood grain.
darken-sill-edge.inside: The darker grain covers most of the ledge, from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, and gets heavier near the front where the sill turns down.
darken-sill-edge.leave: Leave a long slanting patch running in from the left edge as plain Wood brown: that is where the sunlight will fall. Also leave a thin slanting stripe crossing it near the left edge.
darken-sill-edge.stop: Stop when the ledge looks grained and darker everywhere except the sunlight patch.

light-sill.first: Let the dark grain dry first.
light-sill.start: Start in the slanting sunlight patch near the left edge of the canvas.
light-sill.strokes: With a nearly dry stiff brush, skim Sunlit wood along the patch in level strokes that follow the grain, a few light passes.
light-sill.inside: The light falls where the window throws sun onto the ledge, breaking into small scraps where the patch runs out toward the middle of the sill.
light-sill.leave: Leave the thin dark slanting stripe (the shadow of a window bar) between the small triangle at the left edge and the main patch, and the dark front edge.
light-sill.stop: Stop when the sun patch, about 8 1/4 in wide, glows peachy on the wood and ends in broken scraps.

block-in-blanket.first: The sill must be dry before the gold goes on top.
block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long rounded rectangle for the folded front of the blanket, its rounded end near the window and its other end running off the right edge of the canvas.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Add the curved roll on top as a second piece, then round the ends with ( ) shaped pieces.
block-in-blanket.inside: Mustard gold covers the whole blanket flat, including where the cat will lie.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a thin strip of sill showing along the front of the blanket and on its end nearest the window.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when one flat gold shape about 14 3/4 in wide and 5 in tall lies on the sill, its upper edge about 6 in from the top edge.

shade-blanket.first: Let the Mustard gold dry so the knit lines stay sharp.
shade-blanket.start: Start at the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, along the edge of the top roll.
shade-blanket.strokes: Make short curved strokes of Dark gold in V-shaped chains, bending each one along the roll, like rows of knit. Work along each roll toward the right edge of the canvas.
shade-blanket.inside: The darker gold fills the grooves between the stitches and folds, darkest where the rolls press together and where the blanket meets the sill.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave the raised loops of each stitch as Mustard gold so the knit stands up.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the whole blanket, about 14 in wide, reads as chunky knitted rolls.

dark-stitches.start: Start in the long groove at the back of the top roll, where the blanket dips before rising again.
dark-stitches.strokes: Press the tip of the #8 round down, let the belly spread, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point like a comma. Run a line of them along that groove.
dark-stitches.inside: Then stamp scattered Dark gold commas into the gaps between stitches on the front rolls, more of them toward the right edge of the canvas.
dark-stitches.leave: Leave most stitches as they are; these are only the deepest gaps.
dark-stitches.stop: Stop when the back groove is a clear dark line, about 14 in long, and the front rolls have dark dots of shadow between the loops.

light-stitches.first: The dark commas must be dry before you stamp over them.
light-stitches.start: Start along the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, where the sun hits first.
light-stitches.strokes: Press and lift short Bright gold commas onto the tops of the loops, following the curve of each roll.
light-stitches.inside: Put the bright marks on the raised loops facing the window light: along the rim of the top roll and on the front rolls.
light-stitches.leave: Leave the dark gaps and the deep groove showing between them.
light-stitches.stop: Stop when the blanket sparkles with bright loops over dark gaps, about 14 3/4 in wide. If a comma turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

block-in-cat.start: Start with a big oval for the curled body, lying on the blanket's top roll, about 15 in wide.
block-in-cat.strokes: Add a circle for the head toward the window, two triangles for the ears, and curved ( ) pieces to round the ends of the body. Fill each piece with flat Cat gray.
block-in-cat.inside: The gray covers the whole cat flat, with no shading yet.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the rolls of the blanket showing all around the body, and the window and wall around the head.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when the cat is one flat gray shape, its ear tip about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.

shade-cat.first: The Cat gray must be dry, or the Dark gray will blend away.
shade-cat.start: Start on the head with a few curved bars across the forehead.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend each Dark gray stroke around the body like a hoop, from the ridge of the back down toward the blanket. Pull shorter curves across the cheeks and the tail.
shade-cat.inside: These soft bars map the tabby pattern. Also outline the paws tucked against the chin, and fill the cat's belly where it presses into the blanket.
shade-cat.leave: Leave wide Cat gray bands between the bars.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the cat wears a soft gray striped pattern and looks round.

white-patches.first: Let the Dark gray dry, so the white stays clean.
white-patches.start: Start with the two front paws tucked against the chin.
white-patches.strokes: Curve each stroke of the #8 round around the paw, then up over the muzzle and chin. Paint a separate pointed patch on the chest, curving with the body.
white-patches.inside: Most of the white is on the left half of the cat, on the face and paws; the chest patch is the only white on the body.
white-patches.leave: Leave the gray showing between the two paws and around every patch.
white-patches.stop: Stop when the white is solid. That takes 2 or 3 thin coats, drying between them, rather than one thick one.

cat-stripes.first: The white patches must be dry before you work beside them.
cat-stripes.start: Start on the ear and forehead, where the stripes are short, its top about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
cat-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush to start each stripe, then lighten and turn so it tapers to a point. Follow the soft Dark gray bars around the body and tail.
cat-stripes.inside: Charcoal goes on the stripes, the rims of the ears, and the deep fold where the head tucks into the body.
cat-stripes.leave: Leave the white patches and the gray bands between stripes clean.
cat-stripes.stop: Stop when bold tapering stripes wrap the head, body and tail.

pink-ears.first: Let the charcoal ear rims dry first.
pink-ears.start: Start deep in the far ear, close to the head.
pink-ears.strokes: Press the #8 round, then pull and lift toward the ear tip so the pink tapers into the point.
pink-ears.inside: Soft pink fills the inside of both ears, strongest where the ear joins the head.
pink-ears.leave: Leave a thin gray and charcoal rim around each ear.
pink-ears.stop: Stop when both ears glow pink inside with dark rims.

flick-fur.first: Let the stripes and ears dry so the flicks stay crisp.
flick-fur.start: Start on the head, its middle about 5 1/4 in from the left edge, over the stripes on the forehead and cheek.
flick-fur.strokes: Barely load the fan brush with Cat gray and flick quick short strokes in the way the fur grows, lifting off as you go.
flick-fur.inside: Most of the flicks go on the head, the front of the body and along the ridge of the back, softening the stripe edges on the window side.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the stripes dark between the flicks, and don't touch the white muzzle or pink ears.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the cat looks soft and furry, especially around the face. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

window-light.first: The fur must be dry before you skim over it.
window-light.start: Start on the ear tips and the crown of the head.
window-light.strokes: Wipe the stiff brush almost dry and skim Warm cream lightly in the way the fur grows.
window-light.inside: Catch the light on the ear rims, cheek, a few spots along the ridge of the back, and a few stitch tips on the end of the blanket nearest the window.
window-light.leave: Leave the gray fur and dark stripes showing through.
window-light.stop: Stop when the cat looks touched by soft window light, with broken marks only.

eyes-toes.first: The face must be completely dry, or the lines will feather.
eyes-toes.start: Start on the face with the far closed eye, a curved line like a smile turned down.
eyes-toes.strokes: Thin the Charcoal with water. Hold the liner upright and pull each line steadily, pressing a little more at the start.
eyes-toes.inside: Add the near closed eye, then a few short ticks and dots on the back, tail and ears to sharpen the stripes.
eyes-toes.leave: Leave the white muzzle and paws clean.
eyes-toes.stop: Stop when the cat clearly sleeps. Keep the lines thin; the eyes are small.

paint-nose.first: Let the blanket stitches dry first.
paint-nose.start: Start at the front roll of the blanket, close to the left edge of the canvas.
paint-nose.strokes: Press and lift small Soft pink commas into the dark gaps of the stitches, following each roll.
paint-nose.inside: The warm pink touches only the shadowed gaps on the front rolls, to warm them up.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the bright loops and the cat untouched.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when the blanket's shadows look warmer, not pink.

whiskers.first: Let the face and nose dry completely.
whiskers.start: Start at the side of the white muzzle, just past the nose.
whiskers.strokes: Thin the Pure white well. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one light, curved stroke that tapers away.
whiskers.inside: Sweep a few across the cheek toward the window side, and a few out the other way across the dark stripes of the body.
whiskers.leave: Leave the space between whiskers; three or four on each side is plenty.
whiskers.stop: Stop when fine white whiskers fan from both sides of the muzzle. The painting is done.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket dry completely.

Leave the rolls of the blanket showing all around the body, and the window and wall around the head.
Stop when the cat is one flat gray shape, its ear tip about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.

shade-cat.text: The Cat gray must be dry, or the Dark gray will blend away.
Start on the head with a few curved bars across the forehead.
Bend each Dark gray stroke around the body like a hoop, from the ridge of the back down toward the blanket. Pull shorter curves across the cheeks and the tail.
