Most of the white is on the left half of the cat, on the face and paws; the chest patch is the only white on the body.
Leave the gray showing between the two paws and around every patch.
Stop when the white is solid. That takes 2 or 3 thin coats, drying between them, rather than one thick one.

cat-stripes.text: Let the white patches dry before you start the stripes.
Start on the ear and forehead, where the stripes are short, its top about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Press the full width of the angle brush to start each stripe, then lighten and turn so it tapers to a point. Follow the soft Dark gray bars around the body and tail.
Charcoal goes on the stripes, the rims of the ears, and the deep fold where the head tucks into the body.
Leave the white patches and the gray bands between stripes clean.
Stop when bold tapering stripes wrap the head, body and tail.

pink-ears.text: Let the charcoal ear rims dry first.
Start deep in the far ear, close to the head.
Press the #8 round, then pull and lift toward the ear tip so the pink tapers into the point.
Soft pink fills the inside of both ears, strongest where the ear joins the head.
Leave a thin gray and charcoal rim around each ear.
Stop when both ears glow pink, each with a dark rim.

flick-fur.text: Let the stripes and ears dry so the flicks stay crisp.
Start on the head, its middle about 5 1/4 in from the left edge, over the stripes on the forehead and cheek.
Barely load the fan brush with Cat gray and flick quick short strokes in the way the fur grows, lifting off as you go.
Most of the flicks go on the head, the front of the body and along the ridge of the back, softening the stripe edges on the window side.
Leave the stripes dark between the flicks, and don't touch the white muzzle or pink ears.
Stop when the cat looks soft and furry, especially around the face. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

window-light.text: The fur must be dry before you skim over it.
Start on the ear tips and the crown of the head.
Wipe the stiff brush almost dry and skim Warm cream lightly in the way the fur grows.
Catch the light on the ear rims, cheek, a few spots along the ridge of the back, and a few stitch tips on the end of the blanket nearest the window.
Leave the gray fur and dark stripes showing through.
Stop when the cat looks touched by soft window light, with broken marks only.

eyes-toes.text: The face must be completely dry, or the lines will feather.
Start on the face with the far closed eye, a curved line like a smile turned down.
Thin the Charcoal with water. Hold the liner upright and pull each line steadily, pressing a little more at the start.
Add the near closed eye, then a few short ticks and dots on the back, tail and ears to sharpen the stripes.
Leave the white muzzle and paws clean.
Stop when the cat clearly sleeps. Keep the lines thin; the eyes are small.

paint-nose.text: Let the blanket stitches dry first.
Start on the front roll of the blanket, at the rounded end nearest the window.
Press and lift small Soft pink commas into the dark gaps of the stitches, following each roll.
The warm pink touches only the shadowed gaps on the front rolls, to warm them up.
Leave the bright loops and the cat untouched.
Stop when the blanket's shadows look warmer, not pink.

whiskers.text: Let the face and nose dry completely.
Start at the side of the white muzzle, just past the nose.
Thin the Pure white well. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one light, curved stroke that tapers away.
Sweep a few across the cheek toward the window side, and a few out the other way across the dark stripes of the body.
Leave the space between whiskers; three or four on each side is plenty.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan from both sides of the muzzle. The painting is done.

blend-window-sky.text: Start in the very corner where the top edge and the left edge of the canvas meet, with Sky blue.
Stroke side to side in short rows, working down. Without rinsing, pick up Pale sky blue for the lowest rows, then stroke back up over the join a few times while it is wet.
The deepest blue sits along the top edge; it pales as you go down, the way a sky lightens toward the horizon.
Leave a ragged white cloud gap unpainted, and let the patch end in a soft, broken fringe. The rest of the canvas stays white.
Stop when the patch is about 1 1/4 in wide and 3 1/4 in tall: a small, soft sky with no hard line between the two blues.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky through the window dry, or the green will turn to mud in the blue.
Start where the blue meets the white cloud gap.
Wipe most of the Leaf green off the brush, then tap with just its tips. Don't drag it.
These are only a few tiny taps, the first hint of shaded leaves peeping in at the edge of the cloud.
Leave almost all of the blue and the white gap untouched.
Stop after a handful of small dots. From across the room you should barely see them; if you get blobs, the brush is too wet.

dab-light-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green taps dry first.
Start at the ragged blue fringe where the sky patch fades out, near the left edge of the canvas.
This is the same dry tap you used for the shaded leaves, now with the lighter Light leaf green and only a few dots.
Tap lightly with the tips of the dry, stiff brush, just as before, with very little paint.
The Light leaf green goes on as a few sunny taps where the sky thins out, catching the light from the window side.
Leave the Leaf green dots and the blue sky showing.
Stop after a few small light dots. It is a tiny touch, not a full tree.

blend-wall.text: Let the window sky and leaf taps dry completely before you start.
Start just right of the sky through the window, near the top edge, with Sky blue.
You blended Sky blue wet in the window sky; here it starts the wall, but now you criss-cross it with X strokes over a much bigger area.
Make short criss-cross X strokes, mixing in Soft wall blue as you work down and across. Go back over it while wet with longer, lighter side-to-side strokes to smooth it.
The wall is palest near the top edge. Work a little Deep wall blue in toward the right edge of the canvas and in a soft upright band where the window post will stand.
Leave the sky and leaves showing in the corner where the top edge and left edge of the canvas meet. Paint straight through where the sill, blanket and cat will go.
Stop when the soft blue reaches all four edges of the canvas, smooth with faint criss-cross marks.

block-in-frame.text: The wall must be dry, or the cream will pick up blue.
Start with the tall upright post, a long rectangle standing right of the sky through the window.
Build the frame from flat Warm cream rectangles: the post, a crossbar across the glass, and a slanting ledge at the foot of the window. Keep each edge straight by pulling the flat brush along it.
The cream is flat everywhere for now, with no shading.
Leave the sky and leaves showing in two panes, split by the crossbar.
Stop when the frame is about 3 in wide and 7 in tall, its middle about 1 3/4 in from the left edge, standing clean against the blue wall.

shade-frame.text: Let the cream frame dry completely so your shadow edges stay crisp.
Start at the top edge with a long dark strip running down the outer side of the post, where the window opening turns back into the wall.
This is the Deep wall blue you worked softly into the wall, now laid as crisp, separate pieces along the frame.
Pull long straight strokes of Deep wall blue down the post, then lay thin lines along the edges of the bars and along the foot of the slanting ledge, as small separate pieces.
The shadow sits on the sides of the bars turned away from the light outside, and fades out low on the wall at the foot of the post.
Leave the cream faces of the bars and post clear, and the panes untouched.
Stop when the frame has crisp blue-gray edges and a deep strip down the post about 7 3/4 in tall, so it reads as a real opening.

light-frame.text: The blue-gray shadows must be dry before you skim over the frame.
Start on the face of the crossbar nearest the light, close to the left edge of the canvas.
Dip just the tip of the stiff brush, wipe it nearly dry, and skim lightly along the length of each bar and post.
The Pure white catches the faces that look into the light: the bars, the slanting ledge and the inner post.
Leave the cream showing through the broken marks, and every blue-gray shadow edge untouched.
Stop when the frame glows a little brighter. It should look sunlit, never painted solid white.

lay-in-sill.text: Let the window frame and wall dry first.
Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right across the ledge, working down to the bottom edge.
Wood brown covers the whole ledge flat, straight through where the blanket and cat will lie.
Leave the wall and window frame clean along the far edge of the ledge.
Stop when warm brown fills the lowest part of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, flat and smooth with faint level streaks.

darken-sill-edge.text: The Wood brown must be dry so the streaks stay separate.
Start along the far edge of the ledge, where it meets the wall, near the left edge of the canvas.
The same long level strokes you used to lay in the sill, now with Dark wood brown and allowed to break into grain.
Pull long, level strokes of Dark wood brown across the ledge, letting them break into streaks like wood grain.
The darker grain covers most of the ledge, from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas, and gets heavier near the front where the sill turns down.
Leave a long slanting patch running in from the left edge as plain Wood brown: that is where the sunlight will fall. Also leave a thin slanting stripe crossing it near the left edge.
Stop when the ledge looks grained and darker everywhere except the sunlight patch.

light-sill.text: Let the dark grain dry first.
Start in the slanting sunlight patch near the left edge of the canvas.
This is the dry skim you used to light the window bars, now with Sunlit wood across a wider patch of the ledge.
With a nearly dry stiff brush, skim Sunlit wood along the patch in level strokes that follow the grain, a few light passes.
The light falls where the window throws sun onto the ledge, breaking into small scraps where the patch runs out toward the middle of the sill.
Leave the thin dark slanting stripe (the shadow of a window bar) between the small triangle at the left edge and the main patch, and the dark front edge.
Stop when the sun patch, about 8 1/4 in wide, glows peachy on the wood and ends in broken scraps.

block-in-blanket.text: The sill must be dry before the gold goes on top.
Start with a long rounded rectangle for the folded front of the blanket, its rounded end near the window and its other end running off the right edge of the canvas.
You built the window frame from rectangles; build the blanket the same way, but with rounded pieces and the bigger 1 inch flat.
Add the curved roll on top as a second piece, then round the ends with ( ) shaped pieces.
Mustard gold covers the whole blanket flat, including where the cat will lie.
Leave a thin strip of sill showing along the front of the blanket and on its end nearest the window.
Stop when one flat gold shape about 14 3/4 in wide and 5 in tall lies on the sill.

shade-blanket.text: Let the Mustard gold dry so the knit lines stay sharp.
Start at the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, along the edge of the top roll.
Make short curved strokes of Dark gold in V-shaped chains, bending each one along the roll, like rows of knit. Work along each roll toward the right edge of the canvas.
The darker gold fills the grooves between the stitches and folds, darkest where the rolls press together and where the blanket meets the sill.
Leave the raised loops of each stitch as Mustard gold so the knit stands up.
Stop when the whole blanket reads as chunky knitted rolls.

dark-stitches.text: Let the folds dry first.
Start in the long groove at the back of the top roll, where the blanket dips before rising again.
This is the Dark gold you shaded the folds with, but now stamped as small commas with the #8 round.
Press the tip of the #8 round down, let the belly spread, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point like a comma. Run a line of them along that groove.
Then stamp scattered Dark gold commas into the gaps between stitches on the front rolls, more of them toward the right edge of the canvas.
Leave most stitches as they are; these are only the deepest gaps.
Stop when the back groove is a clear dark line and the front rolls have dark dots of shadow between the loops.

light-stitches.text: The dark commas must be dry before you stamp over them.
Start along the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, where the sun hits first.
The same press-and-lift commas you stamped in dark, now in Bright gold on the raised loops instead of the gaps.
Press and lift short Bright gold commas onto the tops of the loops, following the curve of each roll.
Put the bright marks on the raised loops facing the window light: along the rim of the top roll and on the front rolls.
Leave the dark gaps and the deep groove showing between them.
Stop when the blanket sparkles with bright loops over dark gaps, about 14 3/4 in wide. If a comma turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket dry completely.
Start with a big oval for the curled body, lying on the blanket's top roll, about 15 in wide.
Build the cat from pieces just as you built the blanket: a big oval first this time, then a circle and two triangles.
Add a circle for the head toward the window, two triangles for the ears, and curved ( ) pieces to round the ends of the body. Fill each piece with flat Cat gray.
The gray covers the whole cat flat, with no shading yet.
Leave the rolls of the blanket showing all around the body, and the window and wall around the head.
Stop when the cat is one flat gray shape, its ear tip about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.

shade-cat.text: The Cat gray must be dry, or the Dark gray will blend away.
Start on the head with a few curved bars across the forehead.
These are the curved strokes you bent along the blanket's rolls, now wrapped around the cat's round body in Dark gray.
Bend each Dark gray stroke around the body like a hoop, from the ridge of the back down toward the blanket. Pull shorter curves across the cheeks and the tail.
These soft bars map the tabby pattern. Also outline the paws tucked against the chin, and fill the cat's belly where it presses into the blanket.
Leave wide Cat gray bands between the bars.
Stop when the cat wears a soft gray striped pattern and looks round.

white-patches.text: Let the Dark gray dry, so the white stays clean.
Start with the two front paws tucked against the chin.
You skimmed Pure white dry on the window bars; here it goes on in thin solid coats, so load the brush properly.
Curve each stroke of the #8 round around the paw, then up over the muzzle and chin. Paint a separate pointed patch on the chest, curving with the body.
Most of the white is on the left half of the cat, on the face and paws; the chest patch is the only white on the body.
Leave the gray showing between the two paws and around every patch.
Stop when the white is solid. That takes 2 or 3 thin coats, drying between them, rather than one thick one.

cat-stripes.text: Let the white patches dry before you start the stripes.
Start on the ear and forehead, where the stripes are short, its top about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Press the full width of the angle brush to start each stripe, then lighten and turn so it tapers to a point. Follow the soft Dark gray bars around the body and tail.
Charcoal goes on the stripes, the rims of the ears, and the deep fold where the head tucks into the body.
Leave the white patches and the gray bands between stripes clean.
Stop when bold tapering stripes wrap the head, body and tail.

pink-ears.text: Let the charcoal ear rims dry first.
Start deep in the far ear, close to the head.
The same press-and-lift you used for the knit stitches, now one long comma pulled into each ear in Soft pink.
Press the #8 round, then pull and lift toward the ear tip so the pink tapers into the point.
Soft pink fills the inside of both ears, strongest where the ear joins the head.
Leave a thin gray and charcoal rim around each ear.
Stop when both ears glow pink, each with a dark rim.

flick-fur.text: Let the stripes and ears dry so the flicks stay crisp.
Start on the head, its middle about 5 1/4 in from the left edge, over the stripes on the forehead and cheek.
This is the Cat gray you blocked the cat in with, now flicked lightly with the fan brush so the darker fur shows through.
Barely load the fan brush with Cat gray and flick quick short strokes in the way the fur grows, lifting off as you go.
Most of the flicks go on the head, the front of the body and along the ridge of the back, softening the stripe edges on the window side.
Leave the stripes dark between the flicks, and don't touch the white muzzle or pink ears.
Stop when the cat looks soft and furry, especially around the face. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

window-light.text: The fur must be dry before you skim over it.
Start on the ear tips and the crown of the head.
The same dry skim you used for the sun patch on the sill, now with Warm cream on the cat's fur and a few stitch tips.
Wipe the stiff brush almost dry and skim Warm cream lightly in the way the fur grows.
Catch the light on the ear rims, cheek, a few spots along the ridge of the back, and a few stitch tips on the end of the blanket nearest the window.
Leave the gray fur and dark stripes showing through.
Stop when the cat looks touched by soft window light, with broken marks only.

eyes-toes.text: The face must be completely dry, or the lines will feather.
Start on the face with the far closed eye, a curved line like a smile turned down.
This is the Charcoal from the stripes, now thinned with water and pulled as fine lines with the liner.
Thin the Charcoal with water. Hold the liner upright and pull each line steadily, pressing a little more at the start.
Add the near closed eye, then a few short ticks and dots on the back, tail and ears to sharpen the stripes.
Leave the white muzzle and paws clean.
Stop when the cat clearly sleeps. Keep the lines thin; the eyes are small.

paint-nose.text: Let the blanket stitches dry first.
Start on the front roll of the blanket, at the rounded end nearest the window.
The Soft pink and press-and-lift you used for the cat's ears, now as tiny commas in the blanket's shadowed gaps.
Press and lift small Soft pink commas into the dark gaps of the stitches, following each roll.
The warm pink touches only the shadowed gaps on the front rolls, to warm them up.
Leave the bright loops and the cat untouched.
Stop when the blanket's shadows look warmer, not pink.

whiskers.text: Let the face and nose dry completely.
Start at the side of the white muzzle, just past the nose.
The same thinned liner work you used for the eyes, now with Pure white and longer, lighter strokes that taper away.
Thin the Pure white well. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one light, curved stroke that tapers away.
Sweep a few across the cheek toward the window side, and a few out the other way across the dark stripes of the body.
Leave the space between whiskers; three or four on each side is plenty.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan from both sides of the muzzle. The painting is done.

opening.welcome: You are painting a gray tabby kitten fast asleep on a chunky mustard blanket, curled up on a wooden sill by a sunny window. The heart of the painting is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the little pink nose and the white paws tucked against the chin. Keep everything else soft and warm so the eye rests there.
opening.light: Soft daylight pours in through the window and falls across the scene. It catches the cat's head and ears, the rolls of the blanket and the near end of the sill, while the sides turned away from the window sink into cool blue-gray and deeper gold.

skills.how: You build each big shape from simple pieces: rectangles for the window frame, a long rounded block and a roll for the blanket, an oval, a circle and two triangles for the cat. It turns a hard drawing into a few easy shapes you can trust. Settle the big pieces first, and only soften the joins where the shape should look smooth.

You touch the round brush down, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Here those commas become knit stitches on the blanket and the pink inside the cat's ears. If you get blobs instead of teardrops, use less paint and lift faster.

With almost no paint on a stiff brush, you skim lightly so the color breaks up over the canvas texture. This is how the window light lands: on the frame, the sun patch on the sill and the rims of the cat's fur. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded; let it dry and work over it.

opening.road: You paint from the farthest thing to the nearest. First comes the little sky and leaves seen through the window, then the soft blue wall that fills the canvas. Next the window frame goes over the wall, with its shadows and light, and then the wooden sill with its grain and sun patch. The blanket follows, built from a flat gold shape into chunky knit, because the cat lies in it. The cat comes last and gets the most steps: a flat gray shape, its pattern, white patches, stripes and ears, then fur, window light and finally the sleeping face and whiskers.

the-window-view.for: This stage lays the farthest thing in the picture: a small patch of sky with the first hint of leaves.
the-window-view.end: A small, soft patch of blue sky with a white cloud gap and a few tiny leaf taps sits in the corner of an otherwise white canvas.

the-wall.for: This stage covers the canvas with the soft blue wall that everything else sits against.
the-wall.end: A smooth periwinkle wall fills the canvas, with a glimpse of sky and sunny green leaves still showing in the window corner.

the-window-frame.for: This stage builds the window frame and gives it a shadow side and a lit side, so it reads as a real opening.
the-window-frame.end: Cream window bars and a tall post stand against the wall, with a deep blue-gray strip along the post and a soft glow on the faces catching the light.

the-sill.for: This stage lays the wooden ledge that the blanket and cat will rest on, then gives it grain and a patch of sunlight.
the-sill.end: A warm grained wooden sill runs across the canvas, with a peachy slanting patch of sunlight crossed by the shadow of a window bar.

the-blanket.for: This stage turns one flat gold shape into a chunky folded knit blanket, one layer of stitches at a time.
the-blanket.end: A plump mustard blanket lies on the sill, its rolls covered in dark gaps and bright knit loops that sparkle in the window light.

the-cat.for: This stage builds the sleeping tabby from a flat gray shape into a striped cat with white patches and pink ears.
the-cat.end: A curled gray tabby with bold dark stripes, a white muzzle, chest and paws, and pink ears lies on the blanket, still without a face.

the-light-and-face.for: This stage brings the cat to life with soft fur, window light and the small details of the sleeping face.
the-light-and-face.end: The painting is finished: a soft, furry kitten with closed eyes, a pink nose and fine white whiskers sleeps in the window light on its knit blanket.

back.text: This is the same dry tap you used for the shaded leaves, now with the lighter Light leaf green and only a few dots.
You blended Sky blue wet in the window sky; here it starts the wall, but now you criss-cross it with X strokes over a much bigger area.
This is the Deep wall blue you worked softly into the wall, now laid as crisp, separate pieces along the frame.
The same long level strokes you used to lay in the sill, now with Dark wood brown and allowed to break into grain.
This is the dry skim you used to light the window bars, now with Sunlit wood across a wider patch of the ledge.
You built the window frame from rectangles; build the blanket the same way, but with rounded pieces and the bigger 1 inch flat.
This is the Dark gold you shaded the folds with, but now stamped as small commas with the #8 round.
The same press-and-lift commas you stamped in dark, now in Bright gold on the raised loops instead of the gaps.
Build the cat from pieces just as you built the blanket: a big oval first this time, then a circle and two triangles.
These are the curved strokes you bent along the blanket's rolls, now wrapped around the cat's round body in Dark gray.
You skimmed Pure white dry on the window bars; here it goes on in thin solid coats, so load the brush properly.
The same press-and-lift you used for the knit stitches, now one long comma pulled into each ear in Soft pink.
This is the Cat gray you blocked the cat in with, now flicked lightly with the fan brush so the darker fur shows through.
The same dry skim you used for the sun patch on the sill, now with Warm cream on the cat's fur and a few stitch tips.
This is the Charcoal from the stripes, now thinned with water and pulled as fine lines with the liner.

The same thinned liner work you used for the eyes, now with Pure white and longer, lighter strokes that taper away.

taken_out.sentence: Start where the ledge meets the foot of the window, about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, and lay its far edge as one slanting line all the way across the canvas.
taken_out.why: step 8 (lay-in-sill), line 2 (start): "all the way across" says it reaches the left and right edges (its left side is 0 in from the left edge; its right side is 7 5/8 in from the right edge); sheet: The sill's dark edge and sunlight reaches left

blend-window-sky.start: Start at the top left corner of the canvas with Sky blue, and work down from there.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side with the 1 inch flat. Pick up Pale sky blue without rinsing and paint it below the blue. Then stroke back up over the join a few times while it is wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The deeper blue sits at the top and the paler blue lower down, as if the sky glows near the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave the rest of the canvas bare white. Leave the small ragged white gap near the left edge of the canvas too.
blend-window-sky.stop: You have a small soft blue patch in the top left corner, about 1 1/4 in wide and 3 1/4 in tall, deeper at the top and paler below.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky patch dry so the green doesn't smear into it.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Begin with a few taps in the middle of the sky patch, then spread outward.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the stiff brush and keep it nearly dry. Tap one spot again and again to make it more solid, and let the clumps stay loose and uneven.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Make a few small clumps over the sky, mostly in its upper part. Real leaves hang in separate masses, so don't fill the patch.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave blue sky showing between and around the clumps, and leave the rest of the canvas bare.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: A handful of soft mid-green leaf clumps sit on the sky patch with blue gaps between them.

dab-light-leaves.first: Let the dark green dry first, so the light taps sit on top and don't turn muddy.
dab-light-leaves.start: Start at the top of the highest leaf clump in the sky patch.
dab-light-leaves.strokes: Tap with the dry tip of the stiff brush, using the same dabbing as before. Keep the taps light and few.
dab-light-leaves.inside: Put the yellow-green only on the top and left of each clump, because that's where the sun hits. The light comes from the upper left.
dab-light-leaves.leave: Leave the darker green showing at the bottom of each clump, and leave the blue gaps open.
dab-light-leaves.stop: Each clump is two-toned, yellow-green on top over mid-green, with sky showing between them.

blend-wall.first: Let the leaves and sky patch dry, so the wall blue doesn't drag them.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, just beside the sky patch, with Sky blue.
blend-wall.strokes: Make short strokes that cross each other like overlapping X shapes, and work down and across the canvas. Mix Soft wall blue in as you go lower. Put Deep wall blue in last, at the right edge of the canvas.
blend-wall.inside: The wall is paler at the top and a bit deeper at the far right edge of the canvas, so the light seems to fall off away from the window. It runs behind where the sill, blanket and cat will go.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the sky and leaves in the top left corner untouched.
blend-wall.stop: The wall is a smooth soft periwinkle with faint criss-cross texture across the full 16 in width, and the window view stays at the left edge.

block-in-frame.first: Make sure the wall is dry, or the cream will pick up blue.
block-in-frame.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas with the tall post, about 3 in from the left edge at its outer side.
block-in-frame.strokes: Paint the post as one tall rectangle. Then add the crossbars between the panes and the slanting ledge at the bottom of the window as separate straight pieces.
block-in-frame.inside: All the cream pieces stay flat and plain. They frame the panes, and the shading comes in the next step.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the panes, and the blue wall showing right of the post.
block-in-frame.stop: Flat cream bars and a post run from the top edge down about 7 in, with the sky and leaves seen through the panes.

shade-frame.first: Let the cream dry so the blue-gray stays crisp.
shade-frame.start: Start at the top of the cream post, on its right side where it meets the blue wall.
shade-frame.strokes: Build the shade from straight pieces. Paint one long narrow strip down the post, then add thin pieces under the crossbars and on their right sides.
shade-frame.inside: The shade goes on the inner side of the opening and the undersides and right sides of the bars. The light comes from the upper left, so those faces turn away from it.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the cream faces of the bars and the post bare.
shade-frame.stop: A deep blue-gray strip runs down the right side of the post, fading near its lower end, with narrow blue-gray edges on the bars.

light-frame.start: Start at the top of the post and the top bar, where the light hits first.
light-frame.strokes: Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush lightly along the edges. Make several light passes, and don't press.
light-frame.inside: Put the white only on the left and top faces of the bars and the post, the faces that catch the window light.
light-frame.leave: Leave the cream middles and the blue-gray shadow sides showing.
light-frame.stop: The frame has broken bright white lit edges on cream, with blue-gray shadow sides. It isn't solid white anywhere.

lay-in-sill.first: Let the frame dry so the brown doesn't smear it.
lay-in-sill.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, just under the bottom of the window frame.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and make long strokes left and right. Work down to the bottom edge of the canvas, then across to the right edge.
lay-in-sill.inside: The whole ledge is one flat brown. It runs behind where the blanket will lie, so don't stop short.
lay-in-sill.leave: Leave the blue wall showing above the sill, and the window frame above it.
lay-in-sill.stop: A flat warm-brown ledge about 4 1/2 in tall fills the bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, its back edge rising toward the window. It has level streaks and no dark edge yet.

darken-sill-edge.first: Let the Wood brown dry so the dark doesn't mix into it.
darken-sill-edge.start: Start with the narrow strip along the back of the sill, where it meets the wall, at the left end.
darken-sill-edge.strokes: Use long level strokes from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Do the same along the bottom edge of the canvas. Add a few slanting dark streaks at the left end.
darken-sill-edge.inside: The dark sits at the back and the front of the ledge, so the middle stays lighter and reads as a flat top. The front is darkest because it is in shadow.
darken-sill-edge.leave: Leave a wedge of Wood brown in the middle, with a ragged right end. Leave the light slanting bar at the left end too.
darken-sill-edge.stop: The sill has dark bands at the back and front, a lighter brown wedge between them, and a few dark streaks on the left end.

light-sill.first: Let the dark bands dry first.
light-sill.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, in the brown wedge near the window.
light-sill.strokes: Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush along the wedge with level strokes. Use light pressure and build in a few passes.
light-sill.inside: The sunlight lies where the window light falls on the ledge, strongest near the left end and breaking up as it goes right.
light-sill.leave: Leave the dark bands and streaks showing, and let the brown show through the marks.
light-sill.stop: Peachy-tan sunlight covers the middle of the sill, about 8 1/4 in wide from the left edge of the canvas. It is feathery and not solid.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with the long front fold, about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas, with the 1 inch flat.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Paint a long rounded rectangle first. Then add the curved roll on top, in curved pieces that run up under where the cat will lie.
block-in-blanket.inside: The shape is one flat mustard color, about 14 3/4 in wide, with a rounded left end and a lumpy top edge.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a strip of the brown sill showing below the blanket, the sunny sill at its left end, and the blue wall above it.
block-in-blanket.stop: A flat mustard-gold blanket sits on the sill and runs to the right edge of the canvas, with no folds or stitches.

shade-blanket.first: Let the mustard dry so the dark ochre stays a clear line.
shade-blanket.start: Start at the groove between the two folds, near the left end of the blanket.
shade-blanket.strokes: Pull each curved stroke along the fold and bend it with the roll. Make a second line where the front roll meets the sill, and a third along the top.
shade-blanket.inside: The dark goes in the groove and the underside, where the folds turn away from the window light.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave the mustard bare on the tops of the rolls.
shade-blanket.stop: Deep ochre lines run in the fold, under the front roll and along the top, so the blanket reads as two soft rolls.

dark-stitches.start: Start at the top roll, near its left end.
dark-stitches.strokes: Press the tip of the #8 round down so the belly spreads, then pull and lift to make a comma. Stamp each one in a V pair, following the curve of the roll.
dark-stitches.inside: Put the stitches in rows along both rolls, a little denser in the folds where it is darkest.
dark-stitches.leave: Leave gaps of mustard between the marks.
dark-stitches.stop: Rows of dark ochre V-shaped stitches run along both rolls, with mustard showing between them.

light-stitches.start: Start at the top left of the upper roll, where the light lands first.
light-stitches.strokes: Press and lift the #8 round for each comma, with less paint and a quick lift. Follow the same curve as the dark stitches.
light-stitches.inside: Stamp most of these on the top and left of each roll. Cover most of the dark stitches, but not all of them.
light-stitches.leave: Leave dark ochre showing in the gaps and in the folds.
light-stitches.stop: The blanket looks chunky and knitted: bright yellow stitches over dark ochre, darker in the folds.

block-in-cat.first: Let the blanket dry, so the gray doesn't pick up yellow.
block-in-cat.start: Start with the big oval of the body, in the middle of the canvas, with the 1 inch flat.
block-in-cat.strokes: Add the head as a circle at the left end of the body, against the window frame. Then add two triangle ears and a curved piece for the tail along the front.
block-in-cat.inside: The shape is flat gray and sits down into the blanket, so its underside is hidden in the stitches. It is about 15 in wide.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket showing below it and the blue wall showing above it.
block-in-cat.stop: One flat mid-gray curled cat shape lies on the blanket, with its head at the left end and no marks on it.

shade-cat.start: Start at the top of the cat's back, near the spine.
shade-cat.strokes: Pull each curved stroke over the back, from the spine toward the belly. Then follow the round of the head, and paint the two paw shapes tucked at the front.
shade-cat.inside: The darker gray sits in curved bands over the back and head, and under the body where it meets the blanket. The light comes from the upper left, so the far side is darker.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the lighter gray at the top and left of the body.
shade-cat.stop: The cat looks round, with dark curved bands over the back and head and two paw shapes at the front.

white-patches.start: Start with the chin and muzzle on the cat's face, using the #8 round.
white-patches.strokes: Make curved strokes that follow each shape. Then paint the chest patch on the side of the body, and the two paws under the chin. Use two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
white-patches.inside: The white goes only on the muzzle and chin, the chest patch and the paws. They are the cat's white markings.
white-patches.leave: Leave the gray all around them, and the dark gray between the paws.
white-patches.stop: The cat has a white muzzle, a white chest patch about 2 1/4 in wide, and two white paws on the gray.

cat-stripes.first: Let the white dry so the charcoal stays sharp.
cat-stripes.start: Start at the cat's spine, on the top of the back.
cat-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull down toward the belly. Each stripe thins to a point.
cat-stripes.inside: Curve the stripes around the body, so they look wrapped. Add tapering bars on the forehead and cheeks, and bands across the tail.
cat-stripes.leave: Leave gray between the stripes, and keep the white patches clean.
cat-stripes.stop: Dark tapering stripes wrap around the head, body and tail. The ears are still gray inside.

pink-ears.start: Start at the base of the ear that is nearer the window, with the tip of the #8 round.
pink-ears.strokes: Press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift toward the ear's tip. Make a few strokes side by side to fill it.
pink-ears.inside: The pink fills the inside of each ear. Do the second ear on top of the head the same way.
pink-ears.leave: Leave a gray rim around each ear.
pink-ears.stop: Both ears are pink inside with gray rims.

flick-fur.start: Start on the head, at the base of the fur by the cheek.
flick-fur.strokes: Flick upward from the base with the fan brush, lifting off so each mark thins at the tip. Use very little paint, and follow the way the fur lies.
flick-fur.inside: Flick over the head and over the left and top of the body, more on the window side. Run some flicks over the stripe edges to soften them.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the darker fur showing between the flicks.
flick-fur.stop: The cat looks furry, with soft gray flicks breaking up the shading and the stripe edges.

window-light.start: Start at the tips of the ears.
window-light.strokes: Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush lightly, with almost no paint on it. Pull along the top of the head, then along the top of the back. Build up in several light passes.
window-light.inside: The cream goes only along the rims that face the window. Then touch the tops of the stitches on the upper left of the blanket roll, because the light is the same.
window-light.leave: Leave the gray fur showing through the cream, and keep it from going solid.
window-light.stop: Soft cream light catches the ear tips, the head, the back and the top-left stitches of the blanket.

eyes-toes.first: Let the cream dry, since the lines spread on wet paint.
eyes-toes.start: Start with the eye nearer the window, on the cat's face.
eyes-toes.strokes: Hold the liner upright and use thin paint with light, steady pressure. Draw each closed eye as a thin curved line, then a tiny mouth line under the nose spot.
eyes-toes.inside: Add a few short toe lines on the white paws. Keep them tiny, so they read as toes.
eyes-toes.leave: Leave the white of the muzzle and paws clean around the lines.
eyes-toes.stop: The cat has two closed sleeping eyes, a small mouth line and toe lines on its paws.

paint-nose.start: Start at the top of the white muzzle, between the eyes and above the mouth line.
paint-nose.strokes: Press the #4 round down and pull a short lift to make a small triangle. Use a little paint.
paint-nose.inside: The nose sits at the top of the white muzzle. It is the center of the face.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the white muzzle showing around it.
paint-nose.stop: A small pink nose sits above the mouth line.

whiskers.first: Let the nose dry, so the white doesn't smear into it.
whiskers.start: Start at the cat's muzzle, on its window side.
whiskers.strokes: Use thin Pure white on the liner and sweep each whisker out in one steady motion. Lighten the pressure as you go so it thins at the end. Let them fork a little.
whiskers.inside: Sweep a few from each side of the muzzle, across the cheek and out over the blanket edge and the wall.
whiskers.leave: Leave most of the face clear. Fewer, longer lines look better than many.
whiskers.stop: A few fine white whiskers fan out from each side of the muzzle. The painting is finished.

shade-frame.text: Let the cream dry so the blue-gray stays crisp.
Start at the top of the cream post, on its right side where it meets the blue wall.
You built the cream frame from straight pieces, and you build the shade the same way. Only the paint is different, and it goes on thin, narrow pieces.
Build the shade from straight pieces. Paint one long narrow strip down the post, then add thin pieces under the crossbars and on their right sides.
The shade goes on the inner side of the opening and the undersides and right sides of the bars. The light comes from the upper left, so those faces turn away from it.
Leave the cream faces of the bars and the post bare.
A deep blue-gray strip runs down the right side of the post, fading near its lower end, with narrow blue-gray edges on the bars.

light-frame.text: Let the blue-gray dry completely.
Start at the top of the post and the top bar, where the light hits first.
Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush lightly along the edges. Make several light passes, and don't press.
Put the white only on the left and top faces of the bars and the post, the faces that catch the window light.
Leave the cream middles and the blue-gray shadow sides showing.
The frame has broken bright white lit edges on cream, with blue-gray shadow sides. It isn't solid white anywhere.

lay-in-sill.text: Let the frame dry so the brown doesn't smear it.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, just under the bottom of the window frame.
Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and make long strokes left and right. Work down to the bottom edge of the canvas, then across to the right edge.
The whole ledge is one flat brown. It runs behind where the blanket will lie, so don't stop short.
Leave the blue wall showing above the sill, and the window frame above it.
A flat warm-brown ledge about 4 1/2 in tall fills the bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, its back edge rising toward the window. It has level streaks and no dark edge yet.

darken-sill-edge.text: Let the Wood brown dry so the dark doesn't mix into it.
Start with the narrow strip along the back of the sill, where it meets the wall, at the left end.
These are the same long, level strokes you used to lay in the sill. Now the paint is darker, and you go only where the sill turns into shadow.
Use long level strokes from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Do the same along the bottom edge of the canvas. Add a few slanting dark streaks at the left end.
The dark sits at the back and the front of the ledge, so the middle stays lighter and reads as a flat top. The front is darkest because it is in shadow.
Leave a wedge of Wood brown in the middle, with a ragged right end. Leave the light slanting bar at the left end too.
The sill has dark bands at the back and front, a lighter brown wedge between them, and a few dark streaks on the left end.

light-sill.text: Let the dark bands dry first.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, in the brown wedge near the window.
This is the dry brush you used to light the window bars: a stiff brush skimmed with almost no paint. Now the paint is a peachy wood tone, and it breaks up as it spreads.
Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush along the wedge with level strokes. Use light pressure and build in a few passes.
The sunlight lies where the window light falls on the ledge, strongest near the left end and breaking up as it goes right.
Leave the dark bands and streaks showing, and let the brown show through the marks.
Peachy-tan sunlight covers the middle of the sill, about 8 1/4 in wide from the left edge of the canvas. It is feathery and not solid.

block-in-blanket.text: Let the sill dry completely.
Start with the long front fold, about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas, with the 1 inch flat.
You built the window frame from pieces, and you build the blanket the same way. The brush is bigger, and the pieces are soft rounded folds, not straight bars.
Paint a long rounded rectangle first. Then add the curved roll on top, in curved pieces that run up under where the cat will lie.
The shape is one flat mustard color, about 14 3/4 in wide, with a rounded left end and a lumpy top edge.
Leave a strip of the brown sill showing below the blanket, the sunny sill at its left end, and the blue wall above it.
A flat mustard-gold blanket sits on the sill and runs to the right edge of the canvas, with no folds or stitches.

shade-blanket.text: Let the mustard dry so the dark ochre stays a clear line.
Start at the groove between the two folds, near the left end of the blanket.
Pull each curved stroke along the fold and bend it with the roll. Make another line where the front roll meets the sill, and one more along the top edge of the blanket.
The dark goes in the groove and the underside, where the folds turn away from the window light.
Leave the mustard bare on the tops of the rolls.
Deep ochre lines run in the fold, under the front roll and along the top, so the blanket reads as two soft rolls.

dark-stitches.text: Let the fold shading dry.
Start at the top roll, near its left end.
You used this same Dark gold for the fold shading. Now you stamp it in small commas with a round brush, not pull it in long lines.
Press the tip of the #8 round down so the belly spreads, then pull and lift to make a comma. Stamp each one in a V pair, following the curve of the roll.
Put the stitches in rows along both rolls, a little denser in the folds where it is darkest.
Leave gaps of mustard between the marks.
Rows of dark ochre V-shaped stitches run along both rolls, with mustard showing between them.

light-stitches.text: Let the dark stitches dry.
Start at the top left of the upper roll, where the light lands first.
This is the same press and lift you used for the dark stitches. Now the paint is brighter, and you stamp lightly so the dark still shows through.
Press and lift the #8 round for each comma, with less paint and a quick lift. Follow the same curve as the dark stitches.
Stamp most of these on the upper-left side of each roll, facing the window. Cover most of the dark stitches, but not all of them.
Leave dark ochre showing in the gaps and in the folds.
The blanket looks chunky and knitted: bright yellow stitches over dark ochre, darker in the folds.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket dry, so the gray doesn't pick up yellow.
Start with the big oval of the body, in the middle of the canvas, with the 1 inch flat.
You built the blanket from a long shape plus curved pieces, and the cat is built the same way. This time the oval, circle and triangles are gray.
Add the head as a circle at the left end of the body, against the window frame. Then add two triangle ears and a curved piece for the tail along the front.
The shape is flat gray and sits down into the blanket, so its underside is hidden in the stitches. It is about 15 in wide.
Leave the blanket showing under the cat and the blue wall showing over its back.
One flat mid-gray curled cat shape lies on the blanket, with its head at the left end and no marks on it.

shade-cat.text: Let the gray dry.
Start at the top of the cat's back, near the spine.
You bent these strokes along the blanket's folds. Now you bend them along the cat's round back, with the darker paint going where the form turns away from the window light.
Pull each curved stroke over the back, from the spine toward the belly. Then follow the round of the head, and paint the two paw shapes tucked at the front.
The darker gray sits in curved bands over the back and head, and under the body where it meets the blanket. The light comes from the upper left, so the far side is darker.
Leave the lighter gray on the cat's top and on its window-facing side.
The cat looks round, with dark curved bands over the back and head and two paw shapes at the front.

white-patches.text: Let the dark gray dry.
Start with the chin and muzzle on the cat's face, using the #8 round.
These are curved strokes again, bent to follow each shape, but now with a small round brush. The white goes on in thin coats over the darker gray.
Make curved strokes that follow each shape. Then paint the chest patch on the side of the body, and the two paws under the chin. Use two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
The white goes only on the muzzle and chin, the chest patch and the paws. They are the cat's white markings.
Leave the gray all around them, and the dark gray between the paws.
The cat has a white muzzle, a white chest patch about 2 1/4 in wide, and two white paws on the gray.

cat-stripes.text: Let the white dry so the charcoal stays sharp.
Start at the cat's spine, on the top of the back.
Press the full width of the angle brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull down toward the belly. Each stripe thins to a point.
Curve the stripes around the body, so they look wrapped. Add tapering bars on the forehead and cheeks, and bands across the tail.
Leave gray between the stripes, and keep the white patches clean.
Dark tapering stripes wrap around the head, body and tail. The ears are still gray inside.

pink-ears.text: Let the stripes dry.
Start at the base of the ear that is nearer the window, with the tip of the #8 round.
You stamped the blanket stitches with the same press and lift. Now each comma is a stroke that fills the hollow of an ear.
Press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift toward the ear's tip. Make a few strokes side by side to fill it.
The pink fills the hollow in the middle of each ear. Do the second ear on top of the head the same way.
Leave a gray rim around each ear.
Both ears are pink in the middle, with gray rims.

flick-fur.text: Let the ears dry.
Start on the head, at the base of the fur by the cheek.
This is the same Cat gray you used for the first gray shape. Now it goes on in tiny flicks that break up the shading instead of covering it.
Flick upward from the base with the fan brush, lifting off so each mark thins at the tip. Use very little paint, and follow the way the fur lies.
Flick over the head and over the left and top of the body, more on the window side. Run some flicks over the stripe edges to soften them.
Leave the darker fur showing between the flicks.
The cat looks furry, with soft gray flicks breaking up the shading and the stripe edges.

window-light.text: Let the flicks dry.
Start at the tips of the ears.
This is the dry brush you used on the window bars: almost no paint, light skimming, several passes. Now the paint is warm cream and the light lands on the cat and the blanket.
Skim the dry tip of the stiff brush lightly, with almost no paint on it. Pull along the top of the head, then along the top of the back. Build up in several light passes.
The cream goes only along the rims that face the window. Then touch the tops of the stitches on the upper left of the blanket roll, because the light is the same.
Leave the gray fur showing through the cream, and keep it from going solid.
Soft cream light catches the ear tips, the head, the back and the top-left stitches of the blanket.

eyes-toes.text: Let the cream dry, since the lines spread on wet paint.
Start with the eye nearer the window, on the cat's face.
You painted the stripes with this same Charcoal. Now it goes on with a fine liner, as thin lines for the eyes and toes.
Hold the liner upright and use thin paint with light, steady pressure. Draw each closed eye as a thin curved line, then a tiny mouth line under the nose spot.
Add a few short toe lines on the white paws. Keep them tiny, so they read as toes.
Leave the white of the muzzle and paws clean around the lines.
The cat has two closed sleeping eyes, a small mouth line and toe lines on its paws.

paint-nose.text: Let the eye lines dry.
Start at the top of the white muzzle, between the closed eyes and over the tiny mouth line.
You made the ears pink with this same Soft pink and a press and lift. Now you do it once more with a slightly smaller brush for one small nose.
Press the #4 round down and pull a short lift to make a small triangle. Use a little paint.
The nose sits at the top of the white muzzle. It is the center of the face.
Leave the white muzzle showing around it.
A small pink nose sits on the muzzle, over the tiny mouth line.

whiskers.text: Let the nose dry, so the white doesn't smear into it.
Start at the cat's muzzle, on its window side.
You drew the closed eyes with the same liner and the same upright hold. Now the paint is white, and the lines are longer and sweep out in one go.
Use thin Pure white on the liner and sweep each whisker out in one steady motion. Lighten the pressure as you go so it thins at the end. Let them fork a little.
Sweep a few from each side of the muzzle, across the cheek and out over the blanket edge and the wall.
Leave most of the face clear. Fewer, longer lines look better than many.
A few fine white whiskers fan out from each side of the muzzle. The painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are going to paint a gray tabby kitten fast asleep, curled up on a chunky mustard blanket on a sunny windowsill. The sleeping face, with its closed eyes, pink nose and white paws, is what makes the picture sing. The mood is quiet and warm, like a lazy afternoon.
opening.light: All the light comes from the window. It warms the sill, glows on the blanket and catches the cat's head and back. The faces turned away from the window fall into cool shadow, so a lot of paint in this lesson goes where the window light does or doesn't reach.

skills.how: Dry brush is a stiff brush with only a little paint on its tip, skimmed lightly so the marks come out feathery and broken. Here it is the window light: on the frame, on the sunny wood of the sill, and on the cat's rims. If it goes on solid, let it dry and brush the base color back over part of it.

Press and lift means you touch down with the tip of a round brush, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift to make a comma. You stamp the knit stitches of the blanket this way, then the pink ears and the nose. If you get a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

Building from pieces means you start with a simple shape and add the rest as separate pieces around it. It gives you the window frame, the blanket and the curled cat without any drawing. Let the pieces overlap a little and leave their seams showing.

opening.road: We paint from the farthest thing to the nearest, because paint can cover what is behind it but not what is in front. First comes the view through the window, then the blue wall that fills the back of the room. Next the window frame and the wooden sill go on, so the room has a corner for the kitten to sit in. The blanket comes after, built from a flat gold up to knit stitches, because the cat lies in it. The cat is last and gets the most steps, since she is the point of the picture: a flat gray shape first, then shading, white markings, stripes and ears. Fur, window light and the sleeping face finish it, with the fine whiskers going on last of all so nothing can smudge them.

the-window-view.for: This stage paints the farthest thing in the picture, the sky and leaves outside, so everything else can sit in front of it.
the-window-view.end: A small patch of soft blue sky with two-toned green leaf clumps sits in the corner of the canvas, and the rest is still bare.

the-wall.for: This stage lays the big calm blue wall behind the whole scene, so the cat and blanket have something to stand out against.
the-wall.end: The canvas is a smooth soft periwinkle wall, paler where the light falls and a little deeper far from the window, with the leaves still showing at the edge.

the-window-frame.for: This stage builds the cream window frame and teaches you to put shade on the faces turned away from the light and brightness on the faces that catch it.
the-window-frame.end: The frame has bright white lit edges, cream middles and a blue-gray shadow side, with sky and leaves seen through its panes.

the-sill.for: This stage lays the wooden ledge the kitten will rest on, and shows how window light makes wood glow.
the-sill.end: The sill is warm brown with dark bands at its back and front and a feathery peach patch of sunlight between them.

the-blanket.for: This stage turns a flat gold shape into a chunky knit blanket, working from dark to light.
the-blanket.end: The blanket reads as two soft rolls of knit, with bright yellow stitches over dark ochre that stays deep in the folds.

the-cat.for: This stage builds the kitten from a plain gray shape into a round tabby with markings, adding one thing at a time.
the-cat.end: A curled gray tabby with white muzzle, chest and paws, dark wrapped stripes and pink ears lies in the blanket.

the-light-and-face.for: This stage makes her look alive and asleep: soft fur, the window light on her rims, and the small face details.
the-light-and-face.end: The painting is finished: a furry sleeping tabby with closed eyes, a pink nose and fine white whiskers, glowing in the window light.
