back.text: You blended Sky blue for the window sky, and you use it again here. This time the strokes cross in short X shapes, and the blue is mixed with Soft wall blue as you go.
This is the same dry tap you used for the shaded leaves. Now the paint is lighter and you tap fewer, only where the sun hits.
You built the cream frame from straight pieces, and you build the shade the same way. Only the paint is different, and it goes on thin, narrow pieces.
These are the same long, level strokes you used to lay in the sill. Now the paint is darker, and you go only where the sill turns into shadow.
This is the dry brush you used to light the window bars: a stiff brush skimmed with almost no paint. Now the paint is a peachy wood tone, and it breaks up as it spreads.
You built the window frame from pieces, and you build the blanket the same way. The brush is bigger, and the pieces are soft rounded folds, not straight bars.
You used this same Dark gold for the fold shading. Now you stamp it in small commas with a round brush, not pull it in long lines.
This is the same press and lift you used for the dark stitches. Now the paint is brighter, and you stamp lightly so the dark still shows through.
You built the blanket from a long shape plus curved pieces, and the cat is built the same way. This time the oval, circle and triangles are gray.
You bent these strokes along the blanket's folds. Now you bend them along the cat's round back, with the darker paint going where the form turns away from the window light.
These are curved strokes again, bent to follow each shape, but now with a small round brush. The white goes on in thin coats over the darker gray.
You stamped the blanket stitches with the same press and lift. Now each comma is a stroke that fills the hollow of an ear.
This is the same Cat gray you used for the first gray shape. Now it goes on in tiny flicks that break up the shading instead of covering it.
This is the dry brush you used on the window bars: almost no paint, light skimming, several passes. Now the paint is warm cream and the light lands on the cat and the blanket.
You painted the stripes with this same Charcoal. Now it goes on with a fine liner, as thin lines for the eyes and toes.
You made the ears pink with this same Soft pink and a press and lift. Now you do it once more with a slightly smaller brush for one small nose.
You drew the closed eyes with the same liner and the same upright hold. Now the paint is white, and the lines are longer and sweep out in one go.

taken_out.sentence: Start at the top edge of the canvas with the tall post, whose outer side is about 3 in from the left edge of the canvas.
taken_out.why: step 5 (block-in-frame), line 2 (start): "about 3 in from the left edge" says 3 in from the left edge; sheet: this step: nearest from the left edge 2 1/8 in, 1 15/16 in, 1 7/8 in

taken_out.sentence: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the panes, and the blue wall showing next to the cream post.
taken_out.why: step 5 (block-in-frame), line 5 (leave): "next to the cream post" can't find 'the cream post' on the sheet; sheet: nothing on the sheet

blend-the-sky.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue, working side to side from the upper left corner.
blend-the-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side, tilting the strokes slightly downward toward the right. Without rinsing, add Sunset gold in a wide band below the blue, then stroke back over the join while it's wet.
blend-the-sky.inside: The gold sits in the upper middle and gets strongest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the sun sets. Blue comes back in soft slanting streaks lower down.
blend-the-sky.leave: Keep the joins soft, with no hard line where blue meets gold.
blend-the-sky.stop: The whole canvas is covered edge to edge in a smooth sky with no clouds yet. Blue at the top, a glowing gold band, then soft blue streaks below.

lay-in-clouds.first: The blended sky must be completely dry.
lay-in-clouds.start: Start along the top edge of the canvas at the upper left, with the tip of the brush.
lay-in-clouds.strokes: Work in small circles with the brush tip so the edges come out bumpy and soft. Drag the circles along into long flat streaks that slope slightly down toward the right.
lay-in-clouds.inside: Put a broken band of cloud along the top of the sky, then a few separate flat patches lower down, over the blue. The patches are bigger on the left side of the canvas and smaller and thinner toward the right.
lay-in-clouds.leave: Leave plenty of blue sky and the earlier gold showing between the streaks.
lay-in-clouds.stop: Cream-gold streaks float over the sky like flat-bottomed clouds, with bumpy edges. They are not solid or bright.

light-cloud-tops.first: The cloud streaks must be dry.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start with a thin band along the very top of the canvas, where the top row of clouds sits.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Load only the tip of the brush, with almost no paint on it. Skim lightly over the top edge of each cloud and let the canvas texture break up the marks. Build it in a few light passes.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Cream goes only on the upper edges of the clouds, the edges that face the sun. The long lower streaks get a line of cream along their upper edges too.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the cream-gold showing below each bright edge, and don't touch the blue.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Each cloud has a feathery, broken bright rim along its top. It reads as sunlight catching the clouds, never as a solid white line.

lay-in-far-hills.first: The sky and clouds must be dry.
lay-in-far-hills.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, with the back range's top about 2 in from the top edge.
lay-in-far-hills.strokes: Pull each stroke along the curve of a hill, from the top of each bump down along its slope. Stack the ranges one below another, each with a soft rounded top.
lay-in-far-hills.inside: Make the ranges as a few big overlapping shapes sloping down across the canvas. Fill all the way down to the bottom edge, because the green land will cover them later.
lay-in-far-hills.leave: Leave the clouds and the gold sky above the hilltops untouched.
lay-in-far-hills.stop: A flat, hazy violet band of rolling hills stretches from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas and runs down to the bottom edge. It has no texture or details.

shade-near-ridges.first: The far hills must be dry.
shade-near-ridges.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, just below the back range's top, about 2 in from the top edge.
shade-near-ridges.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Keep them smooth and flat.
shade-near-ridges.inside: This paint is only a thin band in front of the farthest range, and it is a bit heavier toward the right side of the canvas. The ridges are darker than the range behind them, which makes them look nearer.
shade-near-ridges.leave: Leave the pale back range showing above the band, and leave the rest of the hills as they are.
shade-near-ridges.stop: A slightly darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range. It's soft and has no texture.

paint-lake.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the blue ridges end, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
paint-lake.strokes: With the small round, make a few short curved strokes that flatten out and run level, following the curve of the ridge above it.
paint-lake.inside: The lake is a tiny sliver, only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1/2 in tall, tucked at the foot of the ridges where the land dips.
paint-lake.leave: Leave the hills around it as they are. Don't make the lake bigger.
paint-lake.stop: A small flat sliver of pale silvery blue touches the right edge of the canvas, like a glimpse of water.

lay-in-hillside.first: The hills and lake must be dry.
lay-in-hillside.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, where the slope begins.
lay-in-hillside.strokes: Pull long level strokes across, working down. Shape the top edge so it slopes down toward the right edge of the canvas.
lay-in-hillside.inside: The olive covers everything below that sloping top edge, all the way down to the bottom edge of the canvas. The meadow will cover the lower part later.
lay-in-hillside.leave: Leave the violet hills and the lake showing above the slope's top edge, and keep that edge soft and clean.
lay-in-hillside.stop: A flat olive-green slope fills the canvas below the blue hills from the left edge to the right edge, with no texture or light patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.first: The olive slope must be dry.
tap-sunlit-slope.start: Start on the slope's upper left, just below its top edge.
tap-sunlit-slope.strokes: Spread the fan brush bristles, then stamp with the tips in the middle of the fan, working down in a zigzag. Press harder as you go down and use short strokes in different directions.
tap-sunlit-slope.inside: Cover most of the slope with yellow-green taps, lighter near the top of the slope and heavier lower down. Leave small olive clumps showing so they read as bushes.
tap-sunlit-slope.leave: Leave the dark olive gaps between the taps, and leave the hills above untouched.
tap-sunlit-slope.stop: The slope is dappled yellow-green with darker olive bushes between the taps, from the top of the slope all the way down. It shouldn't be solid or clumpy.

lay-in-meadow.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge, where the meadow meets the bottom of the hillside.
lay-in-meadow.strokes: Use short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes. Work across and down, and keep the top edge gently wavy.
lay-in-meadow.inside: The meadow covers the whole lower canvas, from that top edge down to the bottom edge of the canvas and across from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-in-meadow.leave: Leave the speckled hillside showing above the meadow's top edge.
lay-in-meadow.stop: A flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower part of the canvas, with soft criss-cross texture. It has no dark patches or grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with just the tip of the brush loaded.
darken-meadow-front.strokes: Skim lightly, pulling short upward strokes so the marks break up. Build it in several light passes.
darken-meadow-front.inside: Make it heaviest along the bottom of the canvas and lighter as you go up. The top of this paint starts about 8 1/4 in from the top edge. The front is dark because it is the part nearest us.
darken-meadow-front.leave: Leave the yellow-green showing through higher up and between the streaks.
darken-meadow-front.stop: The meadow is yellow-green at the back and darker, streaky green toward the bottom. The landscape is complete and empty, with no cow yet.

block-in-cow.first: The meadow and its dark front must be dry.
block-in-cow.start: Start with the big oval of the body, whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and whose top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
block-in-cow.strokes: Fill the oval, then add curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges. Make the head a smaller rounded shape at the upper right of the body, with the fringe as a curved cap over it. Add two short leg pieces down into the grass.
block-in-cow.inside: The whole cow is one solid rust shape, about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall. Its bottom is about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave the grass showing between the legs and around the shape.
block-in-cow.stop: A flat rust-brown cow shape stands in the field over the hillside and meadow, with a rough shaggy edge. It has no shading, hair, horns or face.

shade-cow.first: The rust shape must be dry.
shade-cow.start: Start at the top of the cow's back, on the left of the body, just below the fringe.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull each curved stroke down along the cow's body, from the back toward the belly, following the round of the body. Use longer strokes on the body and shorter ones under the fringe and chin.
shade-cow.inside: Dark umber goes on the left side of the body, under the fringe, under the chin and low on the belly, because the light comes from the right. It covers a patch about 6 1/4 in wide and 7 3/4 in tall.
shade-cow.leave: Leave rust showing on the lit right side of the cow and the head.
shade-cow.stop: The cow looks round, with a dark umber left side and underside and rust still glowing on the lit side. It still has no locks, horns or face.

block-in-horns.first: The cow's shading must be dry.
block-in-horns.start: Start with the left horn, at the cow's head where it meets the top of the shoulders, about 2 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas.
block-in-horns.strokes: Build each horn from tapering curved pieces. Pull each stroke around the horn's curve, ending in a point at the tip.
block-in-horns.inside: The left horn sweeps up and outward from the top of the head and is about 2 1/4 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall. The right horn is smaller, about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall, and curves up from the right side of the head. Both tips point upward.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the hills behind the horns showing, and keep the horns off the fringe.
block-in-horns.stop: Two flat bone-colored horns curve up from the cow's head against the hills, with no shading or shine yet.

shade-horns.first: The bone paint must be dry.
shade-horns.start: Start at the tip of the left horn, then work down its curve toward the head.
shade-horns.strokes: Pull each stroke along the horn's curve with the small round, thin at the tips.
shade-horns.inside: Put the paint along the undersides of both horns, where they curve away from the light, and darken the tips. Do the right horn the same way, with a smaller patch about 1 1/4 in wide.
shade-horns.leave: Leave the bone color along the top of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Each horn has a gray-brown underside and a dark tip, with pale bone still on top. It looks rounded but not shiny yet.

pull-ginger-locks.start: Start at the cow's fringe, at the top of the head, with the brush full width.
pull-ginger-locks.strokes: Press the full width of the brush for the thick part of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure so the lock tapers to a point. Pull the locks down, from the fringe over the face, and from the back down the body.
pull-ginger-locks.inside: The locks hang over the fringe, the face and the body, with gaps between them. They are fewer on the shadowed side of the body, where the dark umber stays strongest.
pull-ginger-locks.leave: Leave the dark umber and rust showing between the locks.
pull-ginger-locks.stop: Long golden-ginger locks hang over the cow's coat with the darker coat showing between. There are no straw streaks or bright rim yet, and no nose.

pull-straw-locks.first: The ginger locks must be dry.
pull-straw-locks.start: Start along the fringe at the top of the head, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
pull-straw-locks.strokes: Press the small angle brush down, then turn onto its edge and lift to taper each lock. Pull downward, like the ginger locks.
pull-straw-locks.inside: Put fewer, shorter straw locks on the fringe and the upper body. Put more down the lit edge of the chest and face, because that is where the sun reaches, and a few flecks on the legs.
pull-straw-locks.leave: Leave plenty of ginger, rust and umber showing between them.
pull-straw-locks.stop: Light straw-gold streaks sit over the ginger on the fringe, face and upper body. It is still without a bright rim or nose.

light-the-rims.first: The straw locks must be dry.
light-the-rims.start: Start at the top of the fringe, at the top of the cow's head.
light-the-rims.strokes: Put only the tip of the small flat brush in the cream, with almost no paint on it. Skim lightly in short feathery strokes along the edge, and lift off.
light-the-rims.inside: Cream goes only along the top of the fringe, the top of the cow's back and a thin sunlit line on the upper curve of each horn. All of it is on the sunlit upper edges, because the sun is low on the right.
light-the-rims.leave: Leave everything below the fringe, and the lower body, as it is.
light-the-rims.stop: The top of the cow glows with a faint cream rim, and a thin cream shine runs along the top of each horn. It stays broken and feathery.

paint-nose.first: The cream rims must be dry.
paint-nose.start: Start at the middle of the nose, below the fringe, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
paint-nose.strokes: Build the nose in small curved strokes around its roundness, filling a broad rounded shape with the round brush.
paint-nose.inside: The nose is about 1 in wide and 3/4 in tall, under the shaggy fringe in the middle of the face. It's dusty pink and flat for now.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the hair around the nose showing, and keep the pink within the shape.
paint-nose.stop: A plain dusty-pink nose sits under the fringe, without nostrils or a mouth line.

line-nostrils-mouth.first: The pink nose must be completely dry, or the lines will feather.
line-nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the left nostril, near the middle of the nose.
line-nostrils-mouth.strokes: Hold the liner upright and press lightly. Make each nostril a short curved stroke, then add a short mouth line under the nose, thick to thin. Add water if the line skips.
line-nostrils-mouth.inside: Two small dark nostrils go on the nose, and a faint short mouth line runs under it, a patch about 1 3/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall in all. A touch of dark under the chin helps it read.
line-nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave most of the pink showing, and keep the lines thin.
line-nostrils-mouth.stop: The nose has two dark nostrils and a short mouth line below it. The cow looks finished except for the grass in front of its legs.

flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush barely loaded.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Skim lightly and flick quickly upward, in short blades that lean slightly. Build it in a few light passes.
flick-dark-grass.inside: The blades are thickest along the bottom edge of the canvas and thin out upward. They also stand over the cow's legs and lower belly, because the grass is in front of the cow. The top of this paint is about 10 1/4 in from the top edge.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and leave the cow's face and upper body clear.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Dark green blades rise across the lower meadow and hide the cow's legs and belly in grass. They are broken and feathery, not solid.

flick-light-grass.first: The dark blades must be dry.
flick-light-grass.start: Start at the bottom of the canvas, over the dark blades, at the left edge.
flick-light-grass.strokes: Use the stiff brush nearly dry and flick quickly upward, the same direction as the dark blades. Use fewer blades than before.
flick-light-grass.inside: Put these yellow-green blades over the dark ones across the meadow, and a few over the bottom of the cow, because the sun lights the blades' upper parts. The paint begins about 10 3/4 in from the top edge.
flick-light-grass.leave: Leave the dark green showing between the light blades.
flick-light-grass.stop: Yellow-green blades sit over the dark ones across the meadow and in front of the cow's legs, with dark green still between. There are no gold tips yet.

flick-gold-tips.first: The sunlit blades must be dry.
flick-gold-tips.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush almost dry.
flick-gold-tips.strokes: Make short upward dry-brush flicks, one touch for each seed tip, in one pass across the whole foreground.
flick-gold-tips.inside: Make the tips larger and wider apart at the bottom of the canvas, and smaller and closer together toward the back of the meadow. Put a few over the cow's lower legs and a few on the cow's shaggy coat, because the grass stands in front of it.
flick-gold-tips.leave: Leave most of the green showing, since the tips are only sparks.
flick-gold-tips.stop: Scattered golden grass tips sparkle across the meadow and in front of the cow. The painting is finished.

blend-the-sky.text: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue, working side to side from the upper left corner.

Stroke side to side, tilting the strokes slightly downward toward the right. Without rinsing, add Sunset gold in a wide band across the middle of the sky, then stroke back over the join while it's wet.
The gold sits in the upper middle and gets strongest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the sun sets. Blue comes back in soft slanting streaks lower down.
Keep the joins soft, with no hard line where blue meets gold.
The whole canvas is covered edge to edge in a smooth sky with no clouds yet. Blue at the top, a glowing gold band, then soft blue streaks lower down.

lay-in-clouds.text: The blended sky must be completely dry.
Start along the top edge of the canvas at the upper left, with the tip of the brush.
Work in small circles with the brush tip so the edges come out bumpy and soft. Drag the circles along into long flat streaks that slope slightly down toward the right.

Put a broken band of cloud along the top of the sky, then a few separate flat patches lower down, over the blue. The patches are bigger on the left side of the canvas and smaller and thinner toward the right.
Leave plenty of blue sky and the earlier gold showing between the streaks.
Cream-gold streaks float over the sky like flat-bottomed clouds, with bumpy edges. They are not solid or bright.

light-cloud-tops.text: The cloud streaks must be dry.
Start with a thin band along the very top of the canvas, where the top row of clouds sits.
Load only the tip of the brush, with almost no paint on it. Skim lightly over the top edge of each cloud and let the canvas texture break up the marks. Build it in a few light passes.
Cream goes only on the upper edges of the clouds, the edges that face the sun. The long lower streaks get a line of cream along their upper edges too.
Leave the cream-gold showing through, and don't touch the blue.
Each cloud has a feathery, broken bright rim along its top. It reads as sunlight catching the clouds, never as a solid white line.

lay-in-far-hills.text: The sky and clouds must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, with the back range's top about 2 in from the top edge.
Pull each stroke along the curve of a hill, from the top of each bump down along its slope. Stack the ranges in rows, each with a soft rounded top.
Make the ranges as a few big overlapping shapes sloping down across the canvas. Fill all the way down to the bottom edge, because the green land will cover them later.
Leave the clouds and the gold sky clear of violet.
A flat, hazy violet band of rolling hills stretches from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas and runs down to the bottom edge. It has no texture or details.

shade-near-ridges.text: The far hills must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Keep them smooth and flat.

This paint is only a thin strip in front of the farthest range, and it is a bit heavier toward the right side of the canvas. The ridges are darker than the range behind them, which makes them look nearer.
Leave the pale back range showing, and leave the rest of the hills as they are.
A slightly darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range. It's soft and has no texture.

paint-lake.text: The ridges must be dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the lake's top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
With the small round, make a few short curved strokes that flatten out and run level, following the curve of the ridges.
The lake is a tiny sliver, only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1/2 in tall, tucked at the foot of the ridges where the land dips.
Leave the hills around it as they are. Don't make the lake bigger.
A small flat sliver of pale silvery blue touches the right edge of the canvas, like a glimpse of water.

lay-in-hillside.text: The hills and lake must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, where the slope begins.
Pull long level strokes across, working down. Shape the slope's edge so it slopes down toward the right edge of the canvas.
The olive covers the whole slope, from its sloping edge all the way down to the bottom edge of the canvas. The meadow will cover the lower part later.
Leave the violet hills and the lake showing, and keep the slope's edge soft and clean.
A flat olive-green slope fills the canvas in front of the blue hills from the left edge to the right edge, with no texture or light patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: The olive slope must be dry.
Spread the fan brush bristles, then stamp with the tips in the middle of the fan, working down in a zigzag. Press harder as you go down and use short strokes in different directions.
Cover most of the slope with yellow-green taps, lighter near the far edge of the slope and heavier lower down. Leave small olive clumps showing so they read as bushes.
Leave the dark olive gaps between the taps, and keep the hills clear.
The slope is dappled yellow-green with darker olive bushes between the taps, all the way down. It shouldn't be solid or clumpy.

lay-in-meadow.text: The hillside must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge, where the meadow meets the bottom of the hillside.
Use short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes. Work across and down, and keep the top edge gently wavy.
The meadow covers the whole lower canvas, from that top edge down to the bottom edge of the canvas and across from the left edge to the right edge.
Leave the speckled hillside showing above the meadow's top edge.
A flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower part of the canvas, with soft criss-cross texture. It has no dark patches or grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.text: The meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with just the tip of the brush loaded.
Skim lightly, pulling short upward strokes so the marks break up. Build it in several light passes.
Make it heaviest along the bottom of the canvas and lighter as you go up. The top of this paint starts about 8 1/4 in from the top edge. The front is dark because it is the part nearest us.
Leave the yellow-green showing through higher up and between the streaks.
The meadow is yellow-green at the back and darker, streaky green toward the bottom. The landscape is complete and empty, with no cow yet.

Start with the big oval of the body, whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and whose top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.

Fill the oval, then add curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges. Make the head a smaller rounded shape at the upper right of the body, with the fringe as a curved cap over it. Add two short leg pieces down into the grass.
The whole cow is one solid rust shape, about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall. Its bottom is about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
Leave the grass showing between the legs and around the shape.
A flat rust-brown cow shape stands in the field over the hillside and meadow, with a rough shaggy edge. It has no shading, hair, horns or face.

Start along the cow's back, on its shadow side.
Pull each curved stroke down along the cow's body, from the back toward the belly, following the round of the body. Use longer strokes on the body and shorter ones under the chin.
Dark umber goes on the left side of the body, under the fringe, under the chin and low on the belly, because the light comes from the right. It covers a patch about 6 1/4 in wide and 7 3/4 in tall.
Leave rust showing on the lit right side of the cow and the head.
The cow looks round, with a dark umber left side and underside and rust still glowing on the lit side. It still has no locks, horns or face.

Start with the left horn, at the cow's head where it meets the top of the shoulders, about 2 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas.
Build each horn from tapering curved pieces. Pull each stroke around the horn's curve, ending in a point at the tip.

The left horn sweeps up and outward from the top of the head and is about 2 1/4 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall. The right horn is smaller, about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall, and curves up from the right side of the head. Both tips point upward.
Leave the hills behind the horns showing, and keep the horns off the fringe.
Two flat bone-colored horns curve up from the cow's head against the hills, with no shading or shine yet.

shade-horns.text: The bone paint must be dry.
Start at the tip of the left horn, then work down its curve toward the head.
Pull each stroke along the horn's curve with the small round, thin at the tips.
Put the paint along the undersides of both horns, where they curve away from the light, and darken the tips. Do the right horn the same way, with a smaller patch about 1 1/4 in wide.
Leave the bone color along the top of each horn.
Each horn has a gray-brown underside and a dark tip, with pale bone still on top. It looks rounded but not shiny yet.

pull-ginger-locks.text: The horns must be dry.
Start at the cow's fringe, at the top of the head, with the brush full width.

Press the full width of the brush for the thick part of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure so the lock tapers to a point. Pull the locks down, from the fringe over the face, and from the back down the body.
The locks hang over the fringe, the face and the body, with gaps between them. They are fewer on the shadowed side of the body, where the dark umber stays strongest.
Leave the dark umber and rust showing between the locks.
Long golden-ginger locks hang over the cow's coat with the darker coat showing between. There are no straw streaks or bright rim yet, and no nose.

pull-straw-locks.text: The ginger locks must be dry.
Start along the fringe at the top of the head, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
Press the small angle brush down, then turn onto its edge and lift to taper each lock. Pull downward, like the ginger locks.
Put fewer, shorter straw locks on the fringe and the upper body. Put more down the lit edge of the chest and face, because that is where the sun reaches, and a few flecks on the legs.
Leave plenty of ginger, rust and umber showing between them.
Light straw-gold streaks sit over the ginger on the fringe, face and upper body. It is still without a bright rim or nose.

light-the-rims.text: The straw locks must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, at the top of the cow's head.
Put only the tip of the small flat brush in the cream, with almost no paint on it. Skim lightly in short feathery strokes along the edge, and lift off.

Cream goes only along the top of the fringe, the top of the cow's back and a thin sunlit line on the upper curve of each horn. All of it is on the sunlit upper edges, because the sun is low on the right.
Leave the rest of the cow as it is.
The top of the cow glows with a faint cream rim, and a thin cream shine runs along the top of each horn. It stays broken and feathery.

paint-nose.text: The cream rims must be dry.
Start in the middle of the nose, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
Build the nose in small curved strokes around its roundness, filling a broad rounded shape with the round brush.
The nose is about 1 in wide and 3/4 in tall, in the middle of the face. It's dusty pink and flat for now.
Leave the hair around the nose showing, and keep the pink within the shape.
A plain dusty-pink nose sits on the face, without nostrils or a mouth line.

Start with the left nostril, near the middle of the nose.
Hold the liner upright and press lightly. Make each nostril a short curved stroke, then add a short mouth line, thick to thin. Add water if the line skips.
Two small dark nostrils go on the nose, and a faint short mouth line runs under it, a patch about 1 3/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall in all. A touch of dark under the chin helps it read.
Leave most of the pink showing, and keep the lines thin.
The nose has two dark nostrils and a short mouth line. The cow looks finished except for the grass in front of its legs.

flick-dark-grass.text: The face must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush barely loaded.
Skim lightly and flick quickly upward, in short blades that lean slightly. Build it in a few light passes.

The blades are thickest along the bottom edge of the canvas and thin out upward. They also stand over the cow's legs and lower belly, because the grass is in front of the cow. The top of this paint is about 10 1/4 in from the top edge.
Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and leave the cow's face and upper body clear.
Dark green blades rise across the lower meadow and hide the cow's legs and belly in grass. They are broken and feathery, not solid.

flick-light-grass.text: The dark blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom of the canvas, over the dark blades, at the left edge.
Use the stiff brush nearly dry and flick quickly upward, the same direction as the dark blades. Use fewer blades than before.

Put these yellow-green blades over the dark ones across the meadow, and a few over the bottom of the cow, because the sun lights the blades' upper parts. The paint begins about 10 3/4 in from the top edge.
Leave the dark green showing between the light blades.
Yellow-green blades sit over the dark ones across the meadow and in front of the cow's legs, with dark green still between. There are no gold tips yet.

flick-gold-tips.text: The sunlit blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush almost dry.
Make short upward dry-brush flicks, one touch for each seed tip, in one pass across the whole foreground.

Make the tips larger and wider apart at the bottom of the canvas, and smaller and closer together toward the back of the meadow. Put a few over the cow's lower legs and a few on the cow's shaggy coat, because the grass stands in front of it.
Leave most of the green showing, since the tips are only sparks.
Scattered golden grass tips sparkle across the meadow and in front of the cow. The painting is finished.

Stroke side to side, tilting the strokes slightly downward toward the right. Without rinsing, add Sunset gold in a wide band across the middle of the sky, then stroke back over the join while it's wet.
The gold sits in the upper middle and gets strongest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the sun sets. Blue comes back in soft slanting streaks lower down.
Keep the joins soft, with no hard line where blue meets gold.
The whole canvas is covered edge to edge in a smooth sky with no clouds yet. Blue at the top, a glowing gold band, then soft blue streaks lower down.

lay-in-clouds.text: The blended sky must be completely dry.
Start along the top edge of the canvas at the upper left, with the tip of the brush.
This is the Sunset gold you blended into the sky, but now it goes on the dry sky in small circles instead of being blended wet.
Work in small circles with the brush tip so the edges come out bumpy and soft. Drag the circles along into long flat streaks that slope slightly down toward the right.

Put a broken band of cloud along the top of the sky, then a few separate flat patches lower down, over the blue. The patches are bigger on the left side of the canvas and smaller and thinner toward the right.
Leave plenty of blue sky and the earlier gold showing between the streaks.
Cream-gold streaks float over the sky like flat-bottomed clouds, with bumpy edges. They are not solid or bright.

Leave the cream-gold showing through, and don't touch the blue.
Each cloud has a feathery, broken bright rim along its top. It reads as sunlight catching the clouds, never as a solid white line.

lay-in-far-hills.text: The sky and clouds must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, with the back range's top about 2 in from the top edge.
Pull each stroke along the curve of a hill, from the top of each bump down along its slope. Stack the ranges in rows, each with a soft rounded top.
Make the ranges as a few big overlapping shapes sloping down across the canvas. Fill all the way down to the bottom edge, because the green land will cover them later.
Leave the clouds and the gold sky clear of violet.
A flat, hazy violet band of rolling hills stretches from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas and runs down to the bottom edge. It has no texture or details.

shade-near-ridges.text: The far hills must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.
The same Hazy violet you used for the far hills, now pulled in long level strokes instead of following the curves of the hills.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Keep them smooth and flat.

This paint is only a thin strip in front of the farthest range, and it is a bit heavier toward the right side of the canvas. The ridges are darker than the range behind them, which makes them look nearer.
Leave the pale back range showing, and leave the rest of the hills as they are.
A slightly darker slate-blue ridge sits in front of the pale back range. It's soft and has no texture.

paint-lake.text: The ridges must be dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, where the lake's top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
These are the curved strokes you used on the hills, but now with a small round brush and a pale paint, for just a sliver of water.
With the small round, make a few short curved strokes that flatten out and run level, following the curve of the ridges.
The lake is a tiny sliver, only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1/2 in tall, tucked at the foot of the ridges where the land dips.
Leave the hills around it as they are. Don't make the lake bigger.
A small flat sliver of pale silvery blue touches the right edge of the canvas, like a glimpse of water.

lay-in-hillside.text: The hills and lake must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, where the slope begins.
You used these long level strokes on the ridges. Now you use them again with a bigger brush and olive green, to fill a whole slope.
Pull long level strokes across, working down. Shape the slope's edge so it slopes down toward the right edge of the canvas.
The olive covers the whole slope, from its sloping edge all the way down to the bottom edge of the canvas. The meadow will cover the lower part later.
Leave the violet hills and the lake showing, and keep the slope's edge soft and clean.
A flat olive-green slope fills the canvas in front of the blue hills from the left edge to the right edge, with no texture or light patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: The olive slope must be dry.
Spread the fan brush bristles, then stamp with the tips in the middle of the fan, working down in a zigzag. Press harder as you go down and use short strokes in different directions.
Cover most of the slope with yellow-green taps, lighter near the far edge of the slope and heavier lower down. Leave small olive clumps showing so they read as bushes.
Leave the dark olive gaps between the taps, and keep the hills clear.
The slope is dappled yellow-green with darker olive bushes between the taps, all the way down. It shouldn't be solid or clumpy.

lay-in-meadow.text: The hillside must be dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 in from the top edge, where the meadow meets the bottom of the hillside.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, but now it goes on flat, in criss-cross strokes, as one solid base.
Use short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes. Work across and down, and keep the top edge gently wavy.
The meadow covers the whole lower canvas, from that top edge down to the bottom edge of the canvas and across from the left edge to the right edge.
Leave the speckled hillside showing above the meadow's top edge.
A flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower part of the canvas, with soft criss-cross texture. It has no dark patches or grass blades yet.

darken-meadow-front.text: The meadow must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with just the tip of the brush loaded.
This is the same dry brush you used on the clouds, with only the tip loaded, but now with a bigger brush and a deep green.
Skim lightly, pulling short upward strokes so the marks break up. Build it in several light passes.
Make it heaviest along the bottom of the canvas and lighter as you go up. The top of this paint starts about 8 1/4 in from the top edge. The front is dark because it is the part nearest us.
Leave the yellow-green showing through higher up and between the streaks.
The meadow is yellow-green at the back and darker, streaky green toward the bottom. The landscape is complete and empty, with no cow yet.

block-in-cow.text: The meadow and its dark front must be dry.
Start with the big oval of the body, whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and whose top is about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.

Fill the oval, then add curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges. Make the head a smaller rounded shape at the upper right of the body, with the fringe as a curved cap over it. Add two short leg pieces down into the grass.
The whole cow is one solid rust shape, about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall. Its bottom is about 3 in from the bottom edge of the canvas.
Leave the grass showing between the legs and around the shape.
A flat rust-brown cow shape stands in the field over the hillside and meadow, with a rough shaggy edge. It has no shading, hair, horns or face.

shade-cow.text: The rust shape must be dry.
Start along the cow's back, on its shadow side.
You bent your strokes to follow the hills. Now bend them to follow the round of the cow's body, with a dark paint on the shadow side.
Pull each curved stroke down along the cow's body, from the back toward the belly, following the round of the body. Use longer strokes on the body and shorter ones under the chin.
Dark umber goes on the left side of the body, under the fringe, under the chin and low on the belly, because the light comes from the right. It covers a patch about 6 1/4 in wide and 7 3/4 in tall.
Leave rust showing on the lit right side of the cow and the head.
The cow looks round, with a dark umber left side and underside and rust still glowing on the lit side. It still has no locks, horns or face.

block-in-horns.text: The cow's shading must be dry.
Start with the left horn, at the cow's head where it meets the top of the shoulders, about 2 1/2 in from the top edge of the canvas.
You made the lake with a small round brush and curved strokes. Use that same small round brush again, but now to build each horn from tapering curved pieces.
Build each horn from tapering curved pieces. Pull each stroke around the horn's curve, ending in a point at the tip.

The left horn sweeps up and outward from the top of the head and is about 2 1/4 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall. The right horn is smaller, about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall, and curves up from the right side of the head. Both tips point upward.
Leave the hills behind the horns showing, and keep the horns off the fringe.
Two flat bone-colored horns curve up from the cow's head against the hills, with no shading or shine yet.

shade-horns.text: The bone paint must be dry.
Start at the tip of the left horn, then work down its curve toward the head.
These are the same horns, with the same small curved strokes, but now with a smaller brush and a darker pink-brown paint for the shaded parts.
Pull each stroke along the horn's curve with the small round, thin at the tips.
Put the paint along the undersides of both horns, where they curve away from the light, and darken the tips. Do the right horn the same way, with a smaller patch about 1 1/4 in wide.
Leave the bone color along the top of each horn.
Each horn has a gray-brown underside and a dark tip, with pale bone still on top. It looks rounded but not shiny yet.

pull-ginger-locks.text: The horns must be dry.
Start at the cow's fringe, at the top of the head, with the brush full width.

Press the full width of the brush for the thick part of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure so the lock tapers to a point. Pull the locks down, from the fringe over the face, and from the back down the body.
The locks hang over the fringe, the face and the body, with gaps between them. They are fewer on the shadowed side of the body, where the dark umber stays strongest.
Leave the dark umber and rust showing between the locks.
Long golden-ginger locks hang over the cow's coat with the darker coat showing between. There are no straw streaks or bright rim yet, and no nose.

pull-straw-locks.text: The ginger locks must be dry.
Start along the fringe at the top of the head, about 4 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
These are the same tapering locks you pulled in ginger, but now with a smaller brush, a lighter paint, and fewer, shorter locks.
Press the small angle brush down, then turn onto its edge and lift to taper each lock. Pull downward, like the ginger locks.
Put fewer, shorter straw locks on the fringe and the upper body. Put more down the lit edge of the chest and face, because that is where the sun reaches, and a few flecks on the legs.
Leave plenty of ginger, rust and umber showing between them.
Light straw-gold streaks sit over the ginger on the fringe, face and upper body. It is still without a bright rim or nose.

light-the-rims.text: The straw locks must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, at the top of the cow's head.
This is the Sunlit cream you used to light the clouds, and the same dry brush with almost no paint, now with a smaller brush on the cow and horns.
Put only the tip of the small flat brush in the cream, with almost no paint on it. Skim lightly in short feathery strokes along the edge, and lift off.

Cream goes only along the top of the fringe, the top of the cow's back and a thin sunlit line on the upper curve of each horn. All of it is on the sunlit upper edges, because the sun is low on the right.
Leave the rest of the cow as it is.
The top of the cow glows with a faint cream rim, and a thin cream shine runs along the top of each horn. It stays broken and feathery.

paint-nose.text: The cream rims must be dry.
Start in the middle of the nose, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
This is the Nose pink you used to shade the horns, but now with a bigger round brush, building a whole rounded shape in curved strokes.
Build the nose in small curved strokes around its roundness, filling a broad rounded shape with the round brush.
The nose is about 1 in wide and 3/4 in tall, in the middle of the face. It's dusty pink and flat for now.
Leave the hair around the nose showing, and keep the pink within the shape.
A plain dusty-pink nose sits on the face, without nostrils or a mouth line.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: The pink nose must be completely dry, or the lines will feather.
Start with the left nostril, near the middle of the nose.
This is the Dark umber you used to shade the cow's body, but now it goes on thin with a liner brush, for tiny details.
Hold the liner upright and press lightly. Make each nostril a short curved stroke, then add a short mouth line, thick to thin. Add water if the line skips.
Two small dark nostrils go on the nose, and a faint short mouth line runs under it, a patch about 1 3/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall in all. A touch of dark under the chin helps it read.
Leave most of the pink showing, and keep the lines thin.
The nose has two dark nostrils and a short mouth line. The cow looks finished except for the grass in front of its legs.

flick-dark-grass.text: The face must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush barely loaded.
This is the Deep grass green you dry-brushed on the meadow, but now the brush is stiff and the marks flick upward into blades.
Skim lightly and flick quickly upward, in short blades that lean slightly. Build it in a few light passes.

The blades are thickest along the bottom edge of the canvas and thin out upward. They also stand over the cow's legs and lower belly, because the grass is in front of the cow. The top of this paint is about 10 1/4 in from the top edge.
Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and leave the cow's face and upper body clear.
Dark green blades rise across the lower meadow and hide the cow's legs and belly in grass. They are broken and feathery, not solid.

flick-light-grass.text: The dark blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom of the canvas, over the dark blades, at the left edge.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, now flicked upward in thin blades over the dark ones.
Use the stiff brush nearly dry and flick quickly upward, the same direction as the dark blades. Use fewer blades than before.

Put these yellow-green blades over the dark ones across the meadow, and a few over the bottom of the cow, because the sun lights the blades' upper parts. The paint begins about 10 3/4 in from the top edge.
Leave the dark green showing between the light blades.
Yellow-green blades sit over the dark ones across the meadow and in front of the cow's legs, with dark green still between. There are no gold tips yet.

flick-gold-tips.text: The sunlit blades must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, at the left, with the stiff brush almost dry.
This is the Straw gold you used for the lighter locks of hair, but now as short upward flicks, for the seed tips of the grass.
Make short upward dry-brush flicks, one touch for each seed tip, in one pass across the whole foreground.

Make the tips larger and wider apart at the bottom of the canvas, and smaller and closer together toward the back of the meadow. Put a few over the cow's lower legs and a few on the cow's shaggy coat, because the grass stands in front of it.
Leave most of the green showing, since the tips are only sparks.
Scattered golden grass tips sparkle across the meadow and in front of the cow. The painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are going to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass at sunset, with blue hills and a glimpse of a lake behind it. The cow's face and pink nose are what the eye will go to, so everything else is built to frame it. The mood is a warm, golden evening.
opening.light: The low sun is setting behind the hills. It warms the sky and catches the edges of the cow's hair, its fringe, its horns and the tips of the grass. The side of the cow turned away from the sun stays dark and warm brown.

skills.how: You bend every stroke to follow the shape it paints, so the paint looks round or sloped instead of flat. Here it makes the rolling hills, the round body of the cow, the sweep of the horns and the nose. Watch that each stroke follows the curve and doesn't cut straight across it.

You take only a little paint on the tip of a dry brush and skim the canvas, so the marks come out feathery and broken. Here it makes the glowing cloud edges, the streaky dark meadow, the sunlit rim of the cow and every blade of grass. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

You press the brush down for a wide start, then turn onto its edge and lift so the mark tapers to a point. Here it makes the long locks of the cow's coat, first in ginger and then in straw gold. Pull each one in the direction the hair hangs.

opening.road: We begin with the sky, blended wet in one go, because it runs behind everything else. Then come the far hills and the little lake, then the green hillside and meadow, each laid over the one behind it, so you have a whole empty landscape before the cow arrives. The cow is built next as one rust shape that is shaded, given its horns, and then covered in long locks with a sunlit rim. The face goes on once the coat is done, so the nose is the freshest and clearest thing on the cow. The last stage is the grass in front, flicked over the cow's legs so the cow stands inside the meadow instead of on it.

the-sky.for: This stage makes the glowing sunset that lights everything else in the painting.
the-sky.end: The sky is blue fading to gold, with soft cream clouds whose edges catch the sun.

the-distance.for: This stage puts the far hills and the lake in place, so the scene seems to stretch away.
the-distance.end: Soft, hazy violet and blue hills roll across the canvas, with a small pale lake glimpsed between them.

the-green-land.for: This stage builds the grassy ground the cow will stand in, from the far slope to the near meadow.
the-green-land.end: The landscape is complete and empty: a speckled green hillside, then a meadow that grows darker toward the front.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage builds the cow's solid form and its horns before any hair goes on.
the-cow-shape.end: A rust cow, shaded so it looks round, stands in the field with two curved pale horns.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the smooth shape into a shaggy cow with long locks of hair catching the sun.
the-shaggy-coat.end: Long ginger and straw-gold locks cover the coat, with a faint cream glow along the sunlit edges.

the-face.for: This stage gives the cow its face, the part we most want people to look at.
the-face.end: The cow has a dusty-pink nose with dark nostrils and a short mouth, and looks out at us.

the-grass-in-front.for: This stage puts the grass in front of the cow, so it stands inside the meadow.
the-grass-in-front.end: Dark, sunlit and golden blades of grass rise across the meadow and hide the cow's legs, and the painting is finished.

back.text: This is the Sunset gold you blended into the sky, but now it goes on the dry sky in small circles instead of being blended wet.
The same Hazy violet you used for the far hills, now pulled in long level strokes instead of following the curves of the hills.
These are the curved strokes you used on the hills, but now with a small round brush and a pale paint, for just a sliver of water.
You used these long level strokes on the ridges. Now you use them again with a bigger brush and olive green, to fill a whole slope.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, but now it goes on flat, in criss-cross strokes, as one solid base.
This is the same dry brush you used on the clouds, with only the tip loaded, but now with a bigger brush and a deep green.
You bent your strokes to follow the hills. Now bend them to follow the round of the cow's body, with a dark paint on the shadow side.
You made the lake with a small round brush and curved strokes. Use that same small round brush again, but now to build each horn from tapering curved pieces.
These are the same horns, with the same small curved strokes, but now with a smaller brush and a darker pink-brown paint for the shaded parts.
These are the same tapering locks you pulled in ginger, but now with a smaller brush, a lighter paint, and fewer, shorter locks.
This is the Sunlit cream you used to light the clouds, and the same dry brush with almost no paint, now with a smaller brush on the cow and horns.
This is the Nose pink you used to shade the horns, but now with a bigger round brush, building a whole rounded shape in curved strokes.
This is the Dark umber you used to shade the cow's body, but now it goes on thin with a liner brush, for tiny details.
This is the Deep grass green you dry-brushed on the meadow, but now the brush is stiff and the marks flick upward into blades.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped on the hillside, now flicked upward in thin blades over the dark ones.
This is the Straw gold you used for the lighter locks of hair, but now as short upward flicks, for the seed tips of the grass.

taken_out.sentence: Start at the upper left corner of the slope.
taken_out.why: step 8 (tap-sunlit-slope), line 2 (start): "at the upper left" says upper left; sheet: this step: the step's area centered 6 11/16 in from the left, 5 3/8 in from the top; mark 1 centered 5 3/4 in from the left, 9 15/16 in from the top; the sunlit patches on the hillside centered 5 3/4 in from the left, 10 in from the top

blend-sky.start: Start at the sun spot, high in the upper left corner of the canvas, with Sun cream. Work outward from there.
blend-sky.strokes: Use short strokes that cross like overlapping X shapes. Carry Warm gold across the left half, then bring Haze blue in from the right and across the top right. Where the colors meet, keep crossing X strokes so they melt together. Finish with a few light, longer side-to-side strokes while it is still wet.
blend-sky.inside: The cream glow sits around the sun because the light comes from the upper left. The gold fades toward the middle, and the blue gets deeper at the right edge of the canvas and along the top.
blend-sky.leave: Nothing. Cover the white canvas right down to the bottom edge. Don't paint any trees yet.
blend-sky.stop: The whole canvas is one soft, misty glow: pale cream at the upper left, gold across the left half, and blue on the right.

brush-far-treeline.first: Let the wet sky blend dry all the way through.
brush-far-treeline.start: Start at the tops of the far trees, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, right of the middle.
brush-far-treeline.strokes: Put only the tip of the brush in Misty blue and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly over the sky in rough up-and-down strokes to make ragged tree tops. Work down in a few light passes, letting the strokes break up and fade out at the bottom of each tree.
brush-far-treeline.inside: The trees sit from the middle toward the right edge of the canvas, with most of the paint right of the middle. They are soft shapes in the mist, so keep them see-through.
brush-far-treeline.leave: Leave the sky's glow clear at the left of the canvas, and leave the sky showing through the broken marks.
brush-far-treeline.stop: Faint blue tree shapes fill the right of the middle, going soft at their bottoms. They never read as one solid block.

pull-far-trunks.start: Start at the top of one tall trunk whose middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge of the canvas.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush at the top of the trunk, then roll onto its edge and lighten as you pull straight down so the line thins out. Do the same for the other trunks, each one standing straight up, with a few close together near the middle of the canvas.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Make about a dozen thin trunks across the middle, thin and pale because they are far away in the haze. Let them fade out toward the bottom.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave plenty of space between the trunks and keep the left sky glow clear.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Thin, pale trunks stand faintly in the mist, with no bark marks. Don't make them as dark as the trees you'll add next.

stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tallest fir, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, in the group right of the middle.
stamp-pines.strokes: Spread the fan brush and stamp with the middle tips of Pine dark. Work down in a zigzag, pressing harder as you go so the fir widens toward its base. Make two tall firs side by side, a smaller one at their left, and the start of another at the right edge.
stamp-pines.inside: The paint goes only into the fir shapes, each light and thin at the tip and heaviest at the bottom. The group runs from about 10 in from the left edge to near the right edge.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the pale trunks and blue haze showing around the firs, and keep the left of the canvas clear.
stamp-pines.stop: A dark blue-green group of firs sits right of the middle, flat and dark with no lighter side yet. If the marks go clumpy, thin the paint a little and stamp with the middle tips.

tap-pine-light.start: Start at the top of the left side of the tallest fir, where its dark paint faces the sun.
tap-pine-light.strokes: Stamp with the middle tips of the fan, going down each fir in a zigzag. Stamp lightly near the tip and press a little harder lower down.
tap-pine-light.inside: Pine teal goes only on the left side of each fir, because the sun is on the left. The right side of each fir stays dark so the tree looks round.
tap-pine-light.leave: Leave the dark Pine dark showing on the right side of every fir, and some dark between the teal taps.
tap-pine-light.stop: Each fir has dusty teal light down its left side and stays dark on its right. Keep the teal as taps, not a flat coat.

dab-bush-darks.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, a little above where the ground will be, and work toward the path.
dab-bush-darks.strokes: Load only a little Olive moss on the tip of the stiff brush, with no water. Tap in loose masses, tapping a spot again to make it more solid. Do the same along the foot of the pines at the right. Then tap a few small scattered dabs near the top edge of the canvas, as the first leaves.
dab-bush-darks.inside: Most of the paint is in the bottom half of the canvas, in the bush masses. Let the masses run down past where the ground will start.
dab-bush-darks.leave: Leave gaps so the mist shows through between the masses. Keep the middle of the path clear.
dab-bush-darks.stop: Dark olive bush masses sit across the middle of the canvas with mist between them. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-canopy-darks.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas at the left, and tap loose clusters along it.
dab-canopy-darks.strokes: Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the stiff brush, keeping the brush nearly dry. Tap one spot more to make it more solid, and let the clusters hang down in loose, ragged shapes. Then tap a little orange onto the top of the left bush mass, starting at the left edge of the canvas. Last, add a few small dabs low down by the pines.
dab-canopy-darks.inside: Most of the orange is in the left half of the canvas, because the sun glows there. Put just a few clusters in the upper right.
dab-canopy-darks.leave: Leave sky between the clusters, and leave the olive of the bushes showing under the orange.
dab-canopy-darks.stop: Loose orange leaf clusters hang along the top of the canvas, with orange also on the left bush mass. Keep them dappled, not solid.

dab-golden-leaves.start: Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, in the orange cluster nearest the sun.
dab-golden-leaves.strokes: Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the stiff brush, nearly dry. Cover most of each orange cluster, more toward the left. Then tap over the tops and left sides of the bush masses, thickest on the left, using a few more taps where you want it brightest.
dab-golden-leaves.inside: The sunny side catches the gold, so the gold sits over the top and left of each mass. The darker orange and olive stay in the shadows.
dab-golden-leaves.leave: Leave some orange showing in each canopy cluster and some olive under the bushes. Leave the right side of the canvas mostly alone.
dab-golden-leaves.stop: The canopy and bushes glow golden, with orange and olive showing in their shadows. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the canopy clusters nearest the sun.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, using only a little Pale lemon. Make small taps on the left edges of the canopy clusters and on the tops of the left-hand bushes. Then tap a few soft sunny patches in the glow below the bushes, mostly at the left of the canvas.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: These are only the lightest sparkles. They sit where the sun hits first, so keep them on the left sides and tops.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the gold and orange underneath showing around each tap.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Small pale lemon lights sparkle on the sunny side of the leaves, and a few glow patches sit in the lower part of the canvas. Keep them as taps, not a coat.

dab-floor-darks.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, just below the golden bushes.
dab-floor-darks.strokes: Tap Rust brown with the tip of the stiff brush, working along that line and then downward to the bottom edge. Tap the same spots again and again so each patch gets solid, and cover the glowing sky completely.
dab-floor-darks.inside: The leaf floor covers the whole lower third, from the left edge to the right edge. Its top edge is a ragged line along the bottom of the golden undergrowth.
dab-floor-darks.leave: Leave the bushes above untouched, and the golden bush dabs along the top edge of the floor.
dab-floor-darks.stop: The whole lower third is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

pull-path.start: First mark a dot where the path disappears, about 9 1/2 in from the left edge and 8 in from the top edge, just right of the center. Draw two faint lines fanning out from it toward you. Start your first strokes at the dot.
pull-path.strokes: Pull Path tan with the 1/2 inch flat along those lines, thin near the dot, getting a little wider as you come toward you. Check that the strokes run along your two lines and don't cross each other.
pull-path.inside: Only the far end of the path gets solid tan, about 1 1/2 in wide where it is widest. Past that, let the path fade into the leaves, because it lies down and goes toward you.
pull-path.leave: Leave the rust leaves on both sides of the path showing, and keep the strip thin near the dot.
pull-path.stop: A pale tan strip runs into the grove, narrowing to a thread at the dot. It is plain, with no leaves on it yet.

block-in-boulder.start: Start in the middle of the boulder, about 11 3/4 in from the left edge of the canvas, right of the path.
block-in-boulder.strokes: Paint a low dome first with Olive moss, as one simple shape about 2 1/2 in wide. Then add a curved piece on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges. Leave small overlaps so the pieces show.
block-in-boulder.inside: The boulder sits on the leaf floor at the foot of the pines, with its flat bottom resting on the leaves. Fill it as one flat olive color.
block-in-boulder.leave: Leave the path and the leaves around it showing, and don't shade or light it yet.
block-in-boulder.stop: A flat olive boulder sits right of the path, built from three curved pieces with no shading yet.

shade-boulder.start: Start at the top of the dome, just right of its middle, and work down.
shade-boulder.strokes: Pull Dark olive in curved strokes that bend with the dome, down along the right side of the boulder. Then curve along the bottom of the boulder, where it sits on the leaves.
shade-boulder.inside: The shadow goes on the right side and base, because the light comes from the upper left. This is what makes it look round.
shade-boulder.leave: Leave the top and the left side of the boulder as flat olive.
shade-boulder.stop: The boulder is dark on its right side and base, and still flat olive on its top and left.

light-boulder.start: Start at the upper left of the boulder, near the top of the dome, where it faces the sun.
light-boulder.strokes: Dip only the tip of the stiff brush in Pale moss and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly over the top and upper left of the boulder in short curved strokes that follow the dome. Build it up in a few light passes.
light-boulder.inside: The moss catches the light on top and on the sunny left side, in a patch about 1 1/2 in wide. It stays off the dark right side.
light-boulder.leave: Leave the olive in the middle and the dark olive on the right showing through the broken marks.
light-boulder.stop: The boulder looks round: pale moss on the top left, olive in the middle, dark on the right. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the olive back over part of it.

pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of the nearest big trunk, the left-hand one of the two big leaning trunks left of center, down on the leaves.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full width of the 3/4 inch flat for the thick base, then lighten and pull up and slightly right, off the top edge of the canvas, tapering as you go. Make the others the same way. Pull a few thick branches out sideways from the upper trunks, lifting as you go.
pull-birches.inside: There are six trunks: a thin one at the left edge, the two big leaning ones, a thin one at the right of the path, and two at the right, the right-hand one widest. Each is wide at its base.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the golden canopy showing between the trunks and the path and boulder clear.
pull-birches.stop: Six flat pale gray-white trunks with a few branches stand over the leaves and mist, with no shading or marks yet.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top of the left-hand big leaning trunk and work down its right side.
shade-birches.strokes: Load only the tip of the stiff brush with Bark gray and wipe it nearly dry. Skim down each trunk and branch in light, broken strokes, heavier along the right side and across the trunk's middle, a little darker toward the base.
shade-birches.inside: The shade goes on the right side of every trunk and branch, because the light comes from the left. This makes them look round.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged patches of pale gray-white showing, and leave the foot of each trunk pale for now.
shade-birches.stop: The trunks look round, gray with white patches showing, and have no dark marks yet. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the pale gray back over part of it.

mark-birch-bark.start: Start at the foot of the nearest big trunk and work up, where the marks are thickest.
mark-birch-bark.strokes: Press the angle brush on its flat for the thick part of each mark, then lift onto its tip so it tapers. Make short, broken marks across each trunk, and paint the dark branches the same way. Fill in a dark foot where each trunk meets the ground.
mark-birch-bark.inside: Put more marks toward the base and fewer higher up. The dark feet make the trunks sit on the ground.
mark-birch-bark.leave: Leave plenty of pale bark between the marks. Don't make long, even bands.
mark-birch-bark.stop: The trunks are clearly birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet. The bark has no sunlit edge yet.

dab-orange-leaves.first: Let the dark bark marks dry.
dab-orange-leaves.start: Start near the foot of the left-hand big trunk, at the bottom of the canvas, and work across the floor.
dab-orange-leaves.strokes: Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the stiff brush, with no water. Tap in loose dabs so each one reads as a leaf, going edge to edge.
dab-orange-leaves.inside: Cover most of the floor, with a few dabs spilling onto the path, more at its front, and a few over the dark foot of each trunk so they sit in the leaves.
dab-orange-leaves.leave: Leave rust brown showing between the dabs.
dab-orange-leaves.stop: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust-brown in the gaps, orange leaves on the path, and the trunk feet sitting in the leaves.

dab-gold-leaves.start: Start at the far end of the path, about 8 in from the top edge of the canvas, and work toward you.
dab-gold-leaves.strokes: Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, with only a little Golden yellow. Make a trail of dabs down the middle of the path, then scatter more at either side of it.
dab-gold-leaves.inside: Put fewer gold dabs than orange. They go where the sun falls on the leaves, along the path and over the leaves near the foot of the left trunks.
dab-gold-leaves.leave: Leave the orange and rust showing around the gold.
dab-gold-leaves.stop: Golden leaves catch the sun on the floor and down the path, with orange and rust still showing. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

light-birch-bark.start: Start at the top of the left-hand big leaning trunk, down its left edge.
light-birch-bark.strokes: Dip only the tip of the stiff brush in Bark white and wipe it nearly dry. Skim down the left side of each trunk and branch in light, broken strokes. Go over the dark marks in places, so the light catches the bark.
light-birch-bark.inside: The sunny left side of all six trunks gets the light, because the sun is on the left. The right sides stay gray.
light-birch-bark.leave: Leave the gray right side of every trunk, the dark marks, and the dark feet showing.
light-birch-bark.stop: Sunlit white birches with dark bark marks lean over the golden path into the misty blue grove. This is the finished painting.

blend-sky.text: Start at the sun spot, high in the upper left corner of the canvas, with Sun cream. Work outward from there.

Use short strokes that cross like overlapping X shapes. Carry Warm gold across the left half, then bring Haze blue in from the right and across the top right. Where the colors meet, keep crossing X strokes so they melt together. Finish with a few light, longer side-to-side strokes while it is still wet.
The cream glow sits around the sun because the light comes from the upper left. The gold fades toward the middle, and the blue gets deeper at the right edge of the canvas and along the top.
Nothing. Cover the white canvas completely, so no bare white shows. Don't paint any trees yet.
The whole canvas is one soft, misty glow: pale cream at the upper left, gold across the left half, and blue on the right.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the wet sky blend dry all the way through.
Start at the tops of the far trees, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, right of the middle.

Put only the tip of the brush in Misty blue and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly over the sky in rough up-and-down strokes to make ragged tree tops. Work down in a few light passes, letting the strokes break up and fade out at the bottom of each tree.
The trees sit from the middle toward the right edge of the canvas, with most of the paint right of the middle. They are soft shapes in the mist, so keep them see-through.
Leave the sky's glow clear at the left of the canvas, and leave the sky showing through the broken marks.
Faint blue tree shapes fill the right of the middle, going soft at their bottoms. They never read as one solid block.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the far treeline dry.
Start at the top of the tallest far trunk, left of the pines, and pull down.

Press the full width of the angle brush at the top of the trunk, then roll onto its edge and lighten as you pull straight down so the line thins out. Do the same for the other trunks, each one standing straight up, with a few close together near the middle of the canvas.
Make about a dozen thin trunks across the middle, thin and pale because they are far away in the haze. Let them fade out toward the bottom.
Leave plenty of space between the trunks and keep the left sky glow clear.
Thin, pale trunks stand faintly in the mist, with no bark marks. Don't make them as dark as the trees you'll add next.

stamp-pines.text: Let the far trunks dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest fir, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, in the group right of the middle.

Spread the fan brush and stamp with the middle tips of Pine dark. Work down in a zigzag, pressing harder as you go so the fir widens toward its base. Make two tall firs side by side, a smaller one at their left, and the start of another at the right edge.
The paint goes only into the fir shapes, each light and thin at the tip and heaviest at the bottom. The group runs from about 10 in from the left edge to near the right edge.
Leave the pale trunks and blue haze showing around the firs, and keep the left of the canvas clear.
A dark blue-green group of firs sits right of the middle, flat and dark with no lighter side yet. If the marks go clumpy, thin the paint a little and stamp with the middle tips.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the dark pines dry.
Start at the top of the left side of the tallest fir, where its dark paint faces the sun.
Stamp with the middle tips of the fan, going down each fir in a zigzag. Stamp lightly near the tip and press a little harder lower down.
Pine teal goes only on the sun side of each fir, because the sun is on the left. The shadow side of each fir stays dark so the tree looks round.
Leave the dark Pine dark showing on the shadow side of every fir, and some dark between the teal taps.
Each fir has dusty teal light down its sun side and stays dark on the shadow side. Keep the teal as taps, not a flat coat.

dab-bush-darks.text: Let the pines dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, a little above where the ground will be, and work toward the path.

Load only a little Olive moss on the tip of the stiff brush, with no water. Tap in loose masses, tapping a spot again to make it more solid. Do the same along the foot of the pines at the right. Then tap a few small scattered dabs near the top edge of the canvas, as the first leaves.
Most of the paint is in the bottom half of the canvas, in the bush masses. Let the masses run down past where the ground will start.
Leave gaps so the mist shows through between the masses. Keep the middle of the path clear.
Dark olive bush masses sit across the middle of the canvas with mist between them. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-canopy-darks.text: Let the olive dabs dry.
Start at the top edge of the canvas at the left, and tap loose clusters along it.

Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the stiff brush, keeping the brush nearly dry. Tap one spot more to make it more solid, and let the clusters hang down in loose, ragged shapes. Then tap a little orange onto the top of the left bush mass, starting at the left edge of the canvas. Last, add a few small dabs low down by the pines.
Most of the orange is in the left half of the canvas, because the sun glows there. Put just a few clusters in the upper right.
Leave sky between the clusters, and leave the olive of the bushes showing under the orange.
Loose orange leaf clusters hang along the top of the canvas, with orange also on the left bush mass. Keep them dappled, not solid.

dab-golden-leaves.text: Let the orange dabs dry.
Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, in the orange cluster nearest the sun.

Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the stiff brush, nearly dry. Cover most of each orange cluster, more toward the left. Then tap over the tops and left sides of the bush masses, thickest on the left, using a few more taps where you want it brightest.
The sunny side catches the gold, so the gold sits over the tops and sun-facing sides of the clusters and bushes. The darker orange and olive stay in the shadows.
Leave some orange showing in each canopy cluster and some olive in the bushes. Leave the right side of the canvas mostly alone.
The canopy and bushes glow golden, with orange and olive showing in their shadows. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the golden dabs dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the canopy clusters nearest the sun.

Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, using only a little Pale lemon. Make small taps on the left edges of the canopy clusters and on the tops of the left-hand bushes. Then tap a few soft sunny patches in the glowing ground area, mostly toward the sun.
These are only the lightest sparkles. They sit where the sun hits first, so keep them on the sun-facing sides and tops.
Leave the gold and orange underneath showing around each tap.
Small pale lemon lights sparkle on the sunny side of the leaves, and a few glow patches sit in the lower part of the canvas. Keep them as taps, not a coat.
