The leaf floor covers the whole lower third, from the left edge to the right edge. Its top edge is a ragged line along the bottom of the golden undergrowth.
Leave the bushes as they are, with their golden dabs showing where the floor starts.
The whole lower third is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

pull-path.text: Let the rust floor dry.

Pull Path tan with the 1/2 inch flat along those lines, thin near the dot, getting a little wider as you come toward you. Check that the strokes run along your two lines and don't cross each other.
Only the far end of the path gets solid tan, about 1 1/2 in wide where it is widest. Past that, let the path fade into the leaves, because it lies down and goes toward you.
Leave the rust leaves on both sides of the path showing, and keep the strip thin near the dot.
A pale tan strip runs into the grove, narrowing to a thread at the dot. It is plain, with no leaves on it yet.

Start in the middle of the boulder, about 11 3/4 in from the left edge of the canvas, right of the path.
Paint a low dome first with Olive moss, as one simple shape about 2 1/2 in wide. Then add a curved piece on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges. Leave small overlaps so the pieces show.
The boulder sits on the leaf floor at the foot of the pines, with its flat bottom resting on the leaves. Fill it as one flat olive color.
Leave the path and the leaves around it showing, and don't shade or light it yet.
A flat olive boulder sits right of the path, built from three curved pieces with no shading yet.

Pull Dark olive in curved strokes that bend with the dome, down along the right side of the boulder. Then curve along the bottom of the boulder, where it sits on the leaves.
The shadow goes on the right side and base, because the light comes from the upper left. This is what makes it look round.
Leave the top and the left side of the boulder as flat olive.
The boulder is dark on its right side and base, and still flat olive on its top and left.

The moss catches the light on top and on the sunny left side, in a patch about 1 1/2 in wide. It stays off the dark right side.
Leave the olive in the middle and the dark olive on the right showing through the broken marks.
The boulder looks round: pale moss on the top left, olive in the middle, dark on the right. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the olive back over part of it.

Leave plenty of pale bark between the marks. Don't make long, even bands.
The trunks are clearly birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet. The bark has no sunlit edge yet.

Cover most of the floor, with a few dabs spilling onto the path, more at its front, and a few over the dark foot of each trunk so they sit in the leaves.
Leave rust brown showing between the dabs.

Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, with only a little Golden yellow. Make a trail of dabs down the middle of the path, then scatter more at either side of it.
Put fewer gold dabs than orange. They go where the sun falls on the leaves, along the path and over the leaves near the foot of the left trunks.
Leave the orange and rust showing around the gold.
Golden leaves catch the sun on the floor and down the path, with orange and rust still showing. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

The sunny left side of all six trunks gets the light, because the sun is on the left. The right sides stay gray.

Start at the top of the left side of the tallest fir, where its dark paint faces the sun.
You are using the same fan brush and the same zigzag stamping as the dark pines. This time the paint is lighter, and it goes only on the sun side of each fir.

Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, in the orange cluster nearest the sun.
Same stiff brush and same taps as the orange canopy. Golden yellow goes over the orange, and you let the orange show through.

Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the stiff brush, nearly dry. Cover most of each orange cluster, more toward the left. Then tap over the tops and left sides of the bush masses, thickest on the left, using a few more taps where you want it brightest.

Leave some orange showing in each canopy cluster and some olive in the bushes. Leave the right side of the canvas mostly alone.
The canopy and bushes glow golden, with orange and olive showing in their shadows. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the golden dabs dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the canopy clusters nearest the sun.
These are the same taps you made with the golden leaves. This time use the small round brush and a lighter paint, and tap far fewer of them.

Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, using only a little Pale lemon. Make small taps on the left edges of the canopy clusters and on the tops of the left-hand bushes. Then tap a few soft sunny patches in the glowing ground area, mostly toward the sun.

You tap with the same stiff brush as the dark undergrowth. This time tap the same spots again and again until the floor is solid.

light-boulder.text: Let the dark olive dry.

This is the same nearly dry skim you used for the far trees. Here it lets the dark shade of the boulder show through the pale moss.

Start at the foot of the nearest big trunk, the left-hand one of the two big leaning trunks left of center, down on the leaves.
It is the same press-then-lighten pull as the far trunks. Now you use a wide flat brush, so each trunk is bold, wide at its base and thin at the top.

Press the full width of the 3/4 inch flat for the thick base, then lighten and pull up and slightly right, off the top edge of the canvas, tapering as you go. Make the others the same way. Pull a few thick branches out sideways from the upper trunks, lifting as you go.
Each is wide at its base.
Leave the golden canopy showing between the trunks and keep the path and boulder clear.
Six flat pale gray-white trunks with a few branches stand over the leaves and mist, with no shading or marks yet.

shade-birches.text: Let the birch gray dry.
Start at the top of the left-hand big leaning trunk and work down its right side.
This is the same nearly dry skim you used to light the boulder. Here you skim shade down the trunks.

Load only the tip of the stiff brush with Bark gray and wipe it nearly dry. Skim down each trunk and branch in light, broken strokes, heavier along the right side and across the trunk's middle, a little darker toward the base.
The shade goes on the right side of every trunk and branch, because the light comes from the left. This makes them look round.
Leave ragged patches of pale gray-white showing, and leave the foot of each trunk pale for now.
The trunks look round, gray with white patches showing, and have no dark marks yet. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the pale gray back over part of it.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the gray shading dry.
Start at the foot of the nearest big trunk and work up, where the marks are thickest.
You use the same angle brush and the same press-then-lift as the far trunks. Now the marks are short, dark and broken, so they look like bark.

Press the angle brush on its flat for the thick part of each mark, then lift onto its tip so it tapers. Make short, broken marks across each trunk, and paint the dark branches the same way. Fill in a dark foot where each trunk meets the ground.
Put more marks toward the base and fewer higher up. The dark feet make the trunks sit on the ground.
Leave plenty of pale bark between the marks. Don't make long, even bands.
The trunks are clearly birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet. The bark has no sunlit edge yet.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the dark bark marks dry.
Start near the foot of the left-hand big trunk, at the bottom of the canvas, and work across the floor.
Leaf orange is the paint of the canopy, and the stiff brush taps the same way. Now it falls as leaves on the ground.
Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the stiff brush, with no water. Tap in loose dabs so each one reads as a leaf, going edge to edge.
Cover most of the floor, with a few dabs spilling onto the path, more at its front, and a few over the dark foot of each trunk so they sit in the leaves.
Leave rust brown showing between the dabs.
The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust-brown in the gaps, orange leaves on the path, and the trunk feet sitting in the leaves.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the orange leaves dry.
Start at the far end of the path, about 8 in from the top edge of the canvas, and work toward you.
You are using the same small round brush and the same light taps as the sunlit leaf tips. The paint is the golden yellow of the canopy, now on the ground.
Use the #10 round and tap with its tip, with only a little Golden yellow. Make a trail of dabs down the middle of the path, then scatter more at either side of it.
Put fewer gold dabs than orange. They go where the sun falls on the leaves, along the path and over the leaves near the foot of the left trunks.
Leave the orange and rust showing around the gold.
Golden leaves catch the sun on the floor and down the path, with orange and rust still showing. If a patch goes too solid, tap over it with another mix to break it up.

light-birch-bark.text: Let the golden leaves dry.
Start at the top of the left-hand big leaning trunk, down its left edge.
This is the same dry-brush skim you used to shade the trunks. Now it goes on the sunny side, with the shade left showing on the other.

Dip only the tip of the stiff brush in Bark white and wipe it nearly dry. Skim down the left side of each trunk and branch in light, broken strokes. Go over the dark marks in places, so the light catches the bark.
The sunny left side of all six trunks gets the light, because the sun is on the left. The right sides stay gray.
Leave the gray right side of every trunk, the dark marks, and the dark feet showing.
Sunlit white birches with dark bark marks lean over the golden path into the misty blue grove. This is the finished painting.

opening.welcome: You are going to paint a misty autumn birch grove: pale trunks lean over a leaf-covered path that runs into a blue haze. The eye should travel up the path to where it melts into the mist, framed by the trunks. What makes it sing is the glow of the low sun against the cool blue behind.
opening.light: The low sun sits in the glowing mist and shines through it across the whole grove. Everything on its sunny face gets the lightest, warmest paint, and everything turned away from it gets the darkest. The far side of the picture, away from the sun, is cooler and bluer.

skills.how: Dabbing is tapping with only the tip of a nearly dry brush, so the paint lands as dots and dappled patches. Here it builds every leaf in the picture: bushes, canopy and fallen leaves, always dark first and then lighter paint added over it. Watch for blobs; if they appear, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

Dry brush means a barely loaded brush skimmed lightly, so the paint breaks up and lets the earlier paint show through. You use it for the soft far trees, the moss on the boulder and the shade and sun on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

You press the brush down for a wide start, then lighten and turn onto its edge so the line tapers to a point. That one move makes the far trunks, the big birches wide at the ground and thin high up, and the bark marks. The lighter you press, the thinner the line gets.

opening.road: We start with one wet glow over the whole canvas, because the mist and the sun are what everything else sits in. Then we move forward one layer at a time, beginning with the far wood of hazy trees and dark pines. Next come the golden leaves, then the leaf floor and path, and the boulder that sits on it. The birches go on later because they are the nearest things, and they cover what is behind them. The fallen leaves and the last light on the bark finish it, since the brightest touches always go on last.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the glow that every later color and highlight sits in.
the-misty-sky.end: The whole canvas is a soft misty glow, with a pale sun spot warming into gold and cooling into blue.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the far wood in the haze, so the picture has depth behind everything else.
the-far-wood.end: Faint blue trees and thin pale trunks fade into the mist, with a group of dark pines lit by the sun on their sunny faces.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage builds the leaves in the canopy and bushes, dark to light, so they glow.
the-golden-leaves.end: The canopy and undergrowth glow golden, with orange and olive in their shadows and small sparkles of pale lemon where the sun hits.

the-ground.for: This stage gives the picture its floor and the path that leads the eye into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dark rust-brown leaf floor fills the base of the canvas, with a pale path narrowing into the haze.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds a round, mossy rock in three steps: its shape, its shadow, then its light.
the-boulder.end: The boulder sits on the leaves looking round, with pale moss on its sunny face and dark on its shadow side.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the nearest trunks over everything else, then shades and marks them until they read as birches.
the-birches.end: Tall birches with gray shade and broken dark marks lean over the golden leaves and the path.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage covers the dark floor with bright leaves, so the ground matches the glow overhead.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The floor and path are a warm carpet of orange and gold leaves, with rust brown showing in the gaps.

the-last-lights.for: This stage adds the brightest touch last, sunlight along the bark.
the-last-lights.end: The painting is finished: sunlit white birches with dark marks lean over a golden path into the misty blue grove.

back.text: Haze blue is the same misty blue you blended into the sky. Now you pull it as thin lines, so the trunks look like part of the haze.
You are using the same fan brush and the same zigzag stamping as the dark pines. This time the paint is lighter, and it goes only on the sun side of each fir.
This is the same stiff brush and the same dry tapping you used for the dark undergrowth. Only the paint changes, to warm orange.
Same stiff brush and same taps as the orange canopy. Golden yellow goes over the orange, and you let the orange show through.
These are the same taps you made with the golden leaves. This time use the small round brush and a lighter paint, and tap far fewer of them.
You tap with the same stiff brush as the dark undergrowth. This time tap the same spots again and again until the floor is solid.
This is the same nearly dry skim you used for the far trees. Here it lets the dark shade of the boulder show through the pale moss.
It is the same press-then-lighten pull as the far trunks. Now you use a wide flat brush, so each trunk is bold, wide at its base and thin at the top.
This is the same nearly dry skim you used to light the boulder. Here you skim shade down the trunks.
You use the same angle brush and the same press-then-lift as the far trunks. Now the marks are short, dark and broken, so they look like bark.
Leaf orange is the paint of the canopy, and the stiff brush taps the same way. Now it falls as leaves on the ground.
You are using the same small round brush and the same light taps as the sunlit leaf tips. The paint is the golden yellow of the canopy, now on the ground.
This is the same dry-brush skim you used to shade the trunks. Now it goes on the sunny side, with the shade left showing on the other.

taken_out.sentence: There are six trunks: a thin one at the far left of the canvas, the two big leaning ones, a thin one right of the path, and two on the right of the canvas, the right-hand one widest.
taken_out.why: step 15 (pull-birches), line 4 (inside): "left of the canvas" can't find 'the canvas' on the sheet; sheet: nothing on the sheet

blend-sky.start: Start with Sun cream in the misty sky's upper left corner, where the sun glows, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Work short criss-cross X strokes outward from the glow, then go over it while wet with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes.
blend-sky.inside: Sun cream around the sun, Warm gold spreading across the left half, and Haze blue on the right and across the top, because the light comes from the upper left.
blend-sky.leave: Leave no white canvas: the glow runs from the left edge to the right edge and down to the bottom edge.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is one soft misty glow, palest at the sun and bluest at the upper right, with soft blotchy light low down.

brush-far-treeline.start: Start at the top of the far tree line near the right edge; the far wood's middle is about 9 in from the left edge.
brush-far-treeline.strokes: Skim Misty blue down from the ragged tree tops with a dry brush and light pressure, letting it break up as you go.
brush-far-treeline.inside: The tree shapes are tall and deepest on the right side of the far wood, and run lower and fainter toward the sun, where they fade into the gold glow.
brush-far-treeline.leave: Leave the misty sky clear around the sun and the misty ground glow below the trees.
brush-far-treeline.stop: Stop when soft, see-through blue tree shapes show in the haze, their bottoms fading into mist.

pull-far-trunks.first: Let the far tree line dry.
pull-far-trunks.start: Start each trunk at its top in the mist; the first is about 4 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the angle brush full width, then lift onto its edge as you pull straight down, so each trunk tapers.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Haze blue only: a few thin trunks standing upright in the mist among the Misty blue tree shapes.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the glow and the Misty blue tree shapes showing between the trunks.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Stop when a few pale, soft trunks stand faintly in the mist, with no bark marks.

stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tallest pine, its middle about 13 in from the left edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Stamp the fan's middle tips in a zigzag from each tip down, pressing harder as you go so each pine widens toward its base.
stamp-pines.inside: Pine dark fills a group of three or four firs from right of the middle out to the right edge, their bottoms meeting in one dark band.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the Misty blue tree shapes and the misty ground showing around and below the pines.
stamp-pines.stop: Stop when the pines read as flat, dark blue-green fir shapes with ragged needle edges.

tap-pine-light.start: Start along the edges of the pines facing the sun, near the top of the tallest one.
tap-pine-light.strokes: Tap the fan's middle tips lightly along the pine edges and across their bases, short taps in different directions.
tap-pine-light.inside: Pine teal sits along the ragged edges of the pines and in a hazy band where their bottoms meet the mist, softening them back into the haze.
tap-pine-light.leave: Leave the Pine dark showing in the middle of each pine.
tap-pine-light.stop: Stop when the pines are softly edged and their bases melt into the mist.

dab-bush-darks.start: Start with a band of dabs low across the pines' base, then along the top edge of the canvas.
dab-bush-darks.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush; tap more where you want a mass, less where it should break up.
dab-bush-darks.inside: Olive moss goes in loose leaf masses along the top of the canvas, in a heavy band under the pines, and in small clumps and a dappled spread across the misty ground, because these are the shadow leaves.
dab-bush-darks.leave: Leave lots of mist and sky showing through the gaps.
dab-bush-darks.stop: Stop when olive leaf masses are scattered over the canvas with the glow still showing between them.

dab-canopy-darks.start: Start with the big bush mass at the left edge of the canvas, about 4 in from the left edge at its middle.
dab-canopy-darks.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush, building the mass with clustered dabs.
dab-canopy-darks.inside: Leaf orange goes in a wide bush mass on the left, in clusters along the top of the canvas, and in a few dabs over the olive under the pines.
dab-canopy-darks.leave: Leave sky between the top clusters and some Olive moss showing low in the bushes.
dab-canopy-darks.stop: Stop when a solid orange bush sits on the left and loose orange clusters hang along the top.

dab-golden-leaves.start: Start at the top of the left bush and in the clusters near the top edge, close to the sun.
dab-golden-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
dab-golden-leaves.inside: Golden yellow sits on the tops and sunny sides of the left bush and the top clusters, most of it on the left side of the canvas, nearest the sun.
dab-golden-leaves.leave: Leave Leaf orange and Olive moss showing in the shadows under each cluster.
dab-golden-leaves.stop: Stop when the canopy and left bush glow golden with orange still in their shadows.

dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start around the sun, in the upper left corner of the canvas.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the round brush, never dragging.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Pale lemon goes in soft light patches around the sun and the canopy edges, on the sunny tops of the bushes, and in sunlit patches spread across the misty ground.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the golden and orange leaves showing around each light patch.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when sunlight sparkles through the canopy and lies in pale patches on the ground.

dab-floor-darks.start: Start at the bottom edge and work up; the leaf floor's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
dab-floor-darks.strokes: Tap firmly with the tip of the dry brush, tapping often so it covers.
dab-floor-darks.inside: Rust brown covers the whole floor from the left edge to the right edge, over the bottom of the bushes, because it is the darkest layer of leaves.
dab-floor-darks.leave: Leave the lower edge of the bushes showing as a ragged line along the floor's top.
dab-floor-darks.stop: Stop when the whole floor is a dense, dappled rust-brown with no mist showing.

pull-path.start: Mark the dot where the path vanishes into the mist, and start there; the path's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
pull-path.strokes: Pull each stroke along the fanned guide lines, thin at the dot and wider as you come forward.
pull-path.inside: Path tan makes one short strip running from the mist down toward you, narrow at the back.
pull-path.leave: Leave the Rust brown floor showing on both sides of the path.
pull-path.stop: Stop when a short pale tan strip leads back into the grove.

block-in-boulder.start: Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove; its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-boulder.strokes: Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it.
block-in-boulder.inside: Olive moss fills the whole boulder as one flat shape, flat along its bottom where it sits on the leaves.
block-in-boulder.leave: Leave the leaf floor and bushes showing around it.
block-in-boulder.stop: Stop when one flat olive dome sits beside the path, about 2 1/2 in wide.

shade-boulder.start: Start at the top of the boulder's dome.
shade-boulder.strokes: Bend each stroke over the dome and down its curve toward the base.
shade-boulder.inside: Dark olive covers most of the boulder, darkest where it sits on the leaves, because the light comes from the upper left.
shade-boulder.leave: Leave a hint of Olive moss on the side of the dome facing the sun.
shade-boulder.stop: Stop when the boulder reads as a dark, round rock.

light-boulder.start: Start on the top of the boulder, on the side facing the sun.
light-boulder.strokes: Skim the dry brush lightly over the top, following the curve.
light-boulder.inside: Pale moss sits on the top of the boulder, most of it on the left side of the boulder, where the sun hits the moss.
light-boulder.leave: Leave the Dark olive showing on the shadow side and the base.
light-boulder.stop: Stop when a crust of lit moss rides the top and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.start: Start each trunk at its foot in the leaves; the biggest one's middle is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full brush at the foot, then lighten as you pull up past the top edge; pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
pull-birches.inside: Birch gray makes six trunks: one at the left edge, two big ones leaning right, a thin one by the path, and two on the right.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves, pines and boulder showing between the trunks.
pull-birches.stop: Stop when six flat pale trunks stand over the scene with no shading.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top of each trunk.
shade-birches.strokes: Skim the dry brush down each trunk with light pressure.
shade-birches.inside: Bark gray covers most of each trunk and branch in broken patches, because the bark is shaded.
shade-birches.leave: Leave pale gaps of Birch gray in the bark, and the feet of the trunks pale.
shade-birches.stop: Stop when the trunks look gray and broken, with pale patches all down them.

mark-birch-bark.start: Start with the dark foot of the big trunk, about 1 3/4 in from the left edge.
mark-birch-bark.strokes: Press the angle brush across the trunk, then lift onto its edge so each mark tapers; drag the feet up from the leaves.
mark-birch-bark.inside: Bark dark makes short broken marks across every trunk and branch, and a solid dark foot at each base.
mark-birch-bark.leave: Leave the pale bark showing between the marks.
mark-birch-bark.stop: Stop when every trunk reads clearly as a birch with dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.start: Start at the bottom edge and work back toward the path.
dab-orange-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush, leaf-sized dabs.
dab-orange-leaves.inside: Leaf orange covers most of the floor and spills onto the path.
dab-orange-leaves.leave: Leave Rust brown showing between the leaves and the trunk feet dark.
dab-orange-leaves.stop: Stop when the floor is a warm orange carpet with rust in the gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.start: Start on the path where it comes into the light, near the floor's middle, about 8 1/2 in from the left edge.
dab-gold-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the round brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
dab-gold-leaves.inside: Golden yellow sits in a scattered band down the path and across the floor, fewer than the orange.
dab-gold-leaves.leave: Leave the orange and rust showing around them.
dab-gold-leaves.stop: Stop when golden leaves catch the sun along the path.

light-birch-bark.first: Let the leaves and bark marks dry.
light-birch-bark.start: Start at the top of the big trunk, about 3 in from the left edge.
light-birch-bark.strokes: Skim the dry brush down each trunk lightly, so it catches the bark.
light-birch-bark.inside: Bark white goes down the pale parts of every trunk and branch, the sunlit bark, over the gray in places.
light-birch-bark.leave: Leave the dark bark marks, the dark feet and some gray showing.
light-birch-bark.stop: Stop when the birches glow white with crisp dark marks.

blend-sky.text: Start with Sun cream in the misty sky's upper left corner, where the sun glows, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
Work short criss-cross X strokes outward from the glow, then go over it while wet with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes.
Sun cream around the sun, Warm gold spreading across the left half, and Haze blue on the right and across the top, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave no white canvas: the glow runs from the left edge to the right edge and down to the bottom edge.
Stop when the whole canvas is one soft misty glow, palest at the sun and bluest far from it, with soft blotchy light low down.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry completely.
Start at the top of the far tree line near the right edge; the far wood's middle is about 9 in from the left edge.
Skim Misty blue down from the ragged tree tops with a dry brush and light pressure, letting it break up as you go.
The tree shapes are tall and deepest on the right side of the far wood, and run lower and fainter toward the sun, where they fade into the gold glow.
Leave the misty sky clear around the sun, and the misty ground glow clear where the tree shapes fade out.
Stop when soft, see-through blue tree shapes show in the haze, their bottoms fading into mist.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the far tree line dry.
Start each trunk at its top in the mist; the first is about 4 in from the left edge.
Press the angle brush full width, then lift onto its edge as you pull straight down, so each trunk tapers.
Haze blue only: a few thin trunks standing upright in the mist among the Misty blue tree shapes.
Leave the glow and the Misty blue tree shapes showing between the trunks.
Stop when a few pale, soft trunks stand faintly in the mist, with no bark marks.

stamp-pines.text: Let the far trunks dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine, its middle about 13 in from the left edge.
Stamp the fan's middle tips in a zigzag from each tip down, pressing harder as you go so each pine widens toward its base.
Pine dark fills a group of three or four firs from right of the middle out to the right edge, their bottoms meeting in one dark band.
Leave the Misty blue tree shapes and the misty ground showing around and below the pines.
Stop when the pines read as flat, dark blue-green fir shapes with ragged needle edges.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the Pine dark dry.
Start along the edges of the pines facing the sun, near the top of the tallest one.
Tap the fan's middle tips lightly along the pine edges and across their bases, short taps in different directions.
Pine teal sits along the ragged edges of the pines and in a hazy band where their bottoms meet the mist, softening them back into the haze.
Leave the Pine dark showing in the middle of each pine.
Stop when the pines are softly edged and their bases melt into the mist.

dab-bush-darks.text: Let the pines dry.
Start with a band of dabs low across the pines' base, then along the top edge of the canvas.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush; tap more where you want a mass, less where it should break up.

Olive moss goes in loose leaf masses along the top of the canvas, in a heavy band under the pines, and in small clumps and a dappled spread across the misty ground, because these are the shadow leaves.
Leave lots of mist and sky showing through the gaps.
Stop when olive leaf masses are scattered over the canvas with the glow still showing between them.

dab-canopy-darks.text: Let the Olive moss dry.
Start with the big bush mass at the left edge of the canvas, about 4 in from the left edge at its middle.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, building the mass with clustered dabs.
Leaf orange goes in a wide bush mass on the left, in clusters along the top of the canvas, and in a few dabs over the olive under the pines.
Leave sky between the top clusters and some Olive moss showing low in the bushes.
Stop when a solid orange bush sits on the left and loose orange clusters hang along the top.

dab-golden-leaves.text: Let the Leaf orange dry.
Start at the top of the left bush and in the clusters near the top edge, close to the sun.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
Golden yellow sits on the tops and sunny sides of the left bush and the top clusters, most of it on the left side of the canvas, nearest the sun.
Leave Leaf orange and Olive moss showing in the shadows under each cluster.
Stop when the canopy and left bush glow golden with orange still in their shadows.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the Golden yellow dry.
Start around the sun, at the edges of the canopy clusters nearest it.
Tap lightly with the tip of the round brush, never dragging.
Pale lemon goes in soft light patches around the sun and the canopy edges, on the sunny tops of the bushes, and in sunlit patches spread across the misty ground.
Leave the golden and orange leaves showing around each light patch.
Stop when sunlight sparkles through the canopy and lies in pale patches on the ground.

dab-floor-darks.text: Let the leaves dry.
Start at the bottom edge and work up; the leaf floor's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
Tap firmly with the tip of the dry brush, tapping often so it covers.
Rust brown covers the whole floor from the left edge to the right edge, over the bottom of the bushes, because it is the darkest layer of leaves.
Leave the lower edge of the bushes showing as a ragged line along the floor's top.
Stop when the whole floor is a dense, dappled rust-brown with no mist showing.

pull-path.text: Let the Rust brown dry.
Mark the dot where the path vanishes into the mist, and start there; the path's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Pull each stroke along the fanned guide lines, thin at the dot and wider as you come forward.
Path tan makes one short strip running from the mist down toward you, narrow at the back.
Leave the Rust brown floor showing on both sides of the path.
Stop when a short pale tan strip leads back into the grove.

block-in-boulder.text: Let the path dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove; its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it.
Olive moss fills the whole boulder as one flat shape, flat along its bottom where it sits on the leaves.
Leave the leaf floor and bushes showing around it.
Stop when one flat olive dome sits beside the path, about 2 1/2 in wide.

shade-boulder.text: Let the Olive moss dry.
Start at the top of the boulder's dome.
Bend each stroke over the dome and down its curve toward the base.
Dark olive covers most of the boulder, darkest where it sits on the leaves, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave a hint of Olive moss on the side of the dome facing the sun.
Stop when the boulder reads as a dark, round rock.

light-boulder.text: Let the Dark olive dry.
Start on the top of the boulder, on the side facing the sun.
Skim the dry brush lightly over the top, following the curve.
Pale moss sits on the top of the boulder, most of it on the left side of the boulder, where the sun hits the moss.
Leave the Dark olive showing on the shadow side and the base.
Stop when a crust of lit moss rides the top and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.text: Let everything dry completely.
Start each trunk at its foot in the leaves; the biggest one's middle is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
Press the full brush at the foot, then lighten as you pull up past the top edge; pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
Birch gray makes six trunks: a thin one nearest the sun, two big ones leaning toward the path, a thin one by the path, and two beyond the boulder.
Leave the leaves, pines and boulder showing between the trunks.
Stop when six flat pale trunks stand over the scene with no shading.

shade-birches.text: Let the Birch gray dry.
Start at the top of each trunk.
Skim the dry brush down each trunk with light pressure.
Bark gray covers most of each trunk and branch in broken patches, because the bark is shaded.
Leave pale gaps of Birch gray in the bark, and the feet of the trunks pale.
Stop when the trunks look gray and broken, with pale patches all down them.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the Bark gray dry.
Start with the dark foot of the big trunk, about 1 3/4 in from the left edge.
Press the angle brush across the trunk, then lift onto its edge so each mark tapers; drag the feet up from the leaves.
Bark dark makes short broken marks across every trunk and branch, and a solid dark foot at each base.
Leave the pale bark showing between the marks.
Stop when every trunk reads clearly as a birch with dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start at the bottom edge and work back toward the path.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, leaf-sized dabs.
Leaf orange covers most of the floor and spills onto the path.
Leave Rust brown showing between the leaves and the trunk feet dark.
Stop when the floor is a warm orange carpet with rust in the gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the Leaf orange dry.
Start on the path where it comes into the light, near the floor's middle, about 8 1/2 in from the left edge.
Tap with the tip of the round brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
Golden yellow sits in a scattered band down the path and across the floor, fewer than the orange.
Leave the orange and rust showing around them.
Stop when golden leaves catch the sun along the path.

light-birch-bark.text: Let the leaves and bark marks dry.
Start at the top of the big trunk, about 3 in from the left edge.
Skim the dry brush down each trunk lightly, so it catches the bark.
Bark white goes down the pale parts of every trunk and branch, the sunlit bark, over the gray in places.
Leave the dark bark marks, the dark feet and some gray showing.
Stop when the birches glow white with crisp dark marks.

blend-sky.text: Start with Sun cream in the misty sky's upper left corner, where the sun glows, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
Work short criss-cross X strokes outward from the glow, then go over it while wet with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes.
Sun cream around the sun, Warm gold spreading across the left half, and Haze blue on the right and across the top, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave no white canvas: the glow runs from the left edge to the right edge and down to the bottom edge.
Stop when the whole canvas is one soft misty glow, palest at the sun and bluest far from it, with soft blotchy light low down.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry completely.
Start at the top of the far tree line near the right edge; the far wood's middle is about 9 in from the left edge.
Skim Misty blue down from the ragged tree tops with a dry brush and light pressure, letting it break up as you go.
The tree shapes are tall and deepest on the right side of the far wood, and run lower and fainter toward the sun, where they fade into the gold glow.
Leave the misty sky clear around the sun, and the misty ground glow clear where the tree shapes fade out.
Stop when soft, see-through blue tree shapes show in the haze, their bottoms fading into mist.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the far tree line dry.
Start each trunk at its top in the mist; the first is about 4 in from the left edge.
Press the angle brush full width, then lift onto its edge as you pull straight down, so each trunk tapers.
Haze blue only: a few thin trunks standing upright in the mist among the Misty blue tree shapes.
Leave the glow and the Misty blue tree shapes showing between the trunks.
Stop when a few pale, soft trunks stand faintly in the mist, with no bark marks.

stamp-pines.text: Let the far trunks dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine, its middle about 13 in from the left edge.
Stamp the fan's middle tips in a zigzag from each tip down, pressing harder as you go so each pine widens toward its base.
Pine dark fills a group of three or four firs from right of the middle out to the right edge, their bottoms meeting in one dark band.
Leave the Misty blue tree shapes and the misty ground showing around and below the pines.
Stop when the pines read as flat, dark blue-green fir shapes with ragged needle edges.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the Pine dark dry.
Start along the edges of the pines facing the sun, near the top of the tallest one.
The same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines, now with Pine teal and a lighter touch, only along their edges.
Tap the fan's middle tips lightly along the pine edges and across their bases, short taps in different directions.
Pine teal sits along the ragged edges of the pines and in a hazy band where their bottoms meet the mist, softening them back into the haze.
Leave the Pine dark showing in the middle of each pine.
Stop when the pines are softly edged and their bases melt into the mist.

dab-bush-darks.text: Let the pines dry.
Start with a band of dabs low across the pines' base, then along the top edge of the canvas.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush; tap more where you want a mass, less where it should break up.

Olive moss goes in loose leaf masses along the top of the canvas, in a heavy band under the pines, and in small clumps and a dappled spread across the misty ground, because these are the shadow leaves.
Leave lots of mist and sky showing through the gaps.
Stop when olive leaf masses are scattered over the canvas with the glow still showing between them.

dab-canopy-darks.text: Let the Olive moss dry.
Start with the big bush mass at the left edge of the canvas, about 4 in from the left edge at its middle.
The same dry tap you used for the olive undergrowth, now in Leaf orange and built into fuller clusters.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, building the mass with clustered dabs.
Leaf orange goes in a wide bush mass on the left, in clusters along the top of the canvas, and in a few dabs over the olive under the pines.
Leave sky between the top clusters and some Olive moss showing low in the bushes.
Stop when a solid orange bush sits on the left and loose orange clusters hang along the top.

dab-golden-leaves.text: Let the Leaf orange dry.
Start at the top of the left bush and in the clusters near the top edge, close to the sun.
The same dabbing as the orange leaves, now in Golden yellow, smaller dabs, kept to the sunny parts.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
Golden yellow sits on the tops and sunny sides of the left bush and the top clusters, most of it on the left side of the canvas, nearest the sun.
Leave Leaf orange and Olive moss showing in the shadows under each cluster.
Stop when the canopy and left bush glow golden with orange still in their shadows.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the Golden yellow dry.
Start around the sun, at the edges of the canopy clusters nearest it.
The same tapping as the golden leaves, but with the small round brush and the palest mix, just a few lights.
Tap lightly with the tip of the round brush, never dragging.
Pale lemon goes in soft light patches around the sun and the canopy edges, on the sunny tops of the bushes, and in sunlit patches spread across the misty ground.
Leave the golden and orange leaves showing around each light patch.
Stop when sunlight sparkles through the canopy and lies in pale patches on the ground.

dab-floor-darks.text: Let the leaves dry.
Start at the bottom edge and work up; the leaf floor's top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
The same dabbing you used for the undergrowth, but tapped often and firmly so it covers the whole floor.
Tap firmly with the tip of the dry brush, tapping often so it covers.
Rust brown covers the whole floor from the left edge to the right edge, over the bottom of the bushes, because it is the darkest layer of leaves.
Leave the lower edge of the bushes showing as a ragged line along the floor's top.
Stop when the whole floor is a dense, dappled rust-brown with no mist showing.

pull-path.text: Let the Rust brown dry.
Mark the dot where the path vanishes into the mist, and start there; the path's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Pull each stroke along the fanned guide lines, thin at the dot and wider as you come forward.
Path tan makes one short strip running from the mist down toward you, narrow at the back.
Leave the Rust brown floor showing on both sides of the path.
Stop when a short pale tan strip leads back into the grove.

block-in-boulder.text: Let the path dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path into the grove; its middle is about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
Olive moss again, the paint of the shadowed undergrowth, but now laid flat with a flat brush to make one solid shape.
Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it.
Olive moss fills the whole boulder as one flat shape, flat along its bottom where it sits on the leaves.
Leave the leaf floor and bushes showing around it.
Stop when one flat olive dome sits beside the path, about 2 1/2 in wide.

shade-boulder.text: Let the Olive moss dry.
Start at the top of the boulder's dome.
Bend each stroke over the dome and down its curve toward the base.
Dark olive covers most of the boulder, darkest where it sits on the leaves, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave a hint of Olive moss on the side of the dome facing the sun.
Stop when the boulder reads as a dark, round rock.

light-boulder.text: Let the Dark olive dry.
Start on the top of the boulder, on the side facing the sun.
The same dry, skimming brush you used for the misty far trees, now on a small patch of moss with Pale moss.
Skim the dry brush lightly over the top, following the curve.
Pale moss sits on the top of the boulder, most of it on the left side of the boulder, where the sun hits the moss.
Leave the Dark olive showing on the shadow side and the base.
Stop when a crust of lit moss rides the top and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.text: Let everything dry completely.
Start each trunk at its foot in the leaves; the biggest one's middle is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
The same thick-to-thin pull as the far trunks, but with a wider brush, pulled up from the foot, and much bigger.
Press the full brush at the foot, then lighten as you pull up past the top edge; pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
Birch gray makes six trunks: a thin one nearest the sun, two big ones leaning toward the path, a thin one by the path, and two beyond the boulder.
Leave the leaves, pines and boulder showing between the trunks.
Stop when six flat pale trunks stand over the scene with no shading.

shade-birches.text: Let the Birch gray dry.
Start at the top of each trunk.
The same dry brush you skimmed over the boulder's moss, now pulled down the long trunks in Bark gray.
Skim the dry brush down each trunk with light pressure.
Bark gray covers most of each trunk and branch in broken patches, because the bark is shaded.
Leave pale gaps of Birch gray in the bark, and the feet of the trunks pale.
Stop when the trunks look gray and broken, with pale patches all down them.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the Bark gray dry.
Start with the dark foot of the big trunk, about 1 3/4 in from the left edge.
The same angle brush and taper as the far trunks, but pressed across the bark in short broken marks.
Press the angle brush across the trunk, then lift onto its edge so each mark tapers; drag the feet up from the leaves.
Bark dark makes short broken marks across every trunk and branch, and a solid dark foot at each base.
Leave the pale bark showing between the marks.
Stop when every trunk reads clearly as a birch with dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start at the bottom edge and work back toward the path.
The same Leaf orange and dry tap you used for the canopy, now spread across the ground as fallen leaves.
Tap with the tip of the dry brush, leaf-sized dabs.
Leaf orange covers most of the floor and spills onto the path.
Leave Rust brown showing between the leaves and the trunk feet dark.
Stop when the floor is a warm orange carpet with rust in the gaps.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the Leaf orange dry.
Start on the path where it comes into the light, near the floor's middle, about 8 1/2 in from the left edge.
The same Golden yellow as the canopy's sunny leaves, now with the small round brush, fewer dabs, down the path.
Tap with the tip of the round brush, small leaf-sized dabs.
Golden yellow sits in a scattered band down the path and across the floor, fewer than the orange.
Leave the orange and rust showing around them.
Stop when golden leaves catch the sun along the path.

light-birch-bark.text: Let the leaves and bark marks dry.
Start at the top of the big trunk, about 3 in from the left edge.
The same dry skim you used to shade the trunks, now with Bark white for the sunlit bark.
Skim the dry brush down each trunk lightly, so it catches the bark.
Bark white goes down the pale parts of every trunk and branch, the sunlit bark, over the gray in places.
Leave the dark bark marks, the dark feet and some gray showing.
Stop when the birches glow white with crisp dark marks.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint an autumn birch grove: white trunks leaning over a leaf-covered path that runs back into a misty blue wood. The heart of it is the path where it disappears into the mist, framed by the birches. What makes it sing is the warm glow against the cool blue haze, and the bright bark against it all.
opening.light: The light is a low sun shining through the mist, and it sets the whole mood: everything near it glows cream and gold, and everything far from it cools to blue. On each thing you paint, the side facing the sun gets the lightest paint and the side turned away stays darker.

skills.how: Dabbing is tapping with just the tip of a dry brush, so the paint lands as dots and dappled patches instead of strokes. It builds every leaf in this painting, from the canopy and bushes to the carpet on the ground, always dark first and lighter on the sunny side. Watch for blobs: keep water off the brush and wipe most of the paint off before you tap.

Dry brush means only the tip of a dry brush in the paint, skimmed lightly so it breaks up and catches the canvas texture. Here it makes the hazy far trees, the lit moss on the boulder, and the shading and sunlight on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim the base color back over part of it.

Thick to thin is pressing the full brush and then easing onto its edge, so the line starts wide and tapers. It pulls the far trunks, the big birches with their branches, and the broken dark bark marks. Keep the pressure changing through the stroke, or the trunks come out like stiff poles.

opening.road: We start with one wet glow over the whole canvas, because the mist and the sun are what everything else sits in. Then we step forward one layer at a time: the hazy far trees and far trunks, and the dark pines. Next come the golden leaves of the canopy and bushes, dark to light. The leaf floor and path go in after them, then the mossy boulder. The birches go on over all of it, since they are nearest, and the fallen leaves and the sun on the bark finish the picture.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the glow of the low sun and the mist that everything else will sit in.
the-misty-sky.end: The whole canvas is a soft misty glow, warm cream and gold near the sun and cool haze blue away from it.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the far wood, from hazy blue tree shapes to the dark pines, so the grove has depth.
the-far-wood.end: Soft blue trees and pale far trunks stand in the mist, with a group of dark pines softened into the haze at their base.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage dabs the autumn leaves of the canopy and undergrowth, dark first and sunlit last.
the-golden-leaves.end: Golden leaves glow overhead and in the bushes, with sunlight sparkling through them and pale light lying on the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage lays the leaf floor and pulls the path that leads the eye into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor runs across the ground, with a pale tan path leading back into the mist.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder by the path and makes it look round with shade and light.
the-boulder.end: A round mossy boulder sits by the path, dark in its shadow with lit moss on its crown.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the near birches over everything and gives them their shading and dark bark marks.
the-birches.end: Six birches with gray shading, broken dark marks and dark feet lean over the leaves and the path.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage covers the ground and the path with bright fallen leaves catching the sun.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with golden leaves scattered down the path.

the-last-lights.for: This stage catches the sun on the birch bark, the last lights that finish the painting.
the-last-lights.end: The finished painting: sunlit white birches lean over the golden path that runs into the misty blue grove.

blend-window-sky.start: Start at the top left corner of the canvas with Sky blue, where the sky through the window touches the top and left edges.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the small window patch, then pick up Pale sky blue without rinsing and work lower down. Stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The deeper blue sits at the top of the sky through the window and pales lower down, where the light glows behind the trees.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave a ragged bright gap of bare canvas inside the blue for a cloud, and keep the rest of the canvas white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when a small soft blue patch, about 1 1/4 in wide, sits in the corner with a soft, uneven outer edge.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky dry first, or the green will turn muddy.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start at the edge of the white cloud gap inside the sky through the window.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of a nearly dry brush, a few dots at a time, never dragging.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Only a few small dark dots go in, where the leaves will be thickest later.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave almost all of the blue and the cloud gap showing.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop after a handful of small dots; this is a light start, not a tree yet.

dab-light-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green dots dry first.
dab-light-leaves.start: Start at the bottom of the cloud gap, where it meets the blue.
dab-light-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip, with almost no paint on the brush.
dab-light-leaves.inside: A few light taps sit low in the window patch, where the sun would catch the leaf tops.
dab-light-leaves.leave: Leave the blue, the cloud and the Leaf green dots showing around them.
dab-light-leaves.stop: Stop after a few small taps; it barely changes the patch, and that is right. Mistake to avoid: a wet brush makes blobs, so wipe it on a paper towel.

blend-wall.first: Let the window sky and leaves dry first.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, right of the window view, with Sky blue.
blend-wall.strokes: Make short criss-cross X strokes across the whole wall, working down to the bottom edge; blend in Soft wall blue as you go down and Deep wall blue toward the right edge.
blend-wall.inside: Paint the wall right through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go. Paler at the top, deeper at the right edge. While you do this, fill the sky leaf clumps with Sky blue edges, but keep the green trees showing in the window.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the green leaf clumps and a little sky showing in the top left corner.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the canvas is a soft, even periwinkle wall with faint X marks, about 16 in wide, edge to edge.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall dry fully first.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide post right of the window view, from the top edge of the canvas down.
block-in-frame.strokes: Build it from flat rectangles: the tall post first, then the crossbar across the glass, then the slanting ledge at the bottom of the window.
block-in-frame.inside: The cream covers the post and bars only; the panes between them keep the sky and leaves.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the leaves and sky showing in two panes, and keep the wall untouched.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when flat cream bars frame the window, about 3 in wide in all, with no shading yet.

shade-frame.first: Let the cream frame dry first.
shade-frame.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, along the right side of the window frame, where it meets the wall.
shade-frame.strokes: Pull long straight strokes down that narrow strip, then thin straight edges along the bars and the ledge.
shade-frame.inside: The blue-gray goes on the side of the post turned away from the window, and in thin lines on the undersides of the bars, because the light comes from the window.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the cream faces of the bars and post showing between the shadow lines.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when a dark strip runs down beside the post and each bar has a thin shadow edge.

light-frame.first: Let the Deep wall blue shadows dry first.
light-frame.start: Start on the crossbar at the top of the window frame.
light-frame.strokes: Skim the nearly dry brush lightly along each bar and down the post.
light-frame.inside: The white catches the faces of the bars that look toward the window light.
light-frame.leave: Leave the Deep wall blue shadow edges and some cream showing through.
light-frame.stop: Stop when the bars glow a little brighter; it should be broken and soft, never solid.

lay-in-sill.first: Let the frame and wall dry first.
lay-in-sill.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, just below the window ledge.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Pull long level strokes left and right across the sill, down to the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.inside: Fill the whole sill evenly, slanting gently along its back edge where it meets the wall.
lay-in-sill.leave: Leave the wall and window frame clean above it.
lay-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat warm brown ledge, about 4 1/2 in tall, fills the bottom of the canvas.

darken-sill-edge.first: Let the Wood brown dry first.
darken-sill-edge.start: Start along the bottom edge of the canvas, at the front of the sill.
darken-sill-edge.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long streaks side to side across the sill.
darken-sill-edge.inside: Darker streaks go across the whole sill, heavier near the bottom edge for the front of the ledge.
darken-sill-edge.leave: Leave the Wood brown showing between streaks, and a slanting band near the left edge of the canvas where the sun falls.
darken-sill-edge.stop: Stop when the sill looks streaky wood with a darker front edge.

light-sill.first: Let the Dark wood brown streaks dry first.
light-sill.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the sunlit band of the sill.
light-sill.strokes: Skim the dry brush in long level strokes along the band.
light-sill.inside: The tan sits in a slanting patch of sunlight coming from the window, broken by a thin dark bar across it.
light-sill.leave: Leave the dark streaks at the front and back of the sill.
light-sill.stop: Stop when a soft glowing patch, about 8 1/4 in wide, lights the sill. Too solid? Let it dry and dry-brush brown back over part.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long rounded rectangle on the sill for the folded front of the blanket.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Add a curved piece on top for the roll, then round off the ends.
block-in-blanket.inside: Fill it all with one flat coat, running to the right edge of the canvas.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a thin strip of sill showing under its front.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when one flat mustard shape, about 14 3/4 in wide, sits on the sill.

shade-blanket.first: Let the Mustard gold dry first.
shade-blanket.start: Start along the groove between the two rolls of the blanket.
shade-blanket.strokes: Make short curved strokes that bend over each roll like rope twists, following the length of the blanket.
shade-blanket.inside: Dark gold goes in the grooves and folds and between the knit twists, so the rolls look round and chunky.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave Mustard gold showing on the top of each twist.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket reads as knitted rolls with dark folds.

dark-stitches.start: Start on the groove between the two rolls of the blanket.
dark-stitches.strokes: Press the tip down and lift into small commas, following each roll.
dark-stitches.inside: Small dark marks go in the deepest grooves, under the front roll and scattered between stitches.
dark-stitches.leave: Leave most of the knit twists untouched.
dark-stitches.stop: Stop when the grooves look deeper and the stitches stand out more.

light-stitches.first: Let the dark stitches dry first.
light-stitches.start: Start on the top of the front roll of the blanket.
light-stitches.strokes: Press and lift short commas along each stitch, following the curve of the roll.
light-stitches.inside: The bright commas sit on the tops of the stitches, where light from the window hits.
light-stitches.leave: Leave the Dark gold grooves showing between them.
light-stitches.stop: Stop when the knit sparkles with bright stitches over dark gaps. Blobs? Use less paint and lift faster.

block-in-cat.start: Start with a big oval for the curled body on the blanket.
block-in-cat.strokes: Add a circle for the head at the window end, two triangle ears, and a curved piece for the tail.
block-in-cat.inside: Fill it flat with Cat gray, one even coat.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket showing around the bottom of the cat.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when a flat gray cat shape, about 15 in wide, lies on the blanket with no details.

shade-cat.first: Let the Cat gray dry first.
shade-cat.start: Start on the cat's head near the ears.
shade-cat.strokes: Pull curved strokes around the head and down the body, like stripes wrapping a barrel.
shade-cat.inside: Darker marks wrap the body in broad tabby bands and under the head and paws, following the round shape.
shade-cat.leave: Leave plenty of Cat gray between the bands.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when soft bands wrap the cat and it starts to look round.

white-patches.first: Let the Dark gray dry first.
white-patches.start: Start on the muzzle, where the face tucks down to the paws.
white-patches.strokes: Curve each stroke around the muzzle, the two front paws and the chest patch.
white-patches.inside: White goes on the muzzle, the two paws and a chest patch, in 2 or 3 thin coats.
white-patches.leave: Leave the gray and the bands around each white patch.
white-patches.stop: Stop when the muzzle, paws and chest are clean white.

cat-stripes.start: Start on the forehead between the ears.
cat-stripes.strokes: Press the full brush, then lift onto its edge so each stripe tapers to a point as it wraps the body.
cat-stripes.inside: Go over the soft bands, wrapping the head, back and tail.
cat-stripes.leave: Leave Cat gray between stripes and keep the white patches clean.
cat-stripes.stop: Stop when bold dark tabby stripes wrap the whole cat.

pink-ears.start: Start deep inside the near ear.
pink-ears.strokes: Press and lift toward the ear tip.
pink-ears.inside: Pink fills the inside of each ear only.
pink-ears.leave: Leave a gray rim around each ear.
pink-ears.stop: Stop when both ears glow pink with gray rims.

flick-fur.first: Let the pink and stripes dry first.
flick-fur.start: Start on the head, near the ears.
flick-fur.strokes: Make quick light flicks outward with the fur, lifting off.
flick-fur.inside: Flicks break up the stripe edges and the face, so they read soft.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the dark stripes showing between flicks.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the cat looks furry, not flat.

window-light.first: Let the fur flicks dry first.
window-light.start: Start on the cheek by the muzzle.
window-light.strokes: Skim a nearly dry brush lightly over the fur.
window-light.inside: Cream catches the face and ears where window light falls.
window-light.leave: Leave the stripes and pink showing through.
window-light.stop: Stop when the face looks lit and soft.

eyes-toes.first: Let all the paint underneath dry first, or lines will feather.
eyes-toes.start: Start with the closed eye nearest the muzzle.
eyes-toes.strokes: Hold the liner upright and pull thin curved lines.
eyes-toes.inside: Two curved lines make the sleeping eyes, plus a few dark dots along the stripes.
eyes-toes.leave: Leave the face fur untouched around the lines.
eyes-toes.stop: Stop when the cat clearly looks asleep.

paint-nose.start: Start on the stitches of the front roll of the blanket.
paint-nose.strokes: Press and lift small commas along the stitches.
paint-nose.inside: Small marks deepen the stitches across the blanket.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when the blanket stitches look slightly richer.

whiskers.first: Let everything dry first, so the lines stay crisp.
whiskers.strokes: Pull a few thin lines outward with light pressure, tapering at the end.
whiskers.inside: A few whiskers fan from each side of the muzzle across the cheek and paws.
whiskers.leave: Leave most of the face clear.
whiskers.stop: Stop with a few fine whiskers; the painting is done.

blend-window-sky.text: Start at the top left corner of the canvas with Sky blue, where the sky through the window touches the top and left edges.
Stroke side to side across the small window patch, then pick up Pale sky blue without rinsing and work lower down. Stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
The deeper blue sits at the top of the sky through the window and pales lower down, where the light glows behind the trees.
Leave a ragged bright gap of bare canvas within the blue patch for a cloud, and keep the rest of the canvas white.
Stop when a small soft blue patch, about 1 1/4 in wide, sits in the corner with a soft, uneven outer edge.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky dry first, or the green will turn muddy.
Start at the edge of the white cloud gap inside the sky through the window.
Tap with the tip of a nearly dry brush, a few dots at a time, never dragging.
Only a few small dark dots go in, where the leaves will be thickest later.
Leave almost all of the blue and the cloud gap showing.
Stop after a handful of small dots; this is a light start, not a tree yet.

dab-light-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green dots dry first.
Start at the bottom of the cloud gap, where it meets the blue.
Tap lightly with the tip, with almost no paint on the brush.
A few light taps sit low in the window patch, where the sun would catch the leaf tops.
Leave the blue, the cloud and the Leaf green dots showing around them.
Stop after a few small taps; it barely changes the patch, and that is right. Mistake to avoid: a wet brush makes blobs, so wipe it on a paper towel.

blend-wall.text: Let the window sky and leaves dry first.
Start at the top edge of the canvas, right of the window view, with Sky blue.
Make short criss-cross X strokes across the whole wall, working down to the bottom edge; blend in Soft wall blue as you go down and Deep wall blue toward the right edge.

Paint the wall right through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go. Paler at the top, deeper at the right edge. While you do this, fill the sky leaf clumps with Sky blue edges, but keep the green trees showing in the window.
Leave the green leaf clumps and a little sky showing in the window view.
Stop when the canvas is a soft, even periwinkle wall with faint X marks, about 16 in wide, edge to edge.

block-in-frame.text: Let the wall dry fully first.
Start with the wide post right of the window view, from the top edge of the canvas down.
Build it from flat rectangles: the tall post first, then the crossbar across the glass, then the slanting ledge at the bottom of the window.
The cream covers the post and bars only; the panes between them keep the sky and leaves.
Leave the leaves and sky showing in two panes, and keep the wall untouched.
Stop when flat cream bars frame the window, about 3 in wide in all, with no shading yet.

The blue-gray goes on the side of the post turned away from the window, and in thin lines on the undersides of the bars, because the light comes from the window.
Leave the cream faces of the bars and post showing between the shadow lines.
Stop when a dark strip runs down where the frame meets the wall and each bar has a thin shadow edge.

Start on the crossbar at the top of the window frame.
Skim the nearly dry brush lightly along each bar and down the post.
The white catches the faces of the bars that look toward the window light.
Leave the Deep wall blue shadow edges and some cream showing through.
Stop when the bars glow a little brighter; it should be broken and soft, never solid.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a gray tabby kitten fast asleep, curled on a chunky mustard blanket on a sunny wooden windowsill. The heart of it is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white paws tucked in close. Keep the mood soft and warm, like a lazy afternoon nap.
opening.light: Soft daylight pours in through the window and falls on the cat's head, the blanket's rolls and the near end of the sill. Wherever that window light lands you will add lighter paint, and wherever it can't reach you will add darker paint, so the things look round.

skills.how: You build each big shape from simple pieces: rectangles for the window frame, a rounded block and a roll for the blanket, then an oval, a circle and triangles for the cat. It turns a hard drawing into a few easy shapes. Don't fuss over the joins; the pieces can show, and later steps cover them.

Dry brush means only the tip of a dry brush in the paint, skimmed lightly so the mark breaks up on the canvas texture. Here it puts the window light on the frame, the sill and the cat's face. Watch for a solid patch: that means too much paint, so let it dry and brush the base color back over part of it.

You touch the tip down, press so the brush spreads, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point like a comma. It makes the knit stitches of the blanket and the pink inside the ears. If you get blobs instead of commas, use less paint and lift faster.

opening.road: We paint from the farthest thing to the nearest. First the sky and leaves seen through the window, then the plain blue wall, which go in first because everything else sits in front of them. Next the window frame and the wooden sill give the room its shape. The blanket comes after, built up from flat gold to knit stitches, because the cat lies in it. The cat is last and gets the most steps: a flat gray shape, its bands and white patches, stripes and pink ears. The final stage adds the fur, the window light and the sleeping face, so the painting finishes where the eye lands.

the-window-view.for: This stage paints the far-away view through the window, a soft sky with a few leaves.
the-window-view.end: A small patch of soft blue sky with a white cloud gap sits in the corner, and the rest of the canvas is white.

the-wall.for: This stage covers the room's wall in one smooth blue blend, painted straight through where everything else will go.
the-wall.end: A soft periwinkle wall fills the canvas, with green leafy trees and sky showing in the window view.

the-window-frame.for: This stage builds the cream window frame and gives it shadow and light so it looks solid.
the-window-frame.end: Cream window bars with blue-gray shadow edges and bright lit faces frame the sky and leaves.

the-sill.for: This stage lays the wooden sill the blanket and cat will rest on, with a dark front and a patch of sunlight.
the-sill.end: A warm brown wooden sill runs the width of the canvas, with streaky wood and a glowing band of sunlight near the window.

the-blanket.for: This stage turns a flat gold shape into a chunky folded knit blanket.
the-blanket.end: A folded mustard blanket with deep folds and bright knit stitches lies across the sill.

the-cat.for: This stage builds the cat from a flat gray shape into a striped tabby with white patches and pink ears.
the-cat.end: A striped gray tabby with a white muzzle, chest and paws and pink ears lies curled on the blanket, with no face yet.

the-light-and-face.for: This stage makes the cat soft and alive with fur, window light and its sleeping face.
the-light-and-face.end: The finished painting: a furry tabby, lit by the window, sleeping peacefully with whiskers and a pink nose.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a gray tabby kitten fast asleep, curled on a chunky mustard blanket on a sunny wooden windowsill. The heart of it is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white paws tucked in close. Keep the mood soft and warm, like a lazy afternoon nap.
opening.light: Soft daylight pours in through the window and falls on the cat's head, the blanket's rolls and the near end of the sill. Wherever that window light lands you will add lighter paint, and wherever it can't reach you will add darker paint, so the things look round.
