back.text: The same dry tap you used for the shaded leaves, now with the lighter green and even less paint.
You used Sky blue for the sky; now it helps pale the wall, blended with criss-cross strokes instead of side to side.
This is the Deep wall blue you blended into the wall, now laid in straight strips for the frame's shadow.
The same long level strokes as the sill, now in a darker brown and broken into streaks.
The same dry skim you used to light the window bars, now in a warm tan for the sunlight on the wood.
Like the window frame, build the blanket from simple pieces, but rounded this time instead of square.
The same Dark gold you used in the folds, now pressed into small commas with a round brush.
The same press and lift as the dark stitches, now in Bright gold where the light hits.
Build the cat from pieces just as you built the blanket: one big oval first, then the smaller shapes.
The same curved strokes you bent over the blanket's rolls, now wrapping around the cat's round body.
The same Pure white that lit the window bars, but now painted solid in thin coats, not dry-brushed.
The same press and lift you used for the knit stitches, now with Soft pink inside the ears.
This is the Cat gray you blocked the cat in with, now flicked lightly over the stripes to soften them.
The same dry skim as the sunlight on the sill, now in Warm cream on the cat's face and ears.
The same Charcoal as the stripes, now thinned for a liner so the lines stay fine.
The same press and lift as the knit stitches, going back over the blanket to deepen them.
The same upright liner you used for the eyes, now with Pure white and longer, lighter lines.

blend-the-sky.start: Start with Sky blue at the top edge of the canvas and stroke side to side all the way across.
blend-the-sky.strokes: Long side-to-side strokes edge to edge. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold for a warm band through the upper middle of the sky, then go back to Sky blue for the lower sky down to the bottom edge. Stroke back over each join while it is wet.
blend-the-sky.inside: The gold sits in a broad, uneven band where the sunset glows, brightest toward the sun. Blue sits above and below it, in soft slanting streaks.
blend-the-sky.leave: Nothing. The whole white canvas gets covered.
blend-the-sky.stop: Stop when the canvas is a soft sky, blue at the top, a glowing gold band through the upper part, and streaky blue down to the bottom edge, with no hard lines between colors.

lay-in-clouds.start: Start at the top of the sky, laying a ragged gold streak across it.
lay-in-clouds.strokes: Small circles with the tip of the brush, so every cloud gets a soft, bumpy edge.
lay-in-clouds.inside: Most of the paint goes into the long streaks high in the sky. A scatter of smaller flat-bottomed scraps and thin slivers goes lower, in the blue below the gold band.
lay-in-clouds.leave: Leave blue sky showing between the streaks and around each scrap.
lay-in-clouds.stop: Stop when gold cloud scraps float across the blue, big ones high and smaller, thinner ones lower down.

light-cloud-tops.start: Start along the top of the sky, skimming a little Sunlit cream into the cloud edges there.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Dry brush: only the tip in the paint, light pressure, skimming sideways along each cloud.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Lay a broken glow along the top edges of the upper clouds. Then lay long slanting streaks low in the blue sky, following the cloud slivers there, so they read as glowing bands.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the gold and blue showing through. This is never a solid coat.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when the cloud edges and the low streaks glow faintly cream over the blue. If a patch went on solid, let it dry and skim blue back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.start: Start with the farthest hill line, its top about 2 in from the top edge, just under the gold clouds.
lay-in-far-hills.strokes: Curved strokes that follow each hilltop: start on the top of a bump and pull down along its curve.
lay-in-far-hills.inside: Lay one range behind another, each soft rounded top a little lower, all the way down to the bottom edge. Let a little of the sky glow show through faintly where each range meets the one behind it.
lay-in-far-hills.leave: Leave the gold and blue sky above the top hill line untouched.
lay-in-far-hills.stop: Stop when hazy violet ranges fill the canvas from under the clouds to the bottom edge, soft and without texture.

shade-near-ridges.start: Start just under the top hill line, on the second range.
shade-near-ridges.strokes: Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, following the ridge as it slopes down across the canvas.
shade-near-ridges.inside: Lay a deeper band along this one ridge, so the farthest range behind it stays pale. Thicken it where the ridge runs down toward the lake's corner.
shade-near-ridges.leave: Leave the pale back range above it and all the lower ranges as they are.
shade-near-ridges.stop: Stop when one darker slate ridge runs across in front of the pale back range, soft and smooth.

paint-lake.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
paint-lake.strokes: Curved strokes that follow the curve of the shore, pulling the paint in from the edge.
paint-lake.inside: Keep it a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, tapering to a point toward the hills.
paint-lake.leave: Leave the ridge showing above it so the lake sits tucked in the valley.
paint-lake.stop: Stop when a small pale lake sits against the right edge of the canvas.

lay-in-hillside.first: Let the hills and lake dry.
lay-in-hillside.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas with the top of the slope, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-in-hillside.strokes: Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, keeping the top line sloping gently down toward the lake.
lay-in-hillside.inside: Cover everything below that top line with one flat coat, right down to the bottom edge.
lay-in-hillside.leave: Leave the far ranges, the dark ridge and the lake showing above the slope.
lay-in-hillside.stop: Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the lower canvas, with no texture yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.start: Start at the top of the slope, tapping lightly.
tap-sunlit-slope.strokes: Stamp only the middle tips of the fanned brush, working down in a zigzag and pressing a little harder as you go lower, with the dabs angled to follow the slope.
tap-sunlit-slope.inside: Cover most of the slope with light taps where the sun strikes, in long sloping bands.
tap-sunlit-slope.leave: Leave olive clumps and slanting dark bands showing between the taps; they become the bushes. Keep the very top of the slope darker.
tap-sunlit-slope.stop: Stop when the slope is dappled yellow-green with dark bushes running through it.

lay-in-meadow.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas with the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge.
lay-in-meadow.strokes: Short crossing strokes like overlapping X shapes, then go over them while wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
lay-in-meadow.inside: Fill everything below that top edge down to the bottom edge, letting the top edge slope gently down across the canvas.
lay-in-meadow.leave: Leave the dappled hillside showing above the meadow.
lay-in-meadow.stop: Stop when a flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower canvas.

darken-meadow-front.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
darken-meadow-front.strokes: Dry brush: only the tip in paint, light pressure, short upward and slanting skims like grass.
darken-meadow-front.inside: Press most where the meadow comes nearest you, at the bottom. Get lighter and broken going up, with only streaks near the top of the meadow.
darken-meadow-front.leave: Leave plenty of yellow-green showing, most toward the back.
darken-meadow-front.stop: Stop when the meadow reads streaky dark green in front fading to sunlit yellow-green at the back.

block-in-cow.start: Start with the big body oval, its middle about 5 in from the left edge and about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
block-in-cow.strokes: Build from pieces: lay the oval, then add curved pieces around it for the rump, the head and the fringe cap, then short pieces for the legs.
block-in-cow.inside: Fill the whole cow flat, with shaggy, ragged edges all round. The head and fringe sit high on the near side of the body, and the legs go down into the grass.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave gaps of meadow between the legs.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop when one flat rust-brown shaggy cow shape stands in the meadow.

shade-cow.start: Start under the fringe where the face is hidden.
shade-cow.strokes: Long curved strokes that follow the hair, from the top of the back down along the body like hanging locks.
shade-cow.inside: Darken the far side of the body, the hollow under the fringe, under the chin, the belly and the backs of the legs. These are away from the setting sun.
shade-cow.leave: Leave rust showing in long streaks on the sunny side of the body, chest and fringe.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks round and shaggy, dark in the shadows and rust where the sun reaches.

block-in-horns.start: Start each horn where it leaves the head under the fringe.
block-in-horns.strokes: Curved strokes that sweep out from the head and then up, tapering toward the point.
block-in-horns.inside: Make the horn on the far side longer, curving up against the hills; its piece is about 2 1/4 in wide. The other is shorter and hooks up.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the hills showing around both horns.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop when two smooth, flat bone-colored horns curve up from the head.

shade-horns.start: Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the hair.
shade-horns.strokes: Curved strokes along the length of each horn, following its bend.
shade-horns.inside: Lay Nose pink along the lower, shadowed curve of each horn and darken the tips.
shade-horns.leave: Leave bone color along the upper curve of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when each horn has a dark underside and tip, with a pale top.

pull-ginger-locks.start: Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.
pull-ginger-locks.strokes: Thick to thin: press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then lighten onto the edge as you pull down, so it tapers.
pull-ginger-locks.inside: Fill the fringe with locks falling over the face, then pull long locks down the body.
pull-ginger-locks.leave: Leave dark umber showing between the locks, most in the deep shadow under the fringe.
pull-ginger-locks.stop: Stop when long ginger locks hang over the whole coat with dark gaps between them.

pull-straw-locks.start: Start along the top of the fringe.
pull-straw-locks.strokes: Thick to thin, shorter strokes, pulled down with the hair.
pull-straw-locks.inside: Edge the top of the fringe and run a bright strip down the sunlit edge of the face and chest toward the legs. Add a few short locks on the body.
pull-straw-locks.leave: Leave most of the ginger and dark coat untouched.
pull-straw-locks.stop: Stop when the sunlit outline of the head and chest glows straw gold.

light-the-rims.start: Start on the top of the fringe, between the horns.
light-the-rims.strokes: Dry brush: just the tip in paint, skimming tiny feathery touches.
light-the-rims.inside: Add a broken glint along the top of the fringe and the top curve of each horn where the sun catches them, and a few specks along the top of the back.
light-the-rims.leave: Leave the rest of the coat and horns as they are.
light-the-rims.stop: Stop when the top of the head and horns catch a faint, sparkling rim.

paint-nose.start: Start in the middle of the face, just below the fringe.
paint-nose.strokes: Curved strokes around the rounded shape of the muzzle.
paint-nose.inside: Make a small broad nose, about 1 in wide.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the fringe hanging over its top.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a small dusty-pink nose peeks out under the fringe.

line-nostrils-mouth.first: Let the nose dry so the lines don't spread.
line-nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
line-nostrils-mouth.strokes: Hold the liner upright with thin, wet paint and light, steady pressure; reload often.
line-nostrils-mouth.inside: Draw the two nostrils, a short mouth line, and darken around the muzzle so it stands out of the hair. Add a few small dark touches in the shadows of the coat.
line-nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave the pink of the nose showing between the nostrils.
line-nostrils-mouth.stop: Stop when the nose reads as a soft muzzle with nostrils and a mouth.

flick-dark-grass.first: Let the cow and meadow dry.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Dry brush flicked quickly upward, like grass blades.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Lay most blades in the lower meadow, thickest at the bottom, and carry them up over the cow's legs and belly so the legs sink into the grass.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave lighter meadow showing between blades, and the cow's chest and head untouched.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Stop when dark blades rise across the front and swallow the cow's legs.

flick-light-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-light-grass.inside: Lay blades over and between the dark ones across the front meadow and a few over the bottom of the cow.
flick-light-grass.leave: Leave dark green showing between the blades.
flick-light-grass.stop: Stop when light and dark blades mix across the front.

flick-gold-tips.start: Start in the front meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-gold-tips.inside: Scatter tips across the meadow, larger and farther apart in front, smaller toward the back. Put a few over the cow's lower legs.
flick-gold-tips.leave: Leave plenty of green between the tips.
flick-gold-tips.stop: Stop when gold seed tips sparkle across the grass. The painting is finished.

The gold sits in a broad, uneven band where the sunset glows, brightest toward the sun. Blue frames the gold band at the top and runs in soft slanting streaks through the lower sky.
Nothing. The whole white canvas gets covered.
Stop when the canvas is a soft sky, blue at the top, a glowing gold band through the upper part, and streaky blue down to the bottom edge, with no hard lines between colors.

Start at the top of the sky, laying a ragged gold streak across it.

Leave blue sky showing between the streaks and around each scrap.
Stop when gold cloud scraps float across the blue, big ones high and smaller, thinner ones lower down.

light-cloud-tops.text: Let the cloud streaks dry.
Start along the top of the sky, skimming a little Sunlit cream into the cloud edges there.
Dry brush: only the tip in the paint, light pressure, skimming sideways along each cloud.
Lay a broken glow along the top edges of the upper clouds. Then lay long slanting streaks low in the blue sky, following the cloud slivers there, so they read as glowing bands.

Stop when the cloud edges and the low streaks glow faintly cream over the blue. If a patch went on solid, let it dry and skim blue back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.text: Let the sky dry.
Start with the farthest hill line, its top about 2 in from the top edge, just under the gold clouds.
Curved strokes that follow each hilltop: start on the top of a bump and pull down along its curve.
Lay one range behind another, each soft rounded top a little lower, all the way down to the bottom edge. Let a little of the sky glow show through faintly where each range meets the one behind it.
Leave the gold and blue clouds at the top of the sky untouched.
Stop when hazy violet ranges fill the canvas from under the clouds to the bottom edge, soft and without texture.

shade-near-ridges.text: Let the far hills dry.
Start just under the top hill line, on the second range.
Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, following the ridge as it slopes down across the canvas.
Lay a deeper band along this one ridge, so the farthest range behind it stays pale. Thicken it where the ridge runs down toward the lake's corner.
Leave the pale farthest range and all the nearer ranges as they are.
Stop when one darker slate ridge runs across in front of the pale back range, soft and smooth.

paint-lake.text: Let the ridges dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Curved strokes that follow the curve of the shore, pulling the paint in from the edge.
Keep it a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, tapering to a point toward the hills.
Leave the darker ridge showing along the lake's far shore, so the lake sits tucked in the valley.
Stop when a small pale lake sits against the right edge of the canvas.

lay-in-hillside.text: Let the hills and lake dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas with the top of the slope, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, keeping the top line sloping gently down toward the lake.
Cover the whole lower canvas with one flat coat, from that sloping top line right down to the bottom edge.
Leave the far ranges, the dark ridge and the lake showing behind the hillside.
Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the lower canvas, with no texture yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: Let the olive green dry.
Start at the top of the slope, tapping lightly.
Stamp only the middle tips of the fanned brush, working down in a zigzag and pressing a little harder as you go lower, with the dabs angled to follow the slope.
Cover most of the slope with light taps where the sun strikes, in long sloping bands.
Leave olive clumps and slanting dark bands showing between the taps; they become the bushes. Keep the very top of the slope darker.
Stop when the slope is dappled yellow-green with dark bushes running through it.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas with the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge.
Short crossing strokes like overlapping X shapes, then go over them while wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
Fill everything below that top edge down to the bottom edge, letting the top edge slope gently down across the canvas.
Leave the dappled hillside showing above the meadow.
Stop when a flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower canvas.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
Dry brush: only the tip in paint, light pressure, short upward and slanting skims like grass.
Press most where the meadow comes nearest you, at the bottom. Get lighter and broken going up, with only streaks near the top of the meadow.
Leave plenty of yellow-green showing, most toward the back.
Stop when the meadow reads streaky dark green in front fading to sunlit yellow-green at the back.

block-in-cow.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start with the big body oval, its middle about 5 in from the left edge and about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
Build from pieces: lay the oval, then add curved pieces around it for the rump, the head and the fringe cap, then short pieces for the legs.
Fill the whole cow flat, with shaggy, ragged edges all round. The head and fringe sit high on the near side of the body, and the legs go down into the grass.
Leave gaps of meadow between the legs.
Stop when one flat rust-brown shaggy cow shape stands in the meadow.

shade-cow.text: Let the rust brown dry.
Start under the fringe where the face is hidden.
Long curved strokes that follow the hair, from the top of the back down along the body like hanging locks.
Darken the far side of the body, the hollow under the fringe, under the chin, the belly and the backs of the legs. These are away from the setting sun.
Leave rust showing in long streaks on the sunny side of the body, chest and fringe.
Stop when the cow looks round and shaggy, dark in the shadows and rust where the sun reaches.

block-in-horns.text: Let the cow dry.
Start each horn where it leaves the head under the fringe.
Curved strokes that sweep out from the head and then up, tapering toward the point.
Make the horn on the far side longer, curving up against the hills; its piece is about 2 1/4 in wide. The other is shorter and hooks up.
Leave the hills showing around both horns.
Stop when two smooth, flat bone-colored horns curve up from the head.

shade-horns.text: Let the horns dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the hair.
Curved strokes along the length of each horn, following its bend.
Lay Nose pink along the lower, shadowed curve of each horn and darken the tips.
Leave bone color along the upper curve of each horn.
Stop when each horn has a dark underside and tip, with a pale top.

pull-ginger-locks.text: Let the shading dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.
Thick to thin: press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then lighten onto the edge as you pull down, so it tapers.
Fill the fringe with locks falling over the face, then pull long locks down the body.
Leave dark umber showing between the locks, most in the deep shadow under the fringe.
Stop when long ginger locks hang over the whole coat with dark gaps between them.

pull-straw-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry.
Start along the top of the fringe.
Thick to thin, shorter strokes, pulled down with the hair.
Edge the top of the fringe and run a bright strip down the sunlit edge of the face and chest toward the legs. Add a few short locks on the body.
Leave most of the ginger and dark coat untouched.
Stop when the sunlit outline of the head and chest glows straw gold.

light-the-rims.text: Let the straw locks dry.
Start on the top of the fringe, between the horns.
Dry brush: just the tip in paint, skimming tiny feathery touches.
Add a broken glint along the top of the fringe and the top curve of each horn where the sun catches them, and a few specks along the top of the back.
Leave the rest of the coat and horns as they are.
Stop when the top of the head and horns catch a faint, sparkling rim.

paint-nose.text: Let the coat dry.
Start in the middle of the face, where the fringe ends.
Curved strokes around the rounded shape of the muzzle.
Make a small broad nose, about 1 in wide.
Leave the fringe hanging over its top.
Stop when a small dusty-pink nose peeks out under the fringe.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: Let the nose dry so the lines don't spread.
Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
Hold the liner upright with thin, wet paint and light, steady pressure; reload often.
Draw the two nostrils, a short mouth line, and darken around the muzzle so it stands out of the hair. Add a few small dark touches in the shadows of the coat.
Leave the pink of the nose showing between the nostrils.
Stop when the nose reads as a soft muzzle with nostrils and a mouth.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the cow and meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
Dry brush flicked quickly upward, like grass blades.
Lay most blades in the lower meadow, thickest at the bottom, and carry them up over the cow's legs and belly so the legs sink into the grass.
Leave lighter meadow showing between blades, and the cow's chest and head untouched.
Stop when dark blades rise across the front and swallow the cow's legs.

flick-light-grass.text: Let the dark blades dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
Dry brush flicked quickly upward.
Lay blades over and between the dark ones across the front meadow and a few over the bottom of the cow.
Leave dark green showing between the blades.
Stop when light and dark blades mix across the front.

flick-gold-tips.text: Let the green blades dry.
Start in the front meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas.
Short upward dry-brush marks.
Scatter tips across the meadow, larger and farther apart in front, smaller toward the back. Put a few over the cow's lower legs.
Leave plenty of green between the tips.
Stop when gold seed tips sparkle across the grass. The painting is finished.

blend-the-sky.text: Start with Sky blue at the top edge of the canvas and stroke side to side all the way across.

Long side-to-side strokes edge to edge. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold for a warm band through the upper middle of the sky, then go back to Sky blue for the lower sky down to the bottom edge. Stroke back over each join while it is wet.
The gold sits in a broad, uneven band where the sunset glows, brightest toward the sun. Blue frames the gold band at the top and runs in soft slanting streaks through the lower sky.
Nothing. The whole white canvas gets covered.
Stop when the canvas is a soft sky, blue at the top, a glowing gold band through the upper part, and streaky blue down to the bottom edge, with no hard lines between colors.

lay-in-clouds.text: Let the sky dry completely.
Start at the top of the sky, laying a ragged gold streak across it.
Small circles with the tip of the brush, so every cloud gets a soft, bumpy edge.
Most of the paint goes into the long streaks high in the sky. A scatter of smaller flat-bottomed scraps and thin slivers goes lower down, out in the blue streaks of the lower sky.
Leave blue sky showing between the streaks and around each scrap.
Stop when gold cloud scraps float across the blue, big ones high and smaller, thinner ones lower down.

light-cloud-tops.text: Let the cloud streaks dry.
Start along the top of the sky, skimming a little Sunlit cream into the cloud edges there.
Dry brush: only the tip in the paint, light pressure, skimming sideways along each cloud.
Lay a broken glow along the top edges of the upper clouds. Then lay long slanting streaks low in the blue sky, following the cloud slivers there, so they read as glowing bands.
Leave the gold and blue showing through. This is never a solid coat.
Stop when the cloud edges and the low streaks glow faintly cream over the blue. If a patch went on solid, let it dry and skim blue back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.text: Let the sky dry.
Start with the farthest hill line, its top about 2 in from the top edge, just under the gold clouds.
Curved strokes that follow each hilltop: start on the top of a bump and pull down along its curve.
Lay one range behind another, each soft rounded top a little lower, all the way down to the bottom edge. Let a little of the sky glow show through faintly where each range meets the one behind it.
Leave the gold and blue clouds at the top of the sky untouched.
Stop when hazy violet ranges fill the canvas from under the clouds to the bottom edge, soft and without texture.

shade-near-ridges.text: Let the far hills dry.
Start just under the top hill line, on the second range.
This is the same Hazy violet as the far hills, but now you pull long, level strokes along one ridge to make it darker and nearer.
Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, following the ridge as it slopes down across the canvas.
Lay a deeper band along this one ridge, so the farthest range behind it stays pale. Thicken it where the ridge runs down toward the lake's corner.
Leave the pale farthest range and all the nearer ranges as they are.
Stop when one darker slate ridge runs across in front of the pale back range, soft and smooth.

paint-lake.text: Let the ridges dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Curved strokes that follow the curve of the shore, pulling the paint in from the edge.
Keep it a small flat sliver, about 1 1/4 in wide, tapering to a point toward the hills.
Leave the darker ridge showing along the lake's far shore, so the lake sits tucked in the valley.
Stop when a small pale lake sits against the right edge of the canvas.

lay-in-hillside.text: Let the hills and lake dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas with the top of the slope, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
You pulled these same level strokes for the ridge; now use the bigger brush and Olive green to cover a whole slope.
Long, level horizontal strokes, left and right, keeping the top line sloping gently down toward the lake.
Cover the whole lower canvas with one flat coat, from that sloping top line right down to the bottom edge.
Leave the far ranges, the dark ridge and the lake showing behind the hillside.
Stop when one flat olive-green slope fills the lower canvas, with no texture yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: Let the olive green dry.
Start at the top of the slope, tapping lightly.
Stamp only the middle tips of the fanned brush, working down in a zigzag and pressing a little harder as you go lower, with the dabs angled to follow the slope.
Cover most of the slope with light taps where the sun strikes, in long sloping bands.
Leave olive clumps and slanting dark bands showing between the taps; they become the bushes. Keep the very top of the slope darker.
Stop when the slope is dappled yellow-green with dark bushes running through it.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas with the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside, now laid flat and smooth with crossing strokes.
Short crossing strokes like overlapping X shapes, then go over them while wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
Fill everything below that top edge down to the bottom edge, letting the top edge slope gently down across the canvas.
Leave the dappled hillside showing above the meadow.
Stop when a flat yellow-green meadow fills the lower canvas.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
It is the same dry, skimming brush you used to light the clouds, now with deep green and pulled upward like grass.
Dry brush: only the tip in paint, light pressure, short upward and slanting skims like grass.
Press most where the meadow comes nearest you, at the bottom. Get lighter and broken going up, with only streaks near the top of the meadow.
Leave plenty of yellow-green showing, most toward the back.
Stop when the meadow reads streaky dark green in front fading to sunlit yellow-green at the back.

block-in-cow.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start with the big body oval, its middle about 5 in from the left edge and about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
Build from pieces: lay the oval, then add curved pieces around it for the rump, the head and the fringe cap, then short pieces for the legs.
Fill the whole cow flat, with shaggy, ragged edges all round. The head and fringe sit high on the near side of the body, and the legs go down into the grass.
Leave gaps of meadow between the legs.
Stop when one flat rust-brown shaggy cow shape stands in the meadow.

shade-cow.text: Let the rust brown dry.
Start under the fringe where the face is hidden.
The curved strokes that rounded the hills now follow the cow's hair, bending down the body.
Long curved strokes that follow the hair, from the top of the back down along the body like hanging locks.
Darken the far side of the body, the hollow under the fringe, under the chin, the belly and the backs of the legs. These are away from the setting sun.
Leave rust showing in long streaks on the sunny side of the body, chest and fringe.
Stop when the cow looks round and shaggy, dark in the shadows and rust where the sun reaches.

block-in-horns.text: Let the cow dry.
Start each horn where it leaves the head under the fringe.
Curved strokes that sweep out from the head and then up, tapering toward the point.
Make the horn on the far side longer, curving up against the hills; its piece is about 2 1/4 in wide. The other is shorter and hooks up.
Leave the hills showing around both horns.
Stop when two smooth, flat bone-colored horns curve up from the head.

shade-horns.text: Let the horns dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the hair.
Follow each horn's bend just as you did to block it in, now with a smaller brush and only along its shadowed curve.
Curved strokes along the length of each horn, following its bend.
Lay Nose pink along the lower, shadowed curve of each horn and darken the tips.
Leave bone color along the upper curve of each horn.
Stop when each horn has a dark underside and tip, with a pale top.

pull-ginger-locks.text: Let the shading dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.
Thick to thin: press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then lighten onto the edge as you pull down, so it tapers.
Fill the fringe with locks falling over the face, then pull long locks down the body.
Leave dark umber showing between the locks, most in the deep shadow under the fringe.
Stop when long ginger locks hang over the whole coat with dark gaps between them.

pull-straw-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry.
Start along the top of the fringe.
These are the same tapering locks as the ginger ones, but shorter, lighter and with the smaller angle brush.
Thick to thin, shorter strokes, pulled down with the hair.
Edge the top of the fringe and run a bright strip down the sunlit edge of the face and chest toward the legs. Add a few short locks on the body.
Leave most of the ginger and dark coat untouched.
Stop when the sunlit outline of the head and chest glows straw gold.

light-the-rims.text: Let the straw locks dry.
Start on the top of the fringe, between the horns.
This is the same Sunlit cream and dry skim you gave the cloud edges, now as tiny touches where the sun catches the hair and horns.
Dry brush: just the tip in paint, skimming tiny feathery touches.
Add a broken glint along the top of the fringe and the top curve of each horn where the sun catches them, and a few specks along the top of the back.
Leave the rest of the coat and horns as they are.
Stop when the top of the head and horns catch a faint, sparkling rim.

paint-nose.text: Let the coat dry.
Start in the middle of the face, where the fringe ends.
You shaded the horns with this Nose pink; now it becomes the soft round nose.
Curved strokes around the rounded shape of the muzzle.
Make a small broad nose, about 1 in wide.
Leave the fringe hanging over its top.
Stop when a small dusty-pink nose peeks out under the fringe.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: Let the nose dry so the lines don't spread.
Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
This is the Dark umber that shaded the cow, now thinned for the liner to draw fine lines.
Hold the liner upright with thin, wet paint and light, steady pressure; reload often.
Draw the two nostrils, a short mouth line, and darken around the muzzle so it stands out of the hair. Add a few small dark touches in the shadows of the coat.
Leave the pink of the nose showing between the nostrils.
Stop when the nose reads as a soft muzzle with nostrils and a mouth.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the cow and meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
You dry-brushed this Deep grass green over the meadow before; now flick it in distinct blades, right across the cow's legs.
Dry brush flicked quickly upward, like grass blades.
Lay most blades in the lower meadow, thickest at the bottom, and carry them up over the cow's legs and belly so the legs sink into the grass.
Leave lighter meadow showing between blades, and the cow's chest and head untouched.
Stop when dark blades rise across the front and swallow the cow's legs.

flick-light-grass.text: Let the dark blades dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
This is the Sunlit green of the flat meadow, now flicked as single bright blades with the stiff brush.
Dry brush flicked quickly upward.
Lay blades over and between the dark ones across the front meadow and a few over the bottom of the cow.
Leave dark green showing between the blades.
Stop when light and dark blades mix across the front.

flick-gold-tips.text: Let the green blades dry.
Start in the front meadow near the bottom edge of the canvas.
The Straw gold that lit the cow's locks now becomes small seed tips scattered through the grass.
Short upward dry-brush marks.
Scatter tips across the meadow, larger and farther apart in front, smaller toward the back. Put a few over the cow's lower legs.
Leave plenty of green between the tips.
Stop when gold seed tips sparkle across the grass. The painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass on a hillside at sunset, with blue hills and a glint of lake far away. The heart of the painting is the cow's face and pink nose, peeking out from a glowing fringe between two curved horns. Warm gold light and soft blue distance give it a quiet, golden-hour mood.
opening.light: The low sun is setting behind the far hills, so the sky glows gold and the cow is lit from behind. That sun catches the edges of the fringe, the horns and the grass tips with a bright rim, while the shadowed side of the cow and the hollow where the fringe hides the face fall into deep shadow.

skills.how: Dry brush means only the tip of the brush in the paint and no water, skimmed lightly so the marks break up. You use it for the glowing cloud edges, the shadowy front of the meadow, the sunlit rim on the cow and every pass of grass blades. Watch for paint going on solid: that means too much paint on the brush, so wipe it and skim again.

Curved strokes bend with the shape, running from the crest of each bump down along its curve. Here they round off the hills, wrap the cow's body and shape the horns and nose. Following the curve is what makes a flat shape look round.

Press the full width of the angle brush to start, then roll onto its edge and lighten up so each stroke tapers to a point. That one stroke makes every long lock of the cow's shaggy coat. Keep the pressure light at the end of each pull, or the locks end blunt instead of tapered.

opening.road: First you blend the sunset sky across the whole canvas and add the golden clouds. Next come the far hazy hills and the little lake, painted over the dry sky. Then the green hillside and the meadow are laid from far to near, so you have a complete landscape before the cow arrives. The cow is built as one rust-brown shape, shaded, given horns, then covered in long locks and a sunlit rim. The face goes on last, and finally grass is flicked over the cow's legs so it stands inside the meadow.

the-sky.for: This stage lays a smooth sunset sky and soft golden clouds that everything else will sit in front of.
the-sky.end: The canvas is a blue and gold sky with ragged golden clouds and glowing cream streaks.

the-distance.for: This stage pushes the land far away with hazy violet hills and a tiny pale lake.
the-distance.end: Soft violet ranges fill the canvas from the clouds down, with one darker ridge and a small silvery lake tucked into the valley.

the-green-land.for: This stage builds the sunlit green slopes, from the hillside to the meadow nearest you.
the-green-land.end: A dappled green hillside rolls away beyond a streaky meadow that glows yellow-green at the back and darkens toward you.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage gives the cow its whole shape, its shadows and its two horns.
the-cow-shape.end: A shaded rust-brown cow stands in the meadow with two curved horns, each shadowed along its inner curve and pale on its crest.

the-face.for: This stage paints the focal point: the cow's nose peeking out from the fringe.
the-face.end: A soft pink muzzle with dark nostrils and a mouth peeks out from the glowing fringe.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the flat cow into a long-haired Highland cow lit by the setting sun.
the-shaggy-coat.end: The cow is covered in long ginger and straw-gold locks, with a faint sparkling rim of light along its head and horns.

the-grass-in-front.for: This stage sets the cow inside the meadow with layers of grass flicked across its legs.
the-grass-in-front.end: Dark, sunlit and golden grass blades rise across the meadow and hide the cow's legs, and the painting is finished.

back.text: This is the same Hazy violet as the far hills, but now you pull long, level strokes along one ridge to make it darker and nearer.
You pulled these same level strokes for the ridge; now use the bigger brush and Olive green to cover a whole slope.
This is the Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside, now laid flat and smooth with crossing strokes.
It is the same dry, skimming brush you used to light the clouds, now with deep green and pulled upward like grass.
The curved strokes that rounded the hills now follow the cow's hair, bending down the body.

These are the same tapering locks as the ginger ones, but shorter, lighter and with the smaller angle brush.

This is the Sunlit green of the flat meadow, now flicked as single bright blades with the stiff brush.
The Straw gold that lit the cow's locks now becomes small seed tips scattered through the grass.

blend-the-sky.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue, stroking side to side all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-the-sky.strokes: Keep every stroke long and level. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold and paint a gold band below the blue. Stroke back up over the join several times while it is still wet.
blend-the-sky.inside: Blue stays across the top. The gold makes a wide glowing band through the upper middle of the sky, warmest toward the right edge of the canvas where the sun sets. Lower down, go back to Sky blue with soft gold streaks in it, all the way to the bottom edge.
blend-the-sky.leave: No white canvas: this sky runs under everything that comes later.
blend-the-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is covered, top edge to bottom edge, with soft joins. If you see a hard line between two colors, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas in the upper left corner of the sky, with Sunset gold on the tip of the brush.
lay-in-clouds.strokes: Make small circles with the tip so the cloud edges come out bumpy and soft. Keep each streak's bottom fairly flat, and let the streaks lie in long slanting shapes.
lay-in-clouds.inside: Most of the gold goes in the left half: a big ragged cloud along the top edge, a mass reaching down the left edge, then small slanting streaks lower in the blue, smaller and thinner the lower you go.
lay-in-clouds.leave: Leave plenty of blue sky between the streaks.
lay-in-clouds.stop: Stop when you have soft, bumpy gold streaks floating in the blue. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with lighter circles.

light-cloud-tops.first: Let the gold cloud streaks dry.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, on the upper edges of the big gold cloud there.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Dry brush: dip only the tip, with no water. Skim lightly side to side along each cloud edge so the marks break up on the canvas texture.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Sunlit cream goes along the tops of the clouds, the edges that face the light. Most of it goes lower down, though: long wavy streaks across the lower sky that soften the small gold streaks into rippling bands.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the gold showing under the cream and the blue showing between the bands.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when you have broken, see-through glints, never a solid patch. If one went on solid, let it dry and skim the sky color back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.first: Let the sky and clouds dry.
lay-in-far-hills.start: Start with the rounded tops of the far range, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, working from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-in-far-hills.strokes: Bend every stroke with the hills: from the top of each bump, down along its curve.
lay-in-far-hills.inside: Hazy violet covers everything from those hilltops down to the bottom edge. Lay it as layered rows of soft rounded ridges, each row a little lower than the last, sloping down toward the right edge.
lay-in-far-hills.leave: Leave the sky and clouds showing above the hilltops, and let a little warm gold glow through between the ridges.
lay-in-far-hills.stop: Stop when the canvas below the hilltops is a soft violet band of ridges, flat and with no texture.

shade-near-ridges.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, where the pale back range meets the next ridge down.
shade-near-ridges.strokes: Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Let the band drift lower as it crosses toward the right edge of the canvas.
shade-near-ridges.inside: This is one darker ridge just in front of the farthest range. At the middle of the canvas it runs from about 3 in to 4 in from the top edge. Most of it is in the right half, where it is widest and heaviest.
shade-near-ridges.leave: Leave the pale back range and the sky above it untouched, and the lower violet ridges as they are.
shade-near-ridges.stop: Stop when the darker ridge clearly separates the pale distance from the hills in front.

paint-lake.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, with the lake's top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
paint-lake.strokes: Use short curved strokes that follow the shoreline, curving into the hills and tapering to a point.
paint-lake.inside: Pale sky fills one small flat sliver of water, flat along its top and narrowing to a point where it tucks behind the hills.
paint-lake.leave: Leave the violet ridges showing all around it.
paint-lake.stop: Stop when the lake is about 1 1/4 in wide and about 1/2 in tall: a small, pale, still sliver.

lay-in-hillside.first: Let the lake and ridges dry.
lay-in-hillside.start: Start at the top of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-in-hillside.strokes: Cut the top edge of the slope as one line that falls gently to the right edge of the canvas and passes below the lake. Then fill the area with long, level strokes, left and right.
lay-in-hillside.inside: Olive green covers everything from that slope line down to the bottom edge. It is one flat, even shape.
lay-in-hillside.leave: Leave the sky, the violet ridges and the lake showing above the slope line.
lay-in-hillside.stop: Stop when the whole lower canvas is flat olive green, with no patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.start: Start near the top of the hillside at the left edge of the canvas, tapping lightly.
tap-sunlit-slope.strokes: Spread the fan and stamp only its middle tips. Work down in a zigzag and press harder as you go lower. Let the patches drift in long clumps that slope down toward the right edge.
tap-sunlit-slope.inside: Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside, all the way to the bottom edge, because the whole slope faces the low sun.
tap-sunlit-slope.leave: Leave olive clumps between the patches as bushes, and a darker olive band along the very top of the slope.
tap-sunlit-slope.stop: Stop when the hillside is dappled yellow-green with dark bushes throughout. If the marks look heavy and clumpy, thin the paint and spread the fan.

lay-in-meadow.start: Start along the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas, beginning at the left edge.
lay-in-meadow.strokes: Use short X strokes that cross each other in two directions. If you want it smoother, go over it while it is wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
lay-in-meadow.inside: Sunlit green covers everything from that top edge down to the bottom edge, in one solid coat. The top edge is gently bumpy and drops slightly toward the right edge.
lay-in-meadow.leave: Leave the dappled hillside showing above the meadow.
lay-in-meadow.stop: Stop when the lower canvas is flat yellow-green, with no gold or olive showing through.

darken-meadow-front.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
darken-meadow-front.strokes: Dry brush: use only the tip of the brush and no water. Skim short, light strokes upward, leaning a little like windblown grass, and build up in several passes.
darken-meadow-front.inside: Deep grass green is heaviest near the bottom edge, because the front of the meadow sits in shadow. It thins as you go up, with streaks reaching about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
darken-meadow-front.leave: Leave a band of yellow-green along the top of the meadow, and lighter patches of it showing through the streaks.
darken-meadow-front.stop: Stop when the meadow is streaky and darkens toward you. It should still have no separate grass blades.

block-in-cow.start: Start with a big oval for the body. Its middle is about 5 in from the left edge of the canvas.
block-in-cow.strokes: Add the rest in curved pieces like ( ). Put the rounded head and fringe on the side of the body nearest the lake, with its top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge. Then add the shaggy rump, and short leg pieces going down into the grass.
block-in-cow.inside: Rust brown fills the whole cow, flat and solid. Keep the outline ragged so it already looks hairy.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave grass showing between the legs.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop when you have one flat rust shape about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall, with no shading.

shade-cow.start: Start at the top of the cow's back, at the hump behind the head.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs, bending with the round of the body like hanging hair.
shade-cow.inside: Dark umber falls on the hind end and the middle of the body, under the fringe, down the chest and on the legs: the sides turned away from the sun. Most of it is in the left half.
shade-cow.leave: Leave rust streaks showing between the strokes, especially on the face and the front of the chest.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks streaky and rounded, dark at the back and shaded under the fringe.

block-in-horns.start: Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the top of the head.
block-in-horns.strokes: Pull each horn in tapering curves from its base out to its tip.
block-in-horns.inside: Horn bone fills two horns. The long horn sweeps out and up toward the upper left corner of the canvas, with its tip about 2 1/2 in from the top edge. The shorter horn curves out and up near the lake, starting about 8 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the hills showing around both horns.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop when you have two flat bone-colored horns with pointed, upturned tips, and no shading yet.

shade-horns.start: Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the fringe.
shade-horns.strokes: Follow the curve of each horn from the base out toward the tip, with light curved strokes.
shade-horns.inside: Nose pink goes along the underside of each horn, out of the sun. Make it heaviest at the base and at the tip so the horn looks round.
shade-horns.leave: Leave a strip of Horn bone along the upper curve of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when both horns look rounded, with dark bases and tips and pale tops. Keep the strokes thin: it is easy to cover the whole horn.

pull-ginger-locks.start: Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.
pull-ginger-locks.strokes: Press the full width of the brush for the root of each lock, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point. Pull the fringe locks straight down over the eyes. On the body, pull long slanting locks down toward the legs.
pull-ginger-locks.inside: Golden ginger covers the fringe and the whole body. Most of it is in the left half, over the big shaggy rump.
pull-ginger-locks.leave: Leave gaps of rust and Dark umber between the locks, the dark shadow under the fringe, and the muzzle.
pull-ginger-locks.stop: Stop when the cow looks striped with long hanging hair.

pull-straw-locks.start: Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
pull-straw-locks.strokes: Use the same press-then-lift pull, with shorter, thinner locks hanging downward.
pull-straw-locks.inside: Straw gold catches the sun on the edge nearest the lake. Most of it is in the right half: down the edge of the face, the chest and the front leg. Add only a few short locks on the rump.
pull-straw-locks.leave: Leave the ginger, rust and umber showing between the locks.
pull-straw-locks.stop: Stop when one long glowing edge runs down the sunny side of the cow, with fewer, shorter locks elsewhere.

light-the-rims.start: Start on the upper curve of the long horn, near its base.
light-the-rims.strokes: Dry brush: use only the tip, with no water. Skim light, short strokes along each horn's top curve, then dab tiny feathery touches.
light-the-rims.inside: Sunlit cream goes as a thin shine along the upper curve of each horn, and as small touches along the top of the fringe between the horns, where the sun catches the hair. Add a few flecks on the tips of the outer tufts.
light-the-rims.leave: Leave the Nose pink shading on the horn undersides, and all the hair locks below the fringe top.
light-the-rims.stop: Stop early: these are only tiny glints. If one went on solid, let it dry and skim the base color back over it.

paint-nose.first: Let the hair and horns dry.
paint-nose.start: Start in the middle of the nose, just under the fringe, about 7 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Use curved strokes around the round shape of the muzzle.
paint-nose.inside: Nose pink fills one broad, rounded nose peeking out from under the hair.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the hair showing all around it, and the fringe hanging over its top.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when the nose is about 1 in wide and about 3/4 in tall: a plain dusty pink shape, with no nostrils yet.

line-nostrils-mouth.first: Let the nose dry completely, or the lines will spread.
line-nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
line-nostrils-mouth.strokes: Hold the liner upright and use thin, watery paint with light, steady pressure. Make a short dot-like curve for each nostril, then a short wobbling line for the mouth.
line-nostrils-mouth.inside: Dark umber goes in the two nostrils, the mouth line under the nose, and thin dark lines around the edge of the muzzle so it stands out from the hair.
line-nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave most of the Nose pink showing.
line-nostrils-mouth.stop: Stop when the face reads clearly: the area you work in is about 1 3/4 in wide. If a line skips, add water.

flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Dry brush: dip only the tip, with no water. Flick quick, light strokes upward, each one leaning a little like a blade of grass.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Deep grass green is thickest near the bottom edge, because grass up close is darkest. Carry the blades up over the cow's legs and lower belly so the cow stands inside the grass.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and the upper meadow mostly untouched.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Stop when the legs are hidden in dark grass, without any solid patches.

flick-light-grass.start: Start near the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-light-grass.strokes: Use the same quick, light upward flicks with a dry brush.
flick-light-grass.inside: Sunlit green blades go over the dark ones, more of them in the right half where the sun hits. Add a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.
flick-light-grass.leave: Leave dark green showing between the light blades.
flick-light-grass.stop: Stop when you see clear light blades in front of dark ones. A beginner tends to cover the dark: keep it showing.

flick-gold-tips.start: Start low in the meadow, near the bottom edge of the canvas.
flick-gold-tips.strokes: Make short, quick upward dry-brush marks, one small tip at a time.
flick-gold-tips.inside: Straw gold seed tips go across the meadow: bigger and farther apart near the bottom edge, smaller toward the back, with more in the right half toward the sun. Add a few over the cow's lower legs.
flick-gold-tips.leave: Leave most of the green blades untouched.
flick-gold-tips.stop: Stop when golden tips sparkle across the grass. Then the painting is finished.

blend-the-sky.text: Start at the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue, stroking side to side all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge.
Keep every stroke long and level. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold and paint a gold band where the blue ends. Stroke back up over the join several times while it is still wet.

Blue stays across the top. The gold makes a wide glowing band through the upper middle of the sky, warmest toward the right edge of the canvas where the sun sets. Lower down, go back to Sky blue with soft gold streaks in it, all the way to the bottom edge.
No white canvas: this sky runs under everything that comes later.
Stop when the whole canvas is covered, top edge to bottom edge, with soft joins. If you see a hard line between two colors, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

lay-in-clouds.text: Let the sky dry completely.
Start at the top edge of the canvas in the upper left corner of the sky, with Sunset gold on the tip of the brush.
Make small circles with the tip so the cloud edges come out bumpy and soft. Keep each streak's bottom fairly flat, and let the streaks lie in long slanting shapes.
Most of the gold goes in the left half: a big ragged cloud along the top edge, a mass reaching down the left edge, then small slanting streaks lower in the blue, smaller and thinner the lower you go.
Leave plenty of blue sky between the streaks.
Stop when you have soft, bumpy gold streaks floating in the blue. If an edge looks too hard, soften it with lighter circles.

light-cloud-tops.text: Let the gold cloud streaks dry.
Start at the top edge of the canvas, on the upper edges of the big gold cloud there.
Dry brush: dip only the tip, with no water. Skim lightly side to side along each cloud edge so the marks break up on the canvas texture.

Sunlit cream goes along the tops of the clouds, the edges that face the light. Most of it goes lower down, though: long wavy streaks across the lower sky that soften the small gold streaks into rippling bands.
Leave the gold showing under the cream and the blue showing between the bands.
Stop when you have broken, see-through glints, never a solid patch. If one went on solid, let it dry and skim the sky color back over part of it.

lay-in-far-hills.text: Let the sky and clouds dry.
Start with the rounded tops of the far range, about 2 in from the top edge of the canvas, working from the left edge to the right edge.
Bend every stroke with the hills: from the top of each bump, down along its curve.
Hazy violet covers everything from those hilltops down to the bottom edge. Lay it as layered rows of soft rounded ridges, each row a little lower than the last, sloping down toward the right edge.
Keep the sky and clouds clear of violet beyond the line of the hilltops, and let a little warm gold glow through between the ridges.
Stop when the canvas below the hilltops is a soft violet band of ridges, flat and with no texture.

shade-near-ridges.text: Let the far hills dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, where the pale back range meets the next ridge down.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Let the band drift lower as it crosses toward the right edge of the canvas.
This is one darker ridge just in front of the farthest range. Its middle is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of it is in the right half, where it is widest and heaviest.
Leave the pale back range and the sky untouched, and leave the lower violet ridges as they are.
Stop when the darker ridge clearly separates the pale distance from the hills in front.

paint-lake.text: Let the darker ridge dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, with the lake's top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
Use short curved strokes that follow the shoreline, curving into the hills and tapering to a point.
Pale sky fills one small flat sliver of water, flat along its top and narrowing to a point where it tucks behind the hills.
Leave the violet ridges showing all around it.
Stop when the lake is about 1 1/4 in wide and about 1/2 in tall: a small, pale, still sliver.

lay-in-hillside.text: Let the lake and ridges dry.
Start at the top of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
Cut the top edge of the slope as one line that falls gently to the right edge of the canvas and passes below the lake. Then fill the area with long, level strokes, left and right.
Olive green covers everything from that slope line down to the bottom edge. It is one flat, even shape.
Leave the sky, the violet ridges and the lake showing beyond the slope's top edge.
Stop when the whole lower canvas is flat olive green, with no patches yet.

tap-sunlit-slope.text: Let the green from step 7 dry.
Start near the top of the hillside at the left edge of the canvas, tapping lightly.
Spread the fan and stamp only its middle tips. Work down in a zigzag and press harder as you go lower. Let the patches drift in long clumps that slope down toward the right edge.
Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside, all the way down the canvas, because the whole slope faces the low sun.
Leave clumps of the darker green from step 7 showing between the patches as bushes, plus a darker band along the very top of the slope.
Stop when the hillside is dappled yellow-green with dark bushes throughout. If the marks look heavy and clumpy, thin the paint and spread the fan.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside taps dry.
Start along the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas, beginning at the left edge.
Use short X strokes that cross each other in two directions. If you want it smoother, go over it while it is wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
Sunlit green covers the whole lower canvas in one solid coat. Its top edge is gently bumpy and drops slightly toward the right edge.
Leave the dappled hillside showing beyond the meadow's top edge.
Stop when the lower canvas is flat yellow-green, with no gold or olive showing through.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
Dry brush: use only the tip of the brush and no water. Skim short, light strokes upward, leaning a little like windblown grass, and build up in several passes.
Deep grass green is heaviest near the bottom edge, because the front of the meadow sits in shadow. It thins as you go up, with streaks reaching about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
Leave a band of yellow-green along the top of the meadow, and lighter patches of it showing through the streaks.
Stop when the meadow is streaky and darkens toward you. It should still have no separate grass blades.

block-in-cow.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start with a big oval for the body. Its middle is about 5 in from the left edge of the canvas.

Add the rest in curved pieces like ( ). Put the rounded head and fringe on the side of the body nearest the lake, with its top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge. Then add the shaggy rump, and short leg pieces going down into the grass.
Rust brown fills the whole cow, flat and solid. Keep the outline ragged so it already looks hairy.
Leave grass showing between the legs.
Stop when you have one flat rust shape about 7 3/4 in wide and 8 3/4 in tall, with no shading.

shade-cow.text: Let the cow shape from step 11 dry.
Start at the top of the cow's back, at the hump behind the head.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs. Bend each one with the round of the body, like hanging hair.
Dark umber falls on the hind end and the middle of the body, under the fringe, down the chest and on the legs: the sides turned away from the sun. Most of it is in the left half.
Leave streaks of the warm brown from step 11 showing between the strokes, especially on the face and the front of the chest.
Stop when the cow looks streaky and rounded, dark at the back and shaded under the fringe.

block-in-horns.text: Let the cow dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the top of the head.
Pull each horn in tapering curves from its base out to its tip.

Horn bone fills two horns. The long horn sweeps out and up toward the upper left corner of the canvas, with its tip about 2 1/2 in from the top edge. The shorter horn curves out and up near the lake, starting about 8 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the hills showing around both horns.
Stop when you have two flat bone-colored horns with pointed, upturned tips, and no shading yet.

shade-horns.text: Let the horns dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the fringe.
Follow the curve of each horn from the base out toward the tip, with light curved strokes.
Nose pink goes along the underside of each horn, out of the sun. Make it heaviest at the base and at the tip so the horn looks round.
Leave a strip of the pale bone color from step 13 along the upper curve of each horn.
Stop when both horns look rounded, with dark bases and tips and pale tops. Keep the strokes thin: it is easy to cover the whole horn.

pull-ginger-locks.text: Let the shading dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.

Press the full width of the brush for the root of each lock, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point. Pull the fringe locks straight down over the eyes. On the body, pull long slanting locks down toward the legs.
Golden ginger covers the fringe and the whole body. Most of it is in the left half, over the big shaggy rump.
Leave gaps of the darker coat from steps 11 and 12 between the locks. Also leave the dark shadow under the fringe and the muzzle uncovered.
Stop when the cow looks striped with long hanging hair.

pull-straw-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry.
Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
Use the same press-then-lift pull, with shorter, thinner locks hanging downward.
Straw gold catches the sun on the edge nearest the lake. Most of it is in the right half: down the edge of the face, the chest and the front leg. Add only a few short locks on the rump.
Leave the ginger, rust and umber showing between the locks.
Stop when one long glowing edge runs down the sunny side of the cow, with fewer, shorter locks elsewhere.

Start on the upper curve of the long horn, near its base.
Dry brush: use only the tip, with no water. Skim light, short strokes along each horn's top curve, then dab tiny feathery touches.

Sunlit cream goes as a thin shine along the upper curve of each horn. It also goes as small touches along the top of the fringe between the horns, where the sun catches the hair. Add a few flecks on the tips of the outer tufts.
Leave the shading from step 14 on the horn undersides, and the hanging locks of the fringe and body as they are.
Stop early: these are only tiny glints. If one went on solid, let it dry and skim the base color back over it.

paint-nose.text: Let the hair and horns dry.
Start in the middle of the nose, just under the fringe, about 7 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
Use curved strokes around the round shape of the muzzle.
Nose pink fills one broad, rounded nose peeking out from under the hair.
Leave the hair showing all around it, and the fringe hanging over its top.
Stop when the nose is about 1 in wide and about 3/4 in tall: a plain dusty pink shape, with no nostrils yet.

Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
Hold the liner upright and use thin, watery paint with light, steady pressure. Make a short dot-like curve for each nostril, then a short wobbling line for the mouth.
Dark umber goes in the two nostrils and the mouth line under the nose. Add thin dark lines around the edge of the muzzle so it stands out from the hair.
Leave most of the pink from step 18 showing.
Stop when the face reads clearly; the area you work in is about 1 3/4 in wide. If a line skips, add water.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the whole cow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
Dry brush: dip only the tip, with no water. Flick quick, light strokes upward, each one leaning a little like a blade of grass.
Deep grass green is thickest near the bottom edge, because grass up close is darkest. Carry the blades up over the cow's legs and lower belly so the legs disappear among them.
Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and the upper meadow mostly untouched.
Stop when the legs are hidden in dark grass, without any solid patches.

flick-light-grass.text: Let the dark blades dry.
Start near the bottom edge of the canvas.
Use the same quick, light upward flicks with a dry brush.
Sunlit green blades go over the dark ones, more of them in the right half where the sun hits. Add a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.
Leave dark green showing between the light blades.
Stop when you see clear light blades in front of dark ones. A beginner tends to cover the dark: keep it showing.

flick-gold-tips.text: Let the light blades dry.
Start low in the meadow, near the bottom edge of the canvas.
Make short, quick upward dry-brush marks, one small tip at a time.
Straw gold seed tips go across the meadow: bigger and farther apart near the bottom edge, smaller toward the back, with more in the right half toward the sun. Add a few over the cow's lower legs.
Leave most of the green blades untouched.
Stop when golden tips sparkle across the grass. Then the painting is finished.

No white canvas: this sky runs under everything that comes later.
Stop when the whole canvas is covered, top edge to bottom edge, with soft joins. If you see a hard line between two colors, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

shade-near-ridges.text: Let the far hills dry.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, where the pale back range meets the next ridge down.
This is the same Hazy violet you used for the far hills. This time you keep the strokes long and level, and lay one darker ridge instead of many rounded ones.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right. Let the band drift lower as it crosses toward the right edge of the canvas.
This is one darker ridge just in front of the farthest range. Its middle is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of it is in the right half, where it is widest and heaviest.
Leave the pale back range and the sky untouched, and leave the lower violet ridges as they are.
Stop when the darker ridge clearly separates the pale distance from the hills in front.

paint-lake.text: Let the darker ridge dry.
Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the darker ridge, with the lake's top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge.
These are the same bending strokes you used for the far hills, now with a small round brush for one tiny curved shape of water.
Use short curved strokes that follow the shoreline, curving into the hills and tapering to a point.
Pale sky fills one small flat sliver of water, flat along its top and narrowing to a point where it tucks behind the hills.
Leave the violet ridges showing all around it.
Stop when the lake is about 1 1/4 in wide and about 1/2 in tall: a small, pale, still sliver.

lay-in-hillside.text: Let the lake and ridges dry.
Start at the top of the slope at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge.
These are the same long, level strokes you used for the darker ridge, now with a bigger brush and green paint covering much more of the canvas.
Cut the top edge of the slope as one line that falls gently to the right edge of the canvas and passes below the lake. Then fill the area with long, level strokes, left and right.
Olive green covers everything from that slope line down to the bottom edge. It is one flat, even shape.
Leave the sky, the violet ridges and the lake showing beyond the slope's top edge.

Sunlit green goes over most of the hillside, all the way down the canvas, because the whole slope faces the low sun.

lay-in-meadow.text: Let the hillside taps dry.
Start along the meadow's top edge, about 7 in from the top edge of the canvas, beginning at the left edge.
This is the same Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside. Now it goes on as one solid coat, in crossing strokes, with no darker green showing through.
Use short X strokes that cross each other in two directions. If you want it smoother, go over it while it is wet with longer side-to-side strokes.
Sunlit green covers the whole lower canvas in one solid coat. Its top edge is gently bumpy and drops slightly toward the right edge.
Leave the dappled hillside showing beyond the meadow's top edge.
Stop when the lower canvas is flat yellow-green, with no gold or olive showing through.

darken-meadow-front.text: Let the meadow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
This is the same dry, skimming brush you used to light the cloud tops. Now the paint is dark green, the brush is bigger, and the strokes go upward like grass.
Dry brush: use only the tip of the brush and no water. Skim short, light strokes upward, leaning a little like windblown grass, and build up in several passes.
Deep grass green is heaviest near the bottom edge, because the front of the meadow sits in shadow. It thins as you go up, with streaks reaching about 8 1/4 in from the top edge.
Leave a band of yellow-green along the top of the meadow, and lighter patches of it showing through the streaks.

shade-cow.text: Let the cow shape from step 11 dry.
Start at the top of the cow's back, at the hump behind the head.
You bent your strokes over the far hills the same way. Here they follow the round of the cow's body and fall like hanging hair.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the spine toward the belly and legs. Bend each one with the round of the body, like hanging hair.
Dark umber falls on the hind end and the middle of the body, under the fringe, down the chest and on the legs: the sides turned away from the sun. Most of it is in the left half.
Leave streaks of the warm brown from step 11 showing between the strokes, especially on the face and the front of the chest.
Stop when the cow looks streaky and rounded, dark at the back and shaded under the fringe.

block-in-horns.text: Let the cow dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the top of the head.
These are the same curved strokes you just used to shade the cow, now with a small round brush, tapering to a point at each horn's tip.
Pull each horn in tapering curves from its base out to its tip.

Horn bone fills two horns. The long horn sweeps out and up toward the upper left corner of the canvas, with its tip about 2 1/2 in from the top edge. The shorter horn curves out and up near the lake, starting about 8 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the hills showing around both horns.
Stop when you have two flat bone-colored horns with pointed, upturned tips, and no shading yet.

shade-horns.text: Let the horns dry.
Start at the base of each horn, where it meets the fringe.
Follow the same curves you used to block in the horns, with a smaller brush, keeping the darker paint on the side away from the sun.
Follow the curve of each horn from the base out toward the tip, with light curved strokes.
Nose pink goes along the underside of each horn, out of the sun. Make it heaviest at the base and at the tip so the horn looks round.
Leave a strip of the pale bone color from step 13 along the upper curve of each horn.
Stop when both horns look rounded, with dark bases and tips and pale tops. Keep the strokes thin: it is easy to cover the whole horn.

Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns.

Press the full width of the brush for the root of each lock, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point. Pull the fringe locks straight down over the eyes. On the body, pull long slanting locks down toward the legs.
