Stop when the cow looks striped with long hanging hair.

pull-straw-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry.
Start along the top of the fringe, between the horns.
This is the same press-and-lift pull as the ginger locks. The brush is smaller, the paint is lighter, and the locks are shorter and fewer.
Use the same press-then-lift pull, with shorter, thinner locks hanging downward.
Straw gold catches the sun on the edge nearest the lake. Most of it is in the right half: down the edge of the face, the chest and the front leg. Add only a few short locks on the rump.
Leave the ginger, rust and umber showing between the locks.
Stop when one long glowing edge runs down the sunny side of the cow, with fewer, shorter locks elsewhere.

light-the-rims.text: Let the straw-gold locks dry.
Start on the upper curve of the long horn, near its base.
This is the same Sunlit cream and the same dry skim you used to light the cloud tops. Now the marks are tiny, on the horns and the fringe, where the same sun catches them.
Dry brush: use only the tip, with no water. Skim light, short strokes along each horn's top curve, then dab tiny feathery touches.

Sunlit cream goes as a thin shine along the upper curve of each horn. It also goes as small touches along the top of the fringe between the horns, where the sun catches the hair. Add a few flecks on the tips of the outer tufts.
Leave the shading from step 14 on the horn undersides, and the hanging locks of the fringe and body as they are.
Stop early: these are only tiny glints. If one went on solid, let it dry and skim the base color back over it.

paint-nose.text: Let the hair and horns dry.
Start in the middle of the nose, just under the fringe, about 7 1/4 in from the left edge of the canvas and about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
This is the same Nose pink you used to shade the horns. Now it fills one round shape with curved strokes around the muzzle.
Use curved strokes around the round shape of the muzzle.
Nose pink fills one broad, rounded nose peeking out from under the hair.
Leave the hair showing all around it, and the fringe hanging over its top.
Stop when the nose is about 1 in wide and about 3/4 in tall: a plain dusty pink shape, with no nostrils yet.

line-nostrils-mouth.text: Let the nose dry completely, or the lines will spread.
Start with the two nostrils on the nose.
This is the same Dark umber you used for the cow's shadows. Now it goes on thin and watery with a liner, for small lines only.
Hold the liner upright and use thin, watery paint with light, steady pressure. Make a short dot-like curve for each nostril, then a short wobbling line for the mouth.
Dark umber goes in the two nostrils and the mouth line under the nose. Add thin dark lines around the edge of the muzzle so it stands out from the hair.
Leave most of the pink from step 18 showing.
Stop when the face reads clearly; the area you work in is about 1 3/4 in wide. If a line skips, add water.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the whole cow dry.
Start at the bottom edge of the canvas.
This is the same Deep grass green and the same dry brush you used to darken the meadow. Now, with a stiff old brush, each flick becomes a separate blade that runs over the cow's legs.
Dry brush: dip only the tip, with no water. Flick quick, light strokes upward, each one leaning a little like a blade of grass.
Deep grass green is thickest near the bottom edge, because grass up close is darkest. Carry the blades up over the cow's legs and lower belly so the legs disappear among them.
Leave the meadow showing between the blades, and the upper meadow mostly untouched.
Stop when the legs are hidden in dark grass, without any solid patches.

flick-light-grass.text: Let the dark blades dry.
Start near the bottom edge of the canvas.
These are the same quick upward flicks you just made, now in the lighter Sunlit green, and fewer of them, so the dark blades still show.
Use the same quick, light upward flicks with a dry brush.
Sunlit green blades go over the dark ones, more of them in the right half where the sun hits. Add a few over the bottom of the cow's legs.
Leave dark green showing between the light blades.
Stop when you see clear light blades in front of dark ones. A beginner tends to cover the dark: keep it showing.

flick-gold-tips.text: Let the light blades dry.
Start low in the meadow, near the bottom edge of the canvas.
This is the same Straw gold that lit the cow's sunny locks. Now it goes on in short dry-brush marks as the glowing tips of the grass.
Make short, quick upward dry-brush marks, one small tip at a time.
Straw gold seed tips go across the meadow: bigger and farther apart near the bottom edge, smaller toward the back, with more in the right half toward the sun. Add a few over the cow's lower legs.
Leave most of the green blades untouched.
Stop when golden tips sparkle across the grass. Then the painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass on a hillside at sunset, with blue hills and a glimpse of a lake far away. The heart of the painting is the cow's face: a pink nose peeking out of a glowing fringe, framed by a pair of curving horns. Everything else is there to frame that face and fill it with warm evening light.
opening.light: The low sun is setting behind the hills, so the sky glows gold where the sun is going down. The same sun catches the edges of the cow's hair, its fringe, the tops of its horns and the tips of the grass, and leaves the side of the cow that faces away from it in deep shadow.

skills.how: Dry brush means almost no paint and no water: you dip only the tip and skim it lightly, so the paint breaks up on the canvas texture. You use it for the bright edges of the clouds, the shadowy front of the meadow, the sunlit rim of the cow, and every grass blade in front of it. Watch the load: if a mark goes on solid, the brush was too full, so wipe it and let the canvas texture do the work.

Curved strokes bend with the shape you are painting, and that bending is what makes a thing look round. Here they shape the rolling far hills, the curve of the lake, the round body of the cow, its sweeping horns and its soft nose. Before each stroke, ask which way the surface curves, and let the brush follow it.

Thick to thin starts with the full width of the brush and lifts onto its edge as you pull, so each mark tapers to a point. This is how the cow gets its long, hanging locks of hair, first in ginger and then in straw gold. Keep each pull confident and in one motion: a slow, fussy stroke loses the taper.

opening.road: We start with the sky, blended smoothly across the whole canvas, because it sits behind everything else. Next come the far hills and the lake, laid over the sky from the farthest range forward. Then the green hillside and the meadow go on, from far to near, so you have a whole landscape before the cow appears. The cow is built as one simple shape, then shaded and given its horns. After that come its long locks and sunlit rim, and the face goes on last. Finally, grass is flicked over the cow's legs so the cow stands deep in the meadow instead of sitting on it like a sticker.

the-sky.for: This stage covers the canvas with a glowing sunset sky and soft clouds that everything else will sit in front of.
the-sky.end: The whole canvas is a warm blend of blue and gold, with streaky clouds catching bright cream edges.

the-distance.for: This stage builds the far distance: hazy violet hills, a darker ridge in front of them, and a small pale lake.
the-distance.end: Soft violet ridges roll across the canvas in front of the sunset, with a darker ridge and a tiny silver lake tucked into the hills.

the-green-land.for: This stage lays the green land, from the sunlit hillside to the grassy meadow nearest you.
the-green-land.end: A dappled green hillside rolls away toward the hills, and a streaky meadow darkens toward you, still empty of the cow.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage builds the cow as one simple shape, gives it shading so it looks round, then adds its horns.
the-cow-shape.end: A rounded, shaggy brown cow stands in the meadow with a pair of shaded horns curving against the hills.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the plain cow into a long-haired Highland cow lit by the setting sun.
the-shaggy-coat.end: The cow is covered in long ginger and straw-gold locks, glowing along its sunny edge, with a cream shine on its horns.

the-face.for: This stage gives the cow its face, the focal point of the whole painting.
the-face.end: A dusty pink nose with dark nostrils and a mouth peeks out of the glowing fringe.

the-grass-in-front.for: This stage flicks tall grass over the meadow and the cow's legs so the cow stands inside the grass.
the-grass-in-front.end: Dark, light and golden grass blades fill the meadow and hide the cow's legs, and the painting is finished.

the-distance.end: Soft violet ridges roll across the canvas beneath the sunset, with a darker ridge and a tiny silver lake tucked into the hills.

the-green-land.end: A dappled green hillside rolls away toward the hills, and a streaky meadow darkens toward you, still empty of the cow.

the-cow-shape.end: A rounded, shaggy brown cow stands in the meadow with two shaded horns curving against the hills.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage turns the plain cow into a long-haired Highland cow lit by the setting sun.

back.text: This is the same Hazy violet you used for the far hills. This time you keep the strokes long and level, and lay one darker ridge instead of many rounded ones.
These are the same bending strokes you used for the far hills, now with a small round brush for one tiny curved shape of water.
These are the same long, level strokes you used for the darker ridge, now with a bigger brush and green paint covering much more of the canvas.
This is the same Sunlit green you tapped onto the hillside. Now it goes on as one solid coat, in crossing strokes, with no darker green showing through.
This is the same dry, skimming brush you used to light the cloud tops. Now the paint is dark green, the brush is bigger, and the strokes go upward like grass.
You bent your strokes over the far hills the same way. Here they follow the round of the cow's body and fall like hanging hair.
These are the same curved strokes you just used to shade the cow, now with a small round brush, tapering to a point at each horn's tip.
Follow the same curves you used to block in the horns, with a smaller brush, keeping the darker paint on the side away from the sun.
This is the same press-and-lift pull as the ginger locks. The brush is smaller, the paint is lighter, and the locks are shorter and fewer.
This is the same Sunlit cream and the same dry skim you used to light the cloud tops. Now the marks are tiny, on the horns and the fringe, where the same sun catches them.
This is the same Nose pink you used to shade the horns. Now it fills one round shape with curved strokes around the muzzle.
This is the same Dark umber you used for the cow's shadows. Now it goes on thin and watery with a liner, for small lines only.
This is the same Deep grass green and the same dry brush you used to darken the meadow. Now, with a stiff old brush, each flick becomes a separate blade that runs over the cow's legs.
These are the same quick upward flicks you just made, now in the lighter Sunlit green, and fewer of them, so the dark blades still show.
This is the same Straw gold that lit the cow's sunny locks. Now it goes on in short dry-brush marks as the glowing tips of the grass.

blend-sky.start: Start at the sun's glow high on the left side of the canvas with Sun cream, then work Warm gold out around it across the left half.
blend-sky.strokes: Use short X strokes that cross each other, loading two colours at once where they meet. Bring Haze blue in from the right edge and across the top, and carry the whole blend down to the bottom edge.
blend-sky.inside: Keep the palest cream around the sun, with gold spreading out from it and blue toward the right edge and lower down. The light comes from the upper left, so the glow sits there.
blend-sky.leave: Leave no bare white canvas: the blend reaches the left, right, top and bottom edges.
blend-sky.stop: While it is still wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes so the glow fades softly into the blue. The whole canvas reads as a misty glow, paler across the bottom, with no hard edges.

brush-far-treeline.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will drag it into streaks.
brush-far-treeline.start: Begin where the blue tree shapes are tallest, at the top edge on the right side of the canvas.
brush-far-treeline.strokes: Dip only the tip of the old stiff flat in Misty blue and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly downward in short, ragged strokes that make soft, rounded tree tops.
brush-far-treeline.inside: Most of it is on the right side. The shapes run from about 6 3/4 in from the left edge to the right edge. They are deepest near the right edge and thin to a faint band toward the middle, where the glow shines through.
brush-far-treeline.leave: Leave the sun's glow and the left side of the sky clear. Keep the bottoms of the shapes ragged so they fade into the mist.
brush-far-treeline.stop: Soft, broken blue tree shapes stand in the haze with mist below them. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim more lightly next pass.

pull-far-trunks.first: Let the blue tree shapes dry.
pull-far-trunks.start: Start at the top edge, in the glow, with the trunk whose middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the angle brush's full width at the top edge and pull straight down. Lighten the pressure as you go so the trunk thins and fades out, about 7 1/4 in tall.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Then add a short piece hanging from the top edge toward the middle of the canvas. Add a few short, soft trunk pieces lower down in the blue tree shapes. These are far trunks, so keep them pale and plain.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the mist showing between them, and give them no bark marks.
pull-far-trunks.stop: One long, thin, pale trunk stands in the glow, and a few short trunk pieces show faintly in the blue haze.

stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tallest pine on the right side of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Spread the fan and stamp only the middle tips, zigzagging from the tip down and pressing harder as you go, so each pine widens toward the bottom. Make three pines side by side, then part of one more at the right edge.
stamp-pines.inside: The pines run from about 10 1/2 in from the left edge to the right edge. Keep them one flat dark colour for now.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the misty trunks and blue tree shapes showing around and above them. Keep the pines' bottoms ragged in the mist.
stamp-pines.stop: A group of dark blue-green pines, pointed on top and wide at the bottom. Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick or you stamped with the side of the fan.

tap-pine-light.first: Let the dark pines dry so the teal stays separate.
tap-pine-light.start: Start at the feet of the pines, along the band about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, where they meet the mist.
tap-pine-light.strokes: Fan-tap Pine teal in short strokes in different directions, all along the feet. Then add a patch where the smallest pine meets the mist toward the middle, and a few taps between the pine tips near the right edge.
tap-pine-light.inside: The teal goes around the pines, not on them. It softens their feet into the mist and fills the gaps, so the dark trees sit back in the haze.
tap-pine-light.leave: Leave the pine shapes themselves dark and uncovered.
tap-pine-light.stop: The pines' bottoms melt into a teal mist, and their outlines look softer and further away.

dab-bush-darks.first: Let the pines and mist dry.
dab-bush-darks.start: Start along the feet of the pines, on the right side of the canvas, dabbing a band of olive where they meet the mist.
dab-bush-darks.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the dry old flat. Then dab three small clumps across the misty ground and a clump at the left edge. Add thinner scattered dabs down to the bottom edge, then a loose, lacy scatter along the top of the canvas.
dab-bush-darks.inside: Most of it is in the bottom half: the heavy dabs are the undergrowth's shadow. The scatter along the top is only a dark lace for the leaves to sit on later.
dab-bush-darks.leave: Leave plenty of mist showing through the gaps, and keep the sun's glow clear.
dab-bush-darks.stop: Olive masses sit at the pines' feet, with small clumps on the misty ground and an olive lace up top. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-canopy-darks.start: Start with the big bush mass at the left edge. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
dab-canopy-darks.strokes: Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the old flat, tapping a spot more where the bush should look solid.
dab-canopy-darks.inside: Most of it is on the left side. After the bush mass, dab loose clusters hanging from the top edge over the olive lace, and a few small dabs on the olive at the pines' feet.
dab-canopy-darks.leave: Leave olive showing along the bush's base, and sky between the clusters.
dab-canopy-darks.stop: A warm orange bush mass glows at the left edge, with orange clusters hanging along the top of the canvas.

dab-golden-leaves.first: Let the orange dry so the gold stays bright.
dab-golden-leaves.start: Start in the canopy clusters at the top edge, near the sun on the left side of the canvas.
dab-golden-leaves.strokes: Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the old flat in small, leaf-sized dabs.
dab-golden-leaves.inside: Most of it is on the left side and in the top half. Cover most of each canopy cluster and the top of the orange bush mass, where the sun hits them. Only a few dabs go on the clusters toward the right edge.
dab-golden-leaves.leave: Leave orange showing in the shadows of the clusters and along the bush's base, and sky between the leaves.
dab-golden-leaves.stop: The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange still showing underneath.

dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start in the canopy nearest the sun, at the left edge around the cream glow.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap the tip of the #10 round lightly, dot by dot. Tap a spot more where it should glow strongest.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Then tap lemon over the top of the golden bush mass. Spread dappled patches over the misty ground below it, from the left edge across the canvas down to the bottom edge. Most of it is in the bottom half: this is sunlight lying on the mist.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the gold and orange leaves showing under the taps, and blue mist between the lemon patches.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: The canopy sparkles near the sun, and the misty ground glows in warm patches. There is no ground colour yet.

dab-floor-darks.start: Start at the left edge, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, just under the golden bush mass.
dab-floor-darks.strokes: Tap Rust brown with the old flat in rows across the canvas, working down toward the bottom edge.
dab-floor-darks.inside: Cover the whole width from the left edge to the right edge, right down to the bottom edge. Make it dense enough that no mist shows, and tap over the bushes' ragged bottoms.
dab-floor-darks.leave: Leave the bush masses and the pines' teal feet showing above the floor.
dab-floor-darks.stop: The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor. There is no path yet.

pull-path.first: Let the floor dry, so the tan doesn't turn to mud.
pull-path.start: Mark one dot where the path disappears, in the gap at the foot of the bushes. Draw a few faint chalk lines fanning toward you from it.
pull-path.strokes: Pull each stroke along the lines, from the dot toward you, thin near the dot and wider in front.
pull-path.inside: This is only the far end of the path: a short strip whose middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. It ends about 8 3/4 in from the top edge.
pull-path.leave: Leave the rust floor around it, and don't carry the path down to the bottom edge.
pull-path.stop: A short pale tan strip leads back into the gap and narrows to a point, plain with no leaves.

block-in-boulder.start: Start with a low dome right of the path at the pines' feet, its middle about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-boulder.strokes: Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it, like ( ), smaller toward the ends.
block-in-boulder.inside: Fill the whole boulder flat Olive moss, about 2 1/2 in wide, with a flat base sitting on the leaves.
block-in-boulder.leave: Leave the rust floor showing all around it.
block-in-boulder.stop: A plain, flat olive boulder shape sits right of the path, with no shading.

shade-boulder.start: Start on the right side of the boulder, where it sits on the leaves.
shade-boulder.strokes: Bend every stroke with the dome: from the top of it down along its curve, and along the base.
shade-boulder.inside: Most of it is on the right side. Cover the boulder's shadow side and base, and bring curved strokes over most of the dome, because the light comes from the upper left.
shade-boulder.leave: Leave a little flat olive on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
shade-boulder.stop: The boulder reads dark and solid, with only a hint of olive on its sunny shoulder.

light-boulder.first: Let the dark olive dry, or the moss will smear into it.
light-boulder.start: Start on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
light-boulder.strokes: With only the tip loaded, skim short, light dry-brush strokes along the top curve of the dome.
light-boulder.inside: Most of it is on the left side of the boulder, along its top and down the sunny shoulder, where the sun falls.
light-boulder.leave: Leave the dark side and base untouched.
light-boulder.stop: A broken band of pale moss catches the light along the boulder's top, and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.first: Let everything dry: the trunks go over all of it.
pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of the nearest big leaning trunk on the left side of the canvas, down in the leaves.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the 3/4 inch flat's full width at the foot and pull up past the top edge, leaning slightly right. Lighten as you go so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
pull-birches.inside: Make six trunks: a thin one near the left edge, two big leaning ones, and a thinner one whose middle is about 8 in from the left edge. Finish with two on the right side, the widest at the right edge.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the boulder, path and leaves showing between the trunks.
pull-birches.stop: Six flat, pale gray trunks with a few branches, most of it on the left side, with no shading yet.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top edge, on the biggest trunk on the left side.
shade-birches.strokes: With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark gray down each trunk and out along each branch, so it breaks into ragged strokes.
shade-birches.inside: The gray covers most of each trunk's width, most of it on the left side, where the big trunks are.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged pale flecks of the trunk colour all along each trunk. Keep the lowest part of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, pale.
shade-birches.stop: The trunks look gray and flecked with pale bark. If a patch goes solid, the brush was too loaded.

mark-birch-bark.start: Start at the foot of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, and press in a dark foot.
mark-birch-bark.strokes: For each bark mark, press the angle brush's full width, then turn onto its edge and lighten, so each short mark across the trunk tapers. Run thin dark lines along the branches.
mark-birch-bark.inside: Put more marks low on the trunks and fewer higher up. Most of it is in the bottom half and on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
mark-birch-bark.leave: Leave gray and pale bark showing between the marks.
mark-birch-bark.stop: The trunks read as birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.start: Start at the far end of the path, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, and work toward you.
dab-orange-leaves.strokes: Tap Leaf orange with the old flat in leaf-sized dabs.
dab-orange-leaves.inside: Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge, down to the bottom edge. Spill onto the path and over the dark feet of the trunks. Most of it is on the right side.
dab-orange-leaves.leave: Leave rust brown showing in the gaps.
dab-orange-leaves.stop: The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with rust in the gaps, and the trunk feet sit in the leaves.

dab-gold-leaves.start: Start at the far end of the path, then work down along it and out across the floor.
dab-gold-leaves.strokes: Tap the #10 round lightly in small leaf dabs.
dab-gold-leaves.inside: Most of it is on the right side and in the top half. Make a band of gold down the path and across the floor at the trunks' feet, with a few dabs at the left edge and fewer toward the bottom edge.
dab-gold-leaves.leave: Leave orange and rust showing between the gold.
dab-gold-leaves.stop: Gold leaves catch the sun along the path and across the middle of the floor.

light-birch-bark.first: Let the bark marks and leaves dry.
light-birch-bark.start: Start at the top edge on the biggest trunk, on its sunny side, the side facing the glow.
light-birch-bark.strokes: With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark white down each trunk and along its branches, skipping lightly over the dark marks.
light-birch-bark.inside: The light goes on the side of each trunk facing the sun, because the light comes from the upper left. Most of it is on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
light-birch-bark.leave: Leave the shaded side of each trunk gray, and keep the dark feet dark.
light-birch-bark.stop: Sunlit white birches with dark marks lean over the golden path into the misty grove.

blend-sky.text: Start at the sun's glow high on the left side of the canvas with Sun cream, then work Warm gold out around it across the left half.
Use short X strokes that cross each other, loading two colours at once where they meet. Bring Haze blue in from the right edge and across the top, and carry the whole blend down to the bottom edge.
Keep the palest cream around the sun, with gold spreading out from it and blue toward the right edge and lower down. The light comes from the upper left, so the glow sits there.
Leave no bare white canvas: the blend reaches the left, right, top and bottom edges.

While it is still wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes so the glow fades softly into the blue. The whole canvas reads as a misty glow, paler across the bottom, with no hard edges.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will drag it into streaks.
Begin where the blue tree shapes are tallest, at the top edge on the right side of the canvas.
Dip only the tip of the old stiff flat in Misty blue and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly downward in short, ragged strokes that make soft, rounded tree tops.

Most of it is on the right side. The shapes run from about 6 3/4 in from the left edge to the right edge. They are deepest near the right edge and thin to a faint band toward the middle, where the glow shines through.
Leave the sun's glow and the left side of the sky clear. Keep the bottoms of the shapes ragged so they fade into the mist.
Soft, broken blue tree shapes stand in the haze, their ragged feet fading into mist. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim more lightly next pass.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the blue tree shapes dry.
Start at the top edge, in the glow, with the trunk whose middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge.
Press the angle brush's full width at the top edge and pull straight down. Lighten the pressure as you go so the trunk thins and fades out, about 7 1/4 in tall.

Then add a short piece hanging from the top edge toward the middle of the canvas. Add a few short, soft trunk pieces lower down in the blue tree shapes. These are far trunks, so keep them pale and plain.
Leave the mist showing between them, and give them no bark marks.
One long, thin, pale trunk stands in the glow, and a few short trunk pieces show faintly in the blue haze.

stamp-pines.text: Let the far trunks dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine on the right side of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.

Spread the fan and stamp only the middle tips, zigzagging from the tip down and pressing harder as you go, so each pine widens toward the bottom. Make three pines side by side, then part of one more at the right edge.
The pines run from about 10 1/2 in from the left edge to the right edge. Keep them one flat dark colour for now.
Leave the misty trunks and blue tree shapes showing around the pines. Keep the pines' bottoms ragged in the mist.
A group of dark blue-green pines, pointed on top and wide at the bottom. Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick or you stamped with the side of the fan.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the dark pines dry so the teal stays separate.
Start at the feet of the pines, where they meet the mist.

Fan-tap Pine teal in short strokes in different directions, all along the feet. Then add a patch where the smallest pine meets the mist toward the middle, and a few taps between the pine tips near the right edge.
The teal goes around the pines, not on them. It softens their feet into the mist and fills the gaps, so the dark trees sit back in the haze.
Leave the pine shapes themselves dark and uncovered.
The pines' bottoms melt into a teal mist, and their outlines look softer and further away.

dab-bush-darks.text: Let the pines and mist dry.
Start along the feet of the pines, on the right side of the canvas, dabbing a band of olive where they meet the mist.

Tap lightly with the tip of the dry old flat. Then dab three small clumps across the misty ground and a clump at the left edge. Add thinner scattered dabs down to the bottom edge, then a loose, lacy scatter along the top of the canvas.
Most of it is in the bottom half: the heavy dabs are the undergrowth's shadow. The scatter along the top is only a dark lace for the leaves to sit on later.
Leave plenty of mist showing through the gaps, and keep the sun's glow clear.
Olive masses sit at the pines' feet, with small clumps on the misty ground and an olive lace up top. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-canopy-darks.text: Let the olive dry.
Start with the big bush mass at the left edge. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the old flat, tapping a spot more where the bush should look solid.
Most of it is on the left side. After the bush mass, dab loose clusters hanging from the top edge over the olive lace, and a few small dabs on the olive at the pines' feet.
Leave olive showing along the bush's base, and sky between the clusters.
A warm orange bush mass glows at the left edge, with orange clusters hanging along the top of the canvas.

dab-golden-leaves.text: Let the orange dry so the gold stays bright.
Start in the canopy clusters at the top edge, near the sun on the left side of the canvas.
Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the old flat in small, leaf-sized dabs.

Most of it is on the left side and in the top half. Cover most of each canopy cluster and the top of the orange bush mass, where the sun hits them. Only a few dabs go on the clusters toward the right edge.
Leave orange showing in the shadows of the clusters and along the bush's base, and sky between the leaves.
The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange still showing underneath.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the golden leaves dry.
Start in the canopy nearest the sun, at the left edge around the cream glow.
Tap the tip of the #10 round lightly, dot by dot. Tap a spot more where it should glow strongest.

Then tap lemon over the top of the golden bush mass. Spread dappled patches over the misty ground, from the left edge across the canvas down to the bottom edge. Most of it is in the bottom half: this is sunlight lying on the mist.
Leave the gold and orange leaves showing under the taps, and blue mist between the lemon patches.
The canopy sparkles near the sun, and the misty ground glows in warm patches. There is no ground colour yet.

dab-floor-darks.text: Let the lemon dry.
Start at the left edge, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, just under the golden bush mass.
Tap Rust brown with the old flat in rows across the canvas, working down toward you.
Cover the whole width of the canvas and all the way down, dense enough that no mist shows. Tap over the bushes' ragged bottoms as you go.
Leave the bush masses and the pines' teal feet showing above the floor.
The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor. There is no path yet.

pull-path.text: Let the floor dry, so the tan doesn't turn to mud.
Mark one dot where the path disappears, in the gap at the foot of the bushes. Draw a few faint chalk lines fanning toward you from it.
Pull each stroke along the lines, from the dot toward you, thin near the dot and wider in front.
This is only the far end of the path: a short strip whose middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge.
Leave the rust floor around it, and keep the path short.
A short pale tan strip leads back into the gap and narrows to a point, plain with no leaves.

block-in-boulder.text: Let the path dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path at the pines' feet, its middle about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it, like ( ), smaller toward the ends.
Fill the whole boulder flat Olive moss, about 2 1/2 in wide, with a flat base sitting on the leaves.
Leave the rust floor showing all around it.
A plain, flat olive boulder shape sits right of the path, with no shading.

shade-boulder.text: Let the olive dry.
Start on the right side of the boulder, where it sits on the leaves.
Bend every stroke with the dome: from the top of it down along its curve, and along the base.
Most of it is on the right side. Cover the boulder's shadow side and base, and bring curved strokes over most of the dome, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave a little flat olive on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
The boulder reads dark and solid, with only a hint of olive on its sunny shoulder.

light-boulder.text: Let the dark shading from step 13 dry, or the moss will smear into it.
Start on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
With only the tip loaded, skim short, light dry-brush strokes along the top curve of the dome.
Most of it is on the left side of the boulder, along its top and down the sunny shoulder, where the sun falls.
Leave the dark side and base untouched.
A broken band of pale moss catches the light along the boulder's top, and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.text: Let everything dry: the trunks go over all of it.
Start at the foot of the nearest big leaning trunk on the left side of the canvas, down in the leaves.

Press the 3/4 inch flat's full width at the foot and pull up past the top edge, leaning slightly right. Lighten as you go so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
Make six trunks: a thin one near the left edge, two big leaning ones, and a thinner one standing at the gap where the path disappears. Finish with two on the right side, the widest at the right edge.
Leave the boulder, path and leaves showing between the trunks.
Six flat, pale gray trunks with a few branches, most of it on the left side, with no shading yet.

shade-birches.text: Let the trunks dry.
Start at the top edge, on the biggest trunk on the left side.
With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark gray down each trunk and out along each branch, so it breaks into ragged strokes.
The gray covers most of each trunk's width, most of it on the left side, where the big trunks are.
Leave ragged pale flecks of the trunk colour all along each trunk. Keep the lowest part of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, pale.
The trunks look gray and flecked with pale bark. If a patch goes solid, the brush was too loaded.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the gray dry.
Start at the foot of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, and press in a dark foot.
For each bark mark, press the angle brush's full width, then turn onto its edge and lighten, so each short mark across the trunk tapers. Run thin dark lines along the branches.
Put more marks low on the trunks and fewer higher up. Most of it is in the bottom half and on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
Leave gray and pale bark showing between the marks.
The trunks read as birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start at the far end of the path, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, and work toward you.
Tap Leaf orange with the old flat in leaf-sized dabs.
Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge, down to the bottom edge. Spill onto the path and over the dark feet of the trunks. Most of it is on the right side.
Leave the dark leaf floor from step 10 showing in the gaps.
The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with darker leaves in the gaps, and the trunk feet sit in the leaves.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the orange dry.
Start at the far end of the path, then work down along it and out across the floor.
Tap the #10 round lightly in small leaf dabs.
Most of it is on the right side and in the top half. Make a band of gold down the path and across the floor at the trunks' feet, with a few dabs at the left edge and fewer toward the bottom edge.
Leave orange and rust showing between the gold.
Gold leaves catch the sun along the path and across the middle of the floor.

light-birch-bark.text: Let the bark marks and leaves dry.
Start at the top edge on the biggest trunk, on its sunny side, the side facing the glow.
With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark white down each trunk and along its branches, skipping lightly over the dark marks.
The light goes on the side of each trunk facing the sun, because the light comes from the upper left. Most of it is on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
Leave the shaded side of each trunk gray, and keep the dark feet dark.
Sunlit white birches with dark marks lean over the golden path into the misty grove.

blend-sky.text: Start at the sun's glow high on the left side of the canvas with Sun cream, then work Warm gold out around it across the left half.
Use short X strokes that cross each other, loading two colours at once where they meet. Bring Haze blue in from the right edge and across the top, and carry the whole blend down to the bottom edge.
Keep the palest cream around the sun, with gold spreading out from it and blue toward the right edge and lower down. The light comes from the upper left, so the glow sits there.
Leave no bare white canvas: the blend reaches the left, right, top and bottom edges.

While it is still wet, go over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes so the glow fades softly into the blue. The whole canvas reads as a misty glow, paler across the bottom, with no hard edges.

brush-far-treeline.text: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will drag it into streaks.
Begin where the blue tree shapes are tallest, at the top edge on the right side of the canvas.
Dip only the tip of the old stiff flat in Misty blue and wipe it nearly dry. Skim lightly downward in short, ragged strokes that make soft, rounded tree tops.

Most of it is on the right side. The shapes run from about 6 3/4 in from the left edge to the right edge. They are deepest near the right edge and thin to a faint band toward the middle, where the glow shines through.
Leave the sun's glow and the left side of the sky clear. Keep the bottoms of the shapes ragged so they fade into the mist.
Soft, broken blue tree shapes stand in the haze, their ragged feet fading into mist. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim more lightly next pass.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the blue tree shapes dry.
Start at the top edge, in the glow, with the trunk whose middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge.
Press the angle brush's full width at the top edge and pull straight down. Lighten the pressure as you go so the trunk thins and fades out, about 7 1/4 in tall.

Then add a short piece hanging from the top edge toward the middle of the canvas. Add a few short, soft trunk pieces lower down in the blue tree shapes. These are far trunks, so keep them pale and plain.
Leave the mist showing between them, and give them no bark marks.
One long, thin, pale trunk stands in the glow, and a few short trunk pieces show faintly in the blue haze.

stamp-pines.text: Let the far trunks dry.
Start at the tip of the tallest pine on the right side of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.

Spread the fan and stamp only the middle tips, zigzagging from the tip down and pressing harder as you go, so each pine widens toward the bottom. Make three pines side by side, then part of one more at the right edge.
The pines run from about 10 1/2 in from the left edge to the right edge. Keep them one flat dark colour for now.
Leave the misty trunks and blue tree shapes showing around the pines. Keep the pines' bottoms ragged in the mist.
A group of dark blue-green pines, pointed on top and wide at the bottom. Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick or you stamped with the side of the fan.

tap-pine-light.text: Let the dark pines dry so the teal stays separate.
Start at the feet of the pines, where they meet the mist.
This is the same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines, now with Pine teal, tapped into the mist around them instead of on the trees.

Fan-tap Pine teal in short strokes in different directions, all along the feet. Then add a patch where the smallest pine meets the mist toward the middle, and a few taps between the pine tips near the right edge.
The teal goes around the pines, not on them. It softens their feet into the mist and fills the gaps, so the dark trees sit back in the haze.
Leave the pine shapes themselves dark and uncovered.
The pines' bottoms melt into a teal mist, and their outlines look softer and further away.

dab-bush-darks.text: Let the pines and mist dry.
Start along the feet of the pines, on the right side of the canvas, dabbing a band of olive where they meet the mist.

Tap lightly with the tip of the dry old flat. Then dab three small clumps across the misty ground and a clump at the left edge. Add thinner scattered dabs down to the bottom edge, then a loose, lacy scatter along the top of the canvas.
Most of it is in the bottom half: the heavy dabs are the undergrowth's shadow. The scatter along the top is only a dark lace for the leaves to sit on later.
Leave plenty of mist showing through the gaps, and keep the sun's glow clear.
Olive masses sit at the pines' feet, with small clumps on the misty ground and an olive lace up top. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-canopy-darks.text: Let the olive dry.
Start with the big bush mass at the left edge. Its top is about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in wide.
You dabbed the olive undergrowth with this same dry old flat. Now the colour is Leaf orange, and the taps build up into solid leaf masses.
Tap Leaf orange with the tip of the old flat, tapping a spot more where the bush should look solid.
Most of it is on the left side. After the bush mass, dab loose clusters hanging from the top edge over the olive lace, and a few small dabs on the olive at the pines' feet.
Leave olive showing along the bush's base, and sky between the clusters.
A warm orange bush mass glows at the left edge, with orange clusters hanging along the top of the canvas.

dab-golden-leaves.text: Let the orange dry so the gold stays bright.
Start in the canopy clusters at the top edge, near the sun on the left side of the canvas.
Tap Golden yellow with the tip of the old flat in small, leaf-sized dabs.

Most of it is on the left side and in the top half. Cover most of each canopy cluster and the top of the orange bush mass, where the sun hits them. Only a few dabs go on the clusters toward the right edge.
Leave orange showing in the shadows of the clusters and along the bush's base, and sky between the leaves.
The canopy and the big bush glow golden, with orange still showing underneath.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the golden leaves dry.
Start in the canopy nearest the sun, at the left edge around the cream glow.
This is the same dabbing as the golden leaves, but with the small round brush, for smaller, brighter taps where the sun hits.
Tap the tip of the #10 round lightly, dot by dot. Tap a spot more where it should glow strongest.

Then tap lemon over the top of the golden bush mass. Spread dappled patches over the misty ground, from the left edge across the canvas down to the bottom edge. Most of it is in the bottom half: this is sunlight lying on the mist.
Leave the gold and orange leaves showing under the taps, and blue mist between the lemon patches.
The canopy sparkles near the sun, and the misty ground glows in warm patches. There is no ground colour yet.

dab-floor-darks.text: Let the lemon dry.
Start at the left edge, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, just under the golden bush mass.
This is the same dry dabbing as the olive undergrowth, but this time keep tapping until the dabs close up and hide the mist completely.
Tap Rust brown with the old flat in rows across the canvas, working down toward you.
Cover the whole width of the canvas and all the way down, dense enough that no mist shows. Tap over the bushes' ragged bottoms as you go.
Leave the bush masses and the pines' teal feet showing above the floor.
The lower canvas is a dense, dappled rust-brown leaf floor. There is no path yet.

pull-path.text: Let the floor dry, so the tan doesn't turn to mud.
Mark one dot where the path disappears, in the gap at the foot of the bushes. Draw a few faint chalk lines fanning toward you from it.
Pull each stroke along the lines, from the dot toward you, thin near the dot and wider in front.
This is only the far end of the path: a short strip whose middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge.
Leave the rust floor around it, and keep the path short.
A short pale tan strip leads back into the gap and narrows to a point, plain with no leaves.

block-in-boulder.text: Let the path dry.
Start with a low dome right of the path at the pines' feet, its middle about 11 3/4 in from the left edge.
This is the same Olive moss you dabbed for the undergrowth. Here it goes on flat, in curved pieces, to build a solid shape.
Paint the dome first, then add a curved piece on each side of it, like ( ), smaller toward the ends.
Fill the whole boulder flat Olive moss, about 2 1/2 in wide, with a flat base sitting on the leaves.
Leave the rust floor showing all around it.
A plain, flat olive boulder shape sits right of the path, with no shading.

shade-boulder.text: Let the olive dry.
Start on the right side of the boulder, where it sits on the leaves.
Bend every stroke with the dome: from the top of it down along its curve, and along the base.
Most of it is on the right side. Cover the boulder's shadow side and base, and bring curved strokes over most of the dome, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave a little flat olive on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
The boulder reads dark and solid, with only a hint of olive on its sunny shoulder.

light-boulder.text: Let the dark shading from step 13 dry, or the moss will smear into it.
Start on the boulder's sunny shoulder, toward the glow.
This is the same dry skim you used for the misty far trees: only the tip loaded, light pressure. Now it is Pale moss on the boulder's sunny shoulder.
With only the tip loaded, skim short, light dry-brush strokes along the top curve of the dome.
Most of it is on the left side of the boulder, along its top and down the sunny shoulder, where the sun falls.
Leave the dark side and base untouched.
A broken band of pale moss catches the light along the boulder's top, and the boulder looks round.

pull-birches.text: Let everything dry: the trunks go over all of it.
Start at the foot of the nearest big leaning trunk on the left side of the canvas, down in the leaves.
You pulled the far trunks thick to thin. This is the same stroke with a wider flat, pulled up from each trunk's foot instead of down.

Press the 3/4 inch flat's full width at the foot and pull up past the top edge, leaning slightly right. Lighten as you go so the trunk tapers. Pull a few thick branches out from the upper trunks the same way.
Make six trunks: a thin one near the left edge, two big leaning ones, and a thinner one standing at the gap where the path disappears. Finish with two on the right side, the widest at the right edge.
Leave the boulder, path and leaves showing between the trunks.
Six flat, pale gray trunks with a few branches, most of it on the left side, with no shading yet.

shade-birches.text: Let the trunks dry.
Start at the top edge, on the biggest trunk on the left side.
This is the same dry brushing as the moss on the boulder, now skimmed down the length of each trunk so pale bark shows through.
With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark gray down each trunk and out along each branch, so it breaks into ragged strokes.
The gray covers most of each trunk's width, most of it on the left side, where the big trunks are.
Leave ragged pale flecks of the trunk colour all along each trunk. Keep the lowest part of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, pale.
The trunks look gray and flecked with pale bark. If a patch goes solid, the brush was too loaded.

mark-birch-bark.text: Let the gray dry.
Start at the foot of each trunk, where it meets the leaves, and press in a dark foot.
This is the same angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke as the far trunks, but each mark is short and runs across the trunk.
For each bark mark, press the angle brush's full width, then turn onto its edge and lighten, so each short mark across the trunk tapers. Run thin dark lines along the branches.
Put more marks low on the trunks and fewer higher up. Most of it is in the bottom half and on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
Leave gray and pale bark showing between the marks.
The trunks read as birches, with broken dark marks and dark feet.

dab-orange-leaves.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start at the far end of the path, about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, and work toward you.
This is the same Leaf orange and the same dry old flat as the canopy, now dabbed across the ground as fallen leaves.
Tap Leaf orange with the old flat in leaf-sized dabs.
Cover most of the floor from the left edge to the right edge, down to the bottom edge. Spill onto the path and over the dark feet of the trunks. Most of it is on the right side.
Leave the dark leaf floor from step 10 showing in the gaps.
The ground is a warm orange leaf carpet with darker leaves in the gaps, and the trunk feet sit in the leaves.

dab-gold-leaves.text: Let the orange dry.
Start at the far end of the path, then work down along it and out across the floor.
This is the Golden yellow that lit the canopy, now tapped with the small round brush as sunny leaves on the path.
Tap the #10 round lightly in small leaf dabs.
Most of it is on the right side and in the top half. Make a band of gold down the path and across the floor at the trunks' feet, with a few dabs at the left edge and fewer toward the bottom edge.
Leave orange and rust showing between the gold.
Gold leaves catch the sun along the path and across the middle of the floor.

light-birch-bark.text: Let the bark marks and leaves dry.
Start at the top edge on the biggest trunk, on its sunny side, the side facing the glow.
This is the same dry skim you used to gray the trunks, now with Bark white and only on the side of each trunk facing the sun.
With the old flat nearly dry, skim Bark white down each trunk and along its branches, skipping lightly over the dark marks.
The light goes on the side of each trunk facing the sun, because the light comes from the upper left. Most of it is on the left side, where the big trunks stand.
Leave the shaded side of each trunk gray, and keep the dark feet dark.
Sunlit white birches with dark marks lean over the golden path into the misty grove.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint an autumn birch grove: white trunks leaning over a leaf-covered path that runs into a misty blue wood. The heart of the painting is the spot where the path disappears into the mist, framed by the birches. What makes it sing is the warm, hazy light glowing through the trees and catching on the leaves and bark.
opening.light: A low sun shines through the mist, so the glow, the brightest leaves and the sunlit bark all sit toward it. Each thing has a sunny side facing the glow and a shadow side away from it, and the far wood stays cool and blue in the haze.

skills.how: Dabbing is tapping with the tip of a dry brush to make dappled leaves instead of smooth paint. Keep the brush dry: a wet or overloaded brush makes blobs instead of dots.

Dry brushing is skimming a nearly dry brush lightly over the surface so the paint breaks up and lets the earlier paint show through. It makes the misty far trees, the moss on the boulder, and the shading and sunlight on the birch bark. If it goes on solid, the brush held too much paint, so wipe it and skim more lightly.

Thick to thin means pressing the brush's full width, then easing onto its edge so the stroke tapers. It pulls the far misty trunks, the big birch trunks and their branches, and the short dark bark marks. Change your pressure slowly and smoothly, so each stroke narrows instead of stopping with a hard end.

opening.road: First you blend one soft, wet glow over the whole canvas, because the mist and the sun are what everything else sits in. Then you work forward one layer at a time: the hazy far trees and trunks, the dark pines, and the golden canopy and undergrowth. Next comes the rust leaf floor with the path running into the grove, and then the mossy boulder by the path. The birches go on last over all of it, since they are nearest to you. Fallen leaves tie the trunks into the ground, and a last touch of sun on the bark finishes the picture.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the glowing, misty light that the whole painting lives in.
the-misty-sky.end: The canvas is one soft glow, cream around the sun and fading into haze blue, with faint pale trunks standing in the mist.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the distant wood, soft and blue in the mist, so the painting gets its depth.
the-far-wood.end: Soft blue tree shapes and pale trunks stand in the haze, with a group of dark pines whose feet melt into a teal mist.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage brings in the warm autumn colour, building the undergrowth and canopy from dark dabs to bright ones.
the-golden-leaves.end: A golden canopy hangs through the glow, a big golden bush shines near the sun, and warm sunlight lies in patches across the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage lays the leaf floor and the path that leads the eye into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor fills the ground, with a short pale path vanishing into the gap between the bushes and the pines.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder and makes it look round with shadow and light.
the-boulder.end: A rounded boulder sits by the path, dark on its shadow side with pale moss catching the sun.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the near birches over everything and turns them into real birch trunks.
the-birches.end: Six birch trunks lean over the grove, gray and flecked, with broken dark marks and dark feet in the leaves.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage carpets the ground in fallen leaves and settles the trunks into it.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The floor and path are a warm orange carpet with golden leaves catching the sun and darker leaves in the gaps.

the-last-lights.for: This stage adds the final sunlight on the bark that makes the birches glow.
the-last-lights.end: The finished painting: sunlit birches lean over a golden leaf-covered path running into the misty blue grove.

opening.road: First you blend one soft, wet glow over the whole canvas, because the mist and the sun are what everything else sits in. Then you work forward one layer at a time: the hazy far trees and trunks, the dark pines, and the golden canopy and undergrowth. Next comes the rust leaf floor with the path running into the grove, and then the mossy boulder beside it. The birches go on last over all of it, since they are nearest to you. Fallen leaves tie the trunks into the ground, and a last touch of sun on the bark finishes the picture.

the-misty-sky.for: This stage lays the glowing, misty light that the whole painting lives in.
the-misty-sky.end: The canvas is one soft glow, cream around the sun and fading into haze blue, with faint pale trunks standing in the mist.

the-far-wood.for: This stage builds the distant wood, soft and blue in the mist, so the painting gets its depth.
the-far-wood.end: Soft blue tree shapes and pale trunks stand in the haze, with a group of dark pines whose feet melt into a teal mist.

the-golden-leaves.for: This stage brings in the warm autumn colour, building the undergrowth and canopy from dark dabs to bright ones.
the-golden-leaves.end: A golden canopy hangs through the glow, a big golden bush shines near the sun, and warm sunlight lies in patches across the misty ground.

the-ground.for: This stage lays the leaf floor and the path that leads the eye into the grove.
the-ground.end: A dense rust-brown leaf floor fills the ground, with a short pale path vanishing into the gap between the bushes and the pines.

the-boulder.for: This stage builds the mossy boulder and makes it look round with shadow and light.
the-boulder.end: A rounded boulder sits beside the path, dark on its shadow side with pale moss catching the sun.

the-birches.for: This stage pulls the near birches over everything and turns them into real birch trunks.
the-birches.end: Six birch trunks lean over the grove, gray and flecked, with broken dark marks and dark feet in the leaves.

the-fallen-leaves.for: This stage carpets the ground in fallen leaves and settles the trunks into it.
the-fallen-leaves.end: The floor and path are a warm orange carpet with golden leaves catching the sun and darker leaves in the gaps.

the-last-lights.for: This stage adds the final sunlight on the bark that makes the birches glow.
the-last-lights.end: The finished painting: sunlit birches lean over a golden leaf-covered path running into the misty blue grove.

back.text: This is the same fan tapping you used to stamp the pines, now with Pine teal, tapped into the mist around them instead of on the trees.
You dabbed the olive undergrowth with this same dry old flat. Now the colour is Leaf orange, and the taps build up into solid leaf masses.
This is the same dabbing as the golden leaves, but with the small round brush, for smaller, brighter taps where the sun hits.
This is the same dry dabbing as the olive undergrowth, but this time keep tapping until the dabs close up and hide the mist completely.
This is the same Olive moss you dabbed for the undergrowth. Here it goes on flat, in curved pieces, to build a solid shape.
This is the same dry skim you used for the misty far trees: only the tip loaded, light pressure. Now it is Pale moss on the boulder's sunny shoulder.
You pulled the far trunks thick to thin. This is the same stroke with a wider flat, pulled up from each trunk's foot instead of down.
This is the same dry brushing as the moss on the boulder, now skimmed down the length of each trunk so pale bark shows through.
This is the same angle brush and thick-to-thin stroke as the far trunks, but each mark is short and runs across the trunk.
This is the same Leaf orange and the same dry old flat as the canopy, now dabbed across the ground as fallen leaves.
This is the Golden yellow that lit the canopy, now tapped with the small round brush as sunny leaves on the path.
This is the same dry skim you used to gray the trunks, now with Bark white and only on the side of each trunk facing the sun.

arc_taken_out.what: an opener says no number and no side word
arc_taken_out.sentence: It builds the undergrowth, the golden canopy and the whole leaf floor, always dark first and then lighter, with the darker taps left showing.

blend-window-sky.start: Start in the canvas's top left corner with Pale sky blue. This patch of sky is about 3 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the patch. Without rinsing, pick up Titanium white, work it in lower down, then stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The blue is strongest along the top edge, where the open sky is. It gets paler lower down, nearer where the trees will be. Keep the lower outline ragged, like the edges of leaf masses.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave a few small gaps of bare canvas inside the patch, and leave the rest of the canvas white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when a soft, ragged patch of pale blue fills the top left corner, deeper at the top, with no hard line where the blue meets the white.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky dry first, or the green will mix into the blue.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Find the bare gap inside the sky patch. Your dab goes at its lower edge, with its middle about 1 in from the left edge and 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Wipe the old stiff brush almost dry, then tap straight down with its tip. Don't drag it sideways.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: This is one small dot of Leaf green, under 1/4 in wide. It is the first hint of a far leaf at the edge of the gap.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the whole sky and the bare gap around the dot as they are.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop after one small, soft green dot. Wet or heavy paint makes a blob, so wipe the brush before you tap.

dab-pale-leaves.start: Start where the bare gap inside the sky meets the blue, next to the green dot, about 1 in from the top edge.
dab-pale-leaves.strokes: With the brush nearly dry, tap a short row of dabs downward along the edge of the gap.
dab-pale-leaves.inside: Pale leaf green goes only along that edge, in a small curl about 1 in tall, where a leaf tip catches the light.
dab-pale-leaves.leave: Leave the green dot, the blue sky and the bare gap showing.
dab-pale-leaves.stop: Stop when a small, broken curl of pale yellow-green edges the gap. It should read as one sunlit leaf tip, not a clump.

blend-wall.first: Let the window view dry, so the wall's edge doesn't drag the sky.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top of the wall, at the edge of the window view, where the wall begins about 3 in from the left edge.
blend-wall.strokes: Put both Wall blue and Pale wall blue on the 1 inch flat. Make short criss-cross strokes like overlapping X's, working across to the right edge and down.
blend-wall.inside: Use more Pale wall blue near the window, where the daylight falls, and more Wall blue toward the right edge and the top edge. The wall's bottom slopes down toward the right edge. Down its middle it stops about 7 in from the top edge.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the sky and leaves of the window view showing, and leave the canvas below the wall bare.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the wall is an even, soft blue with criss-cross texture showing, a little paler near the window.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall and the window view dry first.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the upright post where the window meets the blue wall. Lay it in as one tall rectangle.
block-in-frame.strokes: Build the frame from straight pieces: the post, then the thinner upright, the crossbar across the window view, and the ledge along the bottom. Pull each stroke along the length of its piece.
block-in-frame.inside: Titanium white goes on every frame piece. The whole frame fits in the canvas's top left corner, about 4 1/2 in wide and 7 in tall.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the two panes of sky and leaves showing between the pieces. Keep the frame's outer edge clean against the blue wall.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when a flat white frame stands in front of the window view, with no shading on it yet.

shade-frame.first: Let the white frame dry completely, or the blue will turn milky.
shade-frame.start: Start with the thin strip along the crossbar, about 2 in from the top edge.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay each strip as its own straight piece with the 1/4 inch flat, pulling along the length of the bar. Do the crossbar first, then the inner face of each upright, then the ledge.
shade-frame.inside: Pale wall blue goes only on the thin faces that turn away from the daylight: the undersides and inner sides of the bars, and the lower face of the ledge. That is what makes the frame look deep.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the broad front faces of the frame white, and leave the panes of sky and leaves untouched.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when every bar has a thin lavender edge along its white face, so the frame looks like wood with real thickness.

lay-in-sill.first: Let the wall and frame dry, so the brown doesn't pick up blue.
lay-in-sill.start: Start where the sill meets the wall's sloping bottom edge and work down. The sill's top is about 6 in from the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Keep the 1 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right, all the way across the canvas.
lay-in-sill.inside: Warm wood brown covers the whole bottom of the canvas, straight through where the blanket will go. It also fills the small wedge where the window ledge meets the sill. Let a faint line across the lower part show the sill's front edge.
lay-in-sill.leave: Leave the wall and the window frame clean, and keep the line where the sill meets the wall crisp.
lay-in-sill.stop: Stop when no white canvas shows anywhere. The bottom of the canvas should be a flat, warm brown ledge with level streaks.

darken-sill-front.first: Let the warm brown dry first.
darken-sill-front.start: Start at the back of the sill, where it meets the blue wall, and lay a band of Dark wood brown along it.
darken-sill-front.strokes: Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right. Use a light hand so the strokes break up.
darken-sill-front.inside: The dark goes in a band at the back, where the wall shades the sill, and in broken grain streaks across the top and the front face. Add one slanting line near the left end of the wooden windowsill, where the frame casts a shadow.
darken-sill-front.leave: Leave plenty of warm brown showing between the streaks, especially across the middle of the sill.
darken-sill-front.stop: Stop when the sill looks like old wood: darker at the back, streaked across, with lighter brown in between.

sunlit-sill.first: Let the dark streaks dry, or the peach will turn muddy.
sunlit-sill.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the sill just in front of the window ledge, and work toward the middle.
sunlit-sill.strokes: Dip only the tip of the 1/2 inch flat in Sunlit wood, with no water. Skim it lightly in level strokes, building up with a few light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.
sunlit-sill.inside: This is window light: one wide slanted patch and a narrower one at the canvas edge, with brown between them like a window bar's shadow. A few broken streaks trail on, reaching about 8 in from the left edge.
sunlit-sill.leave: Leave the slanted gap of brown, and let the wood grain show through the peach.
sunlit-sill.stop: Stop when the left end of the wooden windowsill glows with broken peach light. It should never look solid.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with one long rounded rectangle lying along the sill. Its rounded end is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Build from pieces with the 3/4 inch flat: the long rounded rectangle first, then curved pieces at the ends and along its top for the rolled edge.
block-in-blanket.inside: Golden yellow fills the whole blanket, straight through where the cat will lie. It runs off the right edge, and its bottom sits about 1 in from the bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a strip of sill showing along the bottom of the canvas, and leave the wall and window frame clean.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when a flat, solid golden-yellow shape lies across the sill, with a slightly lumpy top like a roll. No shading yet.

shade-blanket.first: Let the golden yellow dry first.
shade-blanket.start: Start at the rounded end nearest the window. Curve around it, then follow the crease where the top roll folds in.
shade-blanket.strokes: Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each roll down along its curve, and around the ends.
shade-blanket.inside: Dark gold goes where the window light can't reach: in the hollow in the middle, where the cat will lie, along the fold between the two rolls, and along the base where it meets the sill.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave the tops of the rolls golden yellow, so they look lit and round.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket reads as a thick folded ring: a raised roll around a hollow, with a lower roll at the front. No knit loops yet.

dark-knit-loops.first: Let the shadows dry, so the loops stay crisp.
dark-knit-loops.start: Start on the top roll at the window end of the blanket. The marks begin about 2 in from the left edge.
dark-knit-loops.strokes: Load the #8 round fully. Touch down, press, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Set the marks in pairs leaning together like V's, in rows that follow each roll's curve.
dark-knit-loops.inside: Put rows across the top roll, along the fold, and along the base of the lower roll. Scatter fewer, looser commas over the hollow and the front face.
dark-knit-loops.leave: Leave golden yellow between the commas so each loop shows.
dark-knit-loops.stop: Stop when knit rows run around the whole blanket out to the right edge. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-knit-loops.start: Start at the blanket's rounded end nearest the window, where the light hits it first.
light-knit-loops.strokes: With the #6 round fully loaded, press and lift short commas, fitting them into the same V rows as the dark ones.
light-knit-loops.inside: Light gold goes on the tops of the loops that face the window. Most of it is on the left half of the blanket, thickest along the front of the lower roll, with only a few dots on the top roll.
light-knit-loops.leave: Leave the dark gold loops and the golden yellow showing. Use fewer light marks than dark ones.
light-knit-loops.stop: Stop when the knit looks chunky and sunlit near the window, fading away toward the far end.

block-in-cat.first: Let the blanket and frame dry fully, since the cat overlaps both.
block-in-cat.start: Start with one big oval for the curled body. It sits in the blanket's hollow and reaches almost to the right edge.
block-in-cat.strokes: Build the rest from pieces with the 1/2 inch flat: a round head at the window end, two triangle ears, and curved ( ) pieces filling out the back.
block-in-cat.inside: Cat gray covers the whole cat flatly, and the head overlaps the window frame. The tip of the ear on the crown is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and the other ear points toward the window, about 1 in from the left edge.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket's front rolls showing below the cat.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when a flat gray silhouette of a curled cat lies on the blanket, with no shading or markings.

shade-cat.start: Start along the right end of the cat, about 12 1/2 in from the left edge, and curve down around its rounded back end.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend every stroke around the body: from the top of the back down along its curve, and around the head.
shade-cat.inside: Dark cat gray goes on the side away from the window: along the top of the back, down the far end, along the bottom where the body meets the blanket, and in a dark crescent where the head tucks against the body. Edge the back rims of the ears too.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the middle of the body, the face and the front of the head lighter, where the window light falls.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the cat looks round, with its dark side curling away from the window.

paint-white-patches.first: Let the shading dry, so the white stays clean.
paint-white-patches.start: Start with the two front paws resting on the blanket. The first paw begins about 3 1/2 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: With the #8 round, curve each stroke around its shape: round the paws, and pull the muzzle and chest strokes down the way the fur grows.
paint-white-patches.inside: White goes on the muzzle and chin, in a blaze down the chest, and on both paws. A separate white patch sits on the cat's side, with its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave gray between the paws and between the paws and the muzzle. Keep the edges of the patches ragged like fur.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop when the face has a white muzzle, the patch shows on the side, and two round white paws rest on the blanket.

paint-ear-insides.first: Let the gray around the ears dry.
paint-ear-insides.start: Start inside the ear nearest the window. Its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ear-insides.strokes: With a full #6 round, touch down at the ear's base and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear tip and lift so the stroke ends in a point.
paint-ear-insides.inside: Rosy pink fills the inner hollow of each ear. Do the ear on the crown the same way.
paint-ear-insides.leave: Leave a gray rim around each ear.
paint-ear-insides.stop: Stop when both ears have pink insides with gray edges. A blob means too much paint or too slow a lift.

paint-stripes.first: Let the white patches and pink ears dry.
paint-stripes.start: Start on the forehead between the ears, pulling stripes back toward the body.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush so each stripe starts thick. Then turn onto its edge and lighten your pressure so the stripe tapers to a point. Curve every stripe around the body.
paint-stripes.inside: Charcoal brown stripes wrap the forehead and cheeks, curve over the back and side, and cross the tail in short bands. Darken the crescent where the head tucks in. Most of the stripes are on the right half of the cat.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave gray between the stripes, and keep them off the white patches and pink ears.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when bold, tapered stripes wrap the whole cat like a tabby coat.

flick-fur.first: Let the stripes dry completely, or the flicks will smear them.
flick-fur.start: Start on the head, by the ear nearest the window, and work back across the body.
flick-fur.strokes: With very little paint on the small fan brush, flick quick short strokes the way the fur grows, lifting as you go so each mark thins at its tip. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
flick-fur.inside: Light cat gray goes over the gray coat and across the edges of the stripes, softening them. Also flick along the cat's outline against the wall, so the edge looks fuzzy.
flick-fur.leave: Leave darker gray and the stripes showing between the flicks, and keep off the white patches.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the coat looks soft and furry all over, with the stripes still clear but feathered at their edges.

line-eyes.first: Everything on the face must be dry, or the lines will spread.
line-eyes.start: Start with the closed eye nearest the window. Its middle is about 4 1/4 in from the left edge.
line-eyes.strokes: Thin the Charcoal brown with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each eye as a gentle downward curve, starting thick and lightening off. Add water if the line skips.
line-eyes.inside: Line both closed eyes with a little shadow beneath each. Then add tiny marks for the nostrils and mouth on the muzzle, a few short dashes on the cheek where the whiskers grow, and a short line where the two paws meet.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the white muzzle clean around the marks.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the face reads as asleep: two curved closed eyes and a tiny mouth.

press-nose.start: Place the nose on the white muzzle, where it narrows between the eyes. The nose's middle is about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.
press-nose.strokes: With a full #2 round, press down for the wide top of the nose, then pull down and lift to a point. It makes a small triangle about 3/4 in wide.
press-nose.inside: Rosy pink goes only on the nose, plus a light touch inside each ear to warm it.
press-nose.leave: Leave white muzzle all around the nose.
press-nose.stop: Stop when a small pink triangle nose sits on the muzzle. Only the whiskers are missing.

line-whiskers.first: Let the face and nose dry, so the white lines stay sharp.
line-whiskers.start: Start where the muzzle meets the cheek nearest the window, and pull whiskers out across the cheek.
line-whiskers.strokes: Thin the Titanium white with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each whisker as one light, slightly curved line that gets lighter as it ends. Reload often.
line-whiskers.inside: On the window side, three or four whiskers fan down across the cheek toward the blanket. On the other side, a few longer ones fan across the chest patch, their middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave the eyes, nose and paws as they are, and don't let whiskers cross the nose.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop when fine white whiskers fan out on both sides of the muzzle. The painting is finished.

Stop when the knit looks chunky and sunlit near the window, fading away toward the far end.
