Start with one big oval for the curled body. It sits in the blanket's hollow and reaches almost to the right edge.
Build the rest from pieces with the 1/2 inch flat: a round head at the window end, two triangle ears, and curved ( ) pieces filling out the back.

Cat gray covers the whole cat flatly, and the head overlaps the window frame. The tip of the ear on the crown is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and the other ear points toward the window, about 1 in from the left edge.
Leave the blanket's front rolls showing below the cat.
Stop when a flat gray silhouette of a curled cat lies on the blanket, with no shading or markings.

shade-cat.text: Let the gray dry first.
Start along the right end of the cat, about 12 1/2 in from the left edge, and curve down around its rounded back end.
Bend every stroke around the body: from the top of the back down along its curve, and around the head.

Dark cat gray goes on the side away from the window: along the top of the back, down the far end, along the bottom where the body meets the blanket, and in a dark crescent where the head tucks against the body. Edge the back rims of the ears too.
Leave the middle of the body, the face and the front of the head lighter, where the window light falls.
Stop when the cat looks round, with its dark side curling away from the window.

paint-white-patches.text: Let the shading dry, so the white stays clean.
Start with the two front paws resting on the blanket. The first paw begins about 3 1/2 in from the left edge.
With the #8 round, curve each stroke around its shape: round the paws, and pull the muzzle and chest strokes down the way the fur grows.
White goes on the muzzle and chin, in a blaze down the chest, and on both paws. A separate white patch sits on the cat's side, with its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave gray between the paws and between the paws and the muzzle. Keep the edges of the patches ragged like fur.
Stop when the face has a white muzzle, the patch shows on the side, and two round white paws rest on the blanket.

paint-ear-insides.text: Let the gray around the ears dry.
Start with the ear that points toward the window. Its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
With a full #6 round, touch down at the ear's base and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear tip and lift so the stroke ends in a point.
Rosy pink fills the inner hollow of each ear. Do the ear on the crown the same way.
Leave a gray rim around each ear.
Stop when both ears have pink insides with gray edges. A blob means too much paint or too slow a lift.

paint-stripes.text: Let the white patches and pink ears dry.
Start on the forehead between the ears, pulling stripes back toward the body.
Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush so each stripe starts thick. Then turn onto its edge and lighten your pressure so the stripe tapers to a point. Curve every stripe around the body.

Charcoal brown stripes wrap the forehead and cheeks, curve over the back and side, and cross the tail in short bands. Darken the crescent where the head tucks in. Most of the stripes are on the right half of the cat.
Leave gray between the stripes, and keep them off the white patches and pink ears.
Stop when bold, tapered stripes wrap the whole cat like a tabby coat.

flick-fur.text: Let the stripes dry completely, or the flicks will smear them.
Start on the head, by the ear nearest the window, and work back across the body.
With very little paint on the small fan brush, flick quick short strokes the way the fur grows, lifting as you go so each mark thins at its tip. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
Light cat gray goes over the gray coat and across the edges of the stripes, softening them. Also flick along the cat's outline against the wall, so the edge looks fuzzy.
Leave darker gray and the stripes showing between the flicks, and keep off the white patches.
Stop when the coat looks soft and furry all over, with the stripes still clear but feathered at their edges.

line-eyes.text: Everything on the face must be dry, or the lines will spread.
Start with the closed eye nearest the window. Its middle is about 4 1/4 in from the left edge.
Thin the Charcoal brown with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each eye as a gentle downward curve, starting thick and lightening off. Add water if the line skips.

Line both closed eyes, with a little soft shadow along each lid. Then add tiny marks for the nostrils and mouth on the muzzle, a few short dashes on the cheek where the whiskers grow, and a short line where the two paws meet.
Leave the white muzzle clean around the marks.
Stop when the face reads as asleep: two curved closed eyes and a tiny mouth.

press-nose.text: Place the nose on the white muzzle, where it narrows between the eyes. The nose's middle is about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.
With a full #2 round, press down for the wide top of the nose, then pull down and lift to a point. It makes a small triangle about 3/4 in wide.
Rosy pink goes on the nose, plus a light touch in the pink hollow of each ear to warm it.
Leave white muzzle all around the nose.
Stop when a small pink triangle nose sits on the muzzle. Only the whiskers are missing.

line-whiskers.text: Let the face and nose dry, so the white lines stay sharp.
Start where the muzzle meets the cheek nearest the window, and pull whiskers out across the cheek.
Thin the Titanium white with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each whisker as one light, slightly curved line that gets lighter as it ends. Reload often.

On the window side, three or four whiskers fan down across the cheek toward the blanket. On the other side, a few longer ones fan across the chest patch, their middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the eyes, nose and paws as they are, and don't let whiskers cross the nose.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan out on both sides of the muzzle. The painting is finished.

blend-window-sky.text: Start in the canvas's top left corner with Pale sky blue. This patch of sky is about 3 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
Stroke side to side across the patch. Without rinsing, pick up Titanium white, work it in lower down, then stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
The blue is strongest along the top edge, where the open sky is. It gets paler lower down, nearer where the trees will be. Keep the lower outline ragged, like the edges of leaf masses.
Leave a few small gaps of bare canvas among the blue, and leave the rest of the canvas white.
Stop when a soft, ragged patch of pale blue fills the top left corner, deeper at the top, with no hard line where the blue meets the white.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky dry first, or the green will mix into the blue.
Find the small bare gap in the blue sky. Your dab goes at its lower edge, with its middle about 1 in from the left edge and 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
Wipe the old stiff brush almost dry, then tap straight down with its tip. Don't drag it sideways.
This is one small dot of Leaf green, under 1/4 in wide. It is the first hint of a far leaf at the edge of the gap.
Leave the whole sky and the bare gap around the dot as they are.
Stop after one small, soft green dot. Wet or heavy paint makes a blob, so wipe the brush before you tap.

dab-pale-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green dot dry.
Start where the small bare gap meets the blue sky, close to the Leaf green dot, about 1 in from the top edge.
The same dry tap of the old stiff brush you used for the leaf dot, now in the paler green and only where a leaf tip catches the light.
With the brush nearly dry, tap a short row of dabs downward along the edge of the gap.
Pale leaf green goes only along that edge, in a small curl about 1 in tall, where a leaf tip catches the light.
Leave the Leaf green dot, the blue sky and the bare gap showing.
Stop when a small, broken curl of pale yellow-green edges the gap. It should read as one sunlit leaf tip, not a clump.

blend-wall.text: Let the window view dry, so the wall's edge doesn't drag the sky.
Start at the top of the wall, at the edge of the window view, where the wall begins about 3 in from the left edge.
Put both Wall blue and Pale wall blue on the 1 inch flat. Make short criss-cross strokes like overlapping X's, working across to the right edge and down.
Use more Pale wall blue near the window, where the daylight falls, and more Wall blue toward the right edge and the top edge. The wall's bottom edge slopes down toward the right edge.
Leave the sky and leaves of the window view showing, and leave the canvas below the wall bare.
Stop when the wall is an even, soft blue with criss-cross texture showing, a little paler near the window.

block-in-frame.text: Let the wall and the window view dry first.
Start with the upright post where the window meets the blue wall. Lay it in as one tall rectangle.
Build the frame from straight pieces: the post, then the thinner upright, the crossbar across the window view, and the ledge along the bottom. Pull each stroke along the length of its piece.
Titanium white goes on every frame piece. The whole frame fits in the canvas's top left corner, about 4 1/2 in wide and 7 in tall.
Leave the two panes of sky and leaves showing between the pieces. Keep the frame's outer edge clean against the blue wall.
Stop when a flat white frame stands in front of the window view, with no shading on it yet.

shade-frame.text: Let the white frame dry completely, or the blue will turn milky.
Start with the thin strip along the crossbar.
You build these strips piece by piece like the white frame, but with the smaller 1/4 inch flat and only thin strips of Pale wall blue.
Lay each strip as its own straight piece with the 1/4 inch flat, pulling along the length of the bar. Do the crossbar first, then the inner face of each upright, then the ledge.
Pale wall blue goes only on the thin faces that turn away from the daylight: the undersides and inner sides of the bars, and the lower face of the ledge. That is what makes the frame look deep.
Leave the broad front faces of the frame white, and leave the panes of sky and leaves untouched.
Stop when every bar has a thin lavender edge along its white face, so the frame looks like wood with real thickness.

lay-in-sill.text: Let the wall and frame dry, so the brown doesn't pick up blue.
Start where the sill meets the wall's sloping bottom edge and work down to the bottom edge.
Keep the 1 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right, all the way across the canvas.

Warm wood brown covers the whole bottom of the canvas, straight through where the blanket will go. It also fills the small wedge where the window ledge meets the sill. Let a faint line across the lower part show the sill's front edge.
Leave the wall and the window frame clean, and keep the line where the sill meets the wall crisp.
Stop when no white canvas shows anywhere. The bottom of the canvas should be a flat, warm brown ledge with level streaks.

darken-sill-front.text: Let the warm brown dry first.
Start at the back of the sill, where it meets the blue wall, and lay a band of Dark wood brown along it.
The same long level strokes you laid the sill with, now in the darker brown with a lighter hand, so the strokes break up into grain.
Keep the 3/4 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right. Use a light hand so the strokes break up.

The dark goes in a band at the back, where the wall shades the sill, and in broken grain streaks across the top and the front face. Add one slanting line near the left end of the wooden windowsill, where the frame casts a shadow.
Leave plenty of warm brown showing between the streaks, especially across the middle of the sill.
Stop when the sill looks like old wood: darker at the back, streaked across, with lighter brown in between.

sunlit-sill.text: Let the dark streaks dry, or the peach will turn muddy.
Start at the left edge of the canvas, on the sill just in front of the window ledge, and work toward the middle.
Dip only the tip of the 1/2 inch flat in Sunlit wood, with no water. Skim it lightly in level strokes, building up with a few light passes. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.
This is window light: one wide slanted patch and a narrower one at the canvas edge, with brown between them like a window bar's shadow. A few broken streaks trail on toward the middle of the sill.
Leave the slanted gap of brown, and let the wood grain show through the peach.
Stop when the left end of the wooden windowsill glows with broken peach light. It should never look solid.

block-in-blanket.text: Let the sill dry first.
Start with one long rounded rectangle lying along the sill. Its rounded end is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
You built the window frame from straight pieces. The blanket is built the same way, but from a long rounded shape and curved pieces.
Build from pieces with the 3/4 inch flat: the long rounded rectangle first, then curved pieces at the ends and along its top for the rolled edge.
Golden yellow fills the whole blanket, straight through where the cat will lie. It runs off the right edge, and its bottom sits about 1 in from the bottom edge.
Leave a strip of sill showing along the bottom of the canvas, and leave the wall and window frame clean.
Stop when a flat, solid golden-yellow shape lies across the sill, with a slightly lumpy top like a roll. No shading yet.

shade-blanket.text: Let the golden yellow dry first.
Start at the rounded end nearest the window. Curve around it, then follow the crease where the top roll folds in.
Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each roll down along its curve, and around the ends.
Dark gold goes where the window light can't reach: in the hollow in the middle, where the cat will lie, along the fold between the two rolls, and along the base where it meets the sill.
Leave the tops of the rolls golden yellow, so they look lit and round.
Stop when the blanket reads as a thick folded ring: a raised roll around a hollow, with a lower roll at the front. No knit loops yet.

dark-knit-loops.text: Let the shadows dry, so the loops stay crisp.
Start on the top roll at the window end of the blanket. The marks begin about 2 in from the left edge.
The same Dark gold you shaded the rolls with, now laid as small comma marks with the #8 round instead of broad curved strokes.
Load the #8 round fully. Touch down, press, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Set the marks in pairs leaning together like V's, in rows that follow each roll's curve.
Put rows across the top roll, along the fold, and along the base of the lower roll. Scatter fewer, looser commas over the hollow and the front face.
Leave golden yellow between the commas so each loop shows.
Stop when knit rows run around the whole blanket out to the right edge. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-knit-loops.text: Start at the blanket's rounded end nearest the window, where the light hits it first.
The same press and lift as the dark loops, now with the smaller #6 round, the paler gold and fewer marks, only where the window light hits.
With the #6 round fully loaded, press and lift short commas, fitting them into the same V rows as the dark ones.
Light gold goes on the tops of the loops that face the window. Most of it is on the left half of the blanket, thickest along the front of the lower roll, with only a few dots on the top roll.
Leave the dark gold loops and the golden yellow showing. Use fewer light marks than dark ones.
Stop when the knit looks chunky and sunlit near the window, fading away toward the far end.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket and frame dry fully, since the cat overlaps both.
Start with one big oval for the curled body. It sits in the blanket's hollow and reaches almost to the right edge.
Like the blanket, start with one big shape and add pieces, this time an oval body, a round head and triangle ears.
Build the rest from pieces with the 1/2 inch flat: a round head at the window end, two triangle ears, and curved ( ) pieces filling out the back.

Cat gray covers the whole cat flatly, and the head overlaps the window frame. The tip of the ear on the crown is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and the other ear points toward the window, about 1 in from the left edge.
Leave the blanket's front rolls showing below the cat.
Stop when a flat gray silhouette of a curled cat lies on the blanket, with no shading or markings.

shade-cat.text: Let the gray dry first.
Start along the right end of the cat, about 12 1/2 in from the left edge, and curve down around its rounded back end.
Bend your strokes around the cat just as you did under the blanket's rolls, now in Dark cat gray on the side away from the window.
Bend every stroke around the body: from the top of the back down along its curve, and around the head.

Dark cat gray goes on the side away from the window: along the top of the back, down the far end, along the bottom where the body meets the blanket, and in a dark crescent where the head tucks against the body. Edge the back rims of the ears too.
Leave the middle of the body, the face and the front of the head lighter, where the window light falls.
Stop when the cat looks round, with its dark side curling away from the window.

paint-white-patches.text: Let the shading dry, so the white stays clean.
Start with the two front paws resting on the blanket. The first paw begins about 3 1/2 in from the left edge.
The same curved strokes you shaded the cat with, now in white with the #8 round, following the way the fur grows.
With the #8 round, curve each stroke around its shape: round the paws, and pull the muzzle and chest strokes down the way the fur grows.
White goes on the muzzle and chin, in a blaze down the chest, and on both paws. A separate white patch sits on the cat's side, with its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave gray between the paws and between the paws and the muzzle. Keep the edges of the patches ragged like fur.
Stop when the face has a white muzzle, the patch shows on the side, and two round white paws rest on the blanket.

paint-ear-insides.text: Let the gray around the ears dry.
Start with the ear that points toward the window. Its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
The same press and lift with the #6 round you used for the light knit loops, now one fuller pink stroke filling each ear.
With a full #6 round, touch down at the ear's base and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear tip and lift so the stroke ends in a point.
Rosy pink fills the inner hollow of each ear. Do the ear on the crown the same way.
Leave a gray rim around each ear.
Stop when both ears have pink insides with gray edges. A blob means too much paint or too slow a lift.

paint-stripes.text: Let the white patches and pink ears dry.
Start on the forehead between the ears, pulling stripes back toward the body.
Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush so each stripe starts thick. Then turn onto its edge and lighten your pressure so the stripe tapers to a point. Curve every stripe around the body.

Charcoal brown stripes wrap the forehead and cheeks, curve over the back and side, and cross the tail in short bands. Darken the crescent where the head tucks in. Most of the stripes are on the right half of the cat.
Leave gray between the stripes, and keep them off the white patches and pink ears.
Stop when bold, tapered stripes wrap the whole cat like a tabby coat.

flick-fur.text: Let the stripes dry completely, or the flicks will smear them.
Start on the head, by the ear nearest the window, and work back across the body.
With very little paint on the small fan brush, flick quick short strokes the way the fur grows, lifting as you go so each mark thins at its tip. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
Light cat gray goes over the gray coat and across the edges of the stripes, softening them. Also flick along the cat's outline against the wall, so the edge looks fuzzy.
Leave darker gray and the stripes showing between the flicks, and keep off the white patches.
Stop when the coat looks soft and furry all over, with the stripes still clear but feathered at their edges.

line-eyes.text: Everything on the face must be dry, or the lines will spread.
Start with the closed eye nearest the window. Its middle is about 4 1/4 in from the left edge.
The same Charcoal brown as the stripes, now thinned with water and pulled as fine lines with the #1 liner.
Thin the Charcoal brown with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each eye as a gentle downward curve, starting thick and lightening off. Add water if the line skips.

Line both closed eyes, with a little soft shadow along each lid. Then add tiny marks for the nostrils and mouth on the muzzle, a few short dashes on the cheek where the whiskers grow, and a short line where the two paws meet.
Leave the white muzzle clean around the marks.
Stop when the face reads as asleep: two curved closed eyes and a tiny mouth.

press-nose.text: Place the nose on the white muzzle, where it narrows between the eyes. The nose's middle is about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.
The same pink and the same press and lift as the ear insides, now tiny, with the #2 round, for one small triangle.
With a full #2 round, press down for the wide top of the nose, then pull down and lift to a point. It makes a small triangle about 3/4 in wide.
Rosy pink goes on the nose, plus a light touch in the pink hollow of each ear to warm it.
Leave white muzzle all around the nose.
Stop when a small pink triangle nose sits on the muzzle. Only the whiskers are missing.

line-whiskers.text: Let the face and nose dry, so the white lines stay sharp.
Start where the muzzle meets the cheek nearest the window, and pull whiskers out across the cheek.
Hold the #1 liner upright just as you did for the eyes, but this time with thinned Titanium white, pulling longer, lighter lines.
Thin the Titanium white with water and hold the #1 liner upright. Pull each whisker as one light, slightly curved line that gets lighter as it ends. Reload often.

On the window side, three or four whiskers fan down across the cheek toward the blanket. On the other side, a few longer ones fan across the chest patch, their middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the eyes, nose and paws as they are, and don't let whiskers cross the nose.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan out on both sides of the muzzle. The painting is finished.

opening.welcome: You're painting a gray tabby kitten curled up asleep on a golden knit blanket in a sunny window. The heart of the painting is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose, the white muzzle with its whiskers, and the white paws tucked close to it. The mood is warm and quiet, so keep the colors soft and let the window light do the work.
opening.light: The window light falls on everything turned toward the window: the sill glows in peach bars, the blanket's rolls catch the gold, and the cat's head and paws stay bright. Shadows gather on the far side of the cat, in the blanket's hollow and folds, and where the blanket meets the sill.

skills.how: Building from pieces means starting with one simple shape, such as a rectangle, an oval or a circle, and adding the rest in smaller pieces. You use it for the window frame's straight bars, the folded blanket and the curled cat. Keep each piece a clear shape, and only soften the joins where the shape should look smooth.

Curved strokes bend with the shape, from the crest of each bump down along its curve and around anything round. They give the blanket its thick rolls and make the cat look round, with dark gray on the side away from the window and white curving around the paws. If a stroke runs straight across a round shape, the shape will look flat.

Press and lift is a touch, then a press so the belly of the round brush spreads, then a pull that lifts off to a point. It makes every knit loop on the blanket, the pink inside the ears and the little pink nose. A blob means too much paint or too slow a lift, so use less paint and lift faster.

opening.road: We paint the farthest things first: the sky and leaves through the window, then the blue wall and the white window frame. Next comes the wooden sill, with its dark grain and bars of window light. The blanket goes on straight through where the cat will lie, then gets its shadows and its dark and light knit loops. The cat is built on the blanket: a flat gray shape, then shading and white patches, then pink ears and stripes, then soft fur. The face comes last, so the focal point gets the sharpest, freshest marks.

the-window-view.for: This stage paints the farthest thing in the picture: the pale sky and soft leaves seen through the window.
the-window-view.end: A ragged patch of pale blue sky sits in a corner of the white canvas, with a few small gaps and the hint of a leaf.

the-wall-and-frame.for: This stage lays the blue wall around the window view, then builds the white frame and shades its inner faces so it looks deep.
the-wall-and-frame.end: A soft criss-cross blue wall meets a white window frame with lavender shadow faces, and the strip where the sill will go is still bare white.

the-windowsill.for: This stage covers the last bare canvas with the wooden sill, then darkens its grain and lays the window light across it.
the-windowsill.end: No white canvas remains: a warm brown sill with dark grain and broken peach bars of window light meets the blue wall.

the-blanket.for: This stage builds the golden blanket the cat will sleep on, from a flat shape to shadows and chunky knit loops.
the-blanket.end: A thick folded blanket of chunky golden loops lies on the sill, lit near the window and fading away from it, with no cat yet.

the-cat-shape.for: This stage builds the sleeping cat as a flat gray shape, rounds it with shadow, and adds its white muzzle, chest and paws.
the-cat-shape.end: A smooth gray cat curls on the blanket, darker on the side away from the window, with a white muzzle, a white chest patch and white paws.

the-markings.for: This stage gives the cat its pink ear insides and its bold tabby stripes.
the-markings.end: The cat has pink ears with gray rims and dark tapered stripes wrapping its head, body and tail, but its coat is still smooth.

the-fur.for: This stage turns the smooth gray coat into soft fur with quick light flicks.
the-fur.end: The coat looks soft and furry, with the stripes still clear but feathered at their edges, and the face has no eyes, nose or whiskers yet.

the-face.for: This stage paints the focal point last: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white whiskers.
the-face.end: The finished kitten sleeps on its golden blanket, with curved closed eyes, a small pink nose and fine white whiskers.

reads.note: The step pictures are identical, so only the words differ, and each lesson has one notable place where its words and pictures disagree (B at step 1, A at step 16). B is slightly more specific in the birch steps, but that is a small edge in the words, not a real difference for the painter. This is a toss-up.

Both lessons use the same paints, brushes and pictures, and their words differ only in small wording and order choices. A's step 19 covers a bit more of the face change, and B gives a few more measurements. Neither difference changes what the beginner would paint, so this is a toss-up.

The pictures are identical, so this comes down to the words. A tells the painter where the birches go in step 15 and describes the bark shading the way the picture shows it; B leaves the trunk layout to guesswork. A's 'no trees yet' in step 1 is a real contradiction, so the edge is slight, close to a toss-up.

The pictures are identical and the words differ only in small ways. A gives a few more measurements, and B's step 19 explains the muzzle change a bit better. Neither fixes the real problems at steps 12, 18 and 19, so this is a toss-up.

Both lessons share every picture, and their words differ only in small ways that don't fix the shared faults: the early leaves and ghosts, the one-step blanket, and the face appearing before its steps. Neither would get a beginner past steps 4, 12 or 20 better than the other. This is a toss-up, so no preference.

The pictures are identical, so only the words differ, and they differ very little. A gives slightly more exact placements; B's step 4 accounts for the post ghost. Neither fixes the real problems: ghosts and magic leaves at step 4, the step 12 jump, the nose appearing early, and step 23's mismatch. It's a toss-up.

The step pictures are identical, so the same picture faults sink both lessons equally. The only difference is the words. A gives more exact placements but contradicts its step 1 picture. B is vaguer but contradicts less. Neither difference amounts to a real preference: a toss-up.

Both lessons share every picture, and the pictures carry the problems that sink a lesson: ghosts and a big jump at step 4, a big jump at step 12, and the face appearing before its steps. B's words are a bit more specific, but that is polish, not a fix for what the pictures show. A toss-up, so none.

Both lessons share identical pictures with the same serious faults, so neither paints well. A's words locate each mark more concretely and agree a little better with what the pictures show. It is a slight preference, close to a toss-up, since the shared picture faults dominate both lessons.

The pictures are identical, so the choice rests only on how well the words describe them. B covers more of what each picture actually shows across steps 3 to 15. B's flat 'no trees yet' on step 1 and the empty step 20 keep the edge small. Slight preference, not clear.

Both lessons share every picture, and the faults that would stop a beginner are in those pictures: steps 12, 18 and 19. B's words place things a bit more exactly, but that is a small edge in wording, not a real difference in what you could paint. I'm calling it a toss-up, leaning very slightly to B.

The pictures are identical, so the two differ only in the words. A gives clearer measurements and left/right placement, which slightly helps a beginner, but both share the same picture problems that would stop the painter at steps 12, 16, 18 and 19. That edge is small, so I call it none, leaning slightly to A.

The pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words match them. B's words describe what each picture actually shows at steps 5, 9, 13, 15, 16 and 19, where A would send a beginner to paint something different from the reference. Both share the step 1 trunk problem, so the edge is moderate: slightly better than slight, not overwhelming.

The pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words match them. B describes what actually lands on the canvas more often (steps 1-3, 12, 16), while A repeatedly promises marks the pictures don't show. It is a slight preference, because both inherit the same step-4 and step-20/21 magic and B has its own muddled step 23.

Both lessons share the same weak cow steps (12's magic rendering, 19's face appearing from a few liner lines), and those decide most of the scores. A's words match what each picture shows more often, especially at step 3, where B's words would actively mislead. The edge is slight but concrete.

The step pictures are identical, so the choice rests on how well the words describe them. B matches what the beginner will see on about five steps where A's words point elsewhere. Both share the face problem at steps 18 and 19. Slight preference for B, not a toss-up.

Slight preference for B. Both share the same weak pictures (ghosts at step 4, the face appearing in 20-21). A has one broken step, though: its nose step paints the blanket, and that hits the focal point. A's words fit the early leaf and shading pictures better, so the margin is small.

With identical pictures, the difference is how well the words match them, and A matches at the steps where B describes something the picture doesn't show (5, 13, 15, 16). A beginner comparing canvas to picture would be misled less often by A. I'm fairly sure of a slight but real preference, not a toss-up.

The pictures and words are identical and the diagrams are about equal: A's step 11 adds a useful 'rough up the edges' panel, while B's are a little cleaner. B wins because its Known problems list tells a beginner how to fix each wrong paint in plain words, and A's leaves the two most-used paints (Sunlit green and Sunlit cream) unfixed and talks in pipeline jargon. It is a slight preference, not a clear one.

The step pictures and words are the same, and they decide almost everything here: early leaves, the step 4 ghosts, the knit jump at step 12, and the misplaced nose step hurt both lessons equally. B's notes give a little more practical help at steps 2-3, 19 and 23, and A flags the step 1 width error. Both sets of diagrams are about equally good. It's a toss-up with a slight lean to B, which is too small to call a preference.

The pictures and words are identical, so this comes down to the add-ons. A's Known problems give an actionable colour fix for every paint that misses its picture. B leaves the two most-used mismatches (Sunlit green and Sunlit cream) without a fix and adds meta notes a beginner can't use. B's diagrams are a little richer but don't outweigh this. Preference is slight.

Everything on the canvas is identical, so the choice rests on the diagrams. A's diagrams contradict its words on three steps (pines, path length, bark order), and a beginner holding a phone would hit those conflicts. B's diagrams agree with the words. The preference is slight: the shared step 1, 3 and 10 problems weigh more than either set of diagrams.

The lessons are identical except for the diagrams and notes. A's diagrams agree with the step words, while B's path and bark diagrams would steer a beginner wrong on two steps. The edge is slight but concrete.

The step pictures and words are identical, so both lessons share the same serious faults. Neither page's extras change what the painter faces. A's notes are cleaner and fix the nose step outright, while B's diagrams fit the face words slightly better. It's a toss-up, with at most a slight lean to A, which is not enough to prefer it.

The steps are identical, so the choice rests on the extras. A's diagrams cover the hard cow steps (shadow, horn shading, the nose under the fringe), and its notes give fixes the painter can act on. B points to a nose diagram it doesn't have. Slight edge to A: neither one repairs the face jump at step 19.

The pictures and words are identical; only the extras differ, and they cancel out. B's Known problems is more accurate and it adds a useful bark diagram, but its path diagram would mislead a beginner where A's matches the words. It's a toss-up.

The paintings are identical, so the choice rests on what each page adds. B's diagrams cover the shading and the nose, and its notes match what's on the page. A's notes point to a nose diagram that isn't there. The edge is slight to clear: the shared step 19 jump and the wrong recipes still hurt both.

The pictures and words are identical, and their faults (step 4 leaves and ghosts, step 12 jump, nose and whiskers early, step 23 mislabeled) sink both lessons equally. The pages add different strengths: A has better technique diagrams and flags more faults; B's diagrams match the words and its fixes are more usable. Neither page outweighs the other, so this is a toss-up.

The pictures and words are identical, so the difference is only the extras. B's problem list warns about the places where the pictures run ahead of the words (steps 4, 20, 21), which A leaves silent, and its stitch and face diagrams fill the most technique-heavy steps. A's clearer pink and nose fixes and better diagram ordering keep this slight, not clear.

Both lessons share every picture and word, so they share the real faults: trunks on the canvas before step 3, and a step 20 that hardly changes anything. Neither the diagrams nor the problem lists fix those. A has slightly more accurate warnings and a useful bark diagram, and B has a better birch-placement diagram. That is a small edge to A, not a preference, so I call it a toss-up.

Everything the painter compares against is the same, so the difference comes only from the diagrams and the warnings. B's diagrams all work, and the ones on the blanket steps give real help at the lesson's biggest jump, where A shows two broken placeholders. B's warnings are also more accurate and more useful, such as mixing the ears pinker and expecting the leaves in step 4. It is a slight preference, not a clear one, because both lessons share the same weak steps.

The two lessons share every picture and word, so the real faults (trunks in step 1, the ghost path in step 10, the blotches in step 6) sink both equally. A's diagrams and notes fit the steps a little better, especially for the bark marks and the boulder, but that is a small edge and not a real difference. Toss-up, leaning slightly to A.

The pictures and words are identical, so the difference is only the diagrams and the Known problems list. B's list tells a beginner what to do about paints that would otherwise come out olive or muddy, where A's only explains why nothing was changed. It's a slight preference: both lessons share the same serious faults at steps 12, 18 and 19, and neither list mentions the step 12 jump or the step 19 magic.

The pictures and words are identical, so the choice rests on the extras. B's diagrams for the pines, path and bark marks look more like what the step pictures show. Its problem list points to the right steps, while A's path and bark diagrams could mislead a beginner a little. Slight preference: the core weaknesses (step 1 trunks, step 10 path ghost) sink both equally.

The pictures, words and diagrams are essentially a wash. A wins because its Known problems tell a beginner how to fix the wrong recipes (nose, ginger, the darker ridge). B only reports the mismatch and adds one misleading item. This is a slight preference, not a clear one, and the shared problems with the cow at steps 12, 18 and 19 dominate both.

The lessons differ only in their extras. In those extras, A beats B in two places: A's diagrams all work, while B shows error text on the two blanket steps, and A's notes are more accurate and more usable. The underlying step pictures are flawed the same way in both, so this is a slight but real preference, not a toss-up.

The pictures, words and paints are identical, and they decide everything that matters: the ghost trunks in step 1, the early path in step 10, and the small change in step 3. A's warning lands at step 1, while B's diagrams are a little closer to the scene. The two extras pull in opposite directions and are each minor, so this is a toss-up and I have no real preference.

The paintings, words and paints are identical, and the faults that matter (trunks and path showing early, step 16's mismatch) are the same in both. B's path diagram and its slightly more directive Known problems notes are a small edge, not enough to prefer it, so this is a toss-up leaning faintly to B.

A, slightly. The lessons differ only in their extras, and A's extras all work and tell the painter what to do. B has a visibly broken diagram on the key block-in step and Known problems that warn without fixing. B's other diagrams are a little nicer because they start from the previous canvas, but that doesn't make up for the broken one.

The pictures and words are identical, so the extras decide it. B has a working diagram for blocking in the cow where A's is broken, and B's problem list tells the painter how to fix the off recipes instead of just naming them. It is a clear preference, though the shared faults (the step 18/19 nose jump and the weak step 5) hold both lessons down.

The only differences are the diagrams and the problem notes, and they trade off. A's diagrams are a little fuller and its list warns about more traps. B's list is easier for a beginner to read. Neither fixes the step 4 magic, the step 12 jump or the face appearing early, which hurt both lessons equally. It's a toss-up with at most a hair toward A, which is not enough to prefer it.

The pictures and words are the same, so the choice comes down to the extras. B's diagrams match the steps better, and its problem list catches the early nose and whiskers that A misses. Against that, B's list is noisy where A's is clean. I would paint from B, but the edge is slight, since the shared picture faults dominate both.
